rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that the Income Tax Department had not complied with the statutory requirements of section 245 of the Income-tax Act before adjusting Tata Communications Ltd.’s refund against outstanding demands. The case arose in AY 2019-20 and concerned a refund/stay-of-demand dispute; the court specifically criticized the Department’s approach to treating its order as not covering matters dealt with by the ITAT on the ground that the Union of India was not a party, calling that justification unacceptable and inconsistent with the conduct expected of a model litigant.

From a compliance perspective, the key requirement reaffirmed is that before any refund is adjusted against a tax demand under section 245, the Department must follow the procedure mandated by that section rather than simply making an adjustment unilaterally. The judgment signals that authorities cannot rely on technical arguments to avoid the effect of a High Court order where the substance of the dispute requires compliance, and that departmental actions in refund adjustment matters are subject to judicial scrutiny. No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines were stated in the excerpt, but the operative compliance point is that refund adjustments must be lawfully and transparently made in conformity with section 245 and the court’s direction, especially where related stay/refund proceedings are already pending or decided.

Mistri, Madhur Agrawal, Shyam Walve DATE: April 9, 2021 (Date of pronouncement) DATE: April 24, 2021 (Date of publication) AY: 2012-13 FILE: Click here to download the file in pdf format CITATION: Article 226/ s. 147: (i) A Writ Petition can be filed in the Bombay High Court against an order passed in Delhi if the assessee is based in Mumbai. The litigant has the right to go to ‘a Court’ where part of cause of action arises. The Bombay High Court held that a writ petition could be maintained in Bombay even though the challenged income-tax order had been passed by Delhi authorities, because the assessee was based in Mumbai and part of the cause of action arose there. For compliance purposes, the more important ruling is that a notice under section 148 and a reassessment order under section 147 issued in the name of an amalgamated company that had already ceased to exist are **void and without jurisdiction**; this is not treated as a mere procedural defect.

The Court specifically rejected the argument that the defect could be cured under section 292B, and it also held that the assessee’s participation in the reassessment proceedings does **not** validate the proceedings or create any estoppel against law. In practical terms, if a company has been amalgamated before reassessment proceedings are initiated, tax notices and reassessment orders must be issued, if at all, in the name of the surviving entity; action taken against the non-existent predecessor entity is invalid.

The case concerned AY 2012–13, and the Court’s decision was pronounced on April 9, 2021 and published on April 24, 2021. The ruling reinforces a key compliance control point for corporate restructuring: once an amalgamation takes effect, the company should ensure tax records, PAN-related communications, and litigation notices are promptly aligned with the successor entity’s name so that any future assessment or reassessment proceedings are not directed at a dissolved legal person.

However, shares issued to shareholders of an amalgamating company in terms of a scheme of amalgamation does not fall within the sweep of the deeming provisions of s. 56(2) (viib). rows.summary:
The ITAT Ahmedabad held in **DCIT v. Ozone India Ltd.** that **section 56(2)(viib)**, which taxes a private company on **excess share premium received over fair market value**, does **not apply** where shares are issued to shareholders pursuant to a **scheme of amalgamation**. The case involved **AY 2013–14**, with the tribunal’s decision **pronounced on April 13, 2021** and published on **April 24, 2021**.  

On the facts, the assessee-company had filed its return for AY 2013–14, and during scrutiny the Assessing Officer found that **M/s. Kalavir Estate Pvt. Ltd. (KEPL)** had amalgamated into the assessee under an approved amalgamation scheme. In that process, the assessee issued shares to the shareholders of the amalgamating company. The tax department sought to treat the value arising from the amalgamation as **deemed income** under section 56(2)(viib), effectively characterizing the issuance as if there were an unjustified premium over face value.  

The tribunal rejected that approach, stating that the purpose of section 56(2)(viib) is to tax **unexplained or excessive premium received by private companies on issuance of shares where the shares do not carry corresponding underlying value**, not to cover share issuance mandated by an amalgamation scheme. It held that the **notional excess of assets vested on amalgamation cannot be treated as share premium** for this deeming provision. The decision also referred to **AS-14 issued by ICAI** and **CBDT Circular No. 3/2012 dated 12-6-2012** in support of the treatment of amalgamation accounting and share issuance as distinct from taxable premium.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that where shares are issued **solely because of a bona fide amalgamation approved under a scheme**, the transaction should not ordinarily be exposed to **section 56(2)(viib)** tax on alleged excess fair market value. However, the ruling is limited to the facts of amalgamation-related issuance and does not change the general rule that **unjustified share premium in ordinary equity issuances** can still be scrutinized under section 56(2)(viib).

This ITAT Mumbai decision concerns **section 50C of the Income-tax Act**, which deems the **stamp duty valuation** of transferred property to be the sale consideration for **capital gains** purposes when the stated sale price is lower than the stamp valuation. The Tribunal stated that the **third proviso to section 50C**, inserted by the **Finance Act, 2018**, creates a tolerance band under which section 50C will **not apply if the difference between stamp duty value and actual consideration does not exceed 5%**; this tolerance was later **increased to 10% by the Finance Act, 2020**. Although those amendments were described as prospective, the Tribunal held them to be **curative in nature** and therefore applicable **retrospectively from 1 April 2003**, the date section 50C was originally introduced.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that where a property transfer’s **stamp duty value is up to 10% higher than the declared sale consideration**, the declared consideration should be accepted at face value and the **anti-avoidance substitution mechanism under section 50C should not be triggered**. The case was an appeal for **Assessment Year 2011–12** in the matter of **Maria Fernandes Cheryl vs. ITO (International Taxation 2(3)(1), Mumbai)**, with the Tribunal’s pronouncement dated **15 January 2021** and publication on **17 April 2021**. The ruling is relevant to taxpayers and tax teams handling **immovable property transfers**, especially where there is a small gap between contractual consideration and stamp duty value, because it supports using the statutory tolerance band rather than mechanically substituting stamp value for capital gains computation.

The Supreme Court held that Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 because Section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act applicable “as far as may be.” As a result, where a corporate debtor makes a written and signed acknowledgement of debt before expiry of the limitation period, that acknowledgement can extend the limitation period for filing an insolvency application. The Court also clarified that an entry in the debtor’s books of account, including a balance sheet entry, can constitute an acknowledgement of liability under Section 18, provided it is read together with the notes annexed to or forming part of the balance sheet and the auditor’s report.

This decision specifically reverses the NCLAT Full Bench ruling in V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund, which had taken a contrary view on balance-sheet acknowledgements. The Court reaffirmed the basic limitation principle that once time begins to run, it cannot be stopped except by a legally recognized process. For compliance purposes, this means companies facing potential debt enforcement or insolvency exposure should treat balance-sheet disclosures, related notes, and auditor commentary as potentially legally significant acknowledgements that may revive or extend limitation periods for creditors. The judgment was pronounced on April 15, 2021 and published on April 17, 2021.

rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **DCIT v. Pepsi Foods Ltd.** examined the **third proviso to section 254(2A)** of the Income-tax Act, which had provided for **automatic vacation of a stay granted by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) after 365 days**, regardless of who caused the delay in hearing the appeal. The Court held that this rule was **unconstitutional** because it was **discriminatory and manifestly arbitrary**: it could punish an assessee even when the ITAT could not hear the appeal in time for reasons beyond the assessee’s control, and it could also benefit the Revenue even when the Revenue itself was responsible for the delay.

As a result, the Court struck down the offending operation of the proviso and directed that the provision be **read down** by deleting the word **“even”** and the words **“is not”** after the phrase **“delay in disposing of the appeal”**. In practical compliance terms, a stay granted by the ITAT **does not automatically lapse merely because 365 days have passed**; the stay will stand vacated **only if the delay in disposing of the appeal is attributable to the assessee**. This means the focus shifts to **fault-based delay** rather than a strict time-based expiration.

For corporate taxpayers with pending appeals and stay orders before the ITAT, the decision materially affects **stay-of-demand management**: companies no longer face automatic loss of stay solely due to passage of time beyond 365 days if they are not at fault for the delay. At the same time, the ruling preserves the possibility of vacation of stay where the assessee’s conduct is responsible for delaying disposal. There is **no new filing deadline or compliance formality created by this judgment**, but it is important for legal and tax teams to document which party caused any adjournments or hearing delays so that stay protection can be defended if challenged.

This Delhi High Court ruling in **CIT v. D. K. Garg** concerns **Section 68 of the Income-tax Act** and the treatment of **accommodation entries**, **cash credits**, and the taxpayer’s attempt to claim the benefit of **peak credit**. The Court held that an accommodation entry provider who seeks peak-credit relief must make a **full and candid disclosure of all facts within his knowledge** about the credit entries in the relevant accounts; this includes explaining **the source of every deposit**, **the destination of every payment**, and the movement of funds through the account structure. In practical terms, the assessee must be able to show that money was moved **through banking channels** from the creditor’s bank account to the assessee’s bank account, that the **identity of the creditors** is established, and that the money later paid out from the assessee’s account returned to the creditors’ accounts; this is the **primary onus** on the assessee under Section 68.

The Court emphasized that a taxpayer cannot claim the benefit of peak credit merely by asserting that only the highest outstanding balance should be taxed; instead, the taxpayer must first produce a clear and credible explanation of the entire transaction flow and the linked accounts involved. Where the taxpayer fails to do this, the unexplained credits remain liable to be treated under Section 68. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court’s decision in **ADIT v. E-Funds IT Solution Inc.** addresses when a foreign company will be treated as having a **Permanent Establishment (PE) in India** under **Article 5 of the India–U.S. DTAA (1990)** for tax purposes. The tax authority had held that the U.S. companies had a **fixed place PE in Delhi** and were therefore taxable in India on income earned through that alleged PE; the CIT(A) also upheld the assessments, additionally reasoning that the companies had **service PE** and **agency PE** status under Article 5.

The Supreme Court explained the law on **fixed place PE, service PE, and agency PE**, and rejected the idea that mere **close association, dependence, or integrated business relationship** between the U.S. company and Indian group entities is enough to create a PE. It held that the correct test is whether the foreign enterprise itself has a sufficiently permanent **place of business in India through which its own business is carried on**, and that the **functions performed, assets used, and risks assumed** test is **not the proper test** for determining a location/fixed-place PE. The Court therefore clarified that a foreign company does not automatically become taxable in India just because related Indian entities perform support functions or because there is operational dependence between the entities.

For compliance purposes, the key practical takeaway is that **foreign enterprises using Indian affiliates or service providers are not automatically exposed to Indian PE risk solely because of group linkage or business dependence**. PE exposure must be assessed based on the actual facts showing whether the foreign company has a **fixed place**, **service presence**, or **agency relationship** in India within the meaning of the treaty, rather than relying on generalized notions of economic presence or business integration. The judgment is dated **October 24, 2017** (pronouncement), with publication on **October 25, 2017**.

rows.summary:
This circular explains how the GST return filings for July and August 2017 were to be handled during the initial rollout period, when the normal monthly return sequence under sections 37, 38, and 39 of the CGST Act, 2017 and rules 59, 60, and 61 of the CGST Rules, 2017 was temporarily disrupted. Ordinarily, registered persons had to file outward supply details in FORM GSTR-1 by the 10th of the next month, inward supply details in FORM GSTR-2 by the 15th, and the monthly return in FORM GSTR-3 by the 20th; however, the GST Council extended the filing dates for GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 for July and August 2017 and allowed a simplified return in FORM GSTR-3B for those two months, to be filed by the notified due dates after payment of tax.  

The circular also notes that taxpayers using transitional credit under section 140 of the CGST Act for their July 2017 liability had to file FORM GST TRAN-1 on or before 28 August 2017, and that this credit would be posted to the electronic credit ledger and could be used to discharge tax liability. Because FORM GSTR-3B was filed instead of the normal return sequence while the GSTR-1/GSTR-2 due dates were extended, the circular says the system would later reconcile the information furnished in GSTR-1 and GSTR-2 with the amounts reported in GSTR-3B once those returns were filed.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the simplified GSTR-3B filing did not replace the underlying reporting obligations permanently; it was an interim mechanism for the initial GST months, with reconciliation to follow once the regular statement/return data became available. The document is addressed to all Principal Chief Commissioners/Chief Commissioners/Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax and all Principal Directors General/Directors General, indicating that field formations were expected to apply and oversee this reconciliation framework.

No. 354/149/2017-TRU Government of India Ministry of Finance Department of Revenue Tax Research Unit ***** New Delhi, the 27 th August, 2017 To, The Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioners/ Principal Commissioner/ Commissioner of Central Tax (All) / Director General of Systems Madam/Sir, Subject: - Issue related to classification and GST rate on lottery tickets – regarding Supply of lottery has been treated as supply of goods under the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017. 2. Accordingly, based on the recommendation of the GST Council, the GST rate for supply of lottery has been notified under relevant GST rate notification relating to CGST/IGST/UTGST/SGST. However, entries in the respective notifications mention classification for lottery as “-”. 3. In this connection, references have been received, inter-alia, stating that due to discrepancy in code allotted, i.e., lottery is defined as goods but code allotted for lottery is under services, the assessees are not able to upload return or deposit tax in time. 4. The matter has been examined. It should be noted that the process of filing return is linked with rate of tax specified for supply. Further, there is complete clarity about rate of tax on lotteries. As mentioned above, in GST, lottery is goods and the classification indicated in relevant notification for lottery is “-”, which means any chapter. 5. That being so, it is clarified that the classification for lottery in respective CGST, IGST, UTGST and SGST notifications shall be ‘Any Chapter’ of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975) and tax on lottery should be paid accordingly at prescribed rates, 12% or 28%, as the case may be. (Ruchi Bisht) Under Secretary (TRU)
rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 27 August 2017 by the Ministry of Finance, clarifies how lottery tickets are to be classified and taxed under GST because assessees were encountering return-filing and tax-payment problems due to a coding mismatch. The circular states that, under the CGST Act, 2017, supply of lottery is treated as a **supply of goods**, even though the GST rate notifications had shown the classification entry for lottery as “-”. For compliance purposes, the government clarifies that this “-” should be read as **“Any Chapter” of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975**, and that lottery must be taxed under the applicable GST rate notifications accordingly.

The circular specifically resolves the issue that the lottery description was appearing as goods while the code allotted in the system was under services, which had prevented some taxpayers from uploading returns or depositing tax on time. It emphasizes that return filing is linked to the rate of tax applicable to the supply, and that there is no ambiguity on the applicable lottery tax rate. The prescribed GST rate for lottery is confirmed as **12% or 28%, as the case may be**, depending on the relevant notified category.

This clarification applies to the GST framework under **CGST, IGST, UTGST, and SGST** rate notifications and is directed to all Central Tax field formations and systems officials. From a compliance standpoint, entities dealing in lottery tickets should ensure their tax classification and return-filing treatment align with the “Any Chapter” classification and the correct notified rate, so tax can be paid and returns filed without system errors or delay.

This means that only such exporters are eligible to LUT facilities who have received a remittance of Rs. one crore or 10% of export turnover, whichever is a higher amount, in the previous financial
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the rules for exporting goods or services without payment of integrated tax by furnishing either a bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT), under section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, in response to inconsistent interpretations of Notification No. 16/2017–Central Tax dated 7 July 2017 and earlier GST circulars. The key policy clarification is that the LUT facility is no longer limited to manufacturer exporters: **any registered person** may use LUT **if** they received foreign inward remittance in the preceding financial year equal to **at least 10% of export turnover, and in any case not less than Rs. 1 crore**; the circular states this effectively means the exporter must have received **whichever is higher: Rs. 1 crore or 10% of export turnover** in the previous financial year. If that threshold is not met, the exporter must export under a **bond** rather than LUT.

The circular also clarifies the process for using and accepting the bond/LUT. The bond must be **executed on non-judicial stamp paper** for an amount determined as per the relevant bond format, and the exporter is required to furnish a **bank guarantee** along with the bond only to the extent required by the proper officer, not as a blanket requirement for all exporters. It further states that the LUT can be furnished on the exporter’s own letterhead in the prescribed format, and it must be accepted by the jurisdictional Assistant/Deputy Commissioner. The circular instructs tax officers not to insist on unnecessary guarantees or documentation beyond what the notification and circular require.

Another important compliance clarification is that the LUT/bond is a **pre-export** undertaking: it must be furnished **before exports are made** under the zero-rated/without payment route. The circular also explains that exports under bond/LUT are subject to the condition that the exporter will comply with the export provisions, including export of goods or services within the prescribed time limits and maintenance of proof of export. If the exporter fails to comply, the bond can be enforced for tax, interest, and any other applicable amount. The circular is intended to create uniformity across field formations, so compliance teams should ensure exporter eligibility is checked against the prior-year remittance threshold and that the correct instrument—LUT or bond—is used before undertaking exports without payment of integrated tax.

It is observed consign
rows.summary:
This circular clarifies the bond/LUT procedure for **exports of goods or services without payment of integrated tax** under **rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017**. It was issued by the **CBEC GST Policy Wing on 7 July 2017** under **section 168(1) of the CGST Act, 2017** to ensure uniform implementation after complaints from exporters and field offices about difficulties with the prescribed process. The core requirement is that any registered person making such zero-rated exports must furnish either a **bond or a Letter of Undertaking (LUT) in FORM GST RFD-11** before exporting without IGST payment.

The circular then distinguishes who may use an LUT and who must furnish a bond. It points to **Notification No. 16/2017-Central Tax dated 01-07-2017**, which specifies the class of exporters eligible to export under LUT, together with the applicable conditions and safeguards. **Exporters not covered by that notification must furnish a bond instead of an LUT.** The circular also reiterates that the **procedure for submission and acceptance of the bond was already laid down in Circular No. 2/2/2017-GST dated 4 July 2017**.

For the bond itself, the document requires that it be executed on **non-judicial stamp paper** of the **value applicable in the State where the bond is furnished**. A key clarification sought by the field was whether export bonds should be a **running bond with debit/credit facility** or a **separate one-time bond for each consignment/export**. The circular notes this issue and explains that the bond mechanism is intended to operate as a running bond, so exporters do not have to execute a fresh bond for every shipment.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that exporters making zero-rated supplies without IGST must first check whether they qualify for LUT under the 1 July 2017 notification; if not, they must arrange a bond in RFD-11 on the correct state stamp paper and follow the prescribed submission/acceptance process from the earlier circular. The circular is not imposing a new tax rate or deadline, but it does require adherence to the LUT/bond framework as a precondition to exporting without paying integrated tax.

rows.summary:
This circular, issued on 5 July 2017 by the Central Board of Excise and Customs (GST Policy Wing), assigns “proper officer” status for specific GST functions under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (and related rules) to designated Central Tax officers, for matters other than registration and composition. It applies by virtue of section 2(91) of the CGST Act, read with section 20 of the IGST Act and subject to section 5(2) of the CGST Act, and it is intended to clarify which officer rank may legally exercise particular powers under the Act/rules.

For Principal Commissioners/Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns the functions under section 67(7) and the proviso to section 78. For Additional or Joint Commissioners of Central Tax, it assigns powers under sections 67(1), (2), (5), and (9); sections 71(1) and (2); the proviso to section 81; the proviso to section 129(6); and rule 139 sub-rules (1) to (4) and rule 140(2). For Deputy or Assistant Commissioners of Central Tax, the circular assigns a broader set of functions, including sections 54(5), (6), (7), and (10); section 60(1), (2), and (3); sections 63, 64(1), and 65(6); and multiple powers under section 74, including sub-sections (1), (2), (3), (5), (6), (7), (9), and (10), with the listing continuing on the next page. 

From a compliance standpoint, the practical impact is that taxpayers and company compliance teams must ensure that notices, orders, demands, recovery actions, inspections, access requests, search/seizure-related actions, refund-related actions, and other proceedings under the cited provisions are handled by the correct officer rank, because authority is being formally allocated to those officers. The circular does not set new monetary thresholds, tax rates, or filing deadlines; instead, it is an internal administrative authorization that determines which GST officer is empowered to act under the listed sections and rules, effective from the date of the circular itself, 5 July 2017.

Various communications have been received from the field formations and exporters on the issue of difficulties being faced while supplying the goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax and filing the FORM GST RFD -11 on the common portal (www.gst.gov.in), because of which exports are being held up. 2. Whereas, as per rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, any registered person availing the option to supply goods or services for export without payment of integrated tax shall furnish, prior to export, a bond or a Letter of Undertaking. This bond or Letter of Undertaking is required to be furnished in FORM GST RFD-11 on the common portal. Further, Circular No. 26/2017- Customs dated 1 st July, 2017 has clarified that the procedure as prescribed under rule 96A of the said rules requires to be followed for the export of goods from 1 st July, 2017. 3. Another issue being raised by various stakeholders is that the Bond/Letter of Undertaking is required to be given through the proper officer which is to be furnished to the jurisdictional Commissioner as per sub-rule (1) of rule 96A of the said rules. Taking cognizance of the fact that a large number of such Bonds/Letter of Undertakings would be required to be filed by the registered exporters who would be located at a distance from the office of the jurisdictional Commissioner, it is understood that the furnishing of such bonds/undertakings before the jurisdictional Commissioner may cause hardship to the exporters. 4. Thus, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (
rows.summary:
This circular addresses practical problems exporters were facing after GST implementation when supplying goods or services for export **without payment of integrated tax** and then trying to file **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST common portal. The government notes that these difficulties were causing export shipments to be held up, so it clarifies the procedure for furnishing the required **bond or Letter of Undertaking (LUT)** under **rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017**.

The core requirement is unchanged: any **registered person** choosing to export **without paying integrated tax** must furnish, **before export**, a **bond or LUT** in **FORM GST RFD-11**. The circular also confirms that, for **export of goods**, the rule 96A procedure applies **from 1 July 2017**, consistent with **Circular No. 26/2017-Customs dated 1 July 2017**.

The new operational relaxation is that the bond/LUT does **not** need to be physically filed before the **jurisdictional Commissioner**, which had created hardship because many exporters are located far from that office. Instead, the circular allows this filing to be handled through the **proper officer** / jurisdictional tax administration mechanism in a way that avoids travel and administrative delay, so exporters can complete the requirement more easily and prevent export disruption.

For compliance purposes, the document is important because it confirms that exporters using the **zero-rated export without IGST payment route** must still ensure a valid **bond or LUT is in place before export**, but the process is being administratively simplified to reduce delays. The effective date tied to the export procedure is **1 July 2017**, and the requirement remains to use **FORM GST RFD-11** on the GST portal.

Based on the title alone, the document is likely intended to identify which tax authority/officer is authorized to handle actions such as registration-related decisions, composition levy applications, compliance, and any related enforcement or procedural matters under the CGST framework.

rows.summary:
This circular amends Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST dated 9 February 2018 on the question of who is the “proper officer” for adjudicating show cause notices issued under sections 73 and 74 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the IGST Act, 2017. It responds to two prior central tax notifications: Notification No. 02/2022-Central Tax dated 11 March 2022, which had already given certain Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners in specified Central Tax Commissionerates all-India jurisdiction to adjudicate DGGI-issued show cause notices, and Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax dated 25 November 2024, which expanded that arrangement to more such officers by substituting Table V in Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax. The 27/2024 notification took effect on 1 December 2024, and this circular is issued on 4 December 2024 to align the CBIC circular with that expanded adjudication framework.

The operative change is that paragraph 7.1 of Circular No. 31/05/2018-GST (as previously amended by Circular No. 169/01/2022-GST dated 12 March 2022) is substituted. The new text begins by stating that, for show cause notices issued by officers of the Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (DGGI), there may be cases where a single notice is issued to multiple noticees. In such cases, adjudication is to be handled in line with the all-India jurisdiction empowered officers specified under the amended notification framework, rather than being confined by the normal territorial jurisdiction approach.

For compliance purposes, the practical impact is on the adjudication of DGGI-issued show cause notices under sections 73 and 74: companies or other noticees facing such notices may have their matters adjudicated by the centrally empowered Additional Commissioners/Joint Commissioners of Central Tax designated under Notification No. 02/2017-Central Tax as amended, including the broader set added by Notification No. 27/2024-Central Tax. The document does not create a new tax rate, penalty, filing deadline, or monetary threshold; its significance is procedural and jurisdictional, clarifying which officers are authorized to adjudicate DGGI notices, including where one notice covers multiple noticees. The compliance team should therefore ensure that any DGGI show cause notices received on or after the effective change are tracked with attention to the designated adjudicating authority, and that internal responses, representation strategy, and escalation paths reflect this all-India jurisdiction framework.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Clock on ITC: Understanding Time Limits for Claiming Input Tax Credit under GST
rows.desc: Summary: Section 16(4) of the CGST Act generally bars a registered person from availing input tax credit (ITC) after 30 November following the end of the relevant financial year or the date of furnishing the annual return, whichever is earlier. The deadline applies to invoices and debit notes, but ITC eligibility and timely availment remain separate requirements: satisfying the time limit does not itself establish eligibility. The article traces the change from the earlier September-return deadline to 30 November with effect from 1 October 2022, explains why businesses should reconcile ITC before the final cut-off, and highlights the effect of filing the annual return earlier. It also discusses debit notes, reverse-charge supplies from unregistered persons under CBIC Circular No. 211/5/2024-GST, retrospective relief under Sections 16(5) and 16(6) for specified cases, and the distinction between a fresh claim and re-availment of reversed credit. The practical discussion recommends ongoing reconciliation of purchase records, GST data, supplier reporting, reverse-charge transactions, debit notes and reversals, with documentation of when credit became eligible and was availed. The article concludes that businesses should monitor both the statutory date and annual-return filing date and claim eligible ITC within the applicable period. rows.summary:
Section 16(4) of the CGST Act sets a hard time bar on claiming input tax credit (ITC): a registered person cannot take ITC for an invoice or debit note after **30 November following the end of the relevant financial year** or **the date the annual return for that year is furnished, whichever is earlier**. The document notes that this deadline applies specifically to **invoices and debit notes**, and that meeting the deadline does **not** by itself make the credit eligible—businesses still must satisfy the substantive ITC conditions under the GST law before claiming it.

The article explains that this deadline was changed from the earlier **September-return cutoff** to **30 November**, with the change taking effect from **1 October 2022**. It emphasizes that companies should not wait until the last day because filing the **annual return earlier than 30 November** can move the cutoff forward, meaning the effective deadline becomes the annual return filing date if that occurs first. In practice, this means businesses need to reconcile and finalize eligible ITC well before year-end rather than relying on the full November window.

The document also highlights that **debit notes** are covered by the same Section 16(4) timing rule, so credit linked to debit notes must also be claimed within the applicable statutory period. For **reverse charge mechanism (RCM)** supplies, including transactions involving **unregistered persons** discussed in **CBIC Circular No. 211/5/2024-GST**, the article indicates that the Section 16(4) deadline still matters and businesses must track when credit actually becomes available and whether it is claimed within time.

A major 2024 development discussed is **retrospective relief** under **Sections 16(5) and 16(6)** for specified situations. Section **16(5)** provides relief for certain **earlier financial years**, while Section **16(6)** addresses cases involving **registrations that were cancelled and later restored**, allowing ITC claims/re-claims in those covered circumstances despite the normal time restriction. The article also distinguishes between a **fresh ITC claim** and the **re-availment of credit that was previously reversed**, which matters because the compliance treatment may differ depending on whether the credit is being newly claimed or restored.

From a compliance perspective, the article recommends that businesses maintain continuous reconciliation of **purchase invoices, GST returns/data, supplier reporting, reverse-charge items, debit notes, and ITC reversals**, and keep clear documentation showing **when the credit became eligible** and **when it was actually availed**. The practical takeaway is that companies should monitor both the **statutory 30 November deadline** and the **annual return filing date**, claim all eligible ITC within the earlier applicable deadline, and preserve evidence supporting eligibility and timeliness to reduce the risk of denial on limitation grounds.

rows.title: Income Tax | 24-Hour Mistake That Could Cost Your Business Millions: Avoiding EPF Trap
rows.desc: Summary: The Supreme Court in Checkmate Services Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT settled the distinction between an employer’s own contribution to welfare funds and employee contributions deducted from salaries. Employee contributions covered by Section 36(1)(va), read with Section 2(24)(x) of the Income Tax Act, must be deposited within the due date prescribed under the relevant welfare legislation; depositing them before the due date for filing the income-tax return does not bring them within Section 43B. The Court emphasized the distinct character of employees’ contributions as amounts belonging to employees and held in trust by the employer. The practical consequence is significant for businesses: delays in remitting employee PF/ESI contributions can result in denial of the corresponding income-tax deduction even where the amount is subsequently deposited before filing the return. Businesses should therefore segregate employee statutory deductions from ordinary payables, maintain internal deadlines comfortably before the statutory due date, and configure payroll and accounting systems to identify and remit these amounts promptly. You’re juggling cash flow, client deadlines, and payroll. You diligently deduct Provident Fund (EPF) and Employee State Insurance (ESI) from your team’s salaries every month. One month, cash is a little tight, or maybe the government portal is glitching. You end up paying the EPF to the government just a few days past the 15th of the month. But you breathe easy—you paid it completely before filing your Income Tax Return (ITR). In your mind, you are fully compliant. A year later, you receive a notice from the Income Tax Department. They have disallowed the entire amount of the employee contributions and added it straight to your company’s t
rows.summary:
This document explains the Supreme Court’s ruling in **Checkmate Services Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT**, which clarified the tax treatment of **employee contributions to welfare funds** such as **EPF and ESI** versus an employer’s own contributions. The Court held that amounts **deducted from employees’ salaries** are governed by **Section 36(1)(va)** read with **Section 2(24)(x)** of the Income Tax Act and must be deposited **within the due date prescribed under the relevant welfare law**; paying them later, even if still before the **income-tax return filing due date**, does **not** cure the delay under **Section 43B**. In other words, employee contributions are treated as **funds belonging to employees and held in trust by the employer**, so late remittance can trigger **disallowance of the corresponding income-tax deduction**.

For compliance purposes, the key risk is that if a business remits employee PF/ESI contributions even a few days late, the tax department can deny deduction for those amounts in the company’s tax computation, potentially increasing taxable income and tax liability. The document specifically notes the common scenario where an employer pays EPF after the statutory monthly deadline (for example, after the **15th of the month**) but before filing the return; under this ruling, that timing is still insufficient for deduction of employee contributions. The ruling therefore affects **all employers that deduct statutory welfare contributions from payroll**, especially businesses with cash-flow pressure or operational delays in remittance.

The practical compliance obligation is to **separate employee statutory deductions from ordinary payables**, track them with **internal deadlines earlier than the legal due date**, and ensure payroll/accounting systems are configured to identify, prioritize, and remit these sums promptly. The document’s warning is that businesses should not assume “paid before the ITR filing deadline” equals tax deductibility for employee welfare deductions; the controlling deadline is the **welfare statute’s due date**, not the income-tax return deadline.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Exemptions: Relief for Taxpayers and Their Impact on the Tax System
rows.desc: Summary: GST exemptions are an important policy tool, but their economic effect can differ substantially from the headline removal of tax. The distinction between an exempt supply and a zero-rated supply is particularly important because an ordinary exemption generally removes output GST while restricting the supplier’s ability to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC), potentially embedding tax costs into prices. This issue became significant after the 56th GST Council’s September 2025 reforms and Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate), which exempted specified individual life and health insurance services from GST from 22 September 2025. The article examines the statutory exemption powers under Section 11 of the CGST Act and Section 6 of the IGST Act, together with the ITC reversal implications under Section 18(4) and Rule 44. It also traces Supreme Court jurisprudence governing interpretation of exemptions, including Sun Export Corporation, Dilip Kumar & Co., Ambay Cements, Hari Chand Shri Gopal, Mother Superior Adoration Convent and Wood Papers. The practical discussion considers insurance pricing, blocked ITC, transition compliance and anti-profiteering enforcement. The Supreme Court’s decision in State of Karnataka v. Taghar Vasudeva Ambrish provides a second illustration of exemption disputes, showing how the scope and purpose of apparently simple exemption entries can generate prolonged litigation. Table of Contents▸ Introduction Legal Framework The statutory source of the power How courts read exemption notifications Contemporary and Practical Analysis The insurance exemption in practice A second illustration: the hostel accommodation dispute Critical Discussion Conclusion and Suggestions Bibliography Statutes and Rules Notifications Table of Cases Reports and Other Sources Show all 14 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction If the government removes GST from your insurance premium, does your bill drop by exactly 18
rows.summary:
The document explains that GST exemptions are not just a “tax removed” outcome; they often change who can recover input taxes and therefore can affect pricing, margins, and compliance systems. The key new development described is Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate), issued after the 56th GST Council reforms, which exempts specified individual life and health insurance services from GST with effect from 22 September 2025. For compliance purposes, this means businesses in the affected insurance segment must stop charging output GST on those covered supplies from that date, but they must also assess whether the exemption causes a loss of Input Tax Credit (ITC) entitlement because ordinary exemptions generally block ITC recovery and can embed unrecoverable tax costs into the price of the exempt service.

The document focuses on the statutory basis for exemptions under Section 11 of the CGST Act and Section 6 of the IGST Act, and on the ITC reversal consequences under Section 18(4) and Rule 44. In practical terms, once an output supply becomes exempt, suppliers may need to reverse or proportionately adjust ITC associated with inputs/input services used for making exempt supplies, rather than continuing to claim full credits. The article specifically flags transition compliance issues, meaning affected insurers need to review invoicing, tax return treatment, credit reversals, internal accounting, and pricing methodology from the effective date onward so that GST is not incorrectly collected and ITC is not improperly retained.

It also notes that the economic benefit of exemption may be smaller than the headline rate cut because savings can be offset by blocked ITC and embedded taxes. The discussion highlights anti-profiteering enforcement risk, which means suppliers benefiting from the exemption should be able to demonstrate that the tax reduction is appropriately passed through in pricing rather than retained as additional margin. The document does not provide a numerical anti-profiteering threshold, but it clearly indicates that the exemption can trigger scrutiny over whether customers actually receive the benefit of the tax relief.

Finally, the article is partly doctrinal: it surveys Supreme Court cases on how exemption notifications are interpreted, emphasizing that exemption language is often construed strictly and disputes can arise over the scope of an exemption entry. It cites cases including Sun Export Corporation, Dilip Kumar & Co., Ambay Cements, Hari Chand Shri Gopal, Mother Superior Adoration Convent, and Wood Papers, and uses State of Karnataka v. Taghar Vasudeva Ambrish as an example of how exemption scope can lead to prolonged litigation. For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is that exemption wording should be read narrowly and implemented carefully, because a seemingly simple exemption can create filing, credit, pricing, and litigation exposure if the entity’s products or services are not clearly within the covered category.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Blocked Credits under GST: Why Some Business Expenses Do Not Qualify for ITC
rows.desc: Summary: Input Tax Credit (ITC) is a fundamental feature of GST, but GST paid on every legitimate business expense is not necessarily available as credit. Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 establishes the general entitlement to ITC, subject to statutory conditions, while Section 17(5) specifically blocks credit for prescribed categories of goods and services. Major areas include specified motor vehicles, food and catering, certain employee benefits, club and fitness memberships, vacation travel benefits, construction of immovable property, goods lost, stolen, destroyed or written off, gifts and free samples, personal consumption and specified CSR expenditure. Several blocked-credit provisions contain exceptions, making transaction-specific examination essential. Construction-related ITC has generated significant litigation, particularly in Chief Commissioner of Central Goods and Service Tax v. M/s Safari Retreats Private Limited, where the Supreme Court examined Section 17(5)(c) and (d) and the expression “plant or machinery.” The subsequent legislative amendment replacing “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” in Section 17(5)(d), retrospectively from 1 July 2017, is also significant. Businesses must further distinguish permanently blocked credit from ITC reversals and correctly report ineligible credits in GST returns. Invoice-level review, documentation of statutory exceptions, reconciliations and monitoring amendments, CBIC circulars and judicial developments are therefore important for avoiding incorrect ITC claims. Table of Contents▸ Introduction I. General Framework of ITC II. Motor Vehicles III. Food, Catering and Employee Benefits IV. Club Membership and Vacation Travel V. Construction and Immovable Property VI. Safari Retreats: Judicial Development VII. Legislative Development After Safari Retreats VIII. Lost, Stolen, Destroyed or Written-Off Goods IX. Gifts and Free Samples X. Personal Consumption XI. CSR Expenditure XII. Blocked Credit and Revers
rows.summary:
The document explains that although input tax credit (ITC) is generally available under Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 for GST paid on legitimate business expenses, Section 17(5) expressly blocks credit for specified categories of inward supplies, so businesses cannot assume every GST cost is recoverable. It identifies the main blocked-credit buckets as motor vehicles in prescribed cases, food/catering and certain employee benefits, club and fitness memberships, vacation travel benefits, construction of immovable property, goods lost/stolen/destroyed/written off, gifts and free samples, personal consumption, and specified CSR expenditure. A key compliance point is that several of these blocks have exceptions, so entitlement must be tested transaction by transaction rather than by expense category alone.

A major focus is construction-related ITC, which has been heavily litigated. In Chief Commissioner of Central Goods and Service Tax v. M/s Safari Retreats Private Limited, the Supreme Court examined Section 17(5)(c) and (d) and the meaning of “plant or machinery,” which made the scope of blocked credit for construction costs especially important for businesses involved in building commercial properties or assets used in taxable activity. The document notes a later legislative amendment that replaced “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” in Section 17(5)(d), and that this change was made retrospective from 1 July 2017, meaning past periods may also be affected.

For compliance purposes, the document emphasizes that businesses must distinguish permanently blocked credit under Section 17(5) from ITC reversals that arise in other circumstances, and must report ineligible credits correctly in GST returns. It also says companies should perform invoice-level review, keep documentary support for any exception relied on, and regularly reconcile ITC positions against amendments, CBIC circulars, and judicial developments. In practical terms, this means compliance teams should monitor whether a particular expense falls under a statutory exception, whether a blocked-credit rule applies despite the expense being business-related, and whether any judicial or retrospective legislative change alters previously claimed or denied ITC.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan Authority for Advance Ruling held that **fresh psyllium seeds (isabgol)** proposed to be purchased by **RUKHM Industries Limited** are **not exempt** from GST as “fresh or chilled” seeds and are instead **taxable at 5% GST** under the applicable classification for psyllium seeds. The applicant had proposed to buy the seeds **directly from farmers/cultivators through APMC/KUMS auctions, or from traders**, in their natural form, then **store them in godowns without any drying, freezing, crushing, or other processing**, and later resell them; it argued that this should qualify for exemption under **Entry No. 87 of Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17.09.2025**, or alternatively under **Entry No. 77 for “all goods of seed quality.”**  

The Authority examined the product’s nature, the harvesting/threshing process, and the distinction between **fresh/chilled** goods and **dried/processed** goods, and concluded that **threshing is a separate post-harvest mechanical operation** and that the evidence did **not** establish that the psyllium seeds would meet the exemption conditions for “fresh or chilled” seeds. It also rejected the alternative “seed quality” exemption route, indicating that the exemption depends on the relevant statutory conditions being satisfied, which were not shown on the facts presented.  

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that entities **buying and selling psyllium seeds in this trade channel—especially purchases from farmers through APMC/KUMS auctions and onward resale without qualifying processing—should not treat the goods as exempt merely because they are unprocessed or stored in natural form**. Unless the facts clearly fit a specific exemption entry, these goods should be treated as **taxable at 5% GST**, and businesses should ensure their invoicing, tax classification, and input/output tax positions reflect that treatment.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan Authority for Advance Ruling held that rubberised and agglomerated cork sheets manufactured and supplied by Balasaria Agencies Pvt. Ltd. (Pristine Technologies & Industries) are classifiable under tariff item **HSN 4504 10 10** as **agglomerated cork sheets** and attract **GST at 5%** under **serial no. 310 of Schedule I to Notification No. 09/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025**. The applicant’s product was described as industrial sheets made by mixing **cork granules** with **polymer or rubber**, chemicals/curatives, processing oil, and fillers, then moulding, curing, and cutting; the stated composition was **30.99% cork** and **42.47% polymer**. The applicant specifically asked whether the presence of rubber, the absence of natural cork in the finished sheet, or the origin of the cork would prevent use of that tariff entry, and the AAR’s answer was no: it relied on the wording of heading 4504, which covers **agglomerated cork with or without a binding substance**, and noted that the heading does **not impose a minimum cork-content threshold** or require natural cork to remain visible or predominant in the finished product.

The jurisdictional officer had argued that because polymer was the larger component, the goods should be classified in **Chapter 40** and taxed at **18%**, but the AAR rejected that position. In deciding the application, the AAR first confirmed that there was **no pending classification proceeding** that would block the ruling: the applicant said the issue arose only as a **verbal doubt during refund scrutiny**, and the officer confirmed no live proceeding existed. The AAR also **refused to admit the fifth question** on whether the applicant could claim an **inverted duty refund**, because entitlement to refund is **not within the matters listed in Section 97(2)** of the CGST Act and therefore is outside the scope of advance ruling jurisdiction.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that businesses manufacturing or supplying similar **rubberised/agglomerated cork sheets** should assess classification under **HSN 45041010** rather than Chapter 40 where the product is an agglomerated cork article with a binding substance, even if the finished sheet contains significant polymer/rubber content. The ruling is tied to the stated composition and manufacturing process and is relevant to GST rate setting, invoicing, and refund computations for similar goods. No separate effective date for the classification itself was stated in the summary beyond the cited rate notification date of **17 September 2025**.

rows.summary:
Mahesh Transport Company asked the Rajasthan AAR for a ruling on whether its proposed coal transportation arrangement with M/s Mahesh Transport Gujarat would be exempt under Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) or instead taxable under Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate). The applicant said it operated as a goods transport agency (GTA), issued consignment notes, and was transporting coal between Gujarat and Rajasthan; it relied on the GTA definition and on case law about the importance of a consignment note, while also arguing in the alternative that the service should fall under the rate notification rather than exemption. The jurisdictional officer’s comments and the submissions before the AAR also discussed whether the arrangement was really GTA service or merely hiring of vehicles, with a view that simply making vehicles available to another GTA could fall within the exemption for hiring a means of transport under Entry 22(b); however, that was part of the arguments presented, not the ruling itself.

The AAR rejected the application without deciding the GST exemption question on the merits because the same issue was already pending in investigation and had effectively been taken up by the department. The Enforcement Wing had conducted a search at the applicant’s premises on 07.01.2026 under Section 67(2), and the report stated that the applicant had availed input tax credit on invoices for vehicles hired from others and was also hiring out vehicles to other GTAs. The investigating authority viewed those outward vehicle-hiring supplies as exempt and indicated that reversal of common credit under Rules 42 and 43 was required, showing that the tax treatment of the same activity was already under departmental examination.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the AAR did not grant a ruling on the exemption/taxability of the GTA arrangement because the issue was not eligible for advance ruling while it was already pending before the department and had been subject to search/investigation. Any business model involving hiring out vehicles to other GTAs, issuing consignment notes, or claiming exemption versus taxability under the cited notifications should therefore be reviewed carefully, especially where input tax credit has been taken on vehicle-hire invoices and common-credit reversal may arise under Rules 42/43.

The Authority examined the application, annexures, contract documents, rate notifications, officer’s comments and hearing submissions. rows.summary:
The Rajasthan AAR ruling in **In re MTS-EIEL (JV)** concerns the GST rate applicable to a **works contract service for a faecal sludge treatment plant infrastructure project** under **Heading 9954, serial no. 3(iii)(c)**, which covers works contract involving a **pipeline, conduit, plant for water supply, water treatment, sewerage treatment, or disposal**. The applicant, a GST-registered joint venture, had been awarded a contract for **design, supply, construction, testing, trial run, commissioning, and five years of operation and maintenance** under a Rajasthan Urban Infrastructure Development Project package. The tender was issued on **24.04.2022**, the bid was submitted on **28.06.2022**, the **Letter of Acceptance** was issued on **30.09.2022**, and the **Notice to Proceed** followed on **28.11.2022**.

A key commercial issue was the GST rate change around **1 June 2022**. The applicant stated that it had bid assuming GST at **12% total** (**6% CGST + 6% SGST**), but work executed and invoiced after the rate change was taxed at **18%**, creating an extra burden of **6 percentage points**. The accepted contract value was **Rs. 46,34,57,750**, inclusive of a **provisional sum of Rs. 2,11,00,000**. The jurisdictional officer indicated that the earlier applicable rate appeared to be **12%** and the later rate **18%**, but also noted that any contractual recovery of the increased tax from the employer was not something the advance ruling mechanism could decide.

For compliance purposes, the ruling is important mainly because it confirms the tax-rate dispute as a **classification/rate issue for infrastructure works contract services** and shows that the applicant’s rate position turned on the transition from the pre-change **12%** regime to the post-change **18%** regime. However, the Authority did **not** issue a ruling on whether the contractor could contractually recover the additional **6% GST burden** from the customer, because **Section 97(2) of the GST Act** does not allow the AAR to determine that kind of contractual recovery question. In other words, the decision does not create a recovery right or procedure; it only reflects that the tax-rate dispute existed and that the recovery issue was outside AAR jurisdiction.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Psyllium Seeds Not Fresh; 5% GST Applies: Rajasthan AAR

The applicant, M/s Santosh Devi Daga, a proprietorship acting as a licensed commission agent and trader, stated that cultivators bring Psyllium Seeds to the APMC after harvesting and threshing and that no drying, dehydration, freezing, grading, polishing, crushing, milling, roasting, chemical treatment or other processing is undertaken by the applicant. The applicant sought a ruling on whether the goods are classifiable under Tariff Item 12119013 and exempt under Entry No. 87 of Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17.09.2025, and whether threshing by cultivators is merely a harvesting activity rather than processing or manufacture. The Authority accepted the classification of Psyllium Seeds (Isabgol) under Tariff Item 12119013. It examined Heading 1211, the HSN notes, Notification No. 09/2025-Central Tax (Rate), Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate), CBIC FAQ F.No. 332/2/2017-TRU and Circular No. 163/19/2021-GST dated 06.10.2021. The Authority focused on the condition that Entry No. 87 of Notification No. 10/2025 exempts specified plants and parts of plants, including seeds and fruits, only when they are “fresh or chilled”. It observed that the exemption notification must be construed strictly and that the burden of establishing fulfilment of the exemption conditions rests on the person claiming the exemption. On the facts, the Authority did not accept the applicant’s conte
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan AAR held that Psyllium Seeds (Isabgol) traded by the applicant through the APMC at Nokha are correctly classifiable under Tariff Item 12119013, but they do **not** qualify for GST exemption under Entry No. 87 of Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17.09.2025 unless they are “fresh or chilled.” The applicant, M/s Santosh Devi Daga, argued that the seeds are brought by cultivators after harvesting and threshing and that the applicant does no drying, dehydration, freezing, grading, polishing, crushing, milling, roasting, chemical treatment, or other processing, and also asked whether threshing should be treated merely as a harvesting activity rather than processing/manufacture. The Authority reviewed Heading 1211, the HSN notes, Notifications No. 09/2025 and 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate), CBIC FAQ F.No. 332/2/2017-TRU, and Circular No. 163/19/2021-GST dated 06.10.2021, and concluded that the exemption for plants/parts of plants including seeds applies only where the goods are actually fresh or chilled.

The key compliance takeaway is that the exemption is interpreted strictly, and the burden is on the supplier/claimant to prove that the goods satisfy every condition for exemption. On the facts presented, the AAR did not accept the applicant’s position that the seeds were exempt merely because they were unprocessed or because threshing occurred at the cultivation stage; the decisive issue was the absence of the “fresh or chilled” condition. As a result, traders, commission agents, and others dealing in Psyllium Seeds should treat such supplies as taxable unless they can clearly document that the goods meet the specific exemption criteria in Entry No. 87. The ruling is relevant to businesses buying or selling psyllium seeds in APMC channels and similar trade flows, especially where the goods are dried or otherwise not fresh/chilled.

The applicant proposed classification under CTH 1302 as vegetable saps and extracts, whereas the jurisdictional Commissionerate questioned whether the multiple extraction, concentration and purification processes could take the products outside Heading 1302 and potentially bring them under the residual Heading 2106. CAAR examined the manufacturing processes, botanical origin, composition, intended use, HSN Explanatory Notes and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and related regulations. It observed that both products originate from plant materials and undergo solvent-based extraction followed by operations such as filtration, concentration, drying and, in the case of Grape Seed Extract, resin adsorption. However, the material on record did not establish specialised purification or selective concentration/depletion of particular compounds beyond what could be achieved through initial solvent extraction. The Authority held that the processes did not alter the essential identity of the goods as vegetable extracts. It further held that Heading 2106 could not be invoked merely because the extracts were intended for use in nutraceutical products, since they were imported in bulk as single-ingredient botanical extracts/raw materials and not as finished food preparations or dietary supplements put up for direct consumption. Accordingly, Pine Bark Extract and Gra
rows.summary:
CAAR Mumbai held that both Pine Bark Extract and Grape Seed Extract imported by M/s JESSP Chemicals are classifiable under Customs Tariff Heading 1302 as “vegetable saps and extracts,” and not under the residual Heading 2106. The ruling matters for import classification because the jurisdictional Commissionerate had argued that the repeated extraction, concentration, purification, filtration, drying, and—in the case of grape seed extract—resin adsorption steps might change the character of the goods and push them out of Heading 1302. CAAR rejected that view, finding that the products still retained their essential identity as botanical extracts derived from plant material and that the evidence did not show a level of specialized purification, selective concentration, or depletion of specific compounds sufficient to remove them from Heading 1302.

The Authority also specifically rejected the argument that intended use in nutraceutical manufacturing could justify classification under Heading 2106. It noted that the goods were imported in bulk as single-ingredient raw materials for further manufacture by nutraceutical companies, not as finished food preparations or dietary supplements ready for direct consumption. In reaching its conclusion, CAAR considered the manufacturing process, botanical origin, composition, intended use, the HSN Explanatory Notes, and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and related regulations. The practical compliance takeaway is that importers of comparable plant-derived extracts should assess classification based on the product’s essential character and actual form at import, rather than downstream end-use in nutraceuticals, unless the goods are transformed into a finished preparation or otherwise materially altered beyond ordinary extraction/concentration processes.

The department alleged that the tool value was neither included in the cost of production nor amortised, resulting in a duty demand of Rs.7,85,993/- with interest and equal penalty. The appellant contended that duty had already been paid on the tools, that another levy would amount to double taxation, that Notification No.67/95-CE dated 16.03.1995 exempted tools captively used in manufacture and that the extended period under Section 11A(1) was unavailable. The Tribunal followed its decision in M/s Best Cast IT Ltd, which had considered Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai I Vs Mega Rubber Technologies Pvt Ltd and the Larger Bench decision in Mutual Industries Ltd Vs Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai. It held that whether the tools were manufactured in the appellant’s own factory or outsourced did not alter the valuation principle whe
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai held in **Sankar Sealing Systems Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of GST & Central Excise** that where **jigs, fixtures, molds, and dies** were paid for by the buyer-customers but were retained and used by the manufacturer to produce components for those customers, the value of those tools had to be **included in the assessable cost of production and amortised for Central Excise duty purposes under Rule 6 of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000**. In this case, the appellant, a manufacturer of aluminium and rubber gaskets, had manufactured tools for customers, recovered the tool cost through excise invoices, and kept the tools in its factory to make the gaskets; the department treated the omission of the tool value from cost/amortisation as a valuation shortfall and raised a demand of **Rs. 7,85,993**, along with **interest and an equal penalty**.

The appellant argued that duty had already been paid on the tools, so including them again would amount to **double taxation**, and also relied on **Notification No. 67/95-CE dated 16.03.1995**, contending that tools captively used in manufacture were exempt; it further objected to the invocation of the **extended period under Section 11A(1)**. The Tribunal rejected these arguments and followed its earlier ruling in **M/s Best Cast IT Ltd.**, which had considered **Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai I v. Mega Rubber Technologies Pvt. Ltd.** and the Larger Bench decision in **Mutual Industries Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai**. It emphasized that the valuation principle is the same **whether the tools are manufactured in the assessee’s own factory or outsourced**, so the buyer-funded tool cost remains part of the manufacturing cost that must be amortised into the dutiable value of the final goods.

For compliance purposes, the ruling means manufacturers supplying goods using **customer-funded tooling** should ensure that the **full tool cost is captured in valuation and amortised appropriately** when determining excise duty on the final products; simply invoicing the tools separately does not avoid inclusion in assessable value if the tools are used in production. The decision also confirms that the Tribunal accepted the department’s position on valuation and did **not** accept the assessee’s extended-period defense in this matter, so companies with similar arrangements should review historic and current costing/valuation practices for excise exposure.

rows.summary:
CESTAT Chennai held that Brakes India Private Limited’s short payment of excise duty on job-worked automobile components was a bona fide, system-driven valuation error rather than a case of wilful suppression or intent to evade duty. The facts were that, after the parties moved in July 2012 from a job-work procedure to duty-paid clearances, BIPL returned hose ends, sleeves, and other intermediate goods to Wichitra Auto Ltd. after plating; BIPL first used manually computed values, but its system later generated values based only on the purchase cost of raw material plus BIPL’s own conversion cost and failed to include the “anterior” conversion cost already incurred by WAL, causing undervaluation.

Once the Department identified the discrepancy in February 2014, BIPL accepted the error, calculated differential duty of Rs. 1,11,94,846 and paid it along with interest of Rs. 13,10,440 before any show cause notice was issued. Despite that pre-notice payment, the Department alleged suppression, imposed an equivalent penalty on BIPL under Section 11AC, denied WAL CENVAT credit of the differential duty paid under BIPL’s supplementary invoice, and also imposed an equivalent penalty on WAL. The Tribunal rejected the penalty findings because the adjudicating authority did not properly address or rebut the detailed affidavit from BIPL’s Vice President-Finance explaining the system error, and the record did not support a finding of deliberate evasion.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the duty shortfall was treated as a valuation mistake that was voluntarily corrected before notice, so the equivalent penalty under Section 11AC was not sustainable on these facts. The decision also confirms that when a supplier issues a supplementary invoice to make good a genuine pre-notice duty short payment, the recipient’s credit should not be denied solely because the duty arose from that correction, absent evidence of fraud, suppression, or collusion. There are no new prospective regulatory filing deadlines or rate changes in the order itself; the significance is evidentiary and penalty-related: companies should maintain robust valuation logic, document cost-calculation changes in ERP/systems, preserve internal explanations from responsible officers, and ensure prompt payment of any identified differential duty and interest to reduce exposure to penal consequences.

rows.title: Service Tax | Police Security Services Performing Statutory Duties Not Taxable: CESTAT Mumbai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13710 Case Name Superintendent of Police (Rural) Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Mumbai Upgrade to Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Superintendent of Police (Rural) Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Mumbai) Summary: CESTAT Mumbai allowed the appeal of Superintendent of Police (Rural) against the order confirming service tax demand of Rs.3,19,421/- on charges collected for providing armed security guards to public sector banks, undertakings and government departments. The appellant, being part of the Maharashtra State Police force, was responsible for maintenance and enforcement of public law and order and provided armed security guards under Section 13 of the Police Act, 1861 by recovering the actual expenditure/cost. The issue before the Tribunal was whether this activity constituted taxable “security services” under the Finance Act, 1994. The Tribunal observed that the appellant was performing statutory duties and the amounts collected were deposited in the Government treasury. It relied upon Circular No.89/7/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006, under which charges collected by a sovereign/public authority for statutory functions are not liable to service tax where the functions constitute statutory and mandatory obligations, the fee is levied under the relevant law and the amount is deposited into the Government treasury. The Tribunal further relied upon the CESTAT decision in Dy. Commissioner of Police & Others Vs. CCE, Jaipur & Others, where the police department, being an agency of the State Government, was held not to be a person engaged in the business of running security services. It also referred to Mumbai Police Vs. Commissioner of Service Tax, Mumbai-I [2018-TIOL-1067-CESTAT-MUM], where
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai held that the Maharashtra State Police’s provision of armed security guards to public sector banks, public undertakings, and government departments under Section 13 of the Police Act, 1861 was **not taxable as “security services”** under the Finance Act, 1994 when the activity was carried out as part of statutory police functions and the police recovered only the actual expenditure/cost. The appeal was filed by the Superintendent of Police (Rural) against a service tax demand of **Rs. 3,19,421**, and the Tribunal allowed the appeal. A key factual point was that the police department was performing **mandatory public-law and order duties**, and the amounts collected for providing the guards were **deposited into the Government treasury**, rather than retained as commercial consideration.

The Tribunal relied on **Circular No. 89/7/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006**, which states that charges collected by a sovereign/public authority for statutory functions are not subject to service tax where the function is a **statutory and mandatory obligation**, the fee/charge is **levied under the relevant law**, and the amount is **deposited in the Government treasury**. It also followed earlier CESTAT precedent holding that a police department is **not a person engaged in the business of running security services** merely because it provides security in discharge of official duties. The practical compliance takeaway is that government police entities providing security under statutory authority, on a cost-recovery basis and with proceeds paid into the treasury, should not be treated as taxable service providers for service tax on those activities. This ruling does **not** create a new filing deadline or rate change; rather, it confirms a **non-taxability position** for such statutory police functions and helps distinguish them from commercial private security services.
