rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai partly allowed the appeal of Husain Kasam Mukadam & Sons against the Customs authorities’ order revoking its Customs Broker licence, forfeiting its entire security deposit, and imposing a penalty under the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 (CBLR). The case arose from an import made by M/s K.K. Traders, Satara, under Bill of Entry No. 7580019 dated 21.02.2022, for a consignment declared as 27,000 kg of “Raw Cashew Nuts in shell.” After the shipment was cleared at JNCH, Nhava Sheva, Pune Customs intercepted the container based on specific intelligence and found that only 2,487 kg was the declared raw cashew nuts, while 24,753 kg consisted of undeclared broken cashew kernel/cashew baby bits. The Tribunal noted that DGFT Notification No. 08/2015-2020 dated 12.06.2019 prescribed a minimum import price for cashew kernels, and it found that the import itself violated those import conditions because the kernels were brought in below the applicable threshold.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that the Customs Broker was not found to have been part of the importer’s misdeclaration scheme. The Tribunal concluded from the investigation record and statements that the culpable conduct lay with the importer and Shri Chetan Yadav of M/s Ninai Shipping Agency, not with the broker, and it emphasized that the goods had already undergone Customs examination at JNCH without the concealed kernels being detected. On Regulation 10(e) of the CBLR, the Tribunal held that the broker had filed the Bill of Entry based on the documents provided to it, and the concealment was not something the broker was shown to have knowingly participated in or detected from the supplied papers. As a result, while the underlying import violation remained serious, the Tribunal found the extreme broker-side consequences unsustainable on the evidence and therefore only partly upheld the department’s action.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Old Rules Do Not Govern Earlier Vacancies Automatically: Supreme Court
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13697 Case Name State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors. Vs Raj Kumar & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors. Vs Raj Kumar & Ors. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether public posts that became vacant before amendment of recruitment rules must necessarily be filled according to the old rules. The dispute arose after seven additional Labour Officer posts were sanctioned in Himachal Pradesh on 20.07.2006. The governing 1966 Rules contemplated filling Labour Officer posts by promotion. On 25.11.2006, however, new Recruitment and Promotion Rules came into force providing for 75% promotion and 25% direct recruitment. Respondent Labour Inspectors contended that since the additional vacancies had arisen before the amended Rules, they had to be filled entirely under the old Rules. The Himachal Pradesh High Court accepted this contention by relying on Y.V. Rangaiah v. J. Sreenivasa Rao and interfered with appointments made through direct recruitment. The Supreme Court undertook an extensive review of Rangaiah and the numerous subsequent decisions that had either followed or distinguished it. Examining Articles 309, 310 and 311 of the Constitution and the nature of public employment, the Court held that government service is governed by statutory status rather than ordinary contractual rights. A public servant’s rights and obligations must therefore be sourced from the applicable service rules. There is no vested right independent of those rules to insist that vacancies be filled according to the rules prevailing when the vacancies arose. The Court clarified that Rangaiah itself arose from a particular statutory requirement unde
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors. v. Raj Kumar & Ors.** held that **government vacancies that arose before a recruitment-rule amendment do not automatically have to be filled under the old rules**. The case involved **seven additional Labour Officer posts sanctioned on 20.07.2006** in Himachal Pradesh: under the **1966 Rules**, Labour Officer posts were to be filled by **promotion**, but the **new Recruitment and Promotion Rules came into force on 25.11.2006** and changed the method to **75% promotion and 25% direct recruitment**. The affected employees argued that because the vacancies existed before 25.11.2006, the State was bound to fill all of them under the old promotional rule, and the Himachal Pradesh High Court agreed, relying on **Y.V. Rangaiah v. J. Sreenivasa Rao** and setting aside the direct-recruitment appointments.

The Supreme Court reversed that approach and explained that, under **Articles 309, 310, and 311**, public employment is governed by **statutory service rules**, not by any independent vested right of employees to demand that vacancies be filled according to the rules in force when the vacancies first arose. The Court reviewed **Rangaiah** and later cases and clarified that **Rangaiah does not create a universal rule** requiring all earlier vacancies to be filled only under the old rules; rather, its outcome depended on the specific statutory framework in that case. For compliance purposes, the key point is that **when recruitment rules are amended, the applicable rules for filling vacancies depend on the governing legal and factual context, and employees cannot assume a vested right to insist on the old method of appointment merely because the vacancy predated the amendment**. This decision is especially relevant for government departments and public employers managing recruitment after rule changes, because it validates using the **current rules in force at the time of recruitment** unless a statute or rule expressly provides otherwise.

The DCE consisted of four different equipments—Projector, Server, UPS and VSAT—having different HSN classifications, while lease rental for the entire set was charged through a single invoice. The applicant treated the arrangement under section 8 of the CGST/SGST Act. The Authority examined whether the bundle constituted a composite supply or mixed supply. Referring to the definitions of composite supply under Section 2(30), principal supply under Section 2(90) and mixed supply under Section 2(74), it observed that composite supply requires the constituent supplies to be naturally bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business. The Authority also considered the indicators stated in CBIC Flyer No. 4 dated 05.08.2019 for determining whether services are naturally bundled, including consumer perception, normal industry practice, whether the elements are advertised as a package, whether they are separately available and whether they are integral to one overall supply. It found that none of those indicators applied to the applicant’s proposed supply and that similar businesses did not provide such bundling as a matter of course. Consequently, the DCE bundle was held not to constitute a composite supply. The Authority then applied Section 2(74) and held that the equipment leased as DCE was not naturally bundled, was provided for a single lease and was not supplied se
rows.summary:
The Telangana AAR held that leasing Digital Cinema Equipment (DCE) as one packaged arrangement is a **mixed supply, not a composite supply**, for GST purposes. The applicant, UFO Moviez India Limited, leased a DCE bundle made up of four separately classifiable items—**Projector, Server, UPS, and VSAT**—and raised a **single invoice** for the lease rental on the entire set. Because the items had **different HSN classifications** and the Authority found they were **not naturally bundled** or supplied together in the ordinary course of business, the arrangement failed the composite supply test under **Section 2(30)** read with **Section 2(90)** of the CGST/SGST Act.

In reaching that conclusion, the AAR relied on the usual indicators for “naturally bundled” supplies referenced in **CBIC Flyer No. 4 dated 05.08.2019**, including whether customers perceive the items as one package, whether the trade normally supplies them together, whether they are advertised as a package, whether they are separately available, and whether each element is integral to one overall supply. The Authority found those indicators were not satisfied here and noted that similar industry players did not customarily bundle these items in the manner proposed by the applicant. It therefore rejected treatment of the arrangement under the composite supply rule.

Having concluded the bundle was not composite, the AAR applied **Section 2(74)** and classified the arrangement as a **mixed supply**. The practical compliance consequence is that the lease of the DCE bundle must be taxed at the **highest GST rate applicable to any one of the constituent items in the bundle**, rather than by splitting the supply or applying the rate of a supposed principal supply. The document does not specify a separate effective date or new filing deadline; the ruling is a classification decision that affects how taxpayers should invoice and compute GST on similarly bundled equipment-leasing arrangements going forward.

rows.summary:
The Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, through the Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), has issued Notification S.O. 5069(E) dated 14 September 2026 authorizing WDRA and its regulated repositories to use Aadhaar authentication for identity verification of Aadhaar number holders. The permission came after the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, in consultation with UIDAI, approved Aadhaar authentication for WDRA and its regulated repositories for two specific purposes: onboarding depositors, warehousemen, and other stakeholders on the WDRA portal and regulated repository platforms through Aadhaar e-KYC, and conducting service transactions on those platforms.

A key compliance point is that Aadhaar authentication is expressly voluntary. WDRA and regulated repositories must obtain the Aadhaar number holder’s consent before using Aadhaar authentication, and they are prohibited from denying any service merely because a person refuses to use Aadhaar authentication or is unable to complete it. This means entities subject to the WDRA framework must maintain a non-Aadhaar fallback process and cannot make Aadhaar a mandatory gatekeeper for access to portal services or repository-related transactions.

The notification also requires acceptance of alternative, viable identification documents where Aadhaar is not used. The alternatives specified are PAN, Driving Licence, Passport, a photograph-bearing Address Card issued by the Department of Posts, specified photograph-bearing passbooks issued by a post office or a public sector scheduled bank, Kisan Passbook, and Voter Identity Card. Compliance teams should ensure internal onboarding and transaction workflows explicitly incorporate these alternate documents and do not create practical barriers to service for individuals who choose not to authenticate via Aadhaar.

This notification supersedes Notification S.O. 698(E) dated 10 February 2023, except for anything already done or omitted before the new notification took effect. It becomes effective from the date of publication in the Official Gazette, so entities using WDRA-regulated digital onboarding or transaction systems should treat it as immediately operative from publication and align policies, consent capture, and alternate-ID procedures accordingly.

rows.summary:
The Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas has announced that, effective **1 October 2026**, **domestic LPG consumers** must have completed **Biometric Aadhaar Authentication (BAA)** in order to **book refills at the regulated Retail Selling Price (RSP) and receive the applicable subsidy**. Consumers who have already completed BAA do **not** need to repeat it, and consumers who have not yet done so will become eligible for subsidised refills once authentication is completed. BAA can be completed **during cylinder delivery** using the **OMC mobile application**, at the **LPG distributor’s showroom**, or through the relevant **OMC mobile app**.

Consumers who are **unwilling or unable** to complete BAA may still receive LPG, but only after they register that choice through the OMC’s digital channels; in that case, supplies will be provided **at market price without subsidy** and only in **5 kg or 10 kg cylinders**, subject to local availability. As of **19 September 2026**, **27.43 crore** active domestic LPG consumers—representing **89.9% coverage**—had already completed BAA, so the government says those consumers need take no further action. The stated policy objective is to **prevent diversion of subsidised domestic cylinders, eliminate duplicate and ineligible connections, and improve targeting of subsidy benefits**.

The notice also provides financial context: the **implicit subsidy for September 2026** was approximately **₹210 per 14.2 kg cylinder**, and **accumulated under-recoveries of public sector OMCs exceeded ₹62,000 crore as of 31 August 2026**. For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that from the effective date, subsidised domestic LPG refills will be tied to completion of BAA, while non-authenticated consumers must either authenticate or opt into non-subsidised, market-priced supply through the designated digital process.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Multiple Cheques Create Separate Causes of Action under Section 138 of NI Act: SC
rows.desc: Summary: Where several cheques are issued in respect of the same transaction and underlying liability and all are dishonoured, separate complaints under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 can be filed for each cheque where the statutory requirements are independently fulfilled. In Sumit Bansal v. M/s MGI Developers and Promoters & Anr., the Supreme Court held that each dishonour gives rise to a separate cause of action upon completion of the statutory sequence of presentation, dishonour, notice and failure to pay, and multiple cheques arising from one transaction do not merge into a single cause of action. At the same time, multiple cheques arising from the same transaction may be covered by a single complaint, particularly where a common statutory notice is issued, as considered in Pawan Dhanpatrai Malhotra v. Mahender Khari and A. Adinarayana Reddy v. S. Vijayalakshmi & Anr. The Supreme Court further reiterated that jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. must be exercised sparingly and that disputed questions concerning existence of debt or legally enforceable liability ordinarily require trial. The statutory presumption under Section 139 operates in favour of the complainant, and the accused must rebut it during trial. Where the complaint prima facie satisfies the essential ingredients of Section 138, disputed factual defences should not ordinarily result in premature quashing of proceedings. rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **Sumit Bansal v. M/s MGI Developers and Promoters & Anr.** clarified that when **multiple cheques are issued for the same transaction and underlying liability**, each cheque is treated as giving rise to a **separate cause of action** under **Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881** if the statutory steps are independently completed. That means a complainant may file **separate complaints for each dishonoured cheque** so long as the required sequence occurs for each instrument: **presentation of the cheque, dishonour, issuance of statutory notice, and failure to pay within the prescribed period**. The Court rejected the idea that several cheques from one transaction automatically “merge” into a single Section 138 claim.

At the same time, the Court noted that where multiple dishonoured cheques arise from the same transaction, they may also be addressed in a **single consolidated complaint**, especially if a **common statutory notice** is issued, consistent with earlier decisions such as **Pawan Dhanpatrai Malhotra v. Mahender Khari** and **A. Adinarayana Reddy v. S. Vijayalakshmi & Anr.** For compliance purposes, this means entities issuing or receiving multiple cheques tied to one obligation should expect that dishonour of each cheque can trigger **individual prosecution exposure**, not just one combined proceeding.

The Supreme Court also reiterated that the High Court’s inherent power under **Section 482 of the Cr.P.C.** must be used **sparingly** and that disputes about whether a debt or legally enforceable liability actually existed are ordinarily matters for **trial**, not for early quashing. The statutory presumption under **Section 139 of the NI Act** continues to operate in favour of the complainant once the basic Section 138 ingredients are shown, and the accused must rebut that presumption during the trial. Accordingly, if a complaint on its face satisfies the essential requirements of Section 138, factual defences about liability should generally not be used to stop the case at the quashing stage.

The Court observed that disputes relating to the technical qualifications, experience and eligibility of bidders ordinarily involve their individual commercial interests. Such disputes cannot acquire the character of public interest merely because the contract has been awarded by a government authority. The Bench comprising Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu accordingly interfered with the Himachal Pradesh High Court’s decision quashing the road-work contract awarded to the appellant. However, instead of finally disposing of the proceedings, the Supreme Court granted the contractor three months to complete the work and directed the matter to be listed again for submission of a compliance report. High Court Had Quashed the Road-Work Contract The dispute concerned the upgradation of the Matiana-Mahori-Chhaila road under a Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana package. The value of the work was approximately Rs.23 crore. The contract was awarded to the appellant on March 15, 2024. A PIL was subsequently filed before the Himachal Pradesh High Court questioning the tender process
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court of India in **O.P. Mehta v. Mohinder Kalta & Ors. (2026 INSC 1037)** held that a challenge to a government tender award based on the **comparative technical qualifications, experience, and eligibility of rival bidders** should ordinarily not be dressed up as a **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)**, because such disputes are usually commercial in nature and concern the competing private interests of bidders rather than a genuine public-interest issue. The Court criticized the use of PIL to challenge the award of a government contract and disagreed with the Himachal Pradesh High Court’s decision to quash the contract on that basis.

The underlying contract was for the **upgradation of the Matiana-Mahori-Chhaila road** under a **Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana** package, with a value of about **Rs. 23 crore**. The contract had been awarded to the appellant on **15 March 2024**, and a PIL was later filed in the Himachal Pradesh High Court challenging the tender process. The Supreme Court restored the road-work contract rather than leaving the quashing order in place, but it did not give the contractor an unconditional reopening of the award.

Instead, the Court imposed an operational compliance requirement: the contractor was given **three months to complete the work**, and the case is to be **listed again for submission of a compliance report**. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the Court signaled that tender disputes over bidder eligibility generally should not be converted into PILs, but it also required the contractor to meet the accelerated completion timeline and return to court with proof of compliance.

However, noticing that the assessee’s appeal had remained pending before the CIT(A) since January 2020, the Court directed the appellate authority to decide the appeal within two months. The petitioner-company challenged an assessment order dated 31.12.2019 passed under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. At the outset, the Revenue raised a preliminary objection regarding maintainability of the writ petition. It was pointed out that the assessment order had been passed nearly seven years earlier and, more importantly, the assessee had already preferred an appeal before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) on 24.01.2020. That statutory appeal was still pending. According to the Revenue, an assessee could not pursue two parallel remedies by keeping the statutory appeal alive and simultaneously approaching the High Court against the very same assessment order. The assessee, however, contended
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court held that an assessee generally cannot pursue a writ petition under Article 226 challenging an assessment order while a statutory appeal against the same order is already pending before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), even if the assessee’s objection goes to the Assessing Officer’s jurisdiction. In this case, Raj Sheela Growth Fund Pvt. Ltd. had challenged an assessment order dated 31.12.2019 passed under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, but it had already filed a CIT(A) appeal on 24.01.2020, which was still pending when the writ was filed in 2026. The Revenue argued this amounted to impermissible parallel proceedings, and the Court agreed that the writ was ordinarily not maintainable where the statutory appellate remedy had already been invoked and remained available.  

At the same time, the Court noted that the appeal had been pending since January 2020—more than six years—and treated that delay as unacceptable. Rather than decide the merits of the jurisdictional challenge in writ proceedings, the Court directed the CIT(A) to dispose of the pending appeal within two months from the order date, which was 18.09.2026. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is procedural: where an appeal is already on foot, taxpayers should not expect the High Court to entertain a simultaneous writ on the same assessment order, and prolonged inaction in the appellate channel may prompt the Court to require expedited adjudication instead of entertaining the writ directly.

rows.summary:
M/s Ganpati Trader filed five advance-ruling applications on 12.06.2026 seeking Customs classification of imported roasted areca nuts in whole, cut, and split forms; the applications were registered as Nos. 36–40/2026-27. At the personal hearing on 08.09.2026, the applicant’s advocate reiterated the written submissions, but the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings, Delhi first examined whether it could lawfully entertain the requests at all under Section 28-I(2) of the Customs Act, 1962.

The Authority held that the first proviso to Section 28-I(2) bars an application where the same question is pending in the applicant’s own case before a customs officer, the Appellate Tribunal, or a court, and also bars it where the same question has already been decided by the Appellate Tribunal or a court. The order specifically notes the distinction between a pending matter in the applicant’s own case and a question already settled by a higher judicial forum, and it relies on the principle that subordinate authorities must follow binding precedent, citing *Union of India v. Kamlakshi Finance Corporation Ltd.* for judicial discipline.

Applying that principle, CAAR Delhi found that the classification issue for roasted areca nuts was covered by the Madras High Court decision cited as *M/s Shahnaz International Pvt. Ltd.* [2023 (386) E.L.T. 214 (Mad.)]. Because the question had already been decided by a High Court, the Authority declined to issue any classification ruling and rejected the five applications under Section 28-I(2)(b). For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that this order does not establish a new tariff position for Ganpati Trader’s goods; instead, it signals that importers seeking an advance ruling on this roasted areca nut classification issue may be refused where the matter is already governed by existing High Court precedent.

(Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered two connected civil appeals concerning the meaning of “governmental authority” under the Mega Service Tax Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-Service Tax, dated 20 June 2012, as amended by Notification No. 02/2014-Service Tax dated 30 January 2014. The common issue was whether the Indian Institute of Technology, Patna (IIT Patna) and the National Institute of Technology, Rourkela (NIT Rourkela) fell within the amended definition and consequently obtained the exemption applicable to specified construction services provided to the Government, a local authority or a governmental authority. The first appeal arose from the Patna High Court judgment dated 3 March 2016, which had directed refund of service tax collected in relation to construction at IIT Patna. The second arose from the Orissa High Court judgment dated 5 February 2018, which, relying on the Patna decision, directed consideration of SPCL’s refund application concerning construction at NIT Rourkela. The relevant exemption was issued under section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 and clause 12(c) covered structures meant predominantly for educational, clinical, or art or cultural establishments. The original definition of “governmental authority” required 90% or more participation by Government by equity or control, statutory establishment, and performance of a municipal function under Article 243W. The 30 January 2014 amendment recast clause 2(s) into two alternatives: an author
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that the service tax exemption under Mega Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-Service Tax, issued under section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994 and amended by Notification No. 02/2014-Service Tax dated 30 January 2014, applied to construction services provided in relation to IIT Patna and NIT Rourkela. The dispute turned on whether these institutions qualified as a “governmental authority” after the 2014 amendment, which changed the definition from a single test requiring at least 90% Government participation by equity or control, statutory establishment, and performance of a municipal function under Article 243W, into two alternative limbs: an authority or board/body/entity established by Government with 90% or more participation by way of equity or control to carry out functions entrusted by the Government, or an authority or board/body/entity set up by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature to carry out functions entrusted by the Government.

The Court accepted the High Courts’ conclusion that IIT Patna and NIT Rourkela satisfied the amended definition and therefore fell within the exemption for specified construction services, including clause 12(c) covering structures meant predominantly for educational establishments. As a result, service tax that had been collected on construction work for these institutes was held refundable, and the Supreme Court upheld the Patna High Court’s 3 March 2016 order directing refund in the IIT Patna matter and the Orissa High Court’s 5 February 2018 order directing consideration of SPCL’s refund claim for NIT Rourkela. For compliance purposes, the decision confirms that contractors performing construction services for institutions fitting the post-30 January 2014 “governmental authority” definition may claim the exemption, and where tax has already been paid on such covered work, refund treatment may be available subject to the applicable procedural requirements and limitation rules.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Composition Levy: Eligibility, Rates, ITC Limits and Trade-Offs
rows.desc: Summary: The Composition Levy under GST is designed to simplify tax compliance for eligible small taxpayers, but the reduced compliance burden involves important economic and commercial trade-offs. Governed principally by Section 10 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules, the scheme allows qualifying taxpayers to discharge GST at prescribed composition rates subject to turnover thresholds and restrictions concerning the nature and territorial scope of supplies. The notified threshold is generally ₹1.5 crore, with a ₹75 lakh threshold for specified States, while Section 10(2A) provides a separate route for certain taxpayers with aggregate turnover up to ₹50 lakh. The principal economic limitation is the denial of ordinary input tax credit, which can cause GST paid on inputs to become an embedded business cost and may affect B2B competitiveness. Composition taxpayers must also continuously monitor eligibility rather than treating entry into the scheme as a one-time exercise. Legislative and procedural reforms have nevertheless reduced some restrictions. The Finance Act, 2023 enabled eligible composition taxpayers to supply goods through specified electronic commerce operators, while subsequent changes extended the GSTR-4 filing deadline. The scheme therefore presents a continuing policy balance between simplified compliance, input-tax neutrality and the ability of small businesses to expand across markets and distribution channels. rows.summary:
The document explains that the GST Composition Levy is a simplified tax regime under Section 10 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules for eligible small taxpayers, but it comes with important restrictions that compliance teams must monitor continuously. The main entry thresholds are an aggregate turnover limit of generally ₹1.5 crore, a lower ₹75 lakh threshold for specified States, and a separate route under Section 10(2A) for certain taxpayers with aggregate turnover up to ₹50 lakh. Because eligibility is based on aggregate turnover and not just one GST registration, the same PAN cannot ordinarily maintain both composition and regular registrations, so businesses must assess group-level/ PAN-level turnover and not treat enrollment as a one-time decision.

A core trade-off is that composition taxpayers do not get the ordinary input tax credit regime, which means GST paid on inputs can become a built-in cost and may weaken B2B pricing competitiveness. The document emphasizes that composition taxpayers must keep checking whether they remain eligible, since crossing the threshold or otherwise violating scheme conditions can require exit from the scheme and conversion to regular GST compliance. The scheme therefore reduces filing and operational burden, but only if the taxpayer remains within the turnover limits and activity restrictions.

The scheme is governed by Section 10 provisions including Section 10(1), the second proviso to Section 10(1), Section 10(2), Section 10(2A), Section 10(3), reverse charge rules, Section 10(5), and the prescribed composition rates. The document does not provide the exact rate percentages in the excerpt, but it makes clear that taxes are paid at notified composition rates rather than ordinary GST rates. It also notes that legislative/procedural reforms have relaxed some earlier limits.

In particular, the Finance Act, 2023 allowed eligible composition taxpayers to supply goods through specified electronic commerce operators, which is a material expansion because composition taxpayers were previously more restricted in channel access. The document also states that later changes extended the GSTR-4 filing deadline, so compliance teams should verify the current due date rather than relying on older filing calendars. Overall, the practical compliance message is that the composition scheme can simplify return and tax administration for smaller businesses, but only if they continuously track turnover, confirm that their supply type and distribution channels remain permitted, and monitor filing deadlines and any rule changes affecting eligibility.

rows.title: Income Tax | GST on Online Gaming: 40% Rate, Gameskraft Ruling and Prohibition
rows.desc: GST on Online Gaming in India: From 28% to 40%, Games-kraft and the Post-Prohibition Legal Position Summary: The taxation of online gaming has undergone a significant transformation in India. What began as a dispute over whether skill-based gaming platforms were supplying taxable services evolved into a larger controversy concerning betting and gambling, actionable claims, valuation, delegated legislation and constitutional competence. The Central Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced specific definitions of “online gaming”, “online money gaming” and “specified actionable claims”, while Rule 31B of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017, provided a special valuation mechanism for online gaming. These changes took effect from 1 October 2023. The GST Council had recommended taxation at 28% on the full value of the amount paid or deposited by the player, irrespective of whether the underlying game involved skill or chance. The legal position changed further with the Supreme Court’s decision in Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (HQS) v. Gameskraft Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., 2026 INSC 595, decided on 27 May 2026. The Court held that online gaming transactions involving stakes upon uncertain outcomes give rise to actionable-claim interests falling within the GST framework; that gaming platforms themselves may constitute the suppliers; that the amount staked constitutes consideration; and that Rule 31B provides the applicable valuation mechanism. The Court upheld the relevant GST provisions and rejected constitutional challenges to the levy. It also held the 2023 amendments to be clarificatory and retrospective in the manner set out in the judgement. The rate, however, is no longer 28%. Pursuant to the 56th GST Council meeting, the GST rate for specified actionable claims, including online money gaming, was increased from 28% to 40% with effect from 22 September 2025. At the same time, India’s regulatory framework move
rows.summary:
The document explains that India’s GST treatment of online gaming has shifted from a prior 28% levy to a 40% GST rate for specified actionable claims, including online money gaming, with effect from 22 September 2025. It states that the 2023 GST amendments—specifically the Central Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Act, 2023—introduced formal definitions of “online gaming,” “online money gaming,” and “specified actionable claims,” and that Rule 31B of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 established a special valuation method for these activities; those amendments and rules took effect on 1 October 2023. Under the GST Council’s approach described in the document, tax was intended to apply on the full amount paid or deposited by the player, regardless of whether the underlying game was one of skill or chance, and the amount staked is treated as the consideration for GST purposes.

The document further reports that the Supreme Court in Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (HQS) v. Gameskraft Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., 2026 INSC 595, decided on 27 May 2026, upheld the GST framework and rejected constitutional challenges to the levy. The Court held that online gaming transactions involving stakes on uncertain outcomes generate actionable-claim interests within the GST net, that gaming platforms can be treated as the suppliers, and that Rule 31B is the applicable valuation mechanism. It also characterized the 2023 amendments as clarificatory and retrospective to the extent described in the judgment, which means compliance teams should treat the GST treatment as legally reinforced rather than merely prospective from the amendment date.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that online gaming businesses, especially online money gaming platforms and any entity arranging or facilitating wagering on uncertain outcomes, are now subject to a 40% GST rate on the taxable value determined under the special valuation rules, rather than the earlier 28% rate. The document indicates that the post-amendment and post-judgment position is intended to close the skill-versus-chance debate for GST classification by focusing on the existence of actionable claims and stakes, so companies should ensure their invoicing, tax calculation, and reporting systems reflect the full deposit/stake-based valuation model and the updated 40% rate.

rows.summary:
The SAFEMA Appellate Tribunal upheld the freeze of a residential flat under the NDPS framework after finding that the owner had not proved a legitimate, non-illicit source of funds. The case arose from a major narcotics seizure on 16 August 2022, when Gujarat Police recovered 225.053 kg of Mephedrone (reported value about Rs. 1,125.26 crore), Rs. 14 lakh in cash alleged to be sale proceeds of contraband, and 1,753.300 kg of Alprazolam from the premises of Nectar Chem, a partnership firm at Village Moksi, Vadodara; the appellant and four others were arrested for allegedly manufacturing and selling narcotics without a licence. Because the seizure involved commercial quantities and the alleged offences were punishable with rigorous imprisonment of more than three years, the matter triggered the property-freezing provisions applicable to “affected persons” under the NDPS/SAFEMA scheme.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that income-tax returns, a Chartered Accountant’s certificate, and an incomplete loan statement are not enough to establish that a property was purchased from clean, lawful income where the bank trail is missing. The Tribunal stressed that when a property is identified within the statutory period and the person falls within the definition of an “affected person,” the burden shifts to that person under Section 68-J to affirmatively prove that the property was not acquired from illicit income. In this case, the appellant failed because he did not produce the relevant bank statements, loan sanction documents, or proof of repayment that would have substantiated the source of funds.

The practical compliance takeaway is that documentary proof of source-of-funds must be complete and traceable; partial financial records will not defeat a freezing action if authorities link the property to NDPS-related proceedings. Entities and individuals exposed to narcotics investigations should expect courts and tribunals to require a full paper trail showing how the asset was funded, including loan origination and repayment evidence, not just tax filings or professional certifications.

rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, issued Notification No. 23/2026-Customs (ADD) on 22 September 2026 to amend Notification No. 77/2021-Customs (ADD), which imposed anti-dumping duty on **Decor Paper**. The legal basis for the amendment is section 9A(1) and 9A(5) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, read with rules 18 and 23 of the 1995 Anti-Dumping Rules.  

The substantive change is that a new paragraph 3 has been inserted into the principal notification, providing that, **despite paragraph 2**, the anti-dumping duty under Notification No. 77/2021-Customs (ADD) will **continue to remain in force up to and inclusive of 26 March 2027**, unless it is revoked, superseded, or amended earlier. In other words, the duty that was already in place for Decor Paper is not being changed in rate or scope by this amendment; instead, its **operating period is extended** to 26 March 2027.  

For compliance purposes, companies importing Decor Paper should continue to treat the anti-dumping duty as applicable through that date, and customs classification/assessment processes should assume the duty remains payable unless a later order changes or terminates it sooner. The notification also notes that the principal notification had previously been amended by Notification No. 19/2025-Customs (ADD) dated 24 June 2025, but this 2026 amendment is specifically a **time-extension measure** rather than a substantive revision of the underlying anti-dumping duty regime.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | ITC in Special Circumstances: Special Rules for Preserving Input Tax Credit
rows.desc: Section 18 CGST Act governs ITC during registration, composition exit, taxable transitions, restructuring, transfers and special reversals.The post ITC in Special Circumstances: Special Rules for Pres
rows.summary:
Section 18 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 creates a special regime for input tax credit (ITC) when a taxpayer’s GST status or business structure changes, so that credit is preserved only where the statute allows and is reversed or transferred through prescribed procedures where required. It applies when a person becomes liable to register under GST, takes voluntary registration, shifts from the composition scheme to the regular GST regime, or begins making taxable supplies after previously dealing only in exempt supplies. In these cases, the taxpayer may claim ITC in relation to stock, semi-finished goods, finished goods, capital goods, or other eligible assets held at the relevant transition date, but only subject to the conditions and time limits under the Act and Rules.

The document also covers business reorganizations such as sale, merger, demerger, amalgamation, lease, and transfer, where unutilised ITC can be moved from the transferor to the transferee if the statutory requirements are met. Rules 40 and 41 of the CGST Rules are the main procedural provisions here, requiring use of FORM GST ITC-01 for claiming eligible credit in transition situations and FORM GST ITC-02 for transfer of credit in reorganisations; Rule 44 governs reversal of ITC in specified circumstances. These rules are compliance-critical because the preservation of credit depends not just on substantive eligibility but also on correct filing, documentation, and adherence to the prescribed mechanics.

A key compliance issue highlighted is the effect of GST portal restrictions on the transfer of ITC between registrations in different States after amalgamation. In Umicore Autocat India Private Limited v. Union of India, the Bombay High Court allowed the transfer of relevant CGST and IGST credit despite a technical portal restriction, and the Gujarat High Court later dealt with a similar cross-State transfer problem in Emerson Process Management (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India. The practical takeaway for compliance teams is that, while Section 18 is intended to protect genuine credit during tax/status changes, businesses must still monitor filing deadlines, reductions, and reversal obligations closely, and may need to pursue procedural remedies or litigation where the GST portal prevents a legally permitted transfer.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Bribe Recovery Without Proof of Demand Cannot Sustain Conviction: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court sets aside PC Act conviction as demand and conscious acceptance of alleged bribe were not proved beyond reasonable doubt.The post Bribe Recovery Without Proof of Demand Cannot Sustain Co
rows.summary: The Supreme Court held that a conviction under the Prevention of Corruption Act cannot stand where the prosecution proves only recovery of alleged bribe money but fails to prove the core elements of **demand** and **conscious acceptance** beyond a reasonable doubt. In the case referenced, the Court set aside the PC Act conviction because the evidence did not sufficiently establish that the accused had actually asked for the bribe or knowingly accepted it as an illegal gratification. The ruling reinforces that mere recovery of currency from an accused person is not enough, by itself, to sustain a corruption conviction; proof of a prior demand and voluntary acceptance remains essential. For compliance teams, the practical significance is that anti-corruption enforcement outcomes continue to turn on documentary, testimonial, and circumstantial evidence of solicitation and acceptance, not on recovery alone. The document does not announce a new statutory rule, deadline, rate, or threshold; it reports a judicial standard reaffirming the evidentiary burden required for a valid PC Act conviction.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Clock on ITC: Understanding Time Limits for Claiming Input Tax Credit under GST
rows.desc: Summary: Section 16(4) of the CGST Act generally bars a registered person from availing input tax credit (ITC) after 30 November following the end of the relevant financial year or the date of furnishing the annual return, whichever is earlier. The deadline applies to invoices and debit notes, but ITC eligibility and timely availment remain separate requirements: satisfying the time limit does not itself establish eligibility. The article traces the change from the earlier September-return deadline to 30 November with effect from 1 October 2022, explains why businesses should reconcile ITC before the final cut-off, and highlights the effect of filing the annual return earlier. It also discusses debit notes, reverse-charge supplies from unregistered persons under CBIC Circular No. 211/5/2024-GST, retrospective relief under Sections 16(5) and 16(6) for specified cases, and the distinction between a fresh claim and re-availment of reversed credit. The practical discussion recommends ongoing reconciliation of purchase records, GST data, supplier reporting, reverse-charge transactions, debit notes and reversals, with documentation of when credit became eligible and was availed. The article concludes that businesses should monitor both the statutory date and annual-return filing date and claim eligible ITC within the applicable period. rows.summary:
Section 16(4) of the CGST Act sets a hard time bar on claiming input tax credit (ITC): a registered person generally cannot take ITC on invoices or debit notes after **30 November following the end of the relevant financial year** or after the **date the annual return is filed**, whichever comes earlier. The document explains that this was changed from the earlier deadline tied to the **September return**, and that the new 30 November cutoff applies **from 1 October 2022**. For compliance purposes, this means the last date is not fixed only by the calendar; if the annual return is filed earlier, the credit deadline moves up to that filing date, so businesses need to monitor both dates continuously.

A key point is that **timeliness and eligibility are separate tests**: meeting the Section 16(4) deadline does not itself prove the credit is substantively allowable, and a credit can still be disallowed if the underlying conditions for ITC are not met. The article also highlights that this deadline specifically covers **invoices and debit notes**, so companies must track both types of documents when reconciling ITC. Because the cut-off is absolute, the practical recommendation is to reconcile purchase records, GST returns/data, supplier reporting, debit notes, and any reversals well before the final date rather than waiting until the end of November.

The document gives special attention to the **annual return**, because filing it before 30 November can shorten the claim window even though the statutory outside date remains 30 November. It also discusses **debit notes** separately, confirming that they are subject to the same timing discipline and must be accounted for in the ITC clock. In addition, it addresses **reverse-charge transactions**, including supplies from **unregistered persons**, and notes guidance under **CBIC Circular No. 211/5/2024-GST**, which affects how the Section 16(4) deadline should be applied in that context.

Finally, the article notes two retrospective relief provisions introduced in 2024: **Section 16(5)** and **Section 16(6)**. These provide relief for **specified earlier financial years** and for cases where registrations were **cancelled and later restored**, allowing ITC claims in circumstances that would otherwise have been blocked by the ordinary deadline. It also distinguishes between a **fresh ITC claim** and the **re-availment of credit that was previously reversed**, which compliance teams should track separately because the legal treatment may differ. The overall compliance takeaway is that businesses should maintain documented evidence of when credit first became eligible and when it was actually availed, and should actively monitor the statutory deadline and annual-return date to avoid permanent loss of credit.

rows.title: Income Tax | Capital Reduction Cannot Be Taxed as Buyback Under Section 115QA: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: Summary: In normal course of business, a company may cancel its shares for various reasons such as capital reduction, buyback, forfeiture of shares etc. The tax authority closely examines any such cancellation of shares to the extent that it does not amount to evasion of tax. But what if the tax authority itself mis-interpret the mode of cancellation of share and applies wrong law. Here is one such incident where the tax authority recharacterized the cancellation of share done through the Capital Reduction scheme as Buyback. In the case of Seaview Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT (ITAT Delhi), ITA Nos. 2621 & 2719/Del/2024, Pronounced on 8 July 2026, one of the main issue before the tribunal was to clear the confusion regarding the whether Capital reduction is same as buyback? The tribunal held that capital reduction cannot be treated as buyback under Section 115QA. Unlike buyback, capital reduction directly extinguishes shares pursuant to a statutory scheme, without purchasing them back from shareholders. The 2016 amendment which widened the scope of transaction under buyback did not change the nature of distinction. Table of Contents▸ Background Capital Reduction Buyback of shares Point of Confusion Analysis Computation under Rule 40BB and the prevention of Double taxation Conclusion Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Background The assessee, Seaview Developers Pvt. Ltd., is engaged in the business of developing real estate in SEZ in Noida, Uttar Pradesh. The assessee Company had cancelled 36,768 shares of BREP IV for the purpose of Capital reduction. BREP India Office Holdings IV Pte. Ltd. (BREP IV) is a Singapore-incorporated company and a tax resident of Singapore that held shares in the assessee company. The Singaporean Company was remitted ₹4,74,98,74,080 upon the cancellation of shares. The tax treatment of the amount received by BREP IV is as follows: Particulars Amount (₹) Total amount received on cancellation of shares 4,74,98,74
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi in **Seaview Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT (ITA Nos. 2621 & 2719/Del/2024, pronounced 8 July 2026)** held that a **capital reduction resulting in cancellation of shares cannot be taxed as a buyback under Section 115QA** merely because shares were cancelled and money was paid out to the shareholder. The assessee, a real estate developer in Noida SEZ, had cancelled **36,768 shares** held by **BREP India Office Holdings IV Pte. Ltd. (BREP IV)**, a **Singapore tax resident**, in a capital reduction scheme and remitted **₹4,74,98,74,080** to that shareholder. The tax authority attempted to recharacterize this transaction as a buyback and apply the buyback tax regime, but the tribunal rejected that approach.  

The tribunal’s key finding was that **capital reduction and buyback are legally distinct**: in a capital reduction, the company **extinguishes shares pursuant to a statutory scheme**, whereas a buyback involves the company **purchasing shares back from shareholders**. The tribunal emphasized that even though the **2016 amendment broadened the scope of transactions covered under buyback**, it **did not erase the fundamental legal distinction** between the two mechanisms or allow every share cancellation with payout to be taxed as buyback.  

For compliance purposes, the practical implication is that companies implementing **capital reduction schemes** should not automatically assume Section 115QA buyback tax applies; the tax treatment depends on the **legal form and mechanics of the transaction**, not just the economic outcome. The ruling is particularly relevant where a foreign shareholder receives consideration on cancellation of shares, because the tax authority may scrutinize whether the payment is a disguised distribution or an actual capital reduction. Companies should maintain documentation showing that the cancellation was undertaken under a valid **capital reduction process** and not through a share repurchase mechanism, to avoid incorrect buyback characterization and potential disputes over tax computation.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Transactions Without Consideration Treated as Deemed Supplies Under GST
rows.desc: Summary: GST generally applies to supplies of goods or services made for consideration in the course or furtherance of business, but the CGST Act specifically brings certain transactions without consideration within the scope of supply. Section 7(1)(c), read with Schedule I, covers specified activities including permanent transfer or disposal of business assets where input tax credit has been availed, supplies between related or distinct persons in the course or furtherance of business, specified principal-agent transactions, and import of services from related persons or overseas establishments for business purposes. The existence of a deemed supply must be distinguished from its valuation: a transaction must first qualify as a supply before valuation provisions such as Rule 28 become relevant. This distinction assumes particular significance for intra-group arrangements and corporate guarantees. CBIC Circular Nos. 204/16/2023-GST and 225/19/2024-GST address the taxability and valuation of personal and corporate guarantees, while Rule 28(2) provides a specific valuation mechanism in specified corporate guarantee cases. The Gujarat High Court’s decision in Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India further examines the GST treatment of corporate guarantees. Businesses should therefore assess the nature of the transaction, relationship between the parties, business purpose, applicable Schedule I entry and valuation provisions rather than assuming that the absence of a sale or monetary consideration necessarily takes a transaction outside GST. Supplies Between Related or Distinct Persons 3. Principal-Agent Transactions 4. Import of Services from Related Persons or Overseas Establishments Valuation of Deemed Supplies Corporate Guarantees: A Contemporary Development Critical Analysis: Does “No Sale” Mean “No GST”? Practical
rows.summary:
This document explains that GST can apply even where there is no monetary consideration, because section 7(1)(c) of the CGST Act, read with Schedule I, deems certain transactions to be “supplies” for GST purposes. The key point for compliance is that a transaction must first fall within one of the Schedule I deeming categories before valuation rules are even considered; in other words, you cannot assume “no sale” or “no consideration” means “no GST.” The deemed-supply categories highlighted are: permanent transfer or disposal of business assets on which input tax credit has been availed; supplies between related persons or distinct persons when made in the course or furtherance of business; specified principal-agent transactions; and imports of services from related persons or from overseas establishments for business purposes.

The document emphasizes that intra-group and cross-border business arrangements need careful review because they often trigger these deemed-supply rules. It specifically notes that supply between related or distinct persons can be taxable even without payment, and that imports of services from related persons or foreign establishments for business use can also be treated as supplies. Businesses must therefore test each arrangement against the relevant Schedule I entry, the business-purpose requirement, and the relationship between the parties, rather than relying only on whether an invoice or cash consideration exists.

A major focus is the distinction between whether a transaction is taxable as a supply and how it should be valued. Valuation provisions such as Rule 28 only come into play after a transaction is first established to be a supply under Schedule I. The document flags this as especially important for intra-group transactions and corporate guarantees, where valuation issues are often contested only after supply status is determined.

For corporate and personal guarantees, the document points to CBIC Circular No. 204/16/2023-GST and CBIC Circular No. 225/19/2024-GST, which address their taxability and valuation. It also notes that Rule 28(2) provides a specific valuation mechanism in certain corporate guarantee cases, indicating that businesses issuing or receiving corporate guarantees within a group must check both whether GST is triggered and, if so, whether the special valuation rule applies. The Gujarat High Court’s decision in Torrent Power Ltd. v. Union of India is identified as further guidance on the GST treatment of corporate guarantees, reinforcing that this area is legally active and should be monitored closely.

The practical compliance message is that companies should review asset transfers, intercompany charges, principal-agent structures, service imports, and guarantee arrangements under both the deeming provisions and the valuation rules. The document does not announce a new effective date or filing deadline, but it does indicate that existing statutory and circular-based rules must be applied carefully now, with particular attention to whether Schedule I applies before concluding that a transaction falls outside GST.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Trademark Opposition in India: Step-by-Step Guide
rows.desc: Summary: Trademark opposition is the statutory mechanism through which a third party can challenge a trademark application after its advertisement or re-advertisement in the Trade Marks Journal but before registration. Governed principally by Section 21 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Rules 42 to 51 of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017, the process permits “any person” with legally sustainable grounds to oppose registration. Common grounds include similarity with an earlier trademark, prior use, lack of distinctive character, descriptiveness, likelihood of consumer confusion, protection of well-known marks, passing-off rights and bad-faith adoption. A Notice of Opposition in Form TM-O must generally be filed within four months from publication or re-publication. The applicant then has two months from receipt of the opposition to submit a counterstatement, after which the proceeding moves through evidence by the opponent, evidence by the applicant, reply evidence and, where required, a hearing before the Registrar. Documentary proof of prior adoption, use, reputation and goodwill can be crucial. Opposition is also available to an earlier user of an unregistered trademark where sufficient rights can be established. Businesses should therefore monitor the Trade Marks Journal, preserve contemporaneous evidence of trademark use and carefully track procedural deadlines throughout opposition proceedings. Trademark Objection and Trademark Opposition: Understanding the Difference Grounds for Filing a Trademark Opposition Similarity With an Earlier Trademark Prior Use of the Trademark Lack of Distinctive Character Descriptive Trademark Likelihood of Confusion Among Consumers Protection of Well-Known Trademarks Passing Off Rights Bad Faith Adoption Process of Trademark Opposition in India S
rows.summary:
Trademark opposition in India is a pre-registration challenge that allows “any person” with legally sustainable grounds to oppose a trademark application after it is advertised or re-advertised in the Trade Marks Journal but before the mark is registered. The process is governed principally by Section 21 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Rules 42 to 51 of the Trade Marks Rules, 2017, and it is available not only to owners of earlier registered marks but also to earlier users of unregistered marks if they can establish sufficient rights. The document emphasizes that the opposition must be filed using Notice of Opposition in Form TM-O, generally within four months from the date of publication or re-publication in the Journal.

The grounds described as commonly used in opposition proceedings are conflict with an earlier trademark, prior use, lack of distinctive character, descriptiveness, likelihood of consumer confusion, protection of well-known marks, passing off, and bad-faith adoption. For compliance purposes, the practical significance is that an application may be blocked before registration if a third party can show prior rights, market reputation, goodwill, or likely confusion, and the business should expect that documentary evidence of adoption, use, reputation, and goodwill will be critical in defending or pursuing an opposition. The document also notes that businesses should monitor the Trade Marks Journal continuously so they can identify potentially conflicting applications within the opposition window and preserve contemporaneous evidence of their own trademark use.

Once a Notice of Opposition is filed, the applicant has two months from receipt of the opposition to file a counterstatement. If the applicant does not respond within that period, the proceeding continues under the opposition framework rather than moving directly to registration; the process then proceeds through evidence from the opponent, evidence from the applicant, reply evidence, and, where necessary, a hearing before the Registrar. The document does not specify any special filing fee, but it does make clear that the procedural deadlines are strict and that failure to track them can materially affect rights. For a corporate compliance team, the key operational takeaway is to maintain a docketing process for Trade Marks Journal monitoring, deadline tracking for the four-month opposition period and two-month counterstatement period, and retention of proof of trademark use and reputation in anticipation of either asserting or defending opposition proceedings.

rows.title: SEBI | Non-Connected Person Can Still Be Insider Through UPSI Possession: SEBI
rows.desc: Summary: Under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, a person can be an “insider” through two independent routes: by being a connected person or by possessing or having access to unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI). The distinction assumes particular importance in acquisitions, mergers and open offers where the relevant UPSI may originate from an acquirer or investor rather than the listed target company. The SEBI order in the matter of Religare Enterprises Limited illustrates this distinction. SEBI observed that UPSI concerning the impending open offer originated from the Burman Group, the acquirer, rather than REL. The noticee’s position as Executive Chairperson and key managerial personnel of REL was not, by itself, treated as sufficient to make her a connected person in relation to that particular UPSI. Nevertheless, she was held to be an insider under the second limb of Regulation 2(1)(g) on the basis of possession of UPSI. The classification also affects the evidentiary burden under Regulation 4(2): for a connected person, the onus of establishing absence of possession lies on that person, while in other cases SEBI bears the onus of establishing possession. Thus, a person who is neither a connected person nor a designated person may still qualify as an insider if possession of, or access to, the specific UPSI is established. The document explains that under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, “insider” status arises through **two independent routes**: a person is an insider if they are either a **connected person** or if they **possess or have access to unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI)**. This distinction is especially important in **mergers, acquisitions, and open offers**, where the relevant UPSI may come not from the listed target company but from the **acquirer or investor** involved in the transaction.

Using the **Religare Enterprises Limited (REL)** matter as the example, SEBI found that the UPSI relating to the impending open offer **originated from the Burman Group, the acquirer**, rather than from REL itself. The noticee’s status as **Executive Chairperson and key managerial personnel of REL** was **not enough, by itself, to make her a connected person in relation to that specific UPSI**. Even so, she was still treated as an **insider under the second limb of Regulation 2(1)(g)** because she was found to have **possession of UPSI**.

The summary also highlights an important **evidentiary burden** point under **Regulation 4(2)**. Where a person is a **connected person**, the burden is on that person to prove that they **did not possess the UPSI**. In cases where the person is **not** a connected person, SEBI must instead prove that the person **did possess or had access to the UPSI**. As a result, a person who is **neither a connected person nor a designated person** can still be treated as an insider if SEBI establishes possession of the relevant UPSI.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that companies should not assume insider-risk analysis ends with formal titles, designation, or employment status. In transaction-sensitive situations, especially where UPSI is generated outside the listed company, compliance teams should assess **who had access to the specific transaction information**, maintain strict information barriers, and document access and sharing carefully because insider classification can attach even without a formal connection to the listed issuer.

rows.title: Income Tax | 24-Hour Mistake That Could Cost Your Business Millions: Avoiding EPF Trap

Employee contributions covered by Section 36(1)(va), read with Section 2(24)(x) of the Income Tax Act, must be deposited within the due date prescribed under the relevant welfare legislation; depositing them before the due date for filing the income-tax return does not bring them within Section 43B. The Court emphasized the distinct character of employees’ contributions as amounts belonging to employees and held in trust by the employer. The practical consequence is significant for businesses: delays in remitting employee PF/ESI contributions can result in denial of the corresponding income-tax deduction even where the amount is subsequently deposited before filing the return. Businesses should therefore segregate employee statutory deductions from ordinary payables, maintain internal deadlines comfortably before the statutory due date, and configure payroll and accounting systems to identify and remit these amounts promptly. But you breathe easy—you paid it completely before filing your Income Tax Return (ITR). In your mind, you are fully compliant. A year later, you receive a notice from the Income Tax Department. They have disallowed the entire amount of the employee contributions and added it straight to your company’s t
rows.summary:
The document explains the Supreme Court’s ruling in **Checkmate Services Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT**, which clarified a critical tax-compliance distinction between **an employer’s own welfare-fund contributions** and **employee contributions deducted from salaries** for funds such as **EPF and ESI**. The Court held that employee contributions fall under **Section 36(1)(va)** read with **Section 2(24)(x)** of the Income Tax Act and are treated as amounts **belonging to employees and held in trust by the employer**; therefore, they must be deposited **within the due date prescribed under the applicable welfare law**. For EPF/ESI, that means the relevant statutory deadline controls, and **paying the amount before the income-tax return filing deadline is not enough** to preserve the deduction under **Section 43B**.

The practical compliance impact is that if a business remits employee PF/ESI deductions **after the welfare-law due date**, the Income Tax Department can **deny the corresponding income-tax deduction**, even if the money is later deposited before the ITR is filed. The document emphasizes that this can materially increase taxable income and tax liability for employers, creating a potentially significant financial exposure if payroll remittances are delayed even by a few days. The issue affects any employer that deducts statutory employee contributions from wages and is therefore not limited to a particular industry or company size.

The compliance guidance is to **separate employee statutory deductions from ordinary payables**, ensure **internal remittance deadlines are set earlier than the legal due date**, and configure payroll/accounting systems so these amounts are identified, tracked, and paid promptly. In other words, businesses should not treat employee PF/ESI deductions as flexible cash-flow items; they need dedicated controls to prevent late deposit risk. The document’s core message is that the company’s tax deduction depends on **timely deposit under the relevant welfare statute**, not merely eventual payment before tax return filing.

The section permits a meeting to be called at shorter notice if the prescribed consent of members is obtained. But shorter notice does not automatically dispense with the proxy requirements. The document explains that a General Meeting of a company normally must be given **21 clear days’ notice under Section 101(1) of the Companies Act, 2013**, but it can be convened on **shorter notice if the required member consent is obtained**. However, the key compliance point is that **shorter notice does not automatically waive proxy rights or proxy filing deadlines**: Section 105(1) still gives eligible members the right to appoint a proxy, and **Section 105(4)**, as reinforced by **Para 6.6.1 of SS-2**, requires the proxy instrument to be deposited **at least 48 hours before the meeting**.

The article then addresses the practical issue of whether a **Board Meeting and a General Meeting can be held on the same day**. It states that if the company has obtained only the **prescribed shorter-notice consent from 95% of the members**, the proxy requirements still remain in force, which makes an immediate same-day General Meeting after a Board Meeting problematic because the 48-hour proxy deposit window cannot be satisfied. In other words, **95% consent to shorter notice is not enough by itself to eliminate the proxy procedural requirements**.

The document notes an important exception: **where all members entitled to vote consent to the shorter notice**, the ICSI Guidance Note on General Meetings says the proxy requirements **need not be complied with**. On that basis, a **Board Meeting and General Meeting may be held on the same day**, provided all other applicable legal and procedural requirements are also met. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is to verify not just that shorter-notice consent exists, but whether it is **only 95% consent or unanimous consent**, because that distinction determines whether same-day meetings are procedurally permissible under the guidance discussed.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Exemptions: Relief for Taxpayers and Their Impact on the Tax System
rows.desc: Summary: GST exemptions are an important policy tool, but their economic effect can differ substantially from the headline removal of tax. The distinction between an exempt supply and a zero-rated supply is particularly important because an ordinary exemption generally removes output GST while restricting the supplier’s ability to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC), potentially embedding tax costs into prices. This issue became significant after the 56th GST Council’s September 2025 reforms and Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate), which exempted specified individual life and health insurance services from GST from 22 September 2025. The article examines the statutory exemption powers under Section 11 of the CGST Act and Section 6 of the IGST Act, together with the ITC reversal implications under Section 18(4) and Rule 44. It also traces Supreme Court jurisprudence governing interpretation of exemptions, including Sun Export Corporation, Dilip Kumar & Co., Ambay Cements, Hari Chand Shri Gopal, Mother Superior Adoration Convent and Wood Papers. The practical discussion considers insurance pricing, blocked ITC, transition compliance and anti-profiteering enforcement. The Supreme Court’s decision in State of Karnataka v. Taghar Vasudeva Ambrish provides a second illustration of exemption disputes, showing how the scope and purpose of apparently simple exemption entries can generate prolonged litigation. Table of Contents▸ Introduction Legal Framework The statutory source of the power How courts read exemption notifications Contemporary and Practical Analysis The insurance exemption in practice A second illustration: the hostel accommodation dispute Critical Discussion Conclusion and Suggestions Bibliography Statutes and Rules Notifications Table of Cases Reports and Other Sources Show all 14 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction If the government removes GST from your insurance premium, does your bill drop by exactly 18
rows.summary:
This document explains that GST exemptions can reduce tax on the invoice without necessarily reducing the underlying tax burden in the supply chain, because an exemption typically removes output GST but also prevents the supplier from claiming input tax credit (ITC). The specific regulatory change highlighted is Notification No. 16/2025-Central Tax (Rate), issued after the 56th GST Council’s September 2025 reforms, which exempted specified individual life and health insurance services from GST effective 22 September 2025. For compliance purposes, the key issue is that insurers and other affected suppliers must treat these supplies as exempt rather than zero-rated: that means no GST should be charged on the covered insurance premiums, but ITC linked to exempt supplies may need to be reversed under Section 18(4) of the CGST Act and Rule 44, which can create embedded tax costs that may affect pricing and margin calculations.

The article also states that the power to grant exemptions comes from Section 11 of the CGST Act and Section 6 of the IGST Act, and that the legal effect of an exemption depends on how the notification is drafted and interpreted by courts. It emphasizes that courts generally construe exemption entries carefully, and it reviews Supreme Court cases such as Sun Export Corporation, Dilip Kumar & Co., Ambay Cements, Hari Chand Shri Gopal, Mother Superior Adoration Convent, and Wood Papers to show that disputes often turn on the exact scope of the exemption language. The document further notes that the Supreme Court’s decision in State of Karnataka v. Taghar Vasudeva Ambrish is an additional example of how exemption wording can lead to extended litigation over whether a supply falls within the exemption.

From a practical compliance standpoint, the document flags transition issues for insurers and related businesses following the September 2025 change, including pricing adjustments, ITC reversal treatment, and anti-profiteering scrutiny if the tax reduction is not passed through appropriately. In short, any entity providing the specified individual life or health insurance services from 22 September 2025 must stop charging GST on those exempt supplies, reassess ITC eligibility and reversals under the CGST rules, and ensure billing, accounting, and pricing systems reflect the change correctly.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Blocked Credits under GST: Why Some Business Expenses Do Not Qualify for ITC
rows.desc: Summary: Input Tax Credit (ITC) is a fundamental feature of GST, but GST paid on every legitimate business expense is not necessarily available as credit. Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 establishes the general entitlement to ITC, subject to statutory conditions, while Section 17(5) specifically blocks credit for prescribed categories of goods and services. Major areas include specified motor vehicles, food and catering, certain employee benefits, club and fitness memberships, vacation travel benefits, construction of immovable property, goods lost, stolen, destroyed or written off, gifts and free samples, personal consumption and specified CSR expenditure. Several blocked-credit provisions contain exceptions, making transaction-specific examination essential. Construction-related ITC has generated significant litigation, particularly in Chief Commissioner of Central Goods and Service Tax v. M/s Safari Retreats Private Limited, where the Supreme Court examined Section 17(5)(c) and (d) and the expression “plant or machinery.” The subsequent legislative amendment replacing “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery” in Section 17(5)(d), retrospectively from 1 July 2017, is also significant. Businesses must further distinguish permanently blocked credit from ITC reversals and correctly report ineligible credits in GST returns. Invoice-level review, documentation of statutory exceptions, reconciliations and monitoring amendments, CBIC circulars and judicial developments are therefore important for avoiding incorrect ITC claims.
