Construction and Immovable Property VI. Safari Retreats: Judicial Development VII. Legislative Development After Safari Retreats VIII. Lost, Stolen, Destroyed or Written-Off Goods IX. Gifts and Free Samples X. Personal Consumption XI. CSR Expenditure XII. Blocked Credit and Revers
rows.summary:
This document explains that although Input Tax Credit (ITC) is generally available under Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017 for GST paid on business expenses, Section 17(5) creates a list of permanently blocked credits that businesses cannot claim, even if the expense is otherwise business-related. The blocked categories specifically discussed are GST on certain motor vehicles, food and catering, employee welfare/perquisites, club and fitness memberships, vacation travel benefits, construction of immovable property, goods that are lost, stolen, destroyed, or written off, gifts and free samples, personal consumption, and specified CSR expenditure. A compliance team should treat these items as transaction-sensitive rather than assume blanket eligibility, because several of the blocked-credit rules have statutory exceptions that may permit credit only in narrowly defined cases.

A major compliance focus is construction-related ITC, which has been heavily litigated. The Supreme Court’s decision in Chief Commissioner of Central Goods and Service Tax v. M/s Safari Retreats Private Limited examined the blocked-credit rules in Section 17(5)(c) and (d), including the meaning of “plant or machinery.” The document notes that the legislature later amended Section 17(5)(d) by replacing “plant or machinery” with “plant and machinery,” and made that amendment retrospective from 1 July 2017. That retrospective change is significant for historical tax positions and open disputes, so businesses with construction, real estate, or asset-development activities should reassess prior ITC claims and reversals in light of the amended wording and the Safari Retreats line of cases.

The document also draws an important distinction between permanently blocked credit and ITC reversals, which must not be confused in GST accounting and return filing. Businesses are expected to identify ineligible credits at the invoice level, maintain documentation supporting any claimed exception, reconcile blocked-credit items regularly, and monitor changes in law, CBIC circulars, and judicial developments to avoid incorrect ITC claims. In short, the compliance obligation is not just to exclude the obvious blocked items, but to actively review each expenditure against the statutory exceptions and update positions whenever the law or case law changes.

rows.title: Company Law | Managing Director Criminal Liability Depends on Statutory & Personal Involvement
rows.desc: Summary: A Managing Director (MD), defined under Section 2(54) of the Companies Act, 2013, exercises substantial managerial and administrative powers, but the position does not by itself result in unlimited criminal liability. An MD may face liability under the Companies Act, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Negotiable Instruments Act, SEBI Act, FEMA and labour laws where the relevant statutory provision creates liability or where personal involvement, knowledge, consent, connivance or negligence is established. Section 447 of the Companies Act provides punishment for fraud, while provisions relating to oppression and mismanagement may also have consequences for persons managing a company. Under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of a company’s business may incur vicarious liability for cheque dishonour under Section 138. Similar “in charge of and responsible for” principles arise under other corporate regulatory statutes. Judicial decisions including Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation and S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla emphasise the distinction between corporate wrongdoing and the personal criminal responsibility of directors and officers. The central principle discussed in the article is that an MD’s designation alone is insufficient to impose criminal responsibility; liability depends upon the applicable statutory framework and the allegations and evidence concerning the MD’s own role, knowledge, consent, authorisation, connivance or negligence. rows.summary:
The document explains that a Managing Director (MD), as defined in Section 2(54) of the Companies Act, 2013, has broad managerial and administrative authority, but the title alone does not automatically create criminal liability. Instead, whether an MD can be prosecuted depends on the specific statute involved and on proof of the MD’s own conduct — such as knowledge, consent, connivance, authorization, or negligence — rather than merely holding office. The article emphasizes that this principle applies across multiple legal regimes, including the Companies Act, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Negotiable Instruments Act, SEBI Act, FEMA, and labour laws.

Under the Companies Act, the document highlights Section 447, which punishes fraud, and notes that provisions relating to oppression and mismanagement can also have consequences for persons managing a company. In the criminal context, liability is not presumed from designation; instead, the applicable legal provision must itself impose responsibility or the evidence must show personal involvement in the wrongful act. The article cites judicial authority, including *Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation* and *S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla*, to reinforce the rule that corporate wrongdoing and personal criminal liability are separate inquiries and that officers are not vicariously liable unless the statute and pleadings support it.

For cheque dishonour matters, the document specifically points to Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, under which persons “in charge of and responsible for” the company’s business can face vicarious liability for an offence under Section 138. It states that similar “in charge of and responsible for” formulations appear in other corporate regulatory statutes, so compliance teams should not assume that an MD is automatically liable, but they should treat liability risk as fact-specific and documentation-dependent. The practical compliance takeaway is that enforcement exposure turns on the statute, the exact role played by the MD, and whether records and internal controls can show or rebut personal participation, approval, neglect, or direction in the alleged misconduct.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Audit Adjudication, Proper Officer Jurisdiction and Hearing Rights
rows.desc: Enforcement Notice, Audit Adjudication and Denial of Hearing under GST: A Legal Examination of Karnataka Proceedings Summary: The article examines jurisdiction, notice, audit adjudication and denial of personal hearing in GST proceedings, particularly in Karnataka. A GST demand cannot rest merely on uploading FORM GST DRC-01 or displaying hearing dates on the portal; the proceedings must comply with the statutory requirements governing the proper officer, jurisdiction, notice, evidence, service, hearing and reasoned adjudication. Section 2(91) makes assignment of the particular statutory function central to determining the proper officer, while Section 6 permits Centre-State cross-empowerment but restricts parallel proceedings on the same subject matter. FORM GST DRC-01 under Rule 142 is a summary and does not substitute the factual and evidentiary foundation necessary for an effective defence. Section 75(4) requires personal hearing where requested or where an adverse decision is contemplated, while Section 75(7) restricts adjudication to the amount and grounds specified in the notice. The article also examines the natural-justice implications of the same officer participating in audit and adjudication, including the Karnataka High Court ruling in Sumukha Ventures, and explains that Section 74A governs determination for FY 2024-25 onwards while Sections 73 and 74 continue to govern earlier periods as applicable. It concludes with practical objections and a draft representation seeking disclosure of jurisdictional authority, relied-upon documents, independent adjudication and an effective personal hearing. Table of Contents▸ Introduction The real controversy Statutory position Proper officer is not a loose expression Cross-empowerment is real, but not unlimited DRC-01 is not, by itself, a complete adjudication process Mandatory personal hearing Enforcement, audit and adjudication Section 74A: common errors Suggested objections in a taxpayer reply Preliminary objecti
rows.summary:
This document is a legal/compliance analysis of GST enforcement and adjudication practice in Karnataka, emphasizing that a GST demand is not valid merely because the department uploads FORM GST DRC-01 or posts hearing dates on the portal. It says the proceeding must still satisfy the statutory requirements for jurisdiction, notice, evidence, service, hearing, and reasoned adjudication, and that compliance teams should not treat DRC-01 as a substitute for the underlying factual and evidentiary record needed to defend the case.

A central point is jurisdiction: under Section 2(91), the “proper officer” is determined by the specific statutory function assigned to that officer, not by a general designation alone, and under Section 6 Centre-State cross-empowerment exists but does not allow parallel proceedings on the same subject matter. In practical terms, the recipient of a notice should verify whether the officer issuing the notice and/or adjudication order actually has authority over the relevant function and tax period, and should object if jurisdiction is unclear or improperly assumed.

The document also states that FORM GST DRC-01 under Rule 142 is only a summary of the proposed demand and does not by itself constitute a complete adjudication process. For compliance purposes, that means the taxpayer should demand disclosure of the specific documents, evidence, and calculations relied upon, because a bare summary on the portal does not provide the factual basis needed for an effective response.

On hearing rights, the document highlights Section 75(4), which requires a personal hearing if requested and also where an adverse decision is contemplated. It further notes Section 75(7), under which adjudication is limited to the amount and grounds stated in the notice, so the authority should not expand the dispute beyond what was originally alleged. The article also flags natural-justice concerns where the same officer who participated in the audit later adjudicates the matter, citing the Karnataka High Court ruling in Sumukha Ventures as part of that concern.

Finally, the document notes a period-based legal transition: Section 74A governs determination for FY 2024–25 onwards, while Sections 73 and 74 continue to apply to earlier periods as applicable. It closes with practical guidance for a taxpayer reply, including objections seeking disclosure of the jurisdictional basis, production of relied-upon records, adjudication by an independent officer, and a meaningful personal hearing before any adverse order is passed.

rows.title: Income Tax | GST Registration Beyond Turnover: CTP, NRTP and Mandatory Registration Cases
rows.desc: Beyond Turnover Casual Taxable Persons, Non-Residents And Other Mandatory GST Registrations Summary: GST registration under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 is not merely a turnover-based requirement. Although Section 22 provides the general threshold-based framework, Sections 23 and 24 significantly affect the analysis by identifying persons who may not be liable to registration and categories for whom registration can arise because of their legal status, activity or statutory role. Casual Taxable Persons and Non-Resident Taxable Persons illustrate this distinction particularly clearly: temporary or cross-border business activity may attract specialised registration procedures, advance-tax requirements and limited registration validity even though the ordinary turnover analysis may not adequately address the situation. Similar issues arise for inter-State suppliers, persons liable under reverse charge, persons covered by Section 9(5), TDS deductors, agents, Input Service Distributors, e-commerce participants and specified cross-border digital suppliers. The registration framework has also become increasingly technology-driven, including risk-based and simplified mechanisms introduced through amendments to the Rules. Consequently, taxpayers should begin with the facts and legal classification of their activities, read Sections 22, 23 and 24 together, verify applicable Rules and notifications, and only then determine the registration requirement. Turnover remains important, but it is only one component of the wider GST registration architecture. Table of Contents▸ Abstract Keywords PART I – INTRODUCTION 1. The Question That Looks Simple but Is Not 2. A Simple Illustration: The Five-Day Exhibition 3. Why Registration Matters 4. Objectives of This Blog PART II – LEGAL FRAMEWORK 5. Section 22: The General Threshold Rule 6. Section 23: Persons Not Liable in Specified Circumstances 7. Section 24: Compulsory Registration in Specified Cases 8. Casual Taxable Per
rows.summary:
This document explains that GST registration under the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 is not determined by turnover alone, even though Section 22 sets the general threshold-based rule. The key compliance point is that Sections 23 and 24 can override or bypass the ordinary threshold analysis: Section 23 identifies persons who are not liable to registration in specified circumstances, while Section 24 lists categories that must register compulsorily because of their legal status or type of activity, regardless of turnover. For a compliance team, this means the first step is not to calculate turnover, but to classify the entity’s activities and status under Sections 22, 23, and 24 together, then check the relevant Rules and notifications before deciding whether registration is required.

The document highlights Casual Taxable Persons and Non-Resident Taxable Persons as the clearest examples of special registration treatment. Even temporary, event-based, or cross-border business activity may trigger GST registration through specialised procedures, including advance tax/payment requirements and registration that is limited in duration, even where an ordinary turnover review would not obviously require registration. The “five-day exhibition” illustration is specifically mentioned as a way of showing that short-term activity can still create registration obligations, so compliance teams should treat temporary India-facing supply arrangements, exhibitions, fairs, or similar short-duration operations as potential GST registration events.

It also states that several other categories may require mandatory registration beyond normal turnover analysis, including inter-State suppliers, persons liable to pay tax under reverse charge, persons covered under Section 9(5), Tax Deductors at Source (TDS deductors), agents, Input Service Distributors, e-commerce participants, and specified cross-border digital suppliers. These categories are referenced as examples of statutory roles or supply models that can independently create registration obligations. The compliance implication is that business model, supply chain position, and tax-payment mechanism can matter more than revenue level, and the entity may need to register even if sales are below the usual threshold.

The document further notes that the GST registration framework has become increasingly technology-driven, with risk-based and simplified mechanisms introduced through amendments to the Rules. It does not give a specific filing deadline or numeric threshold in the excerpt provided, but it emphasizes that the applicable legal analysis must account for current Rules and notifications, not just the statutory text. Overall, the document’s message for compliance officers is that turnover remains relevant, but it is only one part of a broader registration architecture, and entities engaged in special-status, temporary, non-resident, inter-State, reverse-charge, e-commerce, or digital cross-border activities should be reviewed proactively for immediate registration obligations.

rows.summary:
The Rajasthan Authority for Advance Ruling held that **fresh psyllium seeds (isabgol)** proposed to be purchased by RUKHM Industries Limited are **not exempt from GST** and are instead **taxable at 5% GST**. The applicant had planned to buy the seeds directly from farmers/cultivators through **APMC/KUMS auctions**, or from other traders, and to **store them in godowns without any processing** such as drying, freezing, crushing, or similar treatment before resale. It argued that because the seeds were bought in natural form and remained agricultural produce, they should fall under **Entry No. 87 of Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17.09.2025** as fresh or chilled plant parts/seeds used primarily in perfumery, pharmacy, or insecticidal/fungicidal purposes, or alternatively under **Entry No. 77 for “all goods of seed quality.”**

The Authority rejected the exemption claim after examining the nature of psyllium, its classification under **Chapter 12** and **Tariff Item 12119013**, and the post-harvest handling of the goods. It emphasized that **threshing is a separate mechanical post-harvest operation**, and the material before it did not establish that the seeds would meet the legal meaning of **“fresh or chilled”** psyllium seeds for the claimed exemption. It also noted that the alternative exemption for **seed-quality goods** did not apply on the facts presented. As a result, the ruling means that entities procuring and trading psyllium seeds in this form should **not treat such purchases/resales as exempt**, and should instead apply **GST at 5%** to the supply.

On classification, the Authority applied the express terms of heading 4504, which cover agglomerated cork with or without a binding substance and impose no quantitative limit or
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan Authority for Advance Ruling held that Balasaria Agencies Pvt. Ltd.’s rubberised and agglomerated cork sheets are classifiable under tariff item **HSN 45041010** and therefore attract **GST at 5%** under **serial no. 310 of Schedule I to Notification No. 09/2025-Central Tax (Rate), dated 17 September 2025**. The applicant’s product was described as an industrial sheet made by mixing cork granules with polymer or rubber, chemicals and curatives, processing oil, and fillers, then moulding, curing, and cutting it into sheets; the declared composition was **30.99% cork and 42.47% polymer**. The applicant specifically asked whether the presence of rubber, the fact that the finished sheet may not contain “natural cork” as such, or the origin/source of the cork would prevent classification under heading 4504, and whether it could claim an inverted duty refund.

The jurisdictional officer argued that polymer was the predominant component and that the product should instead fall in **Chapter 40** and be taxed at **18%**. The AAR admitted the four questions relating to classification and rate because there was no pending classification proceeding that would bar the application: the applicant said the issue arose only as a verbal doubt during refund scrutiny, and the officer confirmed that no proceeding was pending. However, the AAR **rejected admission of the fifth question on inverted duty refund**, holding that refund entitlement is not one of the matters that can be decided under **Section 97(2)**.

On the merits, the Authority interpreted heading **4504** as expressly covering **agglomerated cork, with or without a binding substance**, and emphasized that the heading does **not impose any quantitative limit or requirement that cork be the predominant component**. Based on that wording, it concluded that the addition of rubber/polymer or other binding materials does not take the goods out of heading 4504 so long as they are agglomerated cork sheets of the kind described. For compliance purposes, the ruling confirms that businesses manufacturing or supplying similar rubberised/agglomerated cork sheets should assess them under **HSN 45041010** rather than treating the presence of polymer/rubber as decisive for Chapter 40 classification, and the ruling’s tax consequence is the **5% GST rate** under the cited notification.

rows.summary:
Mahesh Transport Company asked the Rajasthan AAR for a ruling on whether transportation services it proposed to provide to M/s Mahesh Transport Gujarat, described as another goods transport agency (GTA), would be exempt under Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) or instead taxable under Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate). The applicant said the arrangement involved coal transport between Gujarat and Rajasthan and that it issued consignment notes, and it relied on the GTA definition and the Gunesh Logistics decision to support the view that issuance of a consignment note is significant for GTA classification. The record also contained jurisdictional officer comments on the substance of the arrangement and a separate view that merely making vehicles available to another GTA could fall under the exemption for hiring a means of transport under Entry 22(b); however, those were submissions in the case, not the final ruling.

The AAR did not decide the GST exemption question on the merits. It noted that the Enforcement Wing had already carried out a search at the applicant’s premises on 07.01.2026 under Section 67(2), and that an investigation was pending. The enforcement report stated that the applicant had taken input tax credit on invoices for vehicles hired from others and was itself hiring out vehicles to other GTAs; the investigating authority viewed those outward hiring supplies as exempt and indicated that reversal of common credit under Rules 42 and 43 was being examined. Because the same issue was already pending before the department and had effectively been decided or was under active adjudication/investigation, the AAR rejected the advance ruling application rather than issuing a substantive exemption/taxability ruling.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the ruling does not create new substantive GST treatment for GTA-vs.-vehicle-hiring arrangements, but it does show that if a company is both availing ITC on hired vehicles and supplying vehicles/hiring services to other GTAs, the department may scrutinize whether those outward supplies are exempt and whether proportional ITC reversal under Rules 42/43 is required. The document also reflects that once an issue is already pending in investigation or has been taken up by the department, an advance ruling may be refused on that ground alone.

The excerpt shown begins the main rate table and establishes that **central tax applies to intra-State service supplies at the rates listed in the table**, subject to any conditions in the table’s last column. rows.summary:
This Rajasthan GST advance ruling concerns a joint venture, M/s MTS-EIEL (JV), that was awarded a works contract for a faecal sludge treatment plant under a Rajasthan Urban Infrastructure Development Project package, covering design, supply, construction, testing, trial run, commissioning, and five years of operation and maintenance. The key tax issue was the applicable GST rate for the works contract service as on **1 June 2022** under **Heading 9954, serial number 3(iii)(c)**, which covers a pipeline, conduit, or plant for water supply, water treatment, sewerage treatment, or disposal. The contract was for **Rs. 46,34,57,750**, including a **provisional sum of Rs. 2,11,00,000**; the tender was invited on **24 April 2022**, the bid was submitted on **28 June 2022**, the **Letter of Acceptance** was issued on **30 September 2022**, and the **Notice to Proceed** was issued on **28 November 2022**.

The applicant stated that it had priced the bid assuming **12% GST** (**6% CGST + 6% SGST**), but GST of **18%** was actually paid on work executed and invoiced after the rate change, resulting in an additional **6 percentage points** of tax burden. The jurisdictional officer’s comments indicated that the earlier applicable rate appeared to be **12%** and the later rate **18%**, but also noted that any contractual right to recover the increased tax from the counterparty was not something the advance ruling authority could decide. The Authority reviewed the application, contract papers, notification history, the officer’s report, and the hearing submissions.

For compliance purposes, the ruling makes clear that the advance ruling forum would not answer whether the applicant could contractually pass on or recover the extra **6%** from the customer, because that question falls outside **Section 97(2) of the CGST Act**. The practical issue for similar suppliers is that GST rate changes can materially affect project pricing and invoicing on long-running infrastructure contracts, but the tax authority will not, through advance ruling, adjudicate private contractual recovery disputes; that must be addressed through the contract terms and commercial arrangements.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Psyllium Seeds Not Fresh; 5% GST Applies: Rajasthan AAR

The Authority accepted the classification of Psyllium Seeds (Isabgol) under Tariff Item 12119013. It observed that the exemption notification must be construed strictly and that the burden of establishing fulfilment of the exemption conditions rests on the person claiming the exemption. On the facts, the Authority did not accept the applicant’s conte
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan AAR held that Psyllium Seeds (Isabgol) sold through the APMC at Nokha are correctly classifiable under Tariff Item 12119013, but they do **not** qualify for GST exemption under Entry No. 87 of Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17.09.2025 because that entry applies only to specified plants and plant parts, including seeds and fruits, when they are **“fresh or chilled.”** The applicant, M/s Santosh Devi Daga, argued that the seeds were brought by cultivators after harvesting and threshing and that no further processing such as drying, dehydration, freezing, grading, polishing, crushing, milling, roasting, chemical treatment, or similar treatment was carried out by the applicant; it also asked whether threshing should be treated merely as harvesting rather than processing or manufacture. The Authority accepted the tariff classification but rejected the exemption claim, reasoning that the exemption notification must be interpreted strictly and that the burden is on the claimant to prove all exemption conditions are met; on the facts presented, the seeds were not shown to be “fresh or chilled,” so the exemption was unavailable.  

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that traders/commission agents dealing in psyllium seeds (and similar goods covered by Heading 1211) cannot assume exemption merely because the goods are sold in an unprocessed form or because processing is limited to harvesting-related activity; the decisive test under this ruling is whether the goods satisfy the specific “fresh or chilled” condition in the exemption entry. The AAR expressly referred to Heading 1211, the HSN notes, Notification No. 09/2025-Central Tax (Rate), Notification No. 10/2025-Central Tax (Rate), CBIC FAQ F.No. 332/2/2017-TRU, and Circular No. 163/19/2021-GST dated 06.10.2021 in reaching its conclusion. There is no separate compliance deadline created by the ruling itself, but the cited exemption notification is dated 17.09.2025, and the ruling underscores that businesses claiming exemption must maintain evidence that the goods actually meet the notification’s specific condition at the time of supply.

Accordingly, Pine Bark Extract and Gra
rows.summary:
CAAR Mumbai held that Pine Bark Extract and Grape Seed Extract imported by M/s JESSP Chemicals are classifiable under Customs Tariff Heading 1302 as vegetable saps and extracts, not under the residuary Heading 2106. The ruling arose because the applicant imported these products as raw materials for nutraceutical manufacturers, while the jurisdictional Commissionerate argued that the extraction, concentration, purification, and in the case of grape seed extract, resin adsorption steps might take the goods out of Heading 1302.

In reaching its conclusion, CAAR reviewed the botanical origin of the products, the manufacturing steps, the HSN Explanatory Notes, and the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and related regulations. It found that both products are derived from plant material and are obtained through solvent-based extraction followed by filtration, concentration, drying, and in one case resin adsorption, but the record did not show any specialised purification or selective concentration/depletion of particular compounds beyond what would normally occur in extraction. On that basis, the Authority said the essential character of the goods remained that of vegetable extracts.

The ruling also rejected the attempt to classify the goods under Heading 2106 simply because they are used in nutraceutical formulations. CAAR emphasized that these imports were bulk single-ingredient botanical extracts/raw materials, not finished food preparations or dietary supplements ready for direct consumption, so their intended downstream use did not change tariff classification. For compliance purposes, importers of similar bulk plant-derived extracts should assess classification based on the nature and processing of the imported product itself, not solely on its eventual use in nutraceuticals; no specific effective date, deadline, or new filing procedure was stated in the excerpt.

rows.summary:
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) notified the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (Liquidation Process) (Fifth Amendment) Regulations, 2026** on **22 September 2026**, issued under **section 196(1)(aa) and (t) read with section 240 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016**. The amendment **takes effect on the date it is published in the Official Gazette**. It updates the **Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016**—the principal regulations originally notified on **15 December 2016** and last amended by the **Fourth Amendment Regulations, 2026** (notified **1 June 2026**).

The substantive change is to **regulation 31**, where the existing **sub-regulations (3) and (4)** are replaced with a new **sub-regulation (3)**. Under the revised rule, a **liquidator is now expressly permitted to modify an entry in the list of stakeholders if additional information comes to light that justifies the change**. This creates an ongoing accuracy obligation: the stakeholder list is no longer fixed once prepared, and liquidators must update it when new information warrants adjustment.

The amendment also adds a reporting requirement: **if the liquidator makes any such modification, the liquidator must inform the Adjudicating Authority within 30 days of making the change**. This requirement is directly relevant to insolvency professionals acting as liquidators and to entities whose claims or stakeholder status may be affected by updates to the liquidation stakeholder list. Compliance teams supporting liquidation matters should ensure that any newly discovered information that affects stakeholder entries is promptly evaluated, the list is amended where justified, and the Adjudicating Authority notification is sent within the 30-day window.

The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in trading rubber goods and allied items, had deposited about Rs.67.62 lakh during demonetisation and explained the source as cash sales and recovery from debtors. The AO considered Rs.57,32,048/- to represent unaccounted income introduced in the guise of cash sales, principally because cash sales were concentrated in October 2016 and up to 08.11.2016, there was no comparable history of cash sales, purchases had been made from a sister concern and the cash was retained instead of being deposited immediately. The AO accordingly invoked Section 69A read with Section 115BBE and the CIT(A) confirmed the addition. The assessee submitted that it maintained audited books comprising cash book, ledger, stock register, sale bills, purchase bills and vouchers; purchases had not been disputed; sales were made from available stock; VAT of Rs.3,25,178/- had been paid; and the sales disclosed in VAT returns were accepted by the Punjab State Sales Tax Department. The Tribunal observed that the cash sales constituted the foundation of the deposits and had already been credited to the profit and loss account and offered to tax. It found the
rows.summary:
This ITAT Amritsar ruling held that cash deposited during the demonetisation period cannot be taxed again under Section 69A where the underlying cash sales were already recorded in the regular books and accepted as genuine. The assessee, R. M. Sales Corporation, a partnership firm trading in rubber goods and allied items for AY 2017-18, had deposited about Rs. 67.62 lakh in cash during demonetisation and explained the source as cash sales and recoveries from debtors; the Assessing Officer treated Rs. 57,32,048 as unexplained money/income introduced as bogus cash sales, and the CIT(A) upheld the addition. The AO’s objections were that the cash sales were heavily concentrated in October 2016 and up to 08.11.2016, there was no comparable past history of such sales, purchases were from a sister concern, and the cash was not deposited immediately, so the AO invoked Section 69A along with Section 115BBE.  

The Tribunal deleted the addition after noting that the assessee maintained audited books including cash book, ledger, stock register, sale bills, purchase bills, and vouchers; the purchases were not disputed; sufficient stock was available to support the sales; and the sales had been disclosed in VAT returns and accepted by the Punjab State Sales Tax Department. It also accepted that VAT of Rs. 3,25,178 had been paid, and emphasized that the cash sales were already credited to the profit and loss account and offered to tax, so the same receipts could not be taxed again merely because the cash was later deposited in the bank during demonetisation.  

For compliance purposes, the practical lesson is that cash sales reflected in proper books, backed by stock records and sales tax/VAT reporting, should not be recharacterized as unexplained cash under Section 69A simply because they were deposited during demonetisation or because the timing appears unusual. However, the decision also shows the importance of contemporaneous documentation: audited books, stock reconciliation, sale invoices, purchase records, tax filings, and proof that the sales were actually reported in indirect tax returns. The case does not create a blanket safe harbor for all demonetisation deposits; it turns on the recorded nature of the sales, the acceptance of purchases/stock, and the fact that the receipts had already been recognized in income.

rows.title: Excise Duty | Buyer-Funded Tool Cost Must Be Amortised; Extended Period Rejected: CESTAT Chennai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13712 Case Name Sankar Sealing Systems Pvt. Ltd. Vs Commissioner of GST & Central Excise (CESTAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Chennai Upgrade to Premium to download. Vs Commissioner of GST & Central Excise (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: CESTAT Chennai held that the cost of tools such as jigs, fixtures, molds and dies, which were paid for by buyer-customers and used by the appellant for manufacturing components for those buyers, was required to be included in the cost of production and amortised for payment of Central Excise duty on the final products under Rule 6 of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000. The appellant, a manufacturer of aluminium and rubber gaskets, had manufactured tools for customers, collected their cost through excise invoices and retained the tools in its factory for manufacturing gaskets. The department alleged that the tool value was neither included in the cost of production nor amortised, resulting in a duty demand of Rs.7,85,993/- with interest and equal penalty. The appellant contended that duty had already been paid on the tools, that another levy would amount to double taxation, that Notification No.67/95-CE dated 16.03.1995 exempted tools captively used in manufacture and that the extended period under Section 11A(1) was unavailable. The Tribunal followed its decision in M/s Best Cast IT Ltd, which had considered Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai I Vs Mega Rubber Technologies Pvt Ltd and the Larger Bench decision in Mutual Industries Ltd Vs Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai. It held that whether the tools were manufactured in the appellant’s own factory or outsourced did not alter the valuation principle whe
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai held that when a manufacturer uses buyer-funded tools such as jigs, fixtures, molds, and dies to make goods for those buyers, the tool cost must be included in the assessable value of the final excisable products and amortized under Rule 6 of the Central Excise Valuation (Determination of Price of Excisable Goods) Rules, 2000. In this case, Sankar Sealing Systems Pvt. Ltd., which manufactured aluminium and rubber gaskets, had manufactured tools for customers, charged the customers for those tools through excise invoices, and kept the tools in its factory for use in producing the gaskets; the department treated the failure to spread that tool cost into the production cost of the final goods as a valuation shortfall. On that basis, the department raised a demand of Rs. 7,85,993, along with interest and an equal penalty.

The appellant argued that the tools had already suffered duty, that including them again in the gasket valuation would amount to double taxation, that Notification No. 67/95-CE dated 16.03.1995 exempted captively used tools, and that the extended limitation period under Section 11A(1) could not be invoked. The Tribunal rejected that defense and followed its earlier ruling in M/s Best Cast IT Ltd., which in turn relied on Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai I v. Mega Rubber Technologies Pvt. Ltd. and the Larger Bench decision in Mutual Industries Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise, Mumbai. The Tribunal specifically held that it made no difference, for valuation purposes, whether the tools were made in the assessee’s own factory or procured from outside; the relevant point was that the buyer-funded tools were used in manufacturing the final goods, so their value had to be amortised into the cost of production.

For compliance purposes, the decision means manufacturers cannot treat customer-paid tooling charges as outside the excise value of the finished goods merely because those tools were separately invoiced or duty was paid on the tools themselves. Where buyer-owned or buyer-funded tools are retained and used to manufacture final dutiable products, the tooling cost must be captured in the production cost and apportioned/amortised into the assessable value of the goods cleared. The Tribunal also upheld the revenue’s position on the demand despite the assessee’s limitation defense, so the case signals litigation risk not only on valuation but also on penalty and interest exposure where tooling has not been amortised correctly.

rows.summary:
The CESTAT Chennai held that Brakes India Private Limited’s undervaluation of job-worked automobile components returned to Wichitra Auto Ltd. was a bona fide, system-driven valuation error rather than a deliberate attempt to evade excise duty. The dispute arose after the parties changed, in July 2012, from the earlier job-work procedure to duty-paid clearances: BIPL first used manually computed values, but its system later generated cost data using only the bare material purchase cost plus BIPL’s own conversion cost and omitted the prior conversion cost already incurred by WAL, causing the assessable value to be understated. When the Department identified the discrepancy in February 2014, BIPL accepted the short payment and, before the show cause notice was issued, paid differential duty of Rs. 1,11,94,846 and interest of Rs. 13,10,440.  

Because the Tribunal found no wilful suppression or intent to evade, it held that the equivalent penalty under Section 11AC could not be sustained against BIPL. The Tribunal also accepted that the value error was inadvertent and that the adjudicating authority had failed to properly deal with the detailed affidavit from BIPL’s Vice President–Finance explaining the system failure. The Department had also denied WAL CENVAT credit on the differential duty reflected in BIPL’s supplementary invoice and imposed an equivalent penalty on WAL, but the Tribunal’s finding that the short payment resulted from a bona fide revenue-neutral valuation mistake undermines that penalty treatment as well. In compliance terms, the case is a reminder that automated valuation and billing systems for excise/job-work clearances must be configured to capture all relevant cost components—especially where processing has occurred at multiple stages—or companies risk duty short-payment disputes even if the error later appears revenue-neutral.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13710 Case Name Superintendent of Police (Rural) Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Mumbai Upgrade to Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Superintendent of Police (Rural) Vs Commissioner of Central Excise (CESTAT Mumbai) Summary: CESTAT Mumbai allowed the appeal of Superintendent of Police (Rural) against the order confirming service tax demand of Rs.3,19,421/- on charges collected for providing armed security guards to public sector banks, undertakings and government departments. The appellant, being part of the Maharashtra State Police force, was responsible for maintenance and enforcement of public law and order and provided armed security guards under Section 13 of the Police Act, 1861 by recovering the actual expenditure/cost. The issue before the Tribunal was whether this activity constituted taxable “security services” under the Finance Act, 1994. The Tribunal observed that the appellant was performing statutory duties and the amounts collected were deposited in the Government treasury. It relied upon Circular No.89/7/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006, under which charges collected by a sovereign/public authority for statutory functions are not liable to service tax where the functions constitute statutory and mandatory obligations, the fee is levied under the relevant law and the amount is deposited into the Government treasury. The Tribunal further relied upon the CESTAT decision in Dy. Commissioner of Police & Others Vs. CCE, Jaipur & Others, where the police department, being an agency of the State Government, was held not to be a person engaged in the business of running security services. It also referred to Mumbai Police Vs. Commissioner of Service Tax, Mumbai-I [2018-TIOL-1067-CESTAT-MUM], where
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai held that service tax was **not payable** on amounts collected by the Maharashtra State Police for providing **armed security guards** to public sector banks, undertakings, and government departments, because the activity was part of the police force’s **statutory public-duty functions** rather than a commercial “security service.” The demand that had been confirmed against the Superintendent of Police (Rural) was **Rs. 3,19,421**, and the Tribunal allowed the appeal, setting aside that tax demand.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the police department in this case was acting under **Section 13 of the Police Act, 1861**, performing responsibilities tied to maintenance and enforcement of law and order, and it recovered only the **actual expenditure/cost** of providing the guards. The Tribunal emphasized that the amounts collected were **deposited into the Government treasury**, which supported the conclusion that this was a sovereign/statutory function, not a taxable business activity. It relied on **CBEC Circular No. 89/7/2006-ST dated 18.12.2006**, which states that charges collected by a sovereign/public authority for statutory functions are not liable to service tax where: the function is a **statutory and mandatory obligation**, the fee is **levied under the relevant law**, and the amount is **credited to the Government treasury**.

The decision also followed earlier CESTAT rulings, including **Dy. Commissioner of Police & Others vs. CCE, Jaipur & Others** and **Mumbai Police vs. Commissioner of Service Tax, Mumbai-I [2018-TIOL-1067-CESTAT-MUM]**, reinforcing the principle that a police department is not “running security services” in a commercial sense when it provides security as part of government/statutory duties. Compliance teams should note that this ruling is relevant where a government authority or sovereign/public body is charging only cost recovery for a mandatory statutory function; in that setting, the service tax exposure may not arise. The document does **not** specify any prospective change in rate or filing deadline, but it does establish that the particular tax demand in this matter was unsustainable on these facts.

rows.title: Income Tax | BookMyShow Convenience Fee Not Subject to Section 194H TDS: ITAT Bangalore
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13708 Case Name Shanthala Enterprises Vs ITO (ITAT Bangalore) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Bangalore Upgrade to Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Shanthala Enterprises Vs ITO (ITAT Bangalore) Summary: ITAT Bangalore allowed the appeal of Shanthala Enterprises for AY 2018-19 and held that the dispute concerning TDS on convenience charges retained by Bigtree Entertainment Pvt. Ltd., operating an online ticket-booking platform, was squarely covered by the Coordinate Bench decision in Shri Srinivas Rudrappa vs. ITO. The assessee operated Veeresh Cinemas in Bangalore. Following a survey conducted on 30/10/2019 at Bigtree’s premises, the Department found that customers booking cinema tickets online paid the ticket price along with a transaction fee of Rs. 5 to 25/-. Bigtree subsequently remitted the ticket cost together with Rs. 3 to 5/- as the assessee’s share of the transaction fee, based on invoices raised biweekly by the assessee. The Assessing Officer considered the convenience charges retained by Bigtree as attracting TDS and consequently treated the assessee as being in default under sections 201(1) and 201(1A). The assessee relied on the Coordinate Bench ruling in Shri Srinivas Rudrappa vs. ITO, ITA Nos. 702 & 703/Bang/2022 dated 02/12/2022. In that decision, the Tribunal had held that transaction charges, service charges or convenience fees collected and retained by Bigtree from end users represented consideration for services provided to those end users and did not establish that Bigtree acted on behalf of theatre owners; consequently, section 194H was not applicable in such circumstances. The Tribunal observed that both the Assessing Officer and CIT(A) had failed to properly consider the earlier Coordinate Benc
rows.summary:
The ITAT Bangalore held in **Shanthala Enterprises v. ITO** that the **convenience fee/transaction charge retained by Bigtree Entertainment Pvt. Ltd. (BookMyShow)** on online cinema-ticket bookings was **not subject to TDS under section 194H** for **AY 2018-19**. The assessee, which operated **Veeresh Cinemas in Bangalore**, had been treated as an assessee in default under **sections 201(1) and 201(1A)** after a **survey on 30/10/2019** at Bigtree’s premises showed that customers paid the ticket price plus a **transaction fee of Rs. 5 to Rs. 25**, while Bigtree later remitted the ticket price plus only **Rs. 3 to Rs. 5** per ticket as the theatre’s share of the fee, based on **biweekly invoices** raised by the assessee. The Assessing Officer had concluded that the convenience charges retained by Bigtree attracted TDS and therefore sought to tax the assessee as non-compliant for failure to deduct tax.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal because the issue was already covered by its earlier coordinate-bench ruling in **Shri Srinivas Rudrappa v. ITO (ITA Nos. 702 & 703/Bang/2022, dated 02/12/2022)**. In that earlier decision, the Tribunal had held that the **transaction charges/service charges/convenience fees collected and retained by Bigtree from end users were consideration for services provided to the customers themselves**, and that this did **not** show Bigtree was acting as an agent on behalf of the theatre owners. On that reasoning, the Tribunal reaffirmed that **section 194H, which applies to commission or brokerage**, does not apply to the convenience fee arrangement in this BookMyShow model.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that, on the facts considered here, **the theatre owner was not required to deduct TDS under section 194H on the amount of convenience fee retained by Bigtree from the customer**; the Tribunal treated the retained fee as Bigtree’s own service revenue rather than commission paid by the theatre. The order specifically concerns the **online ticket-booking platform arrangement** and the **split between ticket price remittance and fee retention** described above, and it was decided in the context of **AY 2018-19**.

rows.title: Income Tax | No Section 194H TDS Where Collection Centres Retain Margin: Bombay HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 13707 Case Name CIT Vs Super Religare Laboratories Ltd. (Bombay High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Bombay High Court Upgrade to Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); CIT Vs Super Religare Laboratories Ltd. (Bombay High Court) Summary: The Bombay High Court considered Revenue’s challenge to an ITAT order concerning applicability of Section 194H of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to discounts allowed by Super Religare Laboratories Ltd. to third-party collection centres. The assessee provided laboratory and testing services through its own centres as well as third-party collection centres. Under the arrangement illustrated before the Court, a collection centre could charge a patient Rs.500 for a blood test, forward the sample to the assessee and pay the assessee Rs.400, retaining Rs.100 as its margin. The Revenue treated this difference as commission and contended that the assessee was required to deduct tax at source under Section 194H. The Assessing Officer consequently treated the assessee as a defaulter under Sections 201(1) and 201(1A). CIT(A) allowed the assessee’s appeal, and the ITAT affirmed that decision, relying upon the assessee’s own case for Assessment Year 2006-07 and holding that the relationship with collection centres was on a principal-to-principal basis rather than principal-agent basis. The High Court examined Section 194H from an additional and fundamental perspective. It noted that the statutory obligation applies to a person responsible for paying income by way of commission or brokerage and requires deduction when such income is credited or paid. Here, the assessee made no payment to the collection centres; instead, the collection centres collected money from patients, retained their margin and paid a reduced amount to the asses
rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court held that Section 194H TDS did **not** apply to the margin retained by third-party collection centres in the Super Religare Laboratories arrangement, because the assessee did not make any payment of “commission or brokerage” to those centres. In the facts before the Court, a collection centre collected **Rs. 500** from a patient for a blood test, sent the sample to the assessee, and remitted **Rs. 400** to the assessee while keeping **Rs. 100** as its own margin; the Revenue argued that this **Rs. 100** was commission on which the assessee should have deducted tax at source under Section 194H. The Assessing Officer had therefore treated the assessee as an assessee in default under **Sections 201(1) and 201(1A)**, but the CIT(A) and ITAT had both ruled for the assessee, with the ITAT emphasizing that the relationship with the collection centres was **principal-to-principal**, not principal-agent.

The High Court upheld that view and added an important statutory point: Section 194H applies only where a person is responsible for **paying** income by way of commission or brokerage and deducting tax when that income is **credited or paid**. Because the collection centres were not being paid commission by the assessee—and instead were themselves collecting the patient’s money, retaining their margin, and remitting the balance to the assessee—there was no TDS obligation on the assessee under Section 194H on that retained margin. For compliance purposes, the decision reinforces that where intermediaries or collection centres retain a spread from amounts they collect from customers and then remit the net amount, the key question is whether the payer is actually making a commission/brokerage payment or merely buying services on a principal-to-principal basis; absent a payment by the assessee to the intermediary, Section 194H should not be triggered on the intermediary’s retained margin.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs Broker Licence Revocation Unsustainable for Importer Misdeclaration: CESTAT Mumbai
rows.desc: CESTAT Mumbai sets aside Customs Broker licence revocation and security forfeiture but imposes ₹10,000 penalty for supervision failure.The post Customs Broker Licence Revocation Unsustainable for Impo
rows.summary:
The CESTAT Mumbai partly allowed the appeal of **Husain Kasam Mukadam & Sons**, holding that **revocation of the Customs Broker licence, forfeiture of the full security deposit, and the penalty imposed under the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018 (CBLR)** were not sustainable on the facts of the case. The matter arose from an import made by **M/s K.K. Traders, Satara**, which declared a consignment as **27,000 kg of “Raw Cashew Nuts in shell”** under **Bill of Entry No. 7580019 dated 21.02.2022**; after clearance at **JNCH, Nhava Sheva**, Pune Customs intercepted the container on specific intelligence and found that only **2,487 kg** matched the declared goods, while **24,753 kg** consisted of undeclared **broken cashew kernel / cashew baby bits**. The Tribunal accepted that the importer’s conduct amounted to misdeclaration and noted that the import violated the applicable trade restrictions because **DGFT Notification No. 08/2015-2020 dated 12.06.2019** had prescribed **minimum import prices for cashew kernels**, which the undeclared kernels effectively breached.  

For compliance purposes, the key finding is that the Tribunal did **not** attribute the import fraud to the Customs Broker: based on the investigation record and statements, the evidence pointed instead to the importer and **Shri Chetan Yadav of M/s Ninai Shipping Agency**, not to the Broker, and the goods had already undergone Customs examination at JNCH without the concealment being detected. On **Regulation 10(e)** of the CBLR, the Tribunal held that the Broker had filed the Bill of Entry **on the basis of the documents provided by the importer** and was not shown to have knowingly participated in the concealment or misdeclaration. The result is a reminder that while Customs can proceed harshly against importers for false declarations and prohibited/value-restricted imports, a Broker’s licence action requires evidence of the Broker’s own culpable involvement or failure beyond merely processing documents supplied by the client.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 115JB MAT Not Applicable to Kerala Electricity Board: Kerala HC
rows.desc: Kerala HC holds Section 115JB inapplicable to KSEB and rules electricity duty collected for State is outside Section 43B.The post Section 115JB MAT Not Applicable to Kerala Electricity Board: Kerala H
rows.summary:
The Kerala High Court held that Section 115JB’s minimum alternate tax regime did **not** apply to the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) for Assessment Years 2002-03 through 2005-06, and it allowed KSEB’s four appeals on that issue. The Court reasoned that although KSEB is treated as a “company” for income-tax purposes, it is **not** a company governed by the Companies Act, 1956, so it is not required to prepare its accounts or hold an annual general meeting in the manner contemplated by that Act. Section 115JB, however, depends on preparation of a profit and loss account in accordance with **Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act**, while KSEB must instead maintain accounts under **Section 69 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948** in the form prescribed by the Central Government and subject them to audit by the Comptroller and Auditor-General or an authorized person.  

In reaching this conclusion, the Court reviewed the legislative history of **Sections 115J, 115JA, and 115JB** and noted that the original Section 115J expressly excluded companies engaged in **generation or distribution of electricity**. Even though that explicit exclusion was not repeated in Section 115JA, the Court relied on **CBDT Circular No. 762 dated 18.02.1998**, which stated that power-generation and distribution companies were exempted from MAT so that infrastructure-development incentives would not be undermined. The Court treated the charging and computation provisions as an integrated code and held that because KSEB’s statutory accounting framework is fundamentally different from the Companies Act framework required by Section 115JB, the MAT mechanism could not be mechanically imposed on it.  

The judgment also dealt with a separate issue under **Section 43B** of the Income Tax Act, though the provided summary does not set out the specific adjustment amount or exact relief granted on that point. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that statutory electricity boards or similarly placed electricity-generation/distribution entities that are **not Companies Act companies** may have a defensible position against MAT under Section 115JB, especially where their accounts are prepared under a special statute rather than Schedule VI of the Companies Act. There are no new filing deadlines or procedural changes announced in the document itself; the ruling is a judicial interpretation of existing law applicable to the assessment years in question.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 54EC Deduction Allowed for Investments Across Two Financial Years: ITAT Bangalore
rows.desc: ITAT Bangalore allows Section 54EC deduction where investments were made across two financial years within six months of property transfers.The post Section 54EC Deduction Allowed for Investments Acro
rows.summary:
The ITAT Bangalore in **DCIT v. Shri Borkatte Ganapathi Hegde** held that, for **AY 2012-13**, the assessee was entitled to claim **Section 54EC deduction on investments made across two financial years** where the **six-month investment window** straddled those years. The assessee had sold **two immovable properties** and invested the capital gains in **REC bonds**; although the investments exceeded **Rs. 50 lakh in total**, they were made within the statutory six-month period, partly in the year of transfer and partly in the immediately succeeding financial year.

The Assessing Officer had capped the exemption at **Rs. 50 lakh** and disallowed the balance **Rs. 49,09,181**, relying on **ACIT v. Shri Raj Kumar Jain & Sons (HUF)**. The CIT(A) deleted the disallowance, and the Tribunal affirmed that view, relying on the Madras High Court decisions in **CIT v. C. Jaichander** and **CIT v. Coromandel Industries Ltd.** The Tribunal’s key conclusion was that, for the law applicable to that assessment year, the **Rs. 50 lakh cap operated financial-year-wise**, so an assessee could invest **Rs. 50 lakh in one financial year and another Rs. 50 lakh in the next financial year** if the investment period under Section 54EC extended across both years.

The Tribunal also noted an important legislative change: the Finance (No. 2) Act, **2014** inserted a **second proviso to Section 54EC(1)**, **effective from 01.04.2015**, expressly limiting the **aggregate investment** in specified bonds, in respect of transfers of one or more original assets during a financial year and the subsequent financial year, to **Rs. 50 lakh**. That amendment is prospective and was highlighted by the Tribunal to show that the stricter aggregate cap did not apply to the assessment year in question. For compliance purposes, the decision matters primarily for historical transactions governed by the pre-01.04.2015 version of Section 54EC; for transactions on or after that date, the aggregate **Rs. 50 lakh** limit across the relevant transfer year and the next year applies.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 271(1)(c) Penalty on Withdrawn Section 35 Donation Deduction Deleted: ITAT Ahmedabad
rows.desc: ITAT Ahmedabad deletes Section 271(1)(c) penalty where Section 35 donation deduction was withdrawn before assessee received reopening reasons.The post Section 271(1)(c) Penalty on Withdrawn Section 35
rows.summary:
ITAT Ahmedabad held that a penalty under section 271(1)(c) could not be sustained merely because the assessee later withdrew a section 35 donation deduction after a reassessment notice was issued. The assessee in **AY 2014-15** had originally filed a return declaring income of **Rs. 4,63,168** and claiming a **section 35 deduction of Rs. 10,50,000** for a donation to **M/s. Herbicure Healthcare Bio-Herbal Research Foundation**; after notice under **section 148**, it filed a revised/reassessment return on **04.04.2017** declaring income of **Rs. 15,13,168** and withdrawing the deduction. The Assessing Officer treated that withdrawal as furnishing inaccurate particulars/concealment and levied a penalty of **Rs. 3,15,000**, and the CIT(A) upheld it, but the Tribunal deleted the penalty.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that a withdrawal of a claimed deduction after reopening does not automatically prove concealment or inaccurate particulars, especially where the taxpayer can plausibly show it did not know the basis for reopening at the time of withdrawal. The assessee argued, and the Tribunal accepted as significant, that the **recorded reasons for reopening were supplied only on 19.04.2017**, after the return withdrawing the deduction had already been filed on **04.04.2017**, so it could not be presumed the withdrawal was made with knowledge of the reopening grounds. The Tribunal also noted that when the donation was made, the recipient institution’s approval/registration under **section 35(1)(ii)** was still in force; the cancellation happened only later. Relying on its earlier decisions involving the same institution and on general penalty principles, the Tribunal concluded that the facts did not justify a concealment penalty and ordered deletion of the **Rs. 3.15 lakh** penalty.

rows.title: Income Tax | Penalty Passed Beyond Extended Limitation Under Section 275 Quashed: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai quashes Section 271(1)(c) penalty passed after extended limitation expired on 30.09.2021 under Section 275(1)(c).The post Penalty Passed Beyond Extended Limitation Under Section 275 Quashe
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that the penalty order under section 271(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 in the case of **Hardik Dayanand Patil v. ITO** was **barred by limitation** and therefore quashed it. The assessee, an individual, had originally filed a return declaring income of **Rs. 14,31,583**, which was assessed under section 143(3); later, reassessment proceedings were opened under sections 147/148 and completed on **30.12.2019** at **Rs. 24,00,830** after the department found that **capital gains arising from a development agreement** had not been reported in the original return. The assessee’s position was that the relevant documents had been provided to his Chartered Accountant, the omission was inadvertent, and once noticed he filed a revised computation and paid the resulting tax.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is procedural: because the assessee did **not appeal the reassessment order**, the Tribunal said the limitation rule in **section 275(1)(c)** applied to the penalty proceedings. On that basis, the ordinary limitation period for passing the penalty order expired on **30.06.2020**. The Tribunal also considered the COVID-era extensions granted under the **Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (TOLA)** and the relevant **CBDT circulars**, but still concluded that even after giving the Revenue the maximum available extension, the penalty order dated **23.11.2021** was passed beyond the permissible outer time limit. The practical takeaway is that where penalty is initiated in reassessment and the reassessment order is not appealed, the department must still pass the penalty order within the section 275 time framework as extended by TOLA; if it is issued after the extended cutoff, it is vulnerable to being struck down as time-barred.

rows.title: Income Tax | CPC Adjustment Merges With Section 143(3) Scrutiny Assessment: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai holds CPC adjustment under Section 143(1) merges with Section 143(3) assessment and only the scrutiny assessment survives.The post CPC Adjustment Merges With Section 143(3) Scrutiny Assess
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that the CPC’s adjustment of **Rs. 35,23,99,063** for “**Abandoned Project Expenses written off and claimed as deductible expenditure**” could not survive once a later **scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3) read with Section 144B** had been completed for the same assessment year. The taxpayer, **National Stock Exchange of India Limited**, had filed its return for **AY 2020-21** declaring total income of **Rs. 2,049,74,12,520**, but CPC processed the return under **Section 143(1)** at **Rs. 2,084,98,11,580** after making the disputed addition.

A key procedural flaw was that the assessee had filed an objection to the proposed **Section 143(1)** adjustment on **29.09.2021**, but CPC did not respond to that objection and passed the final intimation without dealing with it. The assessee also filed a **rectification application under Section 154**, and no order was passed on that either. In parallel, the case was selected for complete scrutiny, and the assessing officer later completed an assessment under **Section 143(3) / 144B on 28.09.2022** without making the disputed disallowance.

The Tribunal found that the Revenue did not dispute that the expenditure was actually incurred; the real issue was whether it was deductible as **business expenditure under Section 37** or whether it was capital in nature. On the facts, the ITAT held that CPC’s failure to consider the taxpayer’s response and failure to dispose of the rectification request meant the adjustment did not satisfy the procedural requirements associated with **Section 143(1)** processing. It also applied the **doctrine of merger**, ruling that once the scrutiny assessment was completed, the earlier CPC adjustment merged into the later assessment, so the final operative order was the **Section 143(3)** assessment and the CPC addition could not stand independently.  

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that when a return-processing adjustment is later followed by a full scrutiny assessment covering the same issue, the later assessment may supersede the CPC intimation; however, taxpayers should still preserve and timely file objections to any proposed **143(1)** adjustment and pursue **Section 154** rectification where the CPC ignores them.

rows.title: Income Tax | Wrong Section 151 Sanction Invalidates Reassessment and Penalty: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashes AY 2017-18 reassessment as Section 151 approval was obtained from PCIT instead of PCCIT; consequential penalty deleted.The post Wrong Section 151 Sanction Invalidates Reassessment a
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi in *Amitabh Tayal v. ITO* allowed both the quantum appeal and the penalty appeal for AY 2017-18, holding that the reassessment was jurisdictionally invalid because the approval under Section 151 was obtained from the PCIT and the notice under Section 148 was issued much later than permitted by law. The case arose from an investigation into Shri Joginder Pal Gupta, described as an entry operator, where the department alleged that the assessee had received accommodation entries through a shell company; the Assessing Officer therefore treated an unsecured loan of Rs. 2.25 crore as income under Section 69D. The assessee’s first appeal had been dismissed in limine by the CIT(A)-NFAC because a six-month delay in filing was not condoned, but the Tribunal did not sustain that outcome because it found a foundational jurisdiction defect in the reopening itself.

The decisive issue was that, for AY 2017-18, sanction under Section 151 from the statutorily correct authority was time-bound. Relying on the Supreme Court’s decision in *Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal* (469 ITR 46), the Tribunal noted that even taking advantage of TOLA extensions, the PCIT could grant approval only up to 30.06.2021 for this assessment year. In this case, the Section 148 notice was issued on 18.07.2022 after approval from PCIT-12, Delhi, which was beyond the permissible sanction window; accordingly, the Tribunal held the reopening notice was invalid. Because the reassessment itself failed on this jurisdictional ground, the corresponding penalty under Section 271AAC(1) also could not survive.

For compliance purposes, the ruling underscores that reassessment notices must be checked not only for substantive allegations but also for strict conformity with Section 151 approval requirements and timing, especially where TOLA extensions were involved. If a notice for AY 2017-18 was issued after 30.06.2021, a PCIT sanction would not cure the defect, and any resulting reassessment and penalty exposure may be vulnerable to annulment.

rows.title: Income Tax | Reassessment Quashed as PCIT Approval Invalid Beyond Three Years: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashes AY 2017-18 reassessment as Section 151 sanction was obtained from PCIT instead of the prescribed PCCIT.The post Reassessment Quashed as PCIT Approval Invalid Beyond Three Years: ITA
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi held that the reassessment of Samunder Saree Centre for AY 2017–18 was invalid and quashed the proceedings because the mandatory approval under Section 151 of the Income-tax Act was obtained from the wrong authority. The reassessment had been initiated through an order under Section 148A(d) dated 23.07.2022 and culminated in an assessment order dated 26.05.2023 under Section 147 read with Section 144B; however, because more than three years had elapsed from the end of the relevant assessment year, the Tribunal found that the competent sanctioning authority was the Principal Chief Commissioner of Income Tax (PCCIT), not the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax (PCIT). Since the approval was actually taken from the PCIT, the jurisdictional defect was fatal and rendered the entire reassessment proceeding void.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the decision reinforces that, in reopened assessments initiated after the three-year period from the end of the assessment year, the identity of the sanctioning authority under Section 151 must strictly match the statutory requirement; obtaining approval from a lower or different authority is not a curable procedural defect. The Tribunal relied on the Delhi High Court’s ruling in Appeal Kids Dream International Private Limited v. ACIT, W.P.(C) 2814/2023 dated 24.02.2025, which held that TOLA does not change the statutory authority prescribed under Section 151. The appeal before the ITAT arose from the NFAC order dated 22.12.2025, and the ruling applies specifically to reassessment jurisdiction issues for AY 2017–18 where the notice/reopening occurred beyond the three-year threshold.

rows.title: Income Tax | Third-Party Search Papers Cannot Sustain Uncorroborated Additions: ITAT Kolkata
rows.desc: ITAT Kolkata upheld search reassessment but deleted coal purchase and cash-loan additions unsupported by corroborative evidence.The post Third-Party Search Papers Cannot Sustain Uncorroborated Additio
rows.summary:
The ITAT Kolkata’s ruling in **Shakambhari Ispat & Power Limited v. DCIT** arises from **search-linked reassessment proceedings** for **AYs 2016-17 to 2021-22** following a search on the **Agarwal Group on 17.09.2021**. For the lead appeal, **ITA No. 931/Kol/2025 for AY 2019-20**, the Tribunal first upheld the **validity of the reopening notice under section 148**, rejecting the assessee’s jurisdictional challenge. It held that, under the **post-01.04.2021 search reassessment framework**, the issuance of a notice under section 148 does **not** depend on incriminating material being found in the search itself; rather, the question whether the material supports additions is to be tested during the assessment proceedings.

On the merits, the Tribunal granted **substantial relief** and deleted the major additions. The central dispute concerned alleged **undisclosed coal purchases from the Anup Majee Group**, which the tax authorities tried to infer from **documents seized in a third-party search**. The assessee consistently denied that these transactions occurred, and the Tribunal found that the alleged purchase papers were **not properly confronted** to the assessee, the relevant persons were **not examined**, and the assessee was **not given cross-examination** of those persons. The Revenue also failed to produce **corroborative evidence** showing corresponding unaccounted manufacture or unrecorded sales that would support the theory of suppressed purchases.

Because of that evidentiary gap, the Tribunal held that the addition under **section 69C** for the alleged purchases could not stand, and it also rejected the CIT(A)’s alternative approach of estimating profit at **8.01%** on those alleged transactions. The Tribunal directed deletion of both the principal purchase addition and the profit estimate. The decision also addressed the separate issue of purchases from **Reeja Trading** in the same reassessment context, indicating that the Tribunal considered additional trade-purchase additions arising from the search material, but the key compliance takeaway is that **third-party search papers alone, without proper confrontation and corroboration, are insufficient to sustain uncorroborated additions**, even though reopening under section 148 may still be upheld.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Old Rules Do Not Govern Earlier Vacancies Automatically: Supreme Court
rows.desc: Supreme Court overrules Rangaiah principle that vacancies arising before rule amendments must necessarily be filled under old rules.The post Old Rules Do Not Govern Earlier Vacancies Automatically: Su
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that government vacancies are **not automatically required to be filled under the recruitment rules that existed when the vacancies first arose**, unless the governing statute or rules specifically create that obligation. The case involved **seven additional Labour Officer posts in Himachal Pradesh sanctioned on 20.07.2006**; the earlier **1966 Rules** contemplated filling Labour Officer posts **by promotion**, but the amended **Recruitment and Promotion Rules that came into force on 25.11.2006** provided a **75% promotion / 25% direct recruitment** split. After the amendment, the High Court had applied **Y.V. Rangaiah v. J. Sreenivasa Rao** to hold that the vacancies had to be filled entirely under the old rules and had interfered with direct recruitment appointments, but the Supreme Court reversed that approach.

The Court reviewed **Articles 309, 310, and 311 of the Constitution** and explained that public employment is governed by **statutory service rules**, not by any independent vested right of employees to demand that vacancies be filled under the rules in force on the date the vacancy arose. The Court clarified that **Rangaiah does not establish a universal rule** requiring old rules to govern every earlier vacancy; rather, it depended on the specific statutory framework in that case. For compliance purposes, the practical rule from this decision is that an employer/government authority should apply the **current valid recruitment rules at the time of filling the post**, unless the applicable rules expressly preserve the earlier method or otherwise mandate filling pre-existing vacancies under the old regime.

This ruling is important for public sector hiring and recruitment administration because it confirms that a change in recruitment rules can validly affect already-existing vacancies, and employees cannot automatically challenge such recruitment simply by pointing to the date the vacancy arose. It also means that, where rules are amended before appointments are finalized, authorities should assess the **exact wording of the new and old service rules** rather than assuming that the old recruitment pattern continues for prior vacancies.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 153C Assessments Quashed for Defective Satisfaction: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashed 40 assessments as Section 153C satisfaction failed to show seized materials bearing on determination of total income.The post Section 153C Assessments Quashed for Defective Satisfac
rows.summary:
This ITAT Delhi ruling holds that the Revenue cannot sustain section 153C assessments unless the satisfaction note clearly shows that the seized material has a bearing on the determination of the other person’s total income. The case arose from a search and seizure operation in the Alankit Group on 18.10.2019, after which the Assessing Officer issued a consolidated satisfaction note dated 24.12.2021 and initiated section 153C proceedings for multiple assessees across AY 2010-11 to AY 2020-21.

The Tribunal allowed a batch of 40 appeals filed by five assessees — Sakshi Agarwal, Alka Agarwal, Pratishtha Images Private Limited, Alankit Forex India Limited, and Alankit Finsec Limited — covering AY 2013-14 to AY 2020-21 in the appeals described in the summary. It quashed the assessments framed under section 153C read with section 143(3) because the satisfaction note merely stated that material/documents relating to the assessee had been found and that the documents belonged to the assessee, but did not clearly establish the jurisdictional requirement that the seized material had a “bearing” on the assessee’s total income.
