The Revenue argued that the exact word “bearing” was not necessary if the relationship between the seized material and escaped income was otherwise evident, citing cases such as Shiv Parkash Bansal, Indian National Congress v. DCIT, and Super Malls Private Limited; however, the Tribunal rejected that position on the facts before it.

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that section 153C proceedings based on search material are vulnerable if the satisfaction recording is defective or conclusory. The Tribunal relied on Delhi High Court authority, particularly Saksham Commodities Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer, to conclude that jurisdiction fails where the note does not expressly or effectively link the seized material to the computation of the other person’s taxable income. No new filing deadline or tax rate was announced, but the decision reinforces a procedural obligation on the tax department: a valid, reasoned satisfaction note is required before proceeding under section 153C, and generic statements that documents “belong to” the assessee may be insufficient unless the income nexus is properly recorded.

rows.title: Income Tax | Mechanical Satisfaction Note Cannot Sustain Section 153C Proceedings: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi quashed Section 153C assessments where AO failed to record how seized material had bearing on assessees total income.The post Mechanical Satisfaction Note Cannot Sustain Section 153C Procee
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi held that the Section 153C proceedings against Anil Chaudhary, proprietor of M/s Chaudhary Trading Company, could not be sustained because the Assessing Officer’s satisfaction note was only a mechanical assertion that the seized material “relates to” the assessee and that action under Section 153C was warranted. The case arose from a search on 12.05.2019 in the group case of M/s Pragati Glass (P) Ltd. (PGPL), where the department relied on documents found with PGPL’s Managing Director and on statements of the Managing Director and accountant to allege that the assessee had made cash purchases from PGPL outside the regular books. On that basis, additions were made under Section 69C for assessment years 2014-15 through 2019-20 in assessments framed under Sections 153C/143(3).

The Tribunal first addressed the jurisdictional time limit under Section 153C and noted that the seized material was received by the assessee’s Assessing Officer on 10.03.2021, making AY 2021-22 the relevant search assessment year for determining the six-year block. Applying CIT v. RRJ Securities Ltd., the Tribunal held that AY 2014-15 fell outside the permissible six-year period, so the assessment for that year was void for lack of jurisdiction. For the remaining years, the Tribunal found the satisfaction note legally deficient because it did not record a real, reasoned satisfaction showing how the seized documents had a bearing on the determination of the assessee’s total income for the relevant years; it merely recited that the documents “relate to” the assessee and that Section 153C action was appropriate.

Relying on Saksham Commodities Ltd., the ITAT emphasized that Section 153C requires more than a mechanical note: the AO must specifically explain the nexus between the seized material and the assessee’s income for the years proposed to be assessed. Because that mandatory satisfaction was absent, the Tribunal held that the 153C proceedings and consequential additions could not stand. The practical compliance implication is that, for search-related third-party assessments, the department must have properly documented satisfaction establishing how the seized items affect the recipient assessee’s income within the statutory assessment period; otherwise, the assessment is vulnerable to being quashed.

rows.title: Income Tax | On-Money From Property Sale Taxable as Capital Gains, Not Section 69A: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: ITAT Delhi holds property sale on-money with explained source forms sale consideration taxable as capital gains, not unexplained money under section 69A.The post On-Money From Property Sale Taxable as
rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi held that “on-money” received in connection with a property sale is to be treated as part of the property’s sale consideration and taxed under the capital gains provisions, rather than being assessed as unexplained money under Section 69A of the Income-tax Act. In other words, where the receipt has an explained source and is directly linked to the transfer of immovable property, tax authorities should not separately invoke Section 69A merely because part of the consideration was received outside the formal documented amount.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that any additional consideration connected to a property transaction can still create tax exposure, but the correct character of that exposure is capital gains treatment on the transfer, not a standalone unexplained-income addition, so long as the source and nexus to the sale are established. This ruling matters for real estate sellers, buyers, and entities involved in structuring or documenting property transfers, because it underscores the importance of maintaining clear records showing the full consideration agreed to and received, including any off-record amounts, to support the transaction’s tax treatment. The document provided is only a short headline-style summary and does not state any separate filing deadline, effective date, monetary threshold, or procedural deadline beyond the general legal principle announced by the ITAT Delhi.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Advocate Gets 15-Day Jail for Baseless “Match-Fixing” Allegation: Karnataka HC
rows.desc: Karnataka HC sentences advocate to 15 days’ simple imprisonment for baseless “match-fixing” and fabricated-order allegations.The post Advocate Gets 15-Day Jail for Baseless “Match-Fixing” Allegation:
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court, in **Criminal Contempt Petition No. 2 of 2026** decided on **18.09.2026**, held an advocate in contempt and sentenced him to **15 days’ simple imprisonment** for making scandalous and unfounded allegations against the judiciary. The court found that he had accused the Trial Court of deciding a matter through **“match-fixing”** and then escalated the misconduct by alleging that the High Court had produced a **false, fabricated, and forged order** in order to implicate him in contempt proceedings. Because of the gravity of those accusations and the advocate’s demeanour before the Bench, the court ordered that he be **taken into custody forthwith**.

The contempt matter arose from proceedings linked to an earlier **order dated 15.09.2025** in **Criminal Appeal No. 1054/2018**, where the Division Bench had taken up the appeal after noticing that the appellant’s aged parents were waiting. The case narrative states that the advocate had previously been directed to file a **written synopsis** explaining the prosecution circumstances and identifying the corresponding witnesses, indicating that the court had already been managing the matter procedurally before the contempt issue escalated.

For compliance purposes, the practical consequence of the ruling is that the High Court treated baseless accusations impugning judicial integrity as punishable contempt and imposed immediate custodial punishment rather than a warning or fine. The Registry was also directed to **send the order to the Bar Council** so that it could consider disciplinary action and determine whether the advocate remained **fit to continue in legal practice**. This means the decision has not only penal consequences in court but also potential **professional disciplinary consequences** before the bar regulator.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 143(1) Intimation Merges With Scrutiny Assessment on Same Issue: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai holds Section 143(1) intimation inoperative after merger with Section 143(3) assessment involving the same Section 80JJAA issue.The post Section 143(1) Intimation Merges With Scrutiny Asse
rows.summary:
The document reports an ITAT Mumbai ruling on how a prior Section 143(1) intimation is treated once a later scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3) covers the same issue. The key holding is that the Section 143(1) intimation becomes inoperative/merged to the extent the same matter is examined in the scrutiny assessment, so the earlier processing-based adjustment cannot stand independently on that point. In the case described, the overlapping issue was the taxpayer’s claim under Section 80JJAA, and the Tribunal held that once the scrutiny assessment addressed that same claim, the earlier 143(1) action ceased to have separate effect for that issue. 

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that companies should treat a Section 143(1) adjustment as potentially displaced if a subsequent regular assessment under Section 143(3) is completed on the same factual/legal issue; any challenge or defense should be focused on the scrutiny assessment rather than assuming both actions operate cumulatively. The document does not describe any new tax rate, filing deadline, monetary threshold, or broadly applicable procedural change beyond this merger principle. It is therefore mainly relevant to taxpayers who have received a processing intimation and later face scrutiny on the same deduction/disallowance item, especially Section 80JJAA claims.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Digital Cinema Equipment Leasing Is Mixed Supply Taxable at Highest GST Rate: Telangana AAR
rows.desc: Telangana AAR holds leasing of projector, server, UPS and VSAT as mixed supply taxable at the highest GST rate applicable to the bundle.The post Digital Cinema Equipment Leasing Is Mixed Supply Taxabl
rows.summary:
The Telangana Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) held that a lease arrangement covering digital cinema equipment—specifically a projector, server, UPS, and VSAT—constitutes a **mixed supply** under GST rather than separate supplies of distinct goods or services. Because the items are being leased together as a bundled offering, the entire transaction must be taxed at the **highest GST rate applicable to any one component in the bundle**, rather than at separate rates for each item.

For compliance purposes, this means businesses leasing this type of cinema equipment should not apportion the bundle across lower-rate and higher-rate categories to reduce tax. Instead, they must determine the highest applicable GST rate among the leased components and apply that rate to the full consideration charged for the package. The ruling is relevant to entities engaged in equipment leasing, especially where multiple items are supplied together under one contract or pricing arrangement.

No effective date, transition period, threshold, or procedural filing deadline is mentioned in the provided text. The practical compliance takeaway is to review bundled leasing contracts for mixed-supply treatment and ensure invoicing and GST classification reflect the highest-rate rule.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CBIC Proposes Mandatory IUPAC Name and CAS Number for 47 Dual-Use Chemicals
rows.desc: CBIC proposes mandatory IUPAC Name and CAS Number in import/export declarations for 47 dual-use chemicals from 15 October 2026.The post CBIC Proposes Mandatory IUPAC Name and CAS Number for 47 Dual-Us
rows.summary:
CBIC has proposed a new customs declaration requirement for imports and exports of **47 dual-use chemicals covered under the Chemical Weapons Convention Act**. For any **Bill of Entry or Shipping Bill** relating to one of these chemicals, importers and exporters would have to **mandatorily declare both the chemical’s IUPAC name and its CAS number**, in addition to the existing product description and other required particulars. The stated purpose is to improve precise chemical identification, help customs detect violations earlier, strengthen enforcement of controls on regulated chemicals, and improve the quality of trade data.

A key compliance change is that the current relaxation in **paragraph 4.2 of Circular No. 23/2023-Customs dated 30.09.2023**, which allows a **self-undertaking where CAS and IUPAC details are unavailable**, would **not be available for these 47 specified chemicals**. In other words, for these covered chemicals, missing CAS/IUPAC information would no longer be an acceptable basis to proceed under that facility. The requirement is proposed to become effective for **Bills of Entry and Shipping Bills filed on or after 15.10.2026**.

CBIC has also indicated that the **Directorate General of Systems and Data Management** will update the **Customs Automated System** by that effective date to support the new mandatory fields. Separately, CBIC has invited **trade and other stakeholders** to submit comments or suggestions on the Draft Circular and Annexure **by email within 15 days from the date of issue of the notice**. For compliance teams, the main action point is to identify whether any current or planned import/export activity involves one of the 47 listed chemicals and ensure systems, documentation workflows, and vendor/master data can supply the **correct CAS number and IUPAC name** before the **15.10.2026** go-live date.

rows.title: Corporate Law | NeSL Regulatory Information Exempt from RTI Disclosure Due to Fiduciary Relationship: IBBI
rows.desc: IBBI upheld denial of NeSL regulatory and supervisory information under Section 8(1)(e) of RTI Act, finding a fiduciary relationship.The post NeSL Regulatory Information Exempt from RTI Disclosure Due
rows.summary:
The IBBI’s First Appellate Authority has upheld the CPIO’s refusal to disclose a range of information requested about National E-Governance Services Limited (NeSL), holding that the material is protected from disclosure under Section 8(1)(e) of the RTI Act because it is shared within a fiduciary/supervisory relationship between NeSL and the IBBI. The appeals, filed by S. Giri and decided by order dated 18 September 2026, sought detailed information on NeSL’s corporate status, user registration and identity verification processes, digital stamping services, authentication of financial information, claimed regulatory exemptions, compliance certifications, inspections and enforcement actions, and the Business Continuity Plan for Digital Document Execution and Electronic Bank Guarantee services. The Authority noted that information concerning the statutory framework is already publicly accessible, and also stated that a CPIO is not obliged to interpret public regulatory material, provide explanatory opinions, or redress grievances through the RTI process.

The document makes clear that the information requested relates to NeSL’s regulatory framework under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the IBBI (Information Utilities) Regulations, 2017, and related technical standards for core and other services. However, because the information had been furnished by NeSL to IBBI in the course of regulatory oversight and supervision, the Authority treated it as fiduciary in nature and therefore exempt from disclosure absent a showing of larger public interest. No such larger public interest was demonstrated, so the CPIO’s original response was affirmed in full. For compliance teams, the practical point is that supervisory information provided by an information utility or similar regulated entity to the regulator may remain non-disclosable under RTI if it is held in a fiduciary context, while the underlying statutory/regulatory framework itself remains public and accessible.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CBIC Invites Comments on Draft Warehousing Operations Regulations, 2026
rows.desc: CBIC seeks stakeholder comments within 15 days on Draft Warehousing Operations Regulations, 2026 governing public and private warehouses.The post CBIC Invites Comments on Draft Warehousing Operations
rows.summary:
CBIC has issued the Draft Warehousing Operations Regulations, 2026 for public comment, under F. No. 473/12/2026-LC dated 21 September 2026, and stakeholders have only 15 days from that date to submit comments, views, and suggestions in the prescribed format. The draft is proposed under section 157 read with sections 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 64, 67, 68, 69 and 72 and section 73A(2) of the Customs Act, 1962, and it would partially supersede the Warehouse (Custody and Handling of Goods) Regulations, 2016 and the Warehoused Goods (Removal) Regulations, 2016 for warehouses covered by the new framework.

Substantively, the regulations would govern how warehoused goods are handled and moved, including transport of warehoused goods with one-time-locks, transit-risk insurance, electronic receipt and accountal of goods, inter-warehouse transfers, removal for home consumption and export, operations on warehoused goods, monthly returns, use of digital warehouse management systems, maintenance of electronic records, risk-based verification, and penalties. Compliance would be shifted to mandatory electronic filing through the Common Customs Electronic Portal, so affected warehouses would need to use that portal for required submissions rather than paper-based processes.

The new framework would apply to public and private warehouses licensed under sections 57 and 58 of the Customs Act, but it would not apply to warehouses authorized to undertake manufacturing or other operations under section 65. It also introduces two specific forms: Form WH-1 for monthly warehouse returns, and Form WH-2 for reporting Bills of Entry whose warehousing period will expire in the following month, which means warehouse operators would need procedures to track expiry dates proactively and report them in advance.

rows.title: Corporate Law | WDRA Aadhaar Authentication for Depositors and Warehousemen Notified
rows.desc: WDRA permits voluntary Aadhaar authentication for depositors, warehousemen and stakeholders, with alternate identification options.The post WDRA Aadhaar Authentication for Depositors and Warehousemen
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, acting through the Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), has issued Notification S.O. 5069(E) dated 14 September 2026 to permit voluntary Aadhaar authentication for identity verification of depositors, warehousemen, and other stakeholders interacting with WDRA-regulated repositories. The permission was granted after the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, in consultation with the Unique Identification Authority of India, authorized WDRA and its regulated repositories to use Aadhaar authentication to establish the identity of Aadhaar number holders. This authentication may be used both for onboarding users onto the WDRA portal and regulated repository platforms via Aadhaar e-KYC and for carrying out service transactions on those platforms.

A key compliance point is that Aadhaar authentication is expressly optional, not mandatory. WDRA and its regulated repositories must obtain the Aadhaar holder’s consent before authentication and must not refuse service merely because a person declines Aadhaar authentication or is unable to complete it. They must therefore maintain and accept alternate, viable identification mechanisms for onboarding and transactions.

The notification specifies the alternative ID documents that may be used instead of Aadhaar: PAN, Driving Licence, Passport, a photograph-bearing Address Card issued by the Department of Posts, photograph-bearing post office passbooks, photograph-bearing public sector scheduled bank passbooks, Kisan Passbook, and Voter Identity Card. Compliance teams should ensure portal workflows, KYC procedures, and service scripts reflect these alternatives and do not create de facto Aadhaar compulsion.

This notification supersedes Notification S.O. 698(E) dated 10 February 2023, except for anything already done or omitted before the supersession took effect. It becomes effective from the date it is published in the Official Gazette.

rows.title: Corporate Law | IRDAI Delegates Penalty and Direction Powers under Insurance Act and Regulations
rows.desc: IRDAI delegates specified powers for penalties and directions under the Insurance Act, regulations and guidelines to designated authorities.The post IRDAI Delegates Penalty and Direction Powers under
rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued Notification F. No. IRDAI/DoP/13/227/2026 dated 10 September 2026, effective immediately on issuance unless otherwise stated, delegating certain enforcement powers under the Insurance Act, 1938 and specified IRDAI regulations/guidelines. The delegation is made under section 23(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999, and it authorizes the Chairperson, a Whole Time Member, a panel of the Chairperson plus one Whole Time Member, or a panel of two Whole Time Members to exercise the delegated powers, with the specific composition to be decided by the Chairperson.

Substantively, the delegation covers the power to issue directions under section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938 in enforcement proceedings against insurers or insurance intermediaries for identified violations, and to impose penalties under section 102 for failures such as not furnishing required documents, not complying with directions, not maintaining the required solvency margin, and failures relating to insurance treaties. It also covers penalties under section 104 for contraventions of sections 27 and 27E, and powers under sections 105C(2) and 105D relating to inquiry reports and fixing the quantum of penalty. In addition, the delegated enforcement powers extend to Regulation 22(6) of the IRDAI (Registration of Corporate Agents) Regulations, 2015 and to clauses 48 through 53 of the Guidelines on Insurance Repositories and electronic issuance of insurance policies, 2015.

For compliance purposes, this means insurers, insurance intermediaries, corporate agents, and entities subject to the insurance repository/e-policy guidelines should expect that penalty and direction decisions may now be issued by the delegated IRDAI authority structure rather than only by the Chairperson personally. The notification also clarifies that not all section 34 direction-making authority has been delegated: directions on other matters under section 34 remain with the Chairperson. There are no new substantive conduct standards created in this text; the change is primarily a shift in enforcement authority and decision-making process, which may affect how quickly and by whom enforcement actions, penalties, and directions are issued.

rows.title: Finance | PMLA Special Court Jurisdiction Revised for Four Himachal Pradesh Districts
rows.desc: Finance Ministry revises PMLA Special Court jurisdiction for Shimla, Kinnaur, Solan and Sirmaur districts through Notification S.O. 5082(E).The post PMLA Special Court Jurisdiction Revised for Four Hi
rows.summary: The Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, issued Notification S.O. 5082(E) dated 16 September 2026 to amend the earlier PMLA court-designation notification S.O. 372(E) dated 5 February 2016 under section 43(1) of the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002, after consulting the Chief Justice of the Himachal Pradesh High Court. The amendment specifically changes the entry for serial number 9 relating to Himachal Pradesh in the original table: the first court entry in column (3) is now “Additional Sessions Judge (CBI) Shimla,” and the corresponding territorial jurisdiction in column (4) is revised to cover the districts of Shimla, Kinnaur, Solan, and Sirmaur at Nahan. In practical terms, PMLA matters that fall within these districts are now assigned to that designated special court rather than any prior court/jurisdiction arrangement reflected in the original notification. The notification does not impose new substantive compliance duties or deadlines for reporting entities, but compliance teams should update internal legal/jurisdiction reference materials, case-routing protocols, and any escalation or litigation-monitoring matrices tied to PMLA proceedings in Himachal Pradesh to reflect the revised special court designation and district coverage. File number: F. No. C-18015/2/2026-Ad.ED.

rows.title: Corporate Law | India-New Zealand FTA to Take Effect from 20 October 2026
rows.desc: India-New Zealand FTA takes effect from 20 October 2026, giving zero-duty access to 100% of India’s exports and boosting trade and investment.The post India-New Zealand FTA to Take Effect from 20 Octo
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Commerce & Industry has announced that the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA), signed on 27 April 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, will enter into force on 20 October 2026, after internal approval processes were completed in both countries. From that date, all tariff lines covering 100% of India’s exports to New Zealand will become duty-free, which is intended to benefit Indian exporters in textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, gems and jewellery, engineering goods, and processed foods.  

The agreement does not liberalize all agricultural trade equally: sensitive Indian agricultural products, including dairy, animal meat other than sheep, key agricultural commodities, sugar, and edible oils, have been excluded from tariff concessions. For New Zealand exports into India, access for apples, kiwifruit, and Manuka honey will be controlled through Tariff Rate Quotas, Minimum Import Prices, and seasonal windows, so these items will not receive unrestricted access.  

The FTA also establishes an Agriculture Productivity Partnership and cooperation through Centres of Excellence, which suggests formal collaboration arrangements in agricultural technology and productivity. On investment, New Zealand has committed to facilitate USD 20 billion of investment into India, which is a material commercial commitment relevant to cross-border investment planning and potential project pipelines.  

On services and mobility, the agreement covers roughly 118 services sectors and grants Most-Favoured Nation treatment across about 139 sub-sectors. It creates a dedicated quota of 5,000 Temporary Employment Entry visas for skilled Indians and 1,000 annual Working Holiday visas for young Indians, and it also provides for student mobility and post-study work rights.  

For regulated products, the FTA is designed to facilitate pharmaceutical and medical-device market access by allowing acceptance of inspection approvals from specified global regulators. Compliance teams should treat 20 October 2026 as the operative date for tariff and market-access changes, and should assess product classification, origin, quota usage, visa planning, and any pharmaceutical or medical-device regulatory reliance in advance of entry into force.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Public Sector and Regional Rural Banks to Open on 27 September 2026
rows.desc: Public Sector Banks and Regional Rural Banks will open on Sunday, 27 September 2026, ahead of the proposed three-day nationwide bank strike.The post Public Sector and Regional Rural Banks to Open on 2
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance announced that all Public Sector Banks and Regional Rural Banks must operate normally on **Sunday, 27 September 2026**, despite it ordinarily being a weekend day, because a **three-day nationwide bank strike** has been called by the **United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU)** for **28–30 September 2026**. The government’s stated objective is to ensure that customers’ genuine banking needs are not disrupted for an extended period, especially since the strike would follow the weekend holidays of **26 and 27 September**.  

The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** has approved full operational continuity on that date for **all bank branches, offices, ATM-linked branches, and Currency Chests**. This means the affected institutions are expected to keep ordinary banking services and related operational infrastructure available on 27 September 2026, rather than observing the usual Sunday closure.  

The notice also states that the government and bank managements have **appealed to the unions to defer the proposed strike**, and that arrangements have been made to ensure **essential banking services continue uninterrupted** during the relevant period. For compliance teams, the key action point is to confirm that the covered banks’ branches, offices, ATM support points, and currency chest operations are staffed and operational on **27 September 2026**, with business continuity measures in place in case the strike proceeds on **28–30 September 2026**.

rows.title: Corporate Law | WAVES OTT and MyWAVES Expand Digital Public Broadcasting and Creator Participation
rows.desc: WAVES OTT and MyWAVES expand Prasar Bharati’s digital broadcasting, creator participation and multilingual content reach in India and globally.The post WAVES OTT and MyWAVES Expand Digital Public Broa
rows.summary:
The document describes Prasar Bharati’s expansion of its digital public-broadcasting ecosystem through WAVES OTT and MyWAVES, signaling a move from traditional broadcasting to an integrated public-service platform with wider online access and creator participation. WAVES OTT was launched on 20 November 2024 and combines live television, radio, on-demand programming, archival content, education, devotional material, and digital publications on a multilingual platform; the platform now reports 1.2 crore registered users, more than 1.5 crore downloads, over 24,000 titles, and roughly 15,000 hours of content, with availability in more than 130 countries. For compliance purposes, the document also notes that WAVES OTT has introduced a Pay-Per-View Content Sourcing Policy, ONDC integration, and railway-related digital distribution initiatives, which indicate new distribution and sourcing arrangements that may affect content partners, platform participants, and any entities involved in monetized digital delivery.  

A separate citizen-creator platform, MyWAVES, was launched on 23 March 2026 and is intended to let users create, upload, and share original short-form, vertical, and episodic content, thereby broadening public participation in the broadcasting ecosystem. The document also highlights the Gems of India Challenge, which is designed to support district-level storytelling and grassroots creators, suggesting a structured initiative for sourcing local content and promoting regional participation. In the broader WAVES ecosystem, Prasar Bharati positions these platforms as tools to connect creators, businesses, investors, policymakers, and technology leaders, with the stated objective of strengthening India’s creative economy and improving the visibility of Indian creators nationally and internationally.  

The backgrounder further states that the inaugural WAVES Summit in 2025 involved participants from more than 100 countries and generated ₹1,328 crore in business transactions through WAVES Bazaar, underscoring the commercial scale of the ecosystem and its relevance to media, content, and technology stakeholders. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that the document does not announce a traditional legal obligation or statutory deadline, but it does identify new platform features, distribution channels, and content-sourcing mechanisms that may require review of licensing, content rights, monetization arrangements, and participation terms for any organization engaging with WAVES OTT, MyWAVES, or related WAVES initiatives.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Whole-of-Industry Approach to Advance India’s Electronics and Semiconductor Ecosystem
rows.desc: SEMICON India 2026 highlights industry collaboration, semiconductor projects, PLI support and a Silicon to Systems approach for India’s electronics growth.The post Whole-of-Industry Approach to Advanc
rows.summary:
This PIB backgrounder is not a binding regulation or rule change; it is a government-industry policy update describing a shift toward a coordinated “whole-of-industry” model to accelerate India’s electronics and semiconductor ecosystem. The main message is that semiconductor fabrication, electronics manufacturing, components, materials, design, packaging, and end-use applications are becoming increasingly interconnected, so industry bodies and participants are being encouraged to collaborate more deeply rather than operate in silos. At SEMICON India 2026, stakeholders discussed creating a permanent community mechanism for ongoing dialogue and collective action, while explicitly preserving the specialized roles of existing associations and institutions.  

For compliance and strategic planning purposes, the document indicates that the Government continues to actively support the sector through the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes and the India Semiconductor Mission, and that this policy environment is intended to reinforce domestic manufacturing and capabilities. It states that the Government has approved 12 semiconductor projects under the Semicon India programme, and that five commercial semiconductor units were already operational as of September 2026. The SEMICON India 2026 event itself was large-scale, with more than 600 exhibitors, including nearly 300 international companies, and it produced 56 memoranda of understanding, strategic initiatives, and industry announcements spanning manufacturing, design, packaging, AI, R&D, logistics, and skilling.  

The practical compliance takeaway is that companies active in these value chains should expect increased emphasis on cross-sector coordination, ecosystem participation, and alignment with broader “Silicon to Systems” objectives that integrate design, manufacturing, packaging, electronics, and technology solutions into a resilient supply chain. No specific reporting deadline, filing obligation, penalty, or mandatory compliance procedure is introduced in the text, but the document signals continuing government-led ecosystem development and a policy direction that may affect investment planning, partnership strategies, localization efforts, and participation in industry forums or government-supported initiatives.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Domestic PNG Connection Incentive Scheme Offers Additional APM Gas Allocation
rows.desc: Domestic PNG incentive scheme offers CGD entities 200 SCM additional APM gas per eligible incremental billed connection to accelerate household coverage.The post Domestic PNG Connection Incentive Sche
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas has launched the **Incentive Scheme for Promotion of Domestic PNG Connections** to speed up active household piped natural gas connections nationwide and improve the economics of City Gas Distribution (CGD) operations. The scheme was **launched on 18 August 2026** and is **effective from 1 September 2026**, and it runs for **six months**, implemented in **two tranches**. It is intended to provide households with cleaner, safer, and more affordable piped cooking gas, while also increasing the commercial viability of domestic connections for CGD entities operating in India’s authorized **309 Geographical Areas** across the mainland.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirement is that **eligible CGD entities** that add **billed domestic PNG connections above the prescribed minimum for each Geographical Area** will receive an **additional allocation of 200 Standard Cubic Metres (SCM) of domestically produced Administered Price Mechanism (APM) gas for each qualifying incremental connection**. This is not a blanket allocation; it is tied specifically to incremental billed domestic connections beyond the minimum threshold applicable to the relevant Geographical Area. The document indicates that this additional APM gas allocation is meant to displace costlier **LNG currently used for the CNG transport segment**, thereby lowering gas sourcing costs and improving domestic connection payback economics.

The stated policy impact is that the availability of cheaper APM gas may reduce the payback period for a domestic connection from **about 10 years to nearly 3 years**. The scheme is accompanied by several supporting measures that compliance and operations teams should note: an **Accelerated Approval Framework**, **uniform pipeline Right-of-Way charges**, encouragement for States to reduce **VAT on natural gas to 5 percent**, **National PNG Drive 2.0**, and development of a **unified PNG registration portal**. The background figures provided show the scale of the market the scheme is targeting: as of **18 August 2026**, there were **1.74 crore domestic PNG connections** already in existence.

For corporate compliance teams, the practical implication is that CGD entities should verify eligibility against the scheme’s geographic and connection-count criteria, track **billed** domestic connection additions carefully, and ensure they can substantiate incremental connections for purposes of claiming the extra **200 SCM per qualifying connection**. Any entity involved in CGD operations should also monitor implementation details of the two-tranche rollout, as well as any state-level tax, land/access, and registration changes that may affect execution and reporting under the scheme.

rows.title: Corporate Law | CCPA Imposes ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Rapido for Dark Patterns and Misleading Tipping Prompts
rows.desc: CCPA penalises Rapido ₹10 lakh for misleading tipping prompts, confirm shaming and interface interference in its ride-booking interface.The post CCPA Imposes ₹10 Lakh Penalty on Rapido for Dark Patter
rows.summary:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), led by Chief Commissioner Smt. Nidhi Khare and Commissioner Shri Anupam Mishra, has imposed a monetary penalty of ₹10 lakh on Roppen Transportation Services Private Limited, the operator of Rapido, after finding that its ride-booking interface used misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices, an unfair contract, and dark patterns. The enforcement action arose from a sector-wide review of pre-ride tipping and dynamic pricing practices used by cab and bike-taxi aggregators, indicating that this was not an isolated review but part of a broader regulatory scrutiny of ride-hailing platforms.

CCPA found that Rapido’s prompts—specifically language such as “Higher the price, higher the chance of getting a ride” and the in-app requests to add ₹10, ₹20, or ₹30 after a ride had been booked at a quoted fare—misled consumers into believing that paying extra would improve the likelihood of getting a ride. The authority treated this as “Confirm Shaming” under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023, because the design and messaging pressured or nudged users toward paying more by implying they would otherwise be less likely to obtain service. It also found that Rapido’s colour-coded “Set your price” slider amounted to “Interface Interference,” because the interface design steered users toward higher fare selections rather than presenting a neutral choice.

A further compliance issue identified by CCPA was the timing of tipping: the authority noted that a tip is ordinarily voluntary and is given after a service is rendered, while the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025 require tipping features to be available only after completion of the ride. Rapido was unable to produce data showing that paying additional amounts actually increased ride availability, which undermined any claim that the prompts were informational or operationally justified. As a result, CCPA ordered Rapido to discontinue the misleading prompts and practices that steer consumers toward paying more.

For compliance teams in ride-hailing, taxi aggregation, and other consumer-facing digital platforms, the key takeaway is that interface design, wording, and timing of payment prompts are now clearly being treated as enforceable consumer-protection issues, not merely product-design choices. The decision underscores that tipping prompts should not be presented before service completion and that any feature or message suggesting that higher payment improves service access must be backed by evidence and must not mislead consumers. The document also notes that scrutiny of other ride-hailing platforms is continuing, so similar tipping, pricing, or “choose-your-price” features may attract enforcement if they can be seen as coercive, deceptive, or structurally biased toward higher payments.

rows.title: Corporate Law | GATC Network Expands Legal Metrology Verification Infrastructure Across India
rows.desc: Government expands GATC network for Legal Metrology verification, with 51 centres recognised and applications under process for 23 instrument categories.The post GATC Network Expands Legal Metrology V
rows.summary:
The Department of Consumer Affairs, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public Distribution, is expanding India’s Legal Metrology verification infrastructure by widening the Government Approved Test Centre (GATC) network under the amended Legal Metrology (Government Approved Test Centre) Rules, 2013. The key change is that GATCs are now authorized to cover 23 categories of weighing and measuring instruments, extending verification capacity across healthcare, energy, transport, retail, manufacturing, infrastructure, and clean-energy sectors. The expanded scope specifically includes water, gas and energy meters; breath analysers; vehicle speedometers; weighing instruments; and dispensers for petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG, LNG, and hydrogen.

For compliance purposes, this means verification activity is no longer limited to the narrower earlier framework, and entities operating or manufacturing the covered instruments may be subject to broader access to approved verification facilities as the network grows. The Ministry says fresh applications from industries, laboratories, and technical institutions are currently under review, with scrutiny focused on documentation, verification infrastructure, qualified personnel, and site inspection, so prospective GATCs must be prepared to demonstrate technical capability and compliance readiness. At present, 51 GATCs have already been recognized, and additional applications are still being considered.

Several States have also finalized and notified their own GATC Rules to align with the amended central framework, indicating that implementation is moving into state-level enforcement and administration as well. The policy objective is to supplement State Legal Metrology infrastructure so that Legal Metrology Officers can concentrate on market surveillance, risk-based inspections, enforcement, and consumer grievance redressal, while technically competent verification capacity is expanded nationwide. The notice is dated 15 September 2026 and reflects an ongoing expansion initiative rather than a single one-time deadline-driven filing requirement.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Biometric Aadhaar Authentication Mandatory for Subsidised LPG Refills From 1 October 2026
rows.desc: Domestic LPG consumers must complete Biometric Aadhaar Authentication to book subsidised refills at regulated prices from 1 October 2026.The post Biometric Aadhaar Authentication Mandatory for Subsidi
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas has announced that, effective **1 October 2026**, **domestic LPG consumers** must have completed **Biometric Aadhaar Authentication (BAA)** in order to book **subsidised refills** at the regulated **Retail Selling Price (RSP)** with the applicable subsidy. Consumers who have already completed BAA do **not** need to repeat the process, and consumers who have not yet authenticated may still become eligible for subsidised refills once BAA is completed. Authentication can be done **during cylinder delivery** through the OMC mobile application, **at the LPG distributor’s showroom**, or through the relevant **OMC mobile app**.

Consumers who are **unwilling or unable** to complete BAA may still receive LPG, but they must register that choice through the OMC’s digital channels and will be supplied LPG **without subsidy** at the **applicable market price**, in **5 kg or 10 kg cylinders**, and only **subject to local availability**. This means the new requirement does not stop supply altogether, but it changes the pricing and product availability for consumers who do not complete authentication. The Government says the measure is intended to **prevent diversion of subsidised domestic cylinders**, **remove duplicate and ineligible connections**, and **ensure targeted subsidy delivery**.

As of **19 September 2026**, **27.43 crore** active domestic LPG consumers had already completed BAA, representing **89.9% coverage**, so those consumers are already compliant and need no further action. The Government also noted that the **implicit subsidy for September 2026** was about **₹210 per 14.2 kg cylinder**, and that accumulated **under-recoveries of public sector OMCs exceeded ₹62,000 crore as on 31 August 2026**. For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that, from 1 October 2026, booking a subsidised domestic LPG refill will require verified BAA status, while non-authenticated consumers must either authenticate or accept non-subsidised, market-priced supply through the designated digital registration process.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Multiple Cheques Create Separate Causes of Action under Section 138 of NI Act: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court holds each dishonoured cheque can create a separate cause of action under Section 138 NI Act despite arising from the same transaction.The post Multiple Cheques Create Separate Causes of
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court in **Sumit Bansal v. M/s MGI Developers and Promoters & Anr.** clarified that when **multiple cheques are issued for the same transaction and underlying liability**, each cheque is treated separately for purposes of **Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881**. If each cheque is **presented, dishonoured, followed by a valid statutory notice, and the drawer still fails to pay within the prescribed time**, then **each dishonour can generate its own independent cause of action**, meaning **separate complaints may be filed for each cheque**; the claims do **not merge into one single cause of action** merely because they arise from the same transaction.

The Court also noted that, as a practical matter, **multiple dishonoured cheques from the same transaction may be included in a single consolidated complaint**, especially where a **common statutory notice** has been issued, consistent with earlier cases such as **Pawan Dhanpatrai Malhotra v. Mahender Khari** and **A. Adinarayana Reddy v. S. Vijayalakshmi & Anr.** This means a complainant is not limited to only one complaint format; the key point is that the **statutory ingredients for each cheque must be independently satisfied**.

On procedure, the Court reiterated that the **High Court’s inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be used sparingly**, and that at the quashing stage, the court should generally **not decide disputed questions of fact** such as whether a legally enforceable debt or liability actually existed. The **Section 139 presumption** continues to operate in favor of the complainant, and the accused must **rebut that presumption at trial**, not typically through premature quashing. So, for corporate compliance purposes, this decision reinforces that **dishonour exposure may arise cheque-by-cheque even within one underlying commercial deal**, and that challenges based on factual disputes about liability will ordinarily need to be litigated rather than disposed of at the threshold.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Registrar Cannot Impose Extra Condition Under Section 63: Karnataka HC
rows.desc: Karnataka HC holds Registrar cannot insist on outgoing partner’s signature to record partnership reconstitution under Section 63.The post Registrar Cannot Impose Extra Condition Under Section 63: Karn
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that a Registrar of Firms cannot refuse to record a change in a registered partnership firm’s constitution merely because the reconstituted deed does not bear the signature of the outgoing partner. The Court interpreted Section 63 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 to mean that a change in constitution may be notified by any incoming, continuing, or outgoing partner, and that the statute does **not** require the consent or signature of every partner as a condition for filing or recording the change. In practical terms, this means registrars cannot add an extra procedural hurdle not found in the Act—specifically, an outgoing partner’s signature cannot be treated as a mandatory prerequisite for recognition of the reconstitution.

The dispute arose in connection with M/s Y. Mahabaleshwarappa and Sons, a registered partnership firm engaged in mining business, which executed a reconstitution deed dated **26 November 2025**. Under that deed, **Y. Harish, Jyothi, and Ria** continued as partners, while **Y. Satish** ceased to be a partner. The Court noted that the reconstitution followed family disputes and related litigation, including **Com. O.S. No. 382 of 2021**, which was ultimately resolved through compromise.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that a firm seeking to update its registration under Section 63 should ensure the constitution-change filing is made by a legally permitted partner category and supported by the reconstitution deed, but it should not assume that the outgoing partner’s signature is required unless the statute or applicable rules expressly say so. The judgment is relevant to partnership firms and registrars handling registration updates, especially where a partner has exited amid internal disputes.

rows.title: Corporate Law | PIL Cannot Become Proxy Tender Dispute Between Rival Bidders: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court questions PIL challenging tender eligibility, allows contractor three months to complete road work at original rates.The post PIL Cannot Become Proxy Tender Dispute Between Rival Bidders
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court held that a Public Interest Litigation cannot be used as a proxy vehicle for a private tender dispute between rival bidders, even where the contract was awarded by a government authority. In **O.P. Mehta v. Mohinder Kalta & Ors., 2026 INSC 1037**, the Court said that challenges centered on a bidder’s **technical qualifications, experience, or eligibility** ordinarily concern the competing bidders’ **commercial interests**, not a genuine public interest issue, and therefore should not be converted into PIL litigation. The dispute arose from the **upgradation of the Matiana-Mahori-Chhaila road** under a **Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana** package, involving a project worth about **Rs. 23 crore**; the contract had been **awarded on March 15, 2024**.

The Himachal Pradesh High Court had quashed the road-work contract, but the Supreme Court interfered with that order and restored the contractor’s position, while stopping short of finally ending the case. Importantly for compliance and project execution, the Court gave the contractor **three months to complete the work** and directed that the matter be **listed again for a compliance report**. For entities involved in public procurement, the decision reinforces that tender award challenges framed as PILs will be scrutinized closely where the real issue is bidder eligibility or comparative merit, and it also shows that courts may impose a time-bound completion condition even while reconsidering an award.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 68 Additions Raise No Substantial Question of Law: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Calcutta HC upheld ITAT deletion of Section 68 additions, holding reasoned factual findings without perversity raise no substantial question of law.The post Section 68 Additions Raise No Substantial Q
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court in **PCIT v. Shelter Infra Projects Ltd.** held that the Revenue’s challenge to the deletion of **₹25.40 crore** in **section 68** additions did not raise any **substantial question of law** under **section 260A**, because the issues turned on factual findings already examined by the ITAT. The ITAT had deleted additions of **₹6.27 crore** and **₹19.13 crore** after considering the documentary record and **additional evidence** submitted before it, and the High Court accepted that the Tribunal gave detailed reasons for finding the transactions genuine; because the Revenue could not show any perversity in those findings, the appeal failed. The Court also held that submission of **additional evidence before the ITAT is legally permissible** in the circumstances considered in this case, so long as the Tribunal evaluates it and records reasons.

Procedurally, the Revenue’s appeal was filed with a **delay of 393 days**, but the High Court **condoned the delay** after finding sufficient cause. Even so, after reviewing the proposed questions in the memorandum of appeal, the Court concluded they were **essentially questions of fact**, not legal questions warranting High Court interference, and therefore **dismissed the appeal at the threshold** without calling on the assessee to argue further.

From the underlying tax history, the assessee had filed its return for **AY 2012-13** declaring **nil income**. The assessment was originally completed under **section 143(3)** at **₹33,00,66,403**, then the Principal Commissioner invoked **section 263** and the assessed income was revised to **₹33,11,79,425**; the CIT(A) later granted partial relief before the matter reached the ITAT and then the High Court. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this decision reinforces that **section 68 additions can be deleted at the appellate stage where the assessee substantiates the transactions with evidence**, and that High Court interference under **section 260A** is unlikely unless the Revenue can demonstrate a genuine legal issue or perversity in the Tribunal’s factual findings.

rows.title: Income Tax | AO Cannot Demand Negative Proof for Section 270AA Immunity: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Delhi HC sets aside Section 270AA immunity rejection; AO cannot demand negative evidence proving no appeal was filed and must reconsider application.The post AO Cannot Demand Negative Proof for Sectio
rows.summary:
In **Shantijanak Estates Private Limited v. ACIT (Delhi High Court), W.P.(C) 12741/2026, decided 17.09.2026**, the Court held that the Assessing Officer (AO) **cannot insist on “negative evidence”** as a condition for granting immunity under **section 270AA**. The assessee had paid the **entire tax demand of ₹37,99,340 on 22.04.2026**, before the payment due date of **26.04.2026**, and then filed an application on **27.04.2026 in Form 68** seeking immunity from penalty/prosecution consequences tied to the assessment.

The dispute arose from the assessment for **AY 2024-25**: the company, engaged in **letting out immovable property**, had declared **₹5,43,52,210** as income under the head **“Profits and Gains of Business or Profession,”** but the AO completed the assessment under **section 143(3) read with section 144B** by order dated **27.03.2026**, recharacterized the rental receipts as **“Income from House Property,”** and determined total income at **₹6,68,07,690**. The AO also initiated **penalty proceedings under section 270A** on the allegation of under-reporting income.

The key compliance holding was that, for a section **270AA** immunity application, the assessee is **not required to prove a negative fact**—specifically, that **no appeal has been filed** against the assessment order. The High Court said that, at most, the AO may ask the assessee for a **declaration** that no appeal has been filed, but cannot reject immunity merely because the assessee did not furnish proof of the absence of an appeal. On that basis, the Court **quashed the rejection order** and restored the assessee’s right to be considered for section 270AA immunity in accordance with law.

For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that when an assessee has **paid the demand within the required time** and otherwise satisfies the section **270AA** conditions, the tax authority should not create additional documentary hurdles that require proving the non-existence of an appeal. The decision is especially relevant for taxpayers who want immunity after assessment orders involving **section 270A penalty initiation**, because it limits the AO’s ability to reject Form 68 applications on technical grounds unrelated to the statutory conditions.

rows.title: Income Tax | Foreign Bank Cannot Claim Domestic Tax Rate Under DTAA: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Calcutta HC holds foreign bank taxable at higher rate, denies head-office interest deduction without TDS and treats ATM as computer.The post Foreign Bank Cannot Claim Domestic Tax Rate Under DTAA: Cal
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court’s decision in **Royal Bank of Scotland N.V. v. Director of Income Tax (International Taxation), Kolkata** (ITA No. 699 of 2007, judgment dated **22.09.2026** as stated in the document) addresses four important international tax issues for a **foreign bank operating in India through a permanent establishment (PE)** under the **India–Netherlands DTAA**. The assessee, formerly **ABN Amro Bank N.V.**, argued that its Indian branch should be taxed at the **domestic company tax rate** under the DTAA’s **non-discrimination clause in Article 24(2)**. The High Court rejected that position, holding that a **foreign company and a domestic company are not similarly placed** for this purpose, so the Indian branch of a foreign bank cannot automatically claim the domestic tax rate merely by invoking the treaty non-discrimination provision.

The court also held that the **Indian PE cannot deduct interest paid to its overseas head office or foreign branches unless tax is deducted at source (TDS)** on such payment, so the claimed interest deduction was disallowed for want of TDS compliance. In addition, the assessee sought to **exclude interest received by the Indian branch from the head office**, but the document indicates the High Court dealt with that issue unfavourably to the assessee as part of the broader ruling against the claimed tax treatment of intra-entity interest flows. A further issue concerned **depreciation on Automated Teller Machines (ATMs)**: the bank sought the **higher depreciation rate applicable to computers**, and the High Court accepted that treatment, holding that **ATMs are to be regarded as computers** for depreciation purposes.

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that a **foreign bank with an Indian branch/PE cannot assume it can apply the lower domestic-company tax rate under a DTAA non-discrimination argument**, and it must ensure **TDS is properly analyzed and withheld** before claiming deductions for interest paid to head office or foreign branches. The ruling is relevant to **AY 2003-04** in the case, but its reasoning is important for ongoing cross-border branch structures and intra-group/ intra-entity payment arrangements.

rows.title: Company Law | Registered Office Change: Companies Act and Other Regulatory Compliance
rows.desc: Compliance for shifting registered office under Companies Act, Income Tax, GST, FEMA, trademark, patent, labour, EPFO and ESIC laws.The post Registered Office Change: Companies Act and Other Regulator
rows.summary:
A shift of a company’s registered office from one ROC jurisdiction to another ROC within the same State is not just an internal address update; it triggers a formal process under the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, plus a separate review of whether other regulatory registrations must also be updated. The corporate-law procedure requires Board approval first, then a Special Resolution, filing Form MGT-14, intimation to the Chief Secretary, an application to the Regional Director in Form INC-23, filing the Regional Director’s order through Form INC-28, and finally completing the registered-office change through Form INC-22. Rule 28 requires declarations covering workmen’s dues, creditors, pending prosecutions, and employee interests, so the company must be prepared to evidence that the transfer does not prejudice these stakeholders.

The document emphasizes that the registered-office change does not automatically amend every other registration: the company must separately assess whether its Income-tax profile and jurisdiction need revision, whether GST registration needs correction, and whether trademark, patent, FEMA, and labour-related records require updates. For GST specifically, a registered-office move alone does not require amendment unless the Principal Place of Business or Additional Place of Business recorded in the GST registration also changes; if that happens, Form GST REG-14 must be filed under Section 28 of the CGST Act read with Rule 19. In practice, this means the compliance team must distinguish between a pure corporate registered-office change and a change affecting the operational premises used for GST purposes.

The document also flags that establishment-level compliance must be reviewed separately for EPFO, ESIC, factory, and contract-labour registrations because those obligations follow the operational establishment, not necessarily the registered office. A registered-office shift and a relocation of the business premises may have different consequences, so the company should not assume that one filing covers all regimes. Overall, the core obligation is to complete the Companies Act filings for the registered-office transfer and then verify, one by one, whether corresponding amendments are required across tax, GST, intellectual property, foreign exchange/FEMA, and labour law registrations.

rows.title: Income Tax | Entire Bogus Purchase Addition Unsustainable When Sales Accepted: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Calcutta HC upholds 0.15% GP on disputed bullion purchases, holding factual ITAT findings raise no substantial question of law.The post Entire Bogus Purchase Addition Unsustainable When Sales Accepted
rows.summary:
This Calcutta High Court decision in **PCIT v. Utkarsh Rai** concerns an assessee engaged in **bullion trading** through a proprietorship concern, for which the Assessing Officer, in **AY 2020–21**, treated purchases totaling **₹85,13,92,096** as bogus and made an addition under **section 69C**. The AO’s basis was that the suppliers had not filed income-tax returns, their business activities allegedly did not match the assessee’s transactions, **section 133(6)** notices went unanswered, and there were alleged documentary discrepancies; however, the Tribunal found that the purchases could not be rejected in full because the assessee’s **sales were accepted**, which supported the existence of genuine trading activity.

The Kolkata Bench of the ITAT therefore restricted the disallowance to a **gross profit addition of 0.15%**, reflecting the commercial realities of bullion trade rather than treating the entire purchase amount as unexplained or nonexistent. The Revenue challenged that relief under **section 260A**, but the High Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the Tribunal’s conclusions were based on appreciation of the evidence and the particular characteristics of bullion dealings. The Court emphasized that the Revenue had not shown any **perversity**, disregard of material evidence, or any substantial question of law that would justify interference.

For compliance purposes, the practical point is that in this case the tax authorities’ attempt to convert the full disputed purchase value into a bogus expenditure addition failed where the business’s **sales were accepted** and the Tribunal found the transaction pattern consistent with genuine trade, even though supplier-level compliance was weak. The ruling does **not** create a blanket safe harbor for unsupported purchases, but it shows that, in bullion trading, tax exposure may be limited to a profit element rather than the entire purchase figure when the factual record supports actual sales and the appellate fact-finding is not shown to be irrational.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Cross-FIR Not Automatic Merely Because Complaint Is Counter-Version: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Delhi HC refuses cross-FIR or fresh CBI case where complaints were verified and no illegality, arbitrariness or jurisdictional failure was shown.The post Cross-FIR Not Automatic Merely Because Complai
rows.summary:
This Delhi High Court decision holds that a dissatisfied complainant cannot force the CBI to register a cross-FIR or fresh criminal case merely because he disagrees with how the agency verified or assessed his allegations. In **Jitendra Pratap Singh v. Union of India & Ors. (W.P.(CRL) 2903/2023, decided 22.09.2026)**, the petitioner—an Indian Revenue Service officer posted with the Enforcement Directorate in Ahmedabad—had earlier been named in a **CBI case registered on 22.09.2015** relating to the conduct of an investigation into **cricket betting and related financial transactions**. A **chargesheet** had already been filed before the competent court at Ahmedabad for offences under the **IPC** and the **Prevention of Corruption Act**, and those proceedings were still pending.  

The petitioner later complained about the conduct of ED and CBI officers and wanted a fresh criminal case, effectively seeking a **cross-FIR** against senior officers based on his allegations. The Court refused to issue such a direction, emphasizing that where the complaints had already been examined by the competent investigative agency—here, after directions of the **Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)**—the High Court’s extraordinary powers under **Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution** read with **Section 482 CrPC** cannot be used simply to obtain a preferred investigative result.  

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that **mere dissatisfaction with a verification process or investigation outcome does not create an entitlement to a new FIR or cross-case**, especially when the matter has already been considered by the authorized investigative machinery. The ruling reinforces that courts will not substitute their view for the investigative agency’s judgment absent a legally cognizable basis, and it limits attempts to use writ or inherent criminal jurisdiction to compel a second investigation against officers involved in prior proceedings.

rows.title: Income Tax | Pending CIT(A) Appeal Bars Parallel Writ on AO Jurisdiction: Delhi High Court
rows.desc: Delhi HC declined writ against assessment as CIT(A) appeal was pending since 2020, but directed disposal within two months.The post Pending CIT(A) Appeal Bars Parallel Writ on AO Jurisdiction: Delhi H
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court held that an assessee generally cannot pursue a writ petition under Article 226 challenging an assessment order when a statutory appeal against that same order is already pending before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), even if the assessee argues that the Assessing Officer lacked jurisdiction. In this case, Raj Sheela Growth Fund Pvt. Ltd. challenged an assessment order dated 31.12.2019 passed under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, but the company had already filed a CIT(A) appeal on 24.01.2020, and that appeal was still pending nearly seven years later. The Revenue raised a maintainability objection on the ground that the assessee could not keep the appellate remedy alive and simultaneously invoke the High Court’s extraordinary writ jurisdiction against the same assessment order.

Although the Court did not entertain the writ as a parallel remedy, it was concerned that the CIT(A) appeal had remained undecided for an unusually long period, since January 2020. To address that delay, the Court directed the appellate authority to dispose of the pending appeal within two months. The practical compliance takeaway is that where an assessment is already under statutory appeal, the taxpayer should expect the High Court to refuse a duplicative writ challenge, and the proper focus should be on obtaining timely adjudication in the appellate forum rather than seeking simultaneous constitutional review.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | FEMA NOC Rejection Without Investigation Nexus Set Aside: Karnataka HC
rows.desc: Karnataka HC upholds ED seizure scrutiny but sets aside FEMA overseas investment NOC rejection for lack of reasoned nexus.The post FEMA NOC Rejection Without Investigation Nexus Set Aside: Karnataka H
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court held that regulatory approval of individual steps in a cross-border restructuring does **not** shield the overall arrangement from scrutiny under FEMA, and it upheld the Enforcement Directorate’s action under **Section 37A of FEMA** against Genpact. The case arose from Genpact group restructuring that began in **2015**, when **Empower Research Knowledge Services Pvt. Ltd. (Empower India)** was used as the Indian vehicle for consolidating the group’s India operations; in **January 2015**, the Singapore holding company borrowed about **USD 660 million** from Morgan Stanley and received an additional **USD 77.50 million** from its holding company, which was then infused as foreign direct investment into Empower India. Empower India then used about **USD 737.50 million (around ₹4,528 crore)** to acquire **49%** of Old Genpact India, and the structure also involved **Genpact Luxembourg**, which had obtained **Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI)** registration and subscribed to shares as part of the arrangement.

For compliance purposes, the ruling means that a company cannot rely on the fact that the **RBI, SEBI, or Income-tax Department** separately accepted or approved parts of a transaction to argue that the entire transaction is immune from FEMA review. The ED is permitted to examine the **connected arrangement as a whole** to determine whether it resulted in a violation of **Section 4 of FEMA** (which restricts dealing in foreign exchange or foreign security except as permitted). The practical compliance takeaway is that multinational restructuring, upstreaming of funds, and share acquisition structures must be assessed not only step-by-step for local approvals, but also for their **overall substance, funding source, and end-use**, because an otherwise approved component can still be scrutinized if the integrated transaction is alleged to violate FEMA.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | RBI Notifies ₹4,850 Crore Exim Bank Line of Credit for Maldives Projects
rows.desc: RBI announces Exim Bank’s ₹4,850 crore GOI-supported Line of Credit for financing developmental projects in Maldives.The post RBI Notifies ₹4,850 Crore Exim Bank Line of Credit for Maldives Projects a
rows.summary:
The document announces that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has notified a Government of India-supported Export-Import Bank of India (Exim Bank) line of credit of ₹4,850 crore for financing developmental projects in the Maldives. The notice indicates that the facility is specifically tied to projects in the Maldives and is intended to support development there through Exim Bank financing, with the Government of India backing the arrangement.

From a compliance perspective, the key material point is that this is a formal RBI notification of a sovereign-supported overseas lending facility, so any internal parties involved in Exim Bank financing, Indian cross-border lending, sovereign support arrangements, or project financing to Maldives-linked counterparties should treat this as an official credit line authorization. The document does not provide operational details such as drawdown dates, repayment terms, interest rates, eligible project categories, borrower identities, or reporting deadlines, so no additional procedural obligations can be inferred from the text beyond recognizing the existence and scale of the ₹4,850 crore facility and its Maldives development purpose.

rows.title: Service Tax | Service Tax Demand on Farm Trading Turnover Remanded: Karnataka HC
rows.desc: Karnataka HC quashes service tax order and remands matter to examine whether turnover from trading in farm products is taxable.The post Service Tax Demand on Farm Trading Turnover Remanded: Karnataka
rows.summary:
The Karnataka High Court partly allowed the writ petition in **Sudarshan Reddy Dhanireddy v. Additional Commissioner of Central Tax**, setting aside the **Order-in-Original dated 06.02.2023** that had been passed under **Section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994** on the basis of information received from the **Central Board of Direct Taxes**. The petitioner argued that **no show cause notice was served** and that, if given notice, he could have shown that the amounts reported in his income-tax returns arose from **trading in farm products**, which he claimed was **exempt from GST/service tax**; he relied on earlier Karnataka High Court decisions restoring similar matters for reconsideration and for filing a detailed reply with supporting documents. The department countered by pointing to the order’s observation that the petitioner had not filed any response or attended personal hearings, but the Court held that the core issue had not been properly examined: namely, whether the petitioner’s turnover from **farm-product trading** was actually **liable to service tax** at all.

The Court found that this taxability question had to be addressed before any enforceable liability could be sustained, so it **quashed the adjudication order dated 06.02.2023** and **remanded the matter for fresh consideration**. Although the document excerpt cuts off before spelling out the full remand directions, the practical compliance implication is that the demand is **not finally upheld** and the matter must be **re-adjudicated after giving the assessee a proper opportunity to respond and produce evidence** on the nature of the farm-trading turnover and its tax treatment. No new rates, thresholds, or substantive tax rule changes are announced in this decision; the key compliance point is procedural and evidentiary: where a demand is based on income-tax data but the taxpayer asserts the turnover is from exempt or non-taxable farm-product trading, the authority must examine that claim before confirming service tax liability.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Expired Railway Way Leave Cannot Be Revived Through Resolution Plan: Calcutta HC
rows.desc: Calcutta HC upheld quashing of expired Way Leave Permission revived after seven years without safety audit or hearing affected party.The post Expired Railway Way Leave Cannot Be Revived Through Resolu
rows.summary:
The Calcutta High Court held that an expired railway way leave permission cannot be brought back to life through a resolution plan, particularly where the permission had lapsed years earlier and the railway authority did not follow the required safety and procedural steps before purporting to revive it. In this case, a way leave permission had expired and was later attempted to be revived after a gap of seven years, but the Court upheld the quashing of that revival because it was done without a fresh safety audit and without hearing the affected party.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that railway-related access permissions are not automatically resurrected by corporate restructuring, insolvency, or resolution-plan language if the underlying permission has already expired; a fresh, lawful process is still required. The ruling underscores that when a right of way or way leave has lapsed, the authority must conduct the necessary safety assessment and provide due process, including giving the impacted party an opportunity to be heard, before any renewed grant or reinstatement can be validly issued.  

This decision affects entities relying on railway way leave permissions, especially companies involved in infrastructure, logistics, industrial access, or insolvency resolution where such permissions are part of the asset package. Compliance teams should treat expired access permissions as non-revivable by assumption and verify whether any attempted continuation or revival is supported by current authorization, proper safety review, and procedural fairness.

rows.title: Income Tax | Section 14A Addition Unsustainable When Own Funds Exceed Investments: Madras HC
rows.desc: Madras HC deleted Section 14A disallowance as Karur Vysya Bank had sufficient own funds exceeding its tax-free investments.The post Section 14A Addition Unsustainable When Own Funds Exceed Investments
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court held in **Karur Vysya Bank Ltd. v. CIT** that the bank was **not subject to a Section 14A disallowance or Rule 8D proportionate expenditure allocation** for the relevant exempt-income investments, because the material on record showed that the assessee’s **own interest-free funds—its equity capital and demand deposits—exceeded the value of the investments generating tax-free income**. The appeals covered **AYs 1996–97, 1997–98, and 1998–99**, and the Court allowed all three Tax Case Appeals in full, answering the substantial questions of law **in favour of the assessee and against the Revenue**, with **no costs**.

For compliance purposes, the key holding is that where a taxpayer can demonstrate that investments yielding exempt income were made out of **sufficient own funds**, the tax authorities cannot mechanically presume that interest-bearing borrowed funds were used and therefore cannot make a **proportionate interest disallowance** under Section 14A. The Court expressly relied on the Supreme Court’s ruling in **South Indian Bank Ltd.** for the principle that **no proportionate disallowance of interest is warranted when own funds exceed exempt-income investments**. The Court also noted the assessee’s position that **no expenditure had been incurred or claimed** for earning the exempt income and that the accounts were maintained under the **Banking Regulation Act**; however, the decisive factor was the sufficiency of own funds relative to investments. The document also references the earlier decision of **20.02.2026** as having already addressed the issue between the parties, but the excerpt does not provide a separate statutory change, deadline, or new filing procedure beyond the litigation outcome and the affirmation that **Section 14A/Rule 8D disallowance was unsustainable on these facts**.

rows.title: Custom Duty | No Interest on MOOWR Capital Goods Intended for Warehouse Use: Rajasthan HC
rows.desc: Rajasthan HC holds Section 61(2) interest inapplicable to MOOWR capital goods intended for use in a Section 65 warehouse.The post No Interest on MOOWR Capital Goods Intended for Warehouse Use: Rajasth
rows.summary:
The supplied text is not the Rajasthan High Court ruling itself; it is the opening/contents page of **The Finance Bill, 2016** (Bill No. 18 of 2016), which lists proposed amendments across direct-tax provisions and related areas. On its face, the document does **not** set out the substantive custom-duty/MOOWR ruling described in the title, nor does it provide the actual legal reasoning or operative directions from the court; instead, it is a legislative index showing that the bill would amend many sections of the Income-tax Act and add several new ones.

From a compliance perspective, the only concrete information available here is that the bill was **introduced in Lok Sabha** as Finance Bill, 2016, and it proposes broad tax-law changes spanning income-tax, deductions, exemptions, capital-gains provisions, presumptive taxation, transfer pricing, advance pricing, and minimum alternate tax.
