The table of contents specifically flags new or revised provisions such as changes to sections **2, 6, 9, 10, 10AA, 17, 24, 28, 32, 35, 36, 40, 43B, 44AA, 44AB, 44AD, 47, 48, 50C, 54EE, 54GB, 55, 56, 80, 80CCD, 80EE, 80GG, 80-IA, 80-IAB, 80-IAC, 80-IB, 80-IBA, 80JJAA, 87A, 92CA, 92D, 112, 115BA, 115BBDA, 115BBE, 115BBF, and 115JB**, among others. However, because the excerpt stops at the contents page and the substantive text is missing, **no effective dates, thresholds, tax rates, compliance deadlines, procedural requirements, or impacted entities can be reliably extracted from this document alone**.

If your compliance team needs the actual substance of the **“No Interest on MOOWR Capital Goods Intended for Warehouse Use: Rajasthan HC”** matter, you would need the court judgment/order text itself rather than this Finance Bill index. As provided, the document is insufficient for determining whether any warehouse operators, importers, MOOWR participants, or customs-duty taxpayers have new obligations or relief, and it should not be treated as a rule-change summary for that topic.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CAAR Delhi Rejects Roasted Areca Nut Classification Applications Citing Prior HC Decision
rows.desc: CAAR Delhi rejected five roasted areca nut classification applications under Section 28-I(2)(b), without ruling on classification.The post CAAR Delhi Rejects Roasted Areca Nut Classification Applicati
rows.summary:
M/s Ganpati Trader filed five advance ruling applications on 12.06.2026 before the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings (CAAR), Delhi, seeking a classification ruling for roasted areca nuts proposed to be imported into India in whole, cut, and split forms. The applications were numbered 36–40/2026-27, and a personal hearing was held on 08.09.2026, at which the applicant’s advocate repeated the written submissions.  

CAAR Delhi first examined whether the applications were even maintainable under the first proviso to Section 28-I(2) of the Customs Act, 1962. It noted that an advance ruling application cannot be admitted if the same question is already pending in the applicant’s own case before a customs officer, the Appellate Tribunal, or a court, or if the same question has already been decided by the Appellate Tribunal or a court. The Authority distinguished between a case-specific pending matter and a question already settled by a higher judicial forum, and emphasized that subordinate authorities must follow binding precedent.  

On that basis, CAAR held that the requested classification issue was already covered by the Madras High Court decision in *M/s Shahnaz International Pvt. Ltd.* [2023 (386) E.L.T. 214 (Mad.)]. Because the legal issue had already been decided by a court, CAAR declined to issue any classification ruling and rejected the applications under Section 28-I(2)(b). For compliance purposes, the key point is that the order does not create a new tariff position for roasted areca nuts; it simply blocks the requested advance ruling because the issue was treated as foreclosed by existing High Court precedent.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST TCS for E-Commerce Operators: Section 52, GSTR-8 and 0.5% Rate
rows.desc: GST TCS under Section 52 explained with 0.5% rate, GSTR-8, e-commerce compliance, Section 9(5), ONDC models and reconciliation.The post GST TCS for E-Commerce Operators: Section 52, GSTR-8 and 0.5% Ra
rows.summary:
The document explains that under Section 52 of the CGST Act, certain electronic commerce operators must collect tax at source on the net value of taxable supplies made through their platforms by other suppliers when the operator collects the consideration. This TCS is not a separate tax in place of GST on the underlying supply; it is mainly a collection, reporting, and transaction-tracking mechanism, and the amount collected is credited to the supplier’s electronic cash ledger. As a result, platform operators need tight reconciliation between marketplace transaction data, GST filings, and supplier books so the correct amount is collected and properly reflected.

A key change highlighted is the reduction in the effective TCS rate, which applies from 10 July 2024. For qualifying intra-State supplies, the rate is now 0.5% total, split as 0.25% CGST and 0.25% SGST/UTGST; for qualifying inter-State supplies, the rate is 0.5% IGST. The document states that this reduction is intended to ease working-capital pressure for businesses while preserving the digital audit trail created through GST reporting.

Compliance obligations focus on reporting through GSTR-8 and accurate payment of TCS by the e-commerce operator. The document emphasizes that operator records must support transaction-level classification and matching so the TCS reported in GSTR-8 aligns with the underlying taxable supplies, because the credit ultimately flows to the supplier’s electronic cash ledger. This makes automated reconciliation, data governance, and timely filing operationally important for affected platforms.

The document also warns that Section 52 TCS must be clearly distinguished from the separate GST liability under Section 9(5), where the e-commerce operator itself becomes liable to pay GST on specified services. It notes that contemporary platform arrangements, including multiple e-commerce operator structures and ONDC-type models, make correct classification especially important. The compliance takeaway is that operators should determine whether they are acting only as a collector under Section 52 or are themselves liable under Section 9(5), then apply the correct rate, filing process, and reconciliation controls accordingly.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Supreme Court Upholds Service Tax Exemption for IIT Patna and NIT Rourkela
rows.desc: Supreme Court holds statutory IIT and NIT institutions qualify as governmental authorities under amended service tax exemption clause 2(s).The post Supreme Court Upholds Service Tax Exemption for IIT
rows.summary:
The Supreme Court addressed whether IIT Patna and NIT Rourkela qualified as a “governmental authority” under Mega Service Tax Exemption Notification No. 25/2012-Service Tax dated 20 June 2012, as amended by Notification No. 02/2014-Service Tax dated 30 January 2014, for purposes of service tax exemption on specified construction services. The exemption, issued under section 93 of the Finance Act, 1994, included clause 12(c), which covered construction of structures predominantly meant for use as educational, clinical, or art/cultural establishments; the dispute was whether construction work for these institutes fell within that exempt category because the recipient entities themselves met the amended definition. Before the 30 January 2014 amendment, “governmental authority” required at least 90% Government participation by equity or control, a statutory basis of establishment, and performance of a municipal function under Article 243W, but the amendment replaced that with two alternative limbs: an authority or board set up by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature, or an authority/board/body/entity established by Government with 90% or more equity or control and entrusted by Government, by law, with functions under Article 243W.  

The case arose from two connected civil appeals: one from the Patna High Court’s 3 March 2016 judgment, which ordered refund of service tax collected on construction at IIT Patna, and another from the Orissa High Court’s 5 February 2018 judgment, which relied on the Patna ruling and directed reconsideration of SPCL’s refund claim for construction at NIT Rourkela. The Supreme Court held that IIT Patna and NIT Rourkela are institutes of national importance established under Parliamentary legislation and therefore fall within the amended “governmental authority” definition; on that basis, construction services provided to them were eligible for the exemption. For compliance purposes, the practical result is that service tax already collected on qualifying construction services for these institutions was held refundable/incorrectly levied under the exemption framework, and the judgment confirms that entities established by central legislation in this manner should be treated as covered by the amended notification for the relevant period after the amendment’s effective date.

rows.title: Income Tax | BVGF Seeks Tax Audit Due Date Extension to 31 October 2026
rows.desc: BVGF urges CBDT to extend AY 2026-27 tax audit deadline to 31 October and audit-case ITR due date to 30 November 2026.The post BVGF Seeks Tax Audit Due Date Extension to 31 October 2026 appeared first
rows.summary:
Bhartiya Vaishya Global Foundation is asking the CBDT to extend the tax-audit filing deadline for AY 2026-27 from **30 September 2026 to 31 October 2026**, and to push the corresponding **income-tax return due date in audit cases from 31 October 2026 to 30 November 2026**. The representation is directed to the Chairman, CBDT, and is dated **22 September 2026**; it relies on the Board’s power under **section 119** to grant deadline extensions and notes that CBDT did so in the prior year, extending the audit date from **30 September 2025 to 31 October 2025**.

The core compliance argument is that the statutory timeline under **section 44AB** only works when the accounting format is settled early, the filing utilities are stable, and auditors have sufficient uninterrupted time, but the petitioner says none of those conditions have been met for AY 2026-27. A major issue cited is that on **31 March 2026**, ICAI announced a mandatory new Guidance Note format for **non-corporate entities**—including **proprietorships, firms, HUFs, AOPs, and trusts**—applicable from **FY 2025-26** for entities with **turnover above ₹5 crore**, meaning books maintained all year in the old structure now have to be regrouped into **current/non-current classification** and aligned to the new format at year-end.

The letter also states that the change was announced at the very end of the financial year, leaving businesses and auditors without adequate time to adapt. It further emphasizes that the affected taxpayer base is large and includes **traders, manufacturers, MSMEs, proprietary concerns, partnership firms, family-owned companies, and the professionals serving them**, many of whom fall within the **44AB tax-audit** population. The practical request is therefore not just for more time to file audit reports, but also for a cascading extension of the linked return-filing deadline so audited taxpayers are not forced to file returns before completing and reviewing their audits.

The submission says it is endorsed by other professional bodies, specifically the **CA Association, Jalandhar (6 Sep 2026)**, the **Rajasthan Tax Consultants Association (8 Sep 2026)**, and **AIMTPA (16 Sep 2026)**, among others. In compliance terms, the document is a policy/advocacy request rather than a binding rule change, but if granted it would directly change the filing calendar for audit cases to **31 October 2026 for tax audit reports** and **30 November 2026 for returns**.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Composition Levy: Eligibility, Rates, ITC Limits and Trade-Offs
rows.desc: Analysis of GST Composition Levy covering eligibility, rates, ITC restrictions, e-commerce changes, compliance and economic trade-offs.The post GST Composition Levy: Eligibility, Rates, ITC Limits and
rows.summary:
The document explains that the GST Composition Levy is a simplified tax regime for eligible small taxpayers under Section 10 of the CGST Act, 2017 and the CGST Rules, but it comes with material commercial trade-offs, especially the loss of ordinary input tax credit. In general, taxpayers may opt in if their aggregate turnover is within the prescribed threshold of ₹1.5 crore, with a lower ₹75 lakh threshold for specified States; it also notes a separate pathway under Section 10(2A) for certain taxpayers with aggregate turnover up to ₹50 lakh. Because composition taxpayers cannot generally claim normal ITC, GST paid on inputs becomes a cost embedded in pricing, which can reduce B2B competitiveness, so eligibility and economics must be reviewed before opting in.  

The document emphasizes that compliance officers should treat composition status as an ongoing eligibility condition rather than a one-time election: the taxpayer must continuously monitor turnover and other restrictions relating to the nature and territorial scope of supplies to ensure continued qualification. It also notes that one PAN cannot ordinarily maintain both composition and regular registrations, so registration structure must be managed carefully across the enterprise. The scheme is intended to reduce filing and reporting burden, but this simplification only applies within the statutory limits and restrictions set out in Section 10 and the rules.  

A key development highlighted is that the Finance Act, 2023 allowed eligible composition taxpayers to make supplies of goods through specified electronic commerce operators, which represents a relaxation of earlier marketplace limitations. The document also says later procedural changes extended the GSTR-4 filing deadline, so composition taxpayers must follow the revised annual/periodic return timetable rather than older due dates.  

For compliance purposes, the main operational issue is that the scheme remains a trade-off between lower compliance burden and reduced tax neutrality: businesses need to assess whether the tax savings and simpler filings outweigh the inability to claim ITC and the constraints on supply channels. The document’s overall point is that the composition levy can be useful for small businesses, but only if they remain within the turnover thresholds, respect the statutory restrictions on business activity and market reach, and keep pace with the updated procedural requirements.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Labour Codes for Banks: RBI Compliance, Governance and Audit Implications
rows.desc: Labour Codes impact banks through payroll, outsourcing, social security, governance, financial reporting, RBI compliance and statutory audit.The post Labour Codes for Banks: RBI Compliance, Governance
rows.summary:
This document explains that India’s four Labour Codes, which consolidate 29 central labour laws, are not just a labour-law change but a significant compliance issue for banks because they affect governance, risk management, financial reporting, and audit under RBI expectations. It states that banks employ a mixed workforce of permanent staff, contractual employees, outsourced workers, security personnel, housekeeping staff, and technology professionals across multiple jurisdictions, so compliance must extend beyond HR to all employment-related arrangements and vendor-managed labour. The key regulatory point is that RBI’s **Commercial Banks – Compliance Function Directions** require banks to have systems to identify and manage compliance risks arising from **all applicable laws**, which would include these Labour Codes; the document also notes that banks are beginning to assess and disclose the **financial implications** of the Labour Codes in line with RBI’s financial reporting framework.

The document does **not** give a single commencement date or a specific implementation deadline in the excerpt provided, but it frames the issue as an active compliance and audit matter that banks must address as part of ongoing governance and reporting. It highlights that the **Code on Wages** has particular implications for banks because it introduces a **uniform definition of “wages,”** which can require salary-structure review, recalculation or reclassification of employee benefits, and payroll audit adjustments to ensure statutory components are correctly identified. For compliance officers, this means bank payrolls, benefit schemes, and employment contracts may need review to verify whether allowances and deductions are being treated consistently with the new wage definition and whether any statutory contributions or payouts change as a result.

The document also indicates that the **Industrial Relations Code** affects banking employment and trade-union related issues, which is material because banking institutions often have structured employee relations frameworks and, in many cases, active union engagement. Overall, the compliance burden described is not limited to direct employees: it extends to outsourced and third-party workforce arrangements, meaning banks must verify whether service providers’ staffing models, labour practices, and documentation meet legal requirements and do not create compliance exposure for the bank. The article is written for compliance officers, internal auditors, and statutory central auditors, signaling that the Labour Codes should be treated as a cross-functional regulatory issue with implications for controls, disclosures, and audit evidence rather than only a legal or HR matter.

rows.title: Income Tax | GST on Online Gaming: 40% Rate, Gameskraft Ruling and Prohibition
rows.desc: GST on online gaming after Gameskraft, Rule 31B, 40% rate and prohibition of online money gaming under the 2025 Act.The post GST on Online Gaming: 40% Rate, Gameskraft Ruling and Prohibition appeared
rows.summary:
India’s GST treatment of online gaming has shifted materially in three stages, and compliance teams should treat the current position as a combination of the 2023 GST amendments, the Supreme Court’s 2026 Gameskraft ruling, and the 2025 rate increase. Effective 1 October 2023, the Central Goods and Services Tax (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced express definitions of “online gaming,” “online money gaming,” and “specified actionable claims,” and Rule 31B of the CGST Rules, 2017 established a special valuation rule for these supplies. The GST Council had originally recommended GST at 28% on the full amount paid or deposited by the player, regardless of whether the game involved skill or chance, and the document states that Rule 31B made the amount staked the relevant valuation base.

The legal position was reinforced by the Supreme Court in Directorate General of Goods and Services Tax Intelligence (HQS) v. Gameskraft Technologies Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., 2026 INSC 595, decided on 27 May 2026. The Court held that online gaming transactions involving stakes on uncertain outcomes create actionable-claim interests that fall within the GST framework, that the gaming platform itself can be treated as the supplier, and that the staked amount is consideration for GST purposes. The Court upheld the relevant GST provisions, rejected constitutional challenges to the levy, and treated the 2023 amendments as clarificatory and retrospective to the extent described in the judgment, which means the GST framework is not limited to future-only application from that amendment date.

Separately, the GST rate for specified actionable claims, including online money gaming, was increased from 28% to 40% pursuant to the 56th GST Council meeting, with effect from 22 September 2025. For compliance purposes, this means businesses offering online money gaming or otherwise dealing in specified actionable claims must apply the 40% GST rate from that date onward, and they must value the tax base using the amount staked/deposited under Rule 31B rather than trying to distinguish the levy based on skill versus chance. The document indicates that India’s regulatory framework also moved toward prohibition, so companies in this sector should assess not only GST collection and invoicing but also whether the underlying activity remains legally permitted under the post-prohibition regime.

rows.title: Income Tax | Income Tax Reassessment Must Be Independent of GST Adjudication: Madras HC
rows.desc: Madras HC declined to quash Section 148 notice but held Income Tax authorities must independently reassess and cannot rely solely on GST adjudication.The post Income Tax Reassessment Must Be Independe
rows.summary:
The Madras High Court considered a writ challenge to a reassessment notice issued under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for AY 2023-24, dated 27.05.2026, where the asserted basis for reopening was an earlier GST adjudication order dated 03.02.2025 passed under the applicable GST laws. The taxpayer argued that the GST order was already under appeal and therefore subject to a deemed stay, and further contended that Section 148(3) permits reassessment to be founded on information from a Tribunal or Court, not merely on an adjudication by a GST proper officer; the concern was that parallel income tax action could produce inconsistent findings. The Revenue responded that the issue had already been addressed in the Section 148A(3) order and maintained that income-tax reassessment must be undertaken independently, rather than mechanically adopting the GST adjudication outcome.

The Court held that initiation under Section 148A(1) requires “information” suggesting escapement of income, and that the statutory definition of “information” under Section 148(3) is broad enough to include information received in line with the CBDT’s risk management strategy. However, the Court noted that no material was placed before it showing what that risk management strategy actually provided, or whether it expressly covered GST adjudication orders as a permissible input for reassessment. Because the matter was still at the preliminary notice stage, the Court declined to interfere with the reassessment proceedings. The practical compliance takeaway is that tax authorities may proceed with reopening only on the basis of statutorily valid “information,” and the Court emphasized that income-tax reassessment cannot simply mirror GST adjudication; it must be independently examined by the Income Tax Department, with proper statutory grounding.

rows.title: Income Tax | Demonetisation Cash Sales Explained by Books and VAT Returns: ITAT Jaipur Deletes Section 69A Addition
rows.desc: ITAT Jaipur deletes Section 69A addition for demonetisation cash deposits where cash sales were supported by books and accepted VAT returns.The post Demonetisation Cash Sales Explained by Books and VA
rows.summary:
The document reports an Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) Jaipur ruling deleting an addition made under Section 69A in a demonetisation-era case involving cash deposits. The key outcome is that cash deposited during the demonetisation period was held to be explained by genuine cash sales, because those sales were supported by the taxpayer’s books of account and were consistent with accepted VAT returns. In other words, where a taxpayer can demonstrate that cash receipts were recorded in the regular books and reflected in statutory tax filings such as VAT returns, the tribunal accepted the source of the cash and rejected the unexplained-money addition.

For compliance purposes, the practical implication is that businesses handling cash sales during demonetisation or similar high-scrutiny periods should maintain strong documentary linkage between cash collections, book entries, and indirect tax filings. The ruling underscores that the revenue authority cannot sustain a Section 69A addition merely because cash was deposited into the bank after demonetisation if the taxpayer can substantiate the cash origin with contemporaneous records. No specific filing deadline, rate, or statutory change is mentioned in the text; the document is a case result rather than a new rule.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Taxable Value Under Section 15: Transaction Value, Discounts & Valuation Rules
rows.desc: Analysis of GST taxable value under Section 15 covering transaction value, inclusions, discounts, related parties and CGST valuation rules.The post GST Taxable Value Under Section 15: Transaction Valu
rows.summary:
This document is a legal/compliance discussion of how taxable value is determined under Section 15 of the GST Act, 2017, and its main point is that GST should be computed on the “transaction value” only when the supplier and recipient are unrelated and the price is the sole consideration. It explains that taxable value is not limited to the invoice amount: the value can also include certain taxes and charges, incidental expenses, amounts the recipient pays on the supplier’s behalf, interest or penalties charged for delayed payment, and subsidies directly linked to the price of supply. For compliance teams, the key operational requirement is to ensure that valuation is supported by proper invoices, agreements, and other records so the business can justify what was included in or excluded from taxable value.

The document also stresses that discounts may be excluded from taxable value only when the statutory conditions are met, so discount treatment must be documented and not assumed automatically. It highlights that special valuation provisions can apply when the ordinary transaction-value rule cannot be used, meaning the company must assess whether a transaction falls outside the standard rule before calculating GST. This is especially relevant for related-party dealings, non-monetary or partially non-monetary arrangements, and other transactions where the price is not the full legal measure of value.

A major compliance warning in the document is that incorrect valuation can cause tax shortfalls, additional GST liabilities, interest exposure, and disputes with tax authorities. The blog frames Section 15 as a framework designed to promote consistency and transparency in valuation, but it also makes clear that taxpayers must analyze the actual nature of each transaction rather than relying only on the face value of the invoice. No specific amendment date, deadline, or numerical threshold/rate is provided in the text beyond the general reference to Section 15 of the GST Act, 2017.

rows.title: Company Law | Different NCLT Jurisdictions in Scheme Proceedings: Filing, Transfer & Effective Date
rows.desc: NCLT jurisdiction for Sections 230–232 schemes, Rule 16(d) transfer between Benches and Effective Date where separate NCLT orders are passed.The post Different NCLT Jurisdictions in Scheme Proceedings
rows.summary:
The document explains how territorial jurisdiction works in scheme proceedings under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013 when the transferor and transferee companies are registered in different NCLT territories. The core rule is that each company should ordinarily file and proceed before its own jurisdictional NCLT Bench based on its registered office; the fact that both companies are parties to the same Scheme of Arrangement or Amalgamation does **not** by itself allow one Bench to assume jurisdiction over a company outside its territory.  

If the same scheme is already pending before different Benches, Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 allows the President of the NCLT, where appropriate, to transfer a pending matter from one Bench to another so that one Bench can hear the connected matters together. The document cites **JAK Builders** as an example of this transfer mechanism, while **M.M. Castings Pvt. Ltd.** and the **Minda TG Rubber Pvt. Ltd. / Toyoda Gosei Minda India Pvt. Ltd.** proceedings are cited as examples where separate proceedings were allowed to continue before the respective jurisdictional Benches rather than being collapsed into one forum.  

A key compliance point is the treatment of the scheme’s **Effective Date** when separate NCLT Benches sanction the same scheme. The Effective Date does **not** automatically become the date of the second NCLT sanction order; instead, it is determined strictly by the wording and conditions in the sanctioned scheme itself. In the example discussed, where the scheme defines the Effective Date as the date on which the **last sanction order is filed with the Registrar of Companies (ROC)**, that later ROC filing date governs as the Effective Date.  

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that filing strategy, jurisdiction analysis, and scheme timing must be managed bench-by-bench unless a formal transfer is ordered under Rule 16(d). Companies should ensure the scheme documents clearly define the Effective Date and any conditions precedent, because that definition will control when the scheme becomes effective for legal and corporate purposes, including ROC filings and implementation timing.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Incomplete Bank Trail Fails to Lift NDPS Property Freeze: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA Tribunal upholds NDPS flat freezing as bank statements, loan documents and repayment evidence failed to establish lawful source.The post Incomplete Bank Trail Fails to Lift NDPS Property Freeze
rows.summary:
This tribunal decision under SAFEMA/NDPS is important for compliance because it confirms that a person cannot defeat a property freeze merely by producing income-tax returns, a Chartered Accountant’s certificate, or a partial loan statement if the underlying banking and funding records are incomplete or withheld. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the freezing of a residential flat after authorities linked the property to a major narcotics case involving a recovery on 16 August 2022 of 225.053 kg of Mephedrone (stated value about Rs. 1,125.26 crore), Rs. 14 lakh in cash alleged to be sale proceeds of contraband, and 1,753.300 kg of Alprazolam from the premises of Nectar Chem, a partnership firm at Village Moksi, Vadodara. The appellant and four others allegedly associated with the firm were arrested for manufacturing and selling narcotic substances without a licence, and the tribunal noted that the quantities involved were “commercial quantity,” meaning the statutory NDPS consequences were triggered.

The compliance takeaway is that once property is identified within the statutory period and the person is treated as an “affected person,” the burden shifts to that person under Section 68-J to prove that the property was not acquired from illicit income. In this case, the tribunal held that the appellant failed to discharge that burden because the evidence submitted did not include the relevant bank statements, loan sanction documents, or proof of repayment that would have demonstrated a legitimate source of funds for the flat. The tribunal therefore accepted the authority’s position that incomplete financial documentation is insufficient to rebut the presumption against property linked to narcotics proceeds.

For compliance teams, the practical implication is that asset provenance defenses must be supported by a complete documentary trail, especially where there is any connection to NDPS-linked entities, partners, or funds. If a property or other asset is challenged as having been acquired from illicit proceeds, the organization or individual must be prepared to produce full bank records, loan approval documents, disbursement details, and repayment evidence—not just tax filings or accountant certifications—to establish lawful source.

rows.title: Income Tax | BookMyShow Convenience Fee Not Commission Under Section 194H: ITAT Bangalore
rows.desc: ITAT Bangalore rules on BookMyShow convenience fee under Section 194H and quashes AY 2013-14 TDS order as time-barred.The post BookMyShow Convenience Fee Not Commission Under Section 194H: ITAT Bangal
rows.summary:
The ITAT Bangalore held that the “convenience fee” charged by BookMyShow is **not “commission”** for purposes of **Section 194H** of the Income-tax Act, meaning BookMyShow was **not required to deduct TDS under that provision** on the fee. The tribunal therefore **quashed the TDS order for Assessment Year 2013–14**, not on the merits alone but because the order was also found to be **time-barred**.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this ruling addresses the tax characterization of platform convenience fees collected in the online ticketing context: if the fee is a service/convenience charge retained by the platform and not an amount paid as commission to an agent for services in procuring sales, Section 194H may not apply. The document does **not** provide any new statutory amendment, rate change, or general deadline beyond the fact that the challenged order related to **AY 2013–14** and was struck down as barred by limitation. In practical terms, entities collecting similar convenience or service fees should review whether their fee structure, contractual arrangements, and payout mechanics create any agency/commission relationship that could trigger TDS obligations, but this document itself is a case-specific tribunal ruling rather than a new rule.

rows.title: Income Tax | Revised Return Correcting F&O Loss Classification Must Be Considered: ITAT Mumbai
rows.desc: ITAT Mumbai restores F&O loss claim where revised return corrected speculative loss classification without introducing any fresh loss.The post Revised Return Correcting F&O Loss Classificati
rows.summary:
The ITAT Mumbai held that the Assessing Officer should not have ignored the assessee’s revised return under section 139(5) for AY 2016-17, where the taxpayer corrected the treatment of Futures and Options derivative loss from a “speculative business loss” to a “non-speculative business loss.” The assessee had originally filed the return on 02.09.2016, disclosed the F&O loss, and mistakenly classified it in a way that affected carry-forward treatment; after noticing the error, it filed a revised return on 17.11.2016, recomputing the set-off to the extent permissible and carrying forward the balance. The Tribunal emphasized that the overall business loss did not materially change: it was Rs. 1,26,05,069 in the original return and Rs. 1,26,05,073 in the revised return, while the amount claimed for carry forward actually reduced from Rs. 1,24,57,323 to Rs. 83,82,855.

The AO had rejected the revised return on the basis that a return claiming business loss should have been filed within the time limit under section 139(1), and the CIT(A) affirmed that approach by relying on the Supreme Court decision in PCIT v. Wipro Ltd. (446 ITR 1). The ITAT disagreed, noting that section 43(5)(d) excludes eligible derivative transactions undertaken on a recognized stock exchange from the definition of speculative transactions, subject to the prescribed conditions, so the correct legal character of the F&O loss had to be applied. In substance, the ruling means that where a taxpayer timely files a revised return within the section 139(5) framework to correct an erroneous classification of derivative/F&O loss, the tax authorities should consider the revised computation rather than mechanically disallow it merely because the original return used the wrong loss category. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is to ensure proper initial classification of derivative transactions under section 43(5)(d), but also that corrected treatment in a valid revised return can be significant for set-off and carry-forward positions where the underlying loss amount is not otherwise changing.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Anti-Dumping Duty on Decor Paper Extended Till 26th March 2027
rows.desc: Notification No. 23/2026-Customs (ADD) extends anti-dumping duty on Decor Paper under Notification 77/2021 till 26 March 2027.The post Anti-Dumping Duty on Decor Paper Extended Till 26th March 2027 ap
rows.summary:
The Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) issued Notification No. 23/2026-Customs (ADD) on 22 September 2026, amending Notification No. 77/2021-Customs (ADD) dated 27 December 2021, which imposes anti-dumping duty on Decor Paper. The amendment was made under sections 9A(1) and 9A(5) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, read with rules 18 and 23 of the Anti-Dumping Rules, 1995.  

The substantive change is the insertion of a new paragraph 3 in the principal notification. This new paragraph provides that, notwithstanding paragraph 2 of the original notification, the anti-dumping duty on Decor Paper will remain in force up to and inclusive of 26 March 2027, unless it is revoked, superseded, or amended earlier. In other words, the duty’s applicability period has been extended, and importers of Decor Paper remain subject to the existing anti-dumping duty regime through that date unless a further legal change occurs first.  

For compliance purposes, any entity importing Decor Paper into India should continue to apply the anti-dumping duty under Notification No. 77/2021-Customs (ADD) as extended by this amendment, and should monitor for any further revocation, supersession, or amendment before 26 March 2027. The notification also notes that the principal notification had previously been amended by Notification No. 19/2025-Customs (ADD) dated 24 June 2025.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Pre-Offence Property Can Be Attached as Equivalent Value Under PMLA: SAFEMA
rows.desc: SAFEMA holds pre-offence and legitimately acquired property can be attached as equivalent value of unavailable proceeds of crime under PMLA.The post Pre-Offence Property Can Be Attached as Equivalent
rows.summary:
The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA held that under the PMLA, property can be attached not only when it is directly “proceeds of crime,” but also when it represents the “equivalent value” of those proceeds. In practical terms, this means a property acquired before the alleged scheduled offence, or even property acquired from legitimate and otherwise explained sources, may still be attached if it is being treated as value substitution for the actual proceeds of crime. The Tribunal also rejected the idea that merely holding property in a spouse’s name provides automatic protection: property standing in the name of the accused’s wife was treated as attachable where the facts showed that the accused had partly or substantially funded the acquisition.

The case concerned two residential properties in Jogeshwari and Bandra, Mumbai, with an aggregate market value of about Rs. 8.58 crore. These properties were attached in the context of an investigation into Geodesic Limited and its directors. Geodesic had raised USD 125 million through Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds in 2008 for overseas investment/acquisition, with redemption due in October 2013 at a maturity value of approximately USD 157.06 million. The Enforcement Directorate alleged default in repayment and used the attachment power in relation to the suspected laundering of funds tied to that default.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that PMLA attachment exposure is not limited to assets purchased after the offence or assets purchased from unexplained money; pre-offence assets and assets acquired through legitimate funds can still be targeted if authorities treat them as substitute value for the alleged crime proceeds. Ownership through a family member, including a wife, is not a safe harbor if the accused has effectively financed the purchase. The Tribunal did, however, indicate that the appellants should retain physical possession of the residential properties during pendency of the prosecution, except in exceptional circumstances, so attachment did not automatically mean immediate dispossession.

rows.title: Income Tax | CBDT Amends TDS Rules for Non-Resident Immovable Property Transfers
rows.desc: CBDT notifies Income-tax (Fifth Amendment) Rules, 2026, revising TDS rules and Forms 132 and 141 for immovable property transfers.The post CBDT Amends TDS Rules for Non-Resident Immovable Property Tra
rows.summary:
The CBDT has issued Notification No. 121/2026-Income Tax, dated 22 September 2026, making the **Income-tax (Fifth Amendment) Rules, 2026**, which take effect **from 1 October 2026**. These rules further amend the Income-tax Rules, 2026, specifically **rules 215, 218 and 219 and Appendix III**, to align tax deduction at source (TDS) reporting and procedure with **section 393(2) of the Income-tax Act, 2025** for cases where a **resident individual or Hindu undivided family (HUF)** is required to deduct tax on consideration paid for the **transfer of immovable property**.

Substantively, **rule 215** is expanded to cover these TDS deductions, and corresponding updates are made to **rules 218 and 219** to reflect the new reporting/compliance framework. The notification also amends **Form No. 132** so it expressly covers transfers of immovable property by a **non-resident to a resident individual or HUF**, while updating related references and notes. In addition, **Form No. 141** is revised to include **section 393(2) transactions** and to add a new **Schedule E** dedicated to reporting TDS on consideration for transfer of immovable property.

Schedule E introduces detailed reporting obligations: it requires disclosure of the **property particulars**, **buyer and non-resident seller details**, **stamp duty value**, **sale consideration**, **instalment information**, **capital gains particulars**, the **applicable TDS rate**, any **certificate under section 395**, and the **tax deducted**. It also requires additional identification and contact information for the non-resident deductee, including **contact details, overseas address details, tax residency certificate information, and tax identification numbers**. For compliance teams, the key operational takeaway is that from **1 October 2026**, transactions involving **resident individual/HUF purchasers deducting TDS on payments for immovable property transfers involving non-residents** will require updated forms and enhanced transaction-level reporting consistent with the amended rules and schedules.

rows.title: Corporate Law | IBBI Flags Delay in RTI Reply on Research Associates and Consultants
rows.desc: IBBI FAA finds delayed RTI disposal violated Section 7 timeline but closes appeal after CPIO satisfactorily provided the information.The post IBBI Flags Delay in RTI Reply on Research Associates and C
rows.summary:
The document concerns an RTI appeal involving the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) and focuses on the timeliness of the response provided by the Central Public Information Officer (CPIO). The First Appellate Authority (FAA) found that the RTI request was not disposed of within the statutory timeline prescribed under Section 7 of the RTI Act, meaning the information was delayed beyond the required deadline, which is a procedural non-compliance relevant to public authorities handling information requests. The subject matter of the RTI request was information relating to research associates and consultants, and the appeal arose because the response was not provided on time.

Although the FAA identified this delay as a violation of the Section 7 timeline, the appeal was ultimately closed because the CPIO later furnished the requested information satisfactorily. In practical compliance terms, the key point is that public bodies must ensure RTI requests are processed within the prescribed statutory period, even if the substantive information is eventually supplied, because delayed disposal can still be treated as a procedural lapse. No additional substantive regulatory requirement, threshold, fee, or sector-wide rule change is described in the text beyond this timing obligation and the fact that the appeal was resolved after disclosure.

rows.title: Corporate Law | IBBI Flags Delay in RTI Reply but Closes Appeal After Satisfactory Disposal
rows.desc: IBBI FAA notes violation of RTI Act Section 7 timeline but closes Priyanka Sony’s appeal after satisfactory disposal of her application.The post IBBI Flags Delay in RTI Reply but Closes Appeal After S
rows.summary:
The document reports an RTI appeal outcome from the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI). It states that the First Appellate Authority (FAA) found that IBBI had violated the Right to Information Act, 2005, by not issuing its reply within the statutory Section 7 timeline, which ordinarily requires a response to an RTI application within 30 days. However, the appeal filed by Priyanka Sony was ultimately closed because the underlying RTI application was considered satisfactorily disposed of by the time the appeal was reviewed.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that IBBI was formally flagged for delay in responding to an RTI request, underscoring the need for public authorities to meet the RTI Act’s prescribed response deadlines. The document does not describe any broader policy change, penalty, or substantive disclosure issue beyond this procedural lapse and the subsequent closure of the matter after the information request was adequately addressed.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | ICAI Warns Against Wrong UDIN Category to Bypass 60 Tax Audit Ceiling
rows.desc: ICAI warns CAs against using incorrect UDIN categories to bypass the 60-tax-audit ceiling effective from 1 April 2026.The post ICAI Warns Against Wrong UDIN Category to Bypass 60 Tax Audit Ceiling app
rows.summary:
ICAI has clarified how the new UDIN-based cap on tax audit assignments will work under the **Chartered Accountants (Limit on Number of Tax Audits) Guidelines, 2025**. The ceiling is **60 tax audit assignments per financial year per member**, and it **takes effect from 1 April 2026**. For purposes of counting toward that ceiling, only the specified “applicable sub-categories” under the **Tax Audit** UDIN category will be included—namely **Form 3CA under the third proviso to Section 44AB**, **Form 3CB under Section 44AB(a)**, **Form 3CB under Section 44AB(b)**, and **combined Form 3CB under Section 44AB**.

ICAI has also stated that certain other **Form 3CB sub-categories under clauses (c), (d), and (e)** are treated as **non-applicable sub-categories** for ceiling computation, meaning they are not to be used to evade the 60-audit limit. The Institute says it has observed some members trying to bypass the notified cap by generating UDINs under these non-applicable categories, and has warned members to generate UDINs **only under the correct category** and **within the prescribed limits**. If a member deliberately uses the wrong UDIN category to circumvent the ceiling, ICAI says the member may face proceedings under the **Chartered Accountants Act, 1949** and the rules made thereunder.

The document’s compliance message is therefore twofold: first, firms and individual CAs must ensure that tax audit UDINs are classified correctly so the 60-per-financial-year limit is counted properly; second, they should treat incorrect categorization as a disciplinary and regulatory risk, not just a technical filing error. The FAQs referenced in the document further confirm that the ceiling is enforced **through the UDIN system**, making accurate category selection part of the compliance process for every tax audit engagement from the effective date onward.

rows.title: Finance | IFSCA Relaxes Qualified Jeweller Eligibility for Gold, Silver Imports Through IIBX
rows.desc: IFSCA relaxes Qualified Jeweller eligibility for DGFT-authorised entities importing gold or silver through IIBX.The post IFSCA Relaxes Qualified Jeweller Eligibility for Gold, Silver Imports Through I
rows.summary:
The IFSCA has amended the framework for importing gold and silver through the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) to make it easier for certain exporters/importers to qualify as “Qualified Jewellers.” Under Circular No. IFSCA-PMTS/10/2023-Precious Metals/2026/5 dated 22 September 2026, entities that hold a valid DGFT-issued Advance Authorisation, a valid Registration-cum-Membership Certificate (RCMC) from the Gem & Jewellery Export Promotion Council, or a DGFT authorisation to import under the specified relevant ITC (HS) codes may now apply through IIBX for notification by IFSCA as Qualified Jewellers. This is a relaxation of the earlier eligibility standard and was issued in response to stakeholder representations, with the stated objective of enabling more seamless and timely bullion imports.

The Circular also replaces the participation rules for these Qualified Jewellers. Going forward, they must participate in the IIBX process through a Bullion Trading Member, and any import activity must be limited to the authorised ITC (HS) codes and, where the importer is operating under an Advance Authorisation, only for the purpose covered by that authorisation. Compliance teams should treat this as an immediate-effective change: the amendments take effect at once and are already reflected in an updated Consolidated Circular that is being issued separately.

This Circular is binding on the IFSCA-regulated bullion ecosystem in the IFSC, including the Bullion Exchange, Bullion Clearing Corporation, Bullion Depository, bullion intermediaries, Vault Managers, and market participants on the Bullion Exchange. It has been issued under Sections 12 and 13 of the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019, read with Regulation 78 of the IFSCA (Bullion Market) Regulations, 2025, so the new eligibility and participation requirements should be incorporated into onboarding, eligibility verification, and import-control procedures without delay.

rows.title: Income Tax | Contractor Label Cannot Defeat Section 80-IA Developer Deduction: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: ITAT Chennai allows Section 80-IA deduction to EPC contractor acting as infrastructure developer and dismisses Revenue’s appeal.The post Contractor Label Cannot Defeat Section 80-IA Developer Deductio
rows.summary:
The ITAT Chennai held in **DCIT vs. Eco Protection Engineers Private Limited** that an assessee executing government infrastructure projects is **not disqualified from Section 80-IA(4) deduction merely because the contract labels it a “contractor.”** The key test is the substance of the arrangement: where the enterprise is responsible for **design, engineering, procurement, construction, erection, testing, commissioning, and maintenance**, and it bears the **financial, technical, and performance risks**, it is functioning as a **developer of infrastructure facilities** rather than a mere works contractor.  

For **Assessment Year 2017-18**, Eco Protection Engineers Private Limited reported **total income of Rs. 4.75 crore** and **book profit of Rs. 6.54 crore under Section 115JB**. It claimed a **Section 80-IA(4) deduction of Rs. 1,96,78,063** on profits from **four infrastructure projects** at **Rajkot, Periyakulam, Aizawl, and Agartala**, all executed for **Government / State Government agencies**. The related **gross receipts were approximately Rs. 32.01 crore**, and the company had filed the required **Form 10CCB audit report within the due date**.  

From a compliance perspective, the ruling reinforces that entitlement to the developer deduction depends on the **actual responsibilities and risk allocation** in the project, not on the title used in the agreement. A company performing turnkey infrastructure work may still qualify if it substantively develops the facility and assumes meaningful project risks, even if the contract uses “contractor” language. This matters for businesses in infrastructure, water supply, sewage treatment, and industrial effluent management projects that claim Section 80-IA benefits and need to document their developer status, scope of work, and timely audit-report compliance.

rows.title: Income Tax | Unproved Opening Cash Balance Cannot Support Cash Deposit Explanation: ITAT Amritsar
rows.desc: ITAT Amritsar restricted cash deposit addition to ₹13.10 lakh after accepting ₹18 lakh deposits as explained by prior withdrawals.The post Unproved Opening Cash Balance Cannot Support Cash Deposit Exp
rows.summary:
The ITAT Amritsar partly allowed Sukhwinder Singh’s appeal for AY 2017–18 and reduced the addition for unexplained cash deposits from ₹25.71 lakh to ₹13.10 lakh. The assessment had been completed ex parte under section 144 on 29.12.2019 after the assessee allegedly did not comply with section 142(1) notices, and the Assessing Officer treated cash deposits in the HDFC Bank account made between 17.05.2016 and 06.08.2016 as unexplained. The assessee was able to substantiate later pre-demonetisation cash deposits made from 11.11.2016 to 01.12.2016 with evidence of agricultural income, including sale receipts and a “J” Form, and those deposits were accepted as explained.

The dispute before the Tribunal centered on the assessee’s cash-flow explanation for the earlier deposits. The CIT(A) rejected the explanation because the document described as a cash flow statement was effectively a ledger, and several amounts the assessee characterized as cash withdrawals were actually cheque payments to third parties, so they could not create cash available for later redeposit. Before the Tribunal, the assessee filed a 218-page paper book without the certificate required under the ITAT Rules, and the paper book included a cash flow statement starting with an opening cash balance of ₹3 lakh as on 01.04.2016. However, the Tribunal held that there was no evidence showing how that opening cash balance was derived from the closing cash balance as on 31.03.2016, and this issue had not been examined in the lower proceedings.

On that basis, the Tribunal concluded that the unproved opening cash balance of ₹3 lakh could not be accepted as a source for the disputed deposits. At the same time, it accepted part of the remaining cash flow explanation and therefore restricted the addition to ₹13.10 lakh. For compliance purposes, the case reinforces that cash deposit explanations must be supported by a verifiable, continuous cash trail backed by contemporaneous evidence; an asserted opening balance is not enough if the prior-period closing balance and source of funds are not proved, and payments mislabeled as cash withdrawals may be disallowed if they were actually cheque payments to others.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Advocate Privilege Cannot Bar GST Search Into Lawyer’s Own Conduct: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Delhi HC upholds GST search at law firm, holding advocate-client privilege cannot bar investigation into an advocate’s own conduct.The post Advocate Privilege Cannot Bar GST Search Into Lawyer’s Own C
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court in **Puneet Batra v. Union of India & Ors.** upheld a **GST search and seizure** conducted at a law firm’s premises, including the Advocate’s cabin, and rejected the argument that **advocate-client privilege** barred the search. The Court found that where the authorities had **properly authorized a search under Section 67(2) of the Central GST Act, 2017** on the basis of **recorded “reasons to believe,”** the mere fact that the searched premises included an advocate’s office/cabin did not make the action unlawful. It further held that privilege is not an absolute shield for all material found in a lawyer’s office; the protection under **Section 132 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023** belongs to the **client**, and it does not prevent inquiry into the **advocate’s own conduct** when there is **prima facie material suggesting involvement beyond a purely legal-adviser role**.

The Court also clarified that the **absence of a show-cause notice (SCN)** did **not** invalidate either the search or the issuance of summons in this context. It rejected the contention that deviations from **administrative instructions or circulars** would automatically vitiate the search, holding that only a breach of a **mandatory statutory requirement affecting jurisdiction** would render the action void. At the same time, the Court preserved confidentiality safeguards: the tax department was directed to rely only on the **cloned data** and to confine its examination to information **relevant to the investigation**, so that **privileged communications and unrelated third-party client data** are not improperly reviewed or used.

For compliance purposes, the decision signals that **law firms and advocates are not immune from GST search and seizure** merely because the premises are legal offices, especially where the department has valid statutory authorization and reasons to believe. It also means that firms should expect that **devices, documents, and data may be seized or cloned** if investigators suspect the lawyer’s own participation in taxable or otherwise examinable conduct. However, the ruling simultaneously reinforces that the department must handle seized electronic data with **narrow relevance-based review** and respect bona fide **client privilege** for communications that fall within the protected scope.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | ITC in Special Circumstances: Special Rules for Preserving Input Tax Credit
rows.desc: Section 18 CGST Act governs ITC during registration, composition exit, taxable transitions, restructuring, transfers and special reversals.The post ITC in Special Circumstances: Special Rules for Pres
rows.summary:
Section 18 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 is the special transitional-credit rule for situations where a taxpayer’s GST status changes or a business is reorganized. It allows Input Tax Credit (ITC) to be preserved, transferred, or, where necessary, reversed when a person first becomes liable for GST registration, takes voluntary registration, shifts from the composition scheme to the normal GST regime, or starts making taxable supplies after previously making exempt supplies. The provision also applies to business transfers such as sale, merger, demerger, amalgamation, lease, or transfer of a business, and it is intended to ensure that legitimate accumulated credit is not lost merely because the business structure or tax status changes.

For the transition cases covered by Section 18, the taxpayer must comply with the procedural requirements in Rules 40 and 41 of the CGST Rules, including filing the relevant declarations in FORM GST ITC-01 and FORM GST ITC-02. These rules govern how unutilised ITC is claimed or transferred and impose documentary and timing conditions; the document emphasizes that Section 18 is not automatic relief, but a controlled mechanism subject to prescribed compliance. Rule 44 separately governs reversal of ITC in specified circumstances, meaning that where credit is no longer eligible, the taxpayer must reverse it rather than retain it.

A further compliance issue highlighted is transfer of credit across registrations in different States after an amalgamation, where GST portal limitations may block the mechanical transfer even though the statute allows it. In Umicore Autocat India Private Limited v. Union of India, the Bombay High Court allowed the transfer of relevant CGST and IGST credit despite the portal restriction, and the Gujarat High Court later addressed a similar dispute in Emerson Process Management (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that Section 18 can support preservation and transfer of credit in restructuring scenarios, but only if the taxpayer meets the statutory conditions, uses the correct forms, observes the applicable time limits, and is prepared to address portal-related filing issues where they arise.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Deleted Chats, Lost Evidence? Indian Law on Preserving Electronic Records Before Litigation
rows.desc: Indian law on preserving emails, WhatsApp chats and digital records when litigation is anticipated, including adverse inference and destruction risks.The post Deleted Chats, Lost Evidence? Indian Law
rows.summary:
This document explains that Indian businesses can face serious legal consequences if potentially relevant electronic evidence disappears through ordinary corporate processes such as email deletion, automated retention expiry, employee offboarding, device handover, or reassignment of business communication accounts. It emphasizes that India does not yet have a single standalone “litigation hold” statute with a precise trigger date, but once a commercial dispute is reasonably anticipated, companies should act as though preservation duties have effectively begun and stop routine deletion or recycling of potentially relevant material.

The key legal framework highlighted is Section 119 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which preserves the evidentiary principle associated with former Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872: courts may draw adverse or other appropriate presumptions from the circumstances when relevant evidence is withheld. The document also cites the Supreme Court’s decision in Gopal Krishnaji Ketkar v. Mohamed Haji Latif as important authority for adverse inference where a party had possession or control of relevant evidence but did not produce it. In addition, Section 241 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is identified as a criminal provision addressing destruction of documents or electronic records done with the intent to prevent their use as evidence.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Bribe Recovery Without Proof of Demand Cannot Sustain Conviction: SC
rows.desc: Supreme Court sets aside PC Act conviction as demand and conscious acceptance of alleged bribe were not proved beyond reasonable doubt.The post Bribe Recovery Without Proof of Demand Cannot Sustain Co
rows.summary:
The document reports a Supreme Court ruling under the Prevention of Corruption Act (PC Act) that sets aside a bribery conviction because the prosecution failed to prove, beyond reasonable doubt, the essential elements of demand and conscious acceptance of the alleged bribe. The Court held that mere recovery of currency notes, by itself, is not sufficient to sustain a conviction unless there is reliable proof that the accused actually demanded the bribe and knowingly accepted it. In this case, the conviction could not stand because the evidence did not establish the required demand/acceptance chain, so the benefit of doubt went to the accused.

For a corporate compliance team, the practical significance is that enforcement risk in bribery matters still turns on documentary and testimonial proof of solicitation and receipt, not just possession or recovery of funds. The ruling reinforces that allegations involving employee or intermediary payments should be assessed for evidence of an actual quid pro quo, explicit demand, and knowing acceptance, since these are the elements that authorities must prove. There are no new compliance deadlines, filing obligations, or threshold amounts announced in this item; it is a judicial clarification on the evidentiary standard applied in PC Act bribery prosecutions.

rows.summary:
The finance ministry said all public sector banks (PSBs) and regional rural banks (RRBs) must remain open on Sunday, September 27, 2026, in response to a planned three-day nationwide bank strike called by the United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) for September 28–30, 2026. This measure is intended to avoid a prolonged service disruption because the strike would otherwise run immediately after the preceding weekend holidays on September 26 and 27, creating a potential five-day interruption in access to banking services. The government described the action as a proactive step to protect citizens’ banking needs during the holiday-and-strike period.  

The Reserve Bank of India approved the opening of all bank branches, offices, ATM-linked branches, and currency chests on September 27, so the compliance expectation is not limited to customer-facing branches alone; operational support functions tied to cash handling and ATM servicing are also required to be available. The document does not state any special transaction limits, reporting forms, or penalties, but the practical requirement is that covered PSBs and RRBs should arrange staff and operations so normal banking services can continue on the designated Sunday despite the impending strike.

rows.title: IRDAI proposes sweeping insurance distribution overhaul; cuts EoM, caps commissions, targets mis-selling
rows.desc: Articles 11 min read IRDAI proposes sweeping insurance distribution overhaul; cuts EoM, caps commissions, targets mis-selling The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has proposed a five-year glide path to bring life insurers’ EoM to 12.5% and general insurers’ to 20%, while commission limits will be linked to product complexity, distribution channel and selling effort. IRDAI said the reforms seek to create a customer-centric, competitive, efficient and transparent distribution ecosystem. Advt The regulator's diagnosis is particularly sharp: insurance distribution costs have risen considerably even as the expansion in the number of insured people has remained limited. IRDAI said the 2023 EoM reforms, which gave insurers greater flexibility at the entity level, have not delivered the expected improvement in affordability, insurance penetration and customer value. Distribution costs have instead returned to historically high levels.Distributor payouts growing much faster than businessOne of the strongest data points in the consultation paper relates to the life insurance corporate agency channel. In a representative sample cover
rows.summary:
IRDAI has released a public consultation proposing a major redesign of India’s insurance distribution framework, with the stated goal of reducing high distribution costs, improving customer outcomes, and curbing mis-selling. The proposal would run on a **five-year glide path** and would bring **life insurers’ Expenses of Management (EoM) down to 12.5%** and **general insurers’ EoM down to 20%**. It would also replace the current broad flexibility on commissions with **segment-, product-, channel-, and effort-linked commission limits**, meaning payouts would no longer be treated as a largely entity-level commercial decision and instead would be tied to how complex the product is, through which channel it is sold, and the amount of selling effort involved.

The regulator’s rationale is that the **2023 EoM reforms** did not produce the intended gains in affordability, penetration, or customer value, and that distribution costs have climbed back to historically high levels even though the number of insured customers has not expanded meaningfully. IRDAI is specifically targeting a market structure that it says is overly dependent on premium acquisition, and is trying to shift incentives toward **affordability, persistency, quality of advice, servicing, and policyholder outcomes**. In other words, insurers and distributors would be expected to demonstrate value creation and customer suitability rather than simply volume-driven sales.

A key compliance implication is that **commission and distributor remuneration structures are expected to tighten materially**, especially for channels and products where sales effort is lower or where the products are simpler. The paper points to strong evidence that distributor payouts have been rising much faster than business growth, particularly in the **life insurance corporate agency channel**, which suggests this channel may be under closer scrutiny in the new framework. Insurers operating through corporate agents, brokers, individual agents, and other intermediaries should expect to review remuneration grids, product categorization, and channel economics once final rules are issued.

IRDAI also proposes to **ease entry into insurance distribution** and to build **digital, pull-based alternatives**, including **Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs)**. That suggests the regulator wants a broader, more competitive distribution ecosystem that reduces dependence on traditional push-selling models. For compliance teams, this likely means new obligations around distribution governance, product design oversight, channel controls, training, and monitoring of sales practices to ensure advice quality and customer suitability, especially if the final framework introduces differentiated rules for digital and traditional channels.

The consultation’s overarching compliance message is that insurers will likely need to adapt quickly to a more interventionist regime on distribution economics and conduct. Companies should anticipate formal changes to **EoM management, commission policy, channel strategy, and mis-selling controls**, with the five-year glide path implying phased implementation rather than an immediate overnight change.

rows.title: IRDAI proposes public mis-selling records, commission clawback to curb insurance sales malpractice
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read IRDAI proposes public mis-selling records, commission clawback to curb insurance sales malpractice The regulator wants customer suitability to become an enforceable obligation and proposes linking the identity of salespersons to policies sold, with mis-selling records made public and commissions clawed back. Anushka Sengupta ETBFSI Published On Sep 23, 2026 at 09:57 PM IST var news_msid = 134442466; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has proposed a tougher framework to tackle mis-selling of insurance, including mandatory suitability assessments, public disclosure of individual mis-selling records and commission clawbacks where a policy is found to have been mis-sold.The proposals form part of IRDAI's consultation paper released today, which identifies mis-selling as a major contributor to premature surrender of life policies and erosion of customer trust.Suitability to become an enforceable obligationIRDAI has proposed that every insurer and Insurance Distribution Entity (IDE) should have a detailed suitability framework. Advt For life insurance sales above a defined ticket size, a documented analysis of the customer's needs and suitability would be mandatory, supported by an audit trail.Importantly, the regulator proposes that simply obtaining a customer's consent or signature should not absolve the insurer or intermediary from responsibility for selling an unsuitable product.Where a customer chooses a product different from the one recommended through the suitability analysis, the reason for that choice would also have to be documented.The consultation paper specifically flags the practice of presenting endowment or other savings insurance products as fixed deposits or equivalent deposit products, particularly in bank-led distribution.12 forms of mis-sel
rows.summary:
IRDAI’s consultation paper proposes a materially stricter anti–mis-selling regime for insurers and insurance distribution entities (IDEs), with the core objective of making customer suitability an enforceable compliance obligation rather than a soft sales guideline. Under the proposal, every insurer and IDE would need a documented suitability framework, and for life insurance sales above a defined ticket size, a recorded assessment of the customer’s needs and product suitability would be mandatory, supported by an auditable trail. The regulator explicitly says that a customer’s consent or signature would not by itself protect the insurer or intermediary if the product sold was unsuitable, and if the customer chooses a product different from the one recommended in the suitability analysis, the reason for that deviation must also be documented.

The paper also targets bank-led and other distribution channels that present endowment or other savings-linked insurance products as if they were fixed deposits or comparable deposit products, identifying this as a specific mis-selling concern. In addition, IRDAI proposes linking the identity of the salesperson to the policy sold so that responsibility can be traced to the individual involved, rather than only to the institution. It further proposes making individual mis-selling records public, which would create reputational consequences for repeat or serious offenders and increase transparency for customers and regulators.

A key enforcement proposal is commission clawback: if a policy is later found to have been mis-sold, the commission paid on that sale could be recovered. The consultation also frames mis-selling as a driver of premature surrender of life policies and a source of erosion of customer trust, indicating that the proposed rules are intended to improve persistency as well as sales conduct. The excerpt does not provide the exact ticket-size threshold, implementation date, or the full list of the “12 forms of mis-selling,” so compliance teams would need to review the full consultation paper to identify the precise operational thresholds, timelines, and any channel-specific obligations once finalized.

rows.title: IRDAI proposes tighter commission caps as distributor payouts rise 125% against 28% premium growth
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read IRDAI proposes tighter commission caps as distributor payouts rise 125% against 28% premium growth The regulator has proposed an all-inclusive commission framework covering incentives, awards, reimbursements and non-cash benefits, with separate caps based on product, channel and distribution effort. Anushka Sengupta ETBFSI Published On Sep 23, 2026 at 09:52 PM IST var news_msid = 134442303; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has proposed a major overhaul of insurance distribution commissions, including hard caps linked to product complexity, distribution channel and the effort involved in selling and servicing a policy.The move comes after the regulator found that distributor remuneration in a representative corporate-agent sample grew 125% between FY23 and FY25, while new business premium increased 28% during the same period.Distributor remuneration grows 4-5 times faster than premiumAccording to IRDAI's consultation paper released today, the sample covers approximately 92% of premium procured through corporate agents. Advt Distributor remuneration now accounts for nearly 27% of first-year premium, with rewards and incentives adding another 30%-60% over the base commission.IRDAI said this means remuneration is growing four to five times faster than the business on which it is paid, making base commission alone an incomplete measure of the actual cost of distribution.The regulator also found wide variation in effective payouts across products. Effective payouts on ULIPs range from around 5% to nearly 40%, while other savings products attract effective commissions of 29%-60% of first-year premium, exceeding 65% in some cases.The NBFC corporate agency channel has nearly tripled since FY23, with effective payouts averaging around 42% of new business premium.
rows.summary:
IRDAI has proposed a major tightening and restructuring of insurance distribution compensation rules in India, aimed at controlling the rapid rise in payouts to distributors. The consultation paper says it will replace a base-commission-only view with an **all-inclusive commission framework** that would capture not just commission but also **incentives, awards, reimbursements, and non-cash benefits**, with **separate caps** depending on the **product type/complexity, distribution channel, and the effort involved in selling and servicing the policy**. The proposal was triggered by IRDAI’s finding that, in a representative corporate-agent sample covering about **92% of premium procured through corporate agents**, distributor remuneration rose **125% from FY23 to FY25**, while **new business premium increased only 28%** over the same period—meaning distributor pay was growing roughly **4–5 times faster** than the business generating it.

The regulator says distributor remuneration now represents **nearly 27% of first-year premium**, and that rewards/incentives can add an additional **30% to 60% on top of base commission**, so base commission alone understates actual distribution cost. IRDAI also identified large product-wise disparities: **ULIP effective payouts** range from around **5% to nearly 40%**, while other savings products have effective commissions of **29% to 60% of first-year premium**, and in some cases **exceed 65%**. The **NBFC corporate agency channel** has grown sharply—nearly **tripling since FY23**—with effective payouts averaging around **42% of new business premium**, which IRDAI appears to view as a particular area of concern.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that insurers and intermediaries should expect future rules to look beyond stated commission rates and assess the **full economic value of all distributor-linked payments and benefits**. Although the article does not provide a final effective date or implementation timeline, it indicates this is currently a **consultation-stage proposal**, so firms should monitor the final IRDAI framework for **product-specific and channel-specific caps**, and be prepared to re-map all distributor compensation structures—including cash and non-cash items—against the new all-inclusive measurement standard.

rows.desc: Articles 2 min read India must move from Make in India to Design, Innovate and Lead from India: PM’s Principal Secretary Mishra Principal Secretary to Prime Minister Narendra Modi Pramod Kumar Mishra said that rising trade barriers and supply-chain disruptions mean the country cannot count on a friendly trade agreement.
