Global supply chains are being reconstituted. Trade agreements are opening markets. Technology is changing the location and organization of production. India has an opportunity to move from being primarily a large market to becoming an important production and innovation hub,” Mishra said while speaking at 13th SBI Banking and Economic Conclave. Advt Mishra said the changing global environment also required India to strengthen domestic manufacturing and reduce its dependence on imports.“Second, our dependence on imports and not just on energy alone. We have a significant merchandise trade deficit. We must make things at home and competitively,” he said.He also addressed the broader changes taking place in global trade and supply chains, including the increasing use of supply chains as a strategic tool and the return of trade barriers.“First, alliances are fragmented. Supply chains are being used as weapons. Capital can be switched on and off. Trade barriers, both tech and non-tech, are rising again. We cannot count on a friend
rows.summary:
This is not a regulatory text with direct compliance deadlines or rule changes, but a policy statement from the Prime Minister’s Principal Secretary that signals the government’s economic direction and the operating environment companies should expect. Pramod Kumar Mishra said India should move beyond “Make in India” toward “Design, Innovate and Lead from India,” with a stronger focus on domestic value addition, component ecosystems, design capability, intellectual property, and globally competitive Indian brands. He framed this as a response to a changing global backdrop in which supply chains are being reconstituted, technology is changing where production happens, alliances are fragmenting, trade barriers are rising again, and supply chains and capital flows are increasingly being used as strategic tools.

The practical message for corporates is that India should become not just a large consumer market but also a production and innovation hub, meaning businesses may face continued pressure to localize manufacturing, source more components domestically, and invest in R&D, design, and IP creation within India. Mishra specifically highlighted India’s dependence on imports, including beyond energy, and pointed to the country’s significant merchandise trade deficit as a reason to “make things at home and competitively.” He also noted that companies and policymakers cannot assume a friendly trade agreement will offset global risks, because trade agreements are opening markets in some places but trade barriers are simultaneously increasing in others.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is strategic rather than procedural: there are no stated effective dates, thresholds, filing obligations, or enforcement requirements in this article. However, the remarks indicate a policy environment that may favor domestic manufacturing, import substitution, technology capability-building, and local value-add, which could affect sourcing, trade, supply-chain, and localization strategies. Businesses operating in or into India should treat this as a signal to review exposure to import dependency, cross-border supply-chain disruption, and potential future policy shifts that could incentivize or require greater domestic production and innovation.

rows.title: RBI DG Poonam Gupta says ‘fair case’ for rupee to appreciate from current levels
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read RBI DG Poonam Gupta says ‘fair case’ for rupee to appreciate from current levels RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta said the rupee’s 13.1 per cent depreciation since March 2025 could be a temporary phenomenon, pointing to an expected improvement in India’s current and capital accounts and saying there is a “fair case” for the currency to not just stabilise but potentially appreciate from current levels. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Sep 23, 2026 at 07:52 PM IST var news_msid = 134440635; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The rupee’s cumulative depreciation over the past year and a half could prove temporary as India’s balance of payments position improves, Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta said on Wednesday, and that there is a “fair case” for the currency to appreciate from current levels.Gupta, speaking at the 13th SBI Banking & Economics Conclave, said India’s current account deficit should shrink further in the coming years, while the capital account could turn more favourable, plausibly from later in the current financial year.“The recent oil price and gold price shocks have pushed CAD temporarily higher,” Gupta said, noting that the capital account surplus had fallen short of the current account deficit in the last two years. Advt India recorded a negative balance of payments of about USD 5 billion in 2024-25 and USD 23.6 billion in 2025-26, she said.However, Gupta said India’s CAD has traditionally remained small and has declined as a share of GDP over time. Net services exports and remittances remain key structural strengths and are large and resilient enough to absorb the merchandise trade deficit, keeping the current account deficit below 1 per cent of GDP, she said.The rupee has cumulatively depreciated by 13.1 per cent on a point-to-point basis between March 31, 2025 and September 16, 2026
rows.summary:
RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta said the rupee’s 13.1% point-to-point depreciation between March 31, 2025 and September 16, 2026 may be temporary, and that there is a “fair case” for the currency to stabilize and potentially appreciate from current levels. Her comments were based on an expected improvement in India’s balance of payments position, with the current account deficit (CAD) projected to shrink further in coming years and the capital account expected to become more favorable, potentially from later in the current financial year.

Gupta said recent oil and gold price shocks have temporarily increased the CAD, while the capital account surplus has been insufficient to cover the CAD over the last two years. She cited India’s negative balance of payments as about USD 5 billion in FY 2024-25 and USD 23.6 billion in FY 2025-26. At the same time, she emphasized that India’s CAD has historically remained small and has declined as a share of GDP over time, supported by structurally strong net services exports and remittances.

For compliance purposes, this is not a rule change or regulatory requirement announcement, but it does signal RBI’s policy view that external-sector pressures on the rupee may ease if India’s balance of payments improves. The practical takeaway for treasury, FX, and risk teams is that RBI appears to view the recent depreciation as potentially transitory rather than a new steady-state trend, with CAD expected to stay below 1% of GDP on the strength of services exports and remittances.

rows.summary:
This article is not a regulation or rule change, but a market/commentary statement by SBI Chairman CS Setty about where India’s next major investment cycle is likely to come from. Setty said the next wave of global investment in India is expected to be driven by “sunrise sectors” such as renewables, battery storage, and green hydrogen, and he framed this as part of India’s broader transition toward higher-value manufacturing, new technologies, and the green economy.

For a compliance team, the practical takeaway is strategic rather than prescriptive: the article signals that banks, investors, and corporates may increasingly need to assess opportunities and risks in these sectors, including financing, project structuring, and intellectual property development, as India’s industrial base evolves. Setty emphasized that India already has the talent, entrepreneurs, and technical capability to participate in these areas, but that the real opportunity is to convert those strengths into globally competitive businesses, manufacturing capacity, technologies, and IP. He also said the financial ecosystem must evolve alongside the economy to support this shift, though the article does not specify any new compliance obligations, deadlines, thresholds, filings, or regulatory requirements.

rows.summary:
The document reports a new UPI merchant discount rate (MDR) framework that becomes effective on **October 15, 2026** and is expected to create an annual fee pool of roughly **Rs 16,000–20,000 crore**, although the final amount will depend on the volume of eligible transactions, exemptions, and the transaction mix. The MDR applies only to **eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above Rs 2,000**, not to all UPI payments, and it is set at **0.4%** of the transaction value. The fee is also **capped at Rs 300 per transaction**, which limits the MDR on large-value payments.

The article says the fee will be split among the **issuing bank, acquiring bank, UPI app, and the app’s payment service provider (PSP) bank**, with banks collectively receiving the largest share. Specifically, the **issuing bank will receive 40% of the MDR** for every Rs 100 collected, while the remainder is distributed across the other participants in the UPI ecosystem. Because of this allocation, the article identifies **Yes Bank, Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, and IndusInd Bank** as likely beneficiaries, depending on each bank’s role as issuer, acquirer, or PSP bank and the volume of eligible transactions they handle.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that the MDR is not a blanket charge on UPI, but a targeted levy on qualifying merchant payments above the **Rs 2,000 threshold**, with **specified exemptions and concessional rates for certain categories**. Institutions involved in UPI issuing, acquiring, or PSP functions will need to ensure their settlement, billing, and revenue-share processes are aligned to the new October 15 framework and to the capped fee structure. The document also notes that the government has tried to allay concerns about any increase in cash usage following the levy, but it does not indicate any additional direct compliance steps beyond implementing the new MDR allocation and eligibility rules.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India is reconsidering its draft proposal to impose a blanket ban on revolving credit facilities offered by non-bank lenders/NBFCs, after industry feedback suggested the measure would affect far more of the NBFC sector than the RBI initially expected. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu met with NBFC representatives and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to hear concerns, and the central bank has already received about 350 industry feedback submissions on the draft proposal.

The main compliance issue under discussion is whether the RBI will proceed with a full prohibition on revolving credit or instead move to a partial restriction. Industry participants say the RBI originally believed the impact would be limited to only three or four NBFCs, but the consultation response indicates that a much broader set of lenders could be caught by the rule. One specific carve-out drawing repeated attention is an exemption for supply chain financing, which the industry has urged the RBI to preserve.

No final contours have been issued yet, so there is no confirmed operative rule to implement at this stage. However, sources cited in the article suggest the final guidelines may be issued in roughly two months, which is the only timeline provided. For compliance teams at NBFCs and other non-bank lenders, the key takeaway is that revolving credit products remain under active regulatory review, and firms offering such facilities should be prepared for either a narrower restriction or a broader ban depending on the RBI’s final decision, with supply chain financing potentially treated differently.

Under the draft, a term loan is a fixed principal amount with a predetermined repayment schedule, w
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has **not yet finalized** its proposed restriction on revolving credit for NBFCs and is still evaluating the issue in light of stakeholder feedback. Deputy Governor S. C. Murmu said the RBI is assessing the risks of allowing revolving credit **both at the level of individual NBFCs and at the systemic level**, and indicated the central bank has not decided in what form the final rule, if any, will come. He also said the RBI has **received a large volume of feedback**, is taking **every submission into account**, and may **discuss the matter further with some participants** to better understand the operational and risk implications.

The underlying proposal being reviewed is the RBI’s **August 6 draft amendment** to its NBFC credit-facility directions. That draft would **restrict NBFCs to term loans only** and would **bar revolving credit products**. The document defines a term loan as a loan of a **fixed principal amount** with a **predetermined repayment schedule**, in contrast to revolving credit, where borrowers can repeatedly draw and repay within a limit. The compliance significance is that NBFCs potentially affected by the draft would need to remove or redesign any revolving-credit offerings if the proposal is adopted, but **no final implementation date or binding deadline has been announced yet** because the matter remains open.

rows.summary:
The Department of Financial Services (DFS) under the Ministry of Finance has directed public sector banks to prepare for the proposed **September 28–30, 2026 bank strike** by ensuring **basic SOP compliance, uninterrupted essential services, adequate cash stocking at ATMs, and sufficient cash availability at business correspondent (BC) outlets**, while also keeping **alternative digital channels** available to reduce disruption. The instruction follows a DFS review meeting with **public sector bank (PSB) chiefs, regional rural banks (RRBs), the Indian Banks’ Association (IBA), and NABARD** to assess strike preparedness. The strike called by the **United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU)** could effectively result in a **five-day disruption** because it is immediately preceded by a weekend, and **September 30** is also **half-year closing**, which makes service continuity especially important.

Banks have been told to take contingency measures so that **cash remains available across delivery channels**, with particular emphasis on **ATM cash loading** and cash support at **BC outlets**. The article also notes that **12 PSBs have already issued customer advisories** in advance of the strike. In parallel, the Finance Ministry has **urged employees to call off the strike**, and a **conciliation meeting with the Chief Labour Commissioner (CLC) is scheduled for September 22, 2026**, which may still alter or avert the planned work stoppage. For compliance teams, the practical requirement is to ensure branch, ATM, BC, and digital-service readiness for the entire strike window and the surrounding weekend, with extra attention to business continuity given the half-year-end operational peak on September 30.

rows.summary:
This article is primarily a business and macroeconomic commentary, not a regulatory notice, so it does not impose a new legal requirement or compliance deadline. The main substantive point is Jamie Dimon’s view that India’s economy could nearly triple in size over the next decade, and that JPMorgan expects to expand its India operations significantly in response.

For corporate compliance purposes, the only directly relevant “change” described is JPMorgan’s stated business expansion in India: the bank reportedly expects to grow its research coverage from nearly 200 Indian companies today to 400 companies, with coverage of 2,000 companies overall, and to deepen work with both the Indian government and Indian businesses. Dimon also said JPMorgan has expanded dramatically in India since his first visit in 2005, noting the firm had 6,000 employees in 2025 and now employs 60,000 professionals across technical areas and investment banking; this is presented as context for the firm’s scale-up, not as a mandated staffing target.

The article also flags a policy point relevant to multinational compliance teams: Dimon urged New Delhi and Washington to conclude a trade agreement and stressed the need for consistency in trade and investment rules. While no specific rule change is announced, the implication is that companies operating across the India-U.S. corridor should watch for potential shifts in trade, investment, and market-access conditions. The piece further notes broader macro risks—persistent inflation, elevated government borrowing, geopolitical tensions, and rising capital demand—and says Dimon expects interest rates and bond markets to matter more, but it cuts off before giving any specific forecast or compliance instruction.

rows.summary:
Unity Small Finance Bank’s first MD & CEO, Inderjit Camotra, has had his tenure extended by the Reserve Bank of India by six months, with the new end date set at **February 4, 2027**. This is a direct governance/leadership continuation measure rather than a change to bank operations, and it means Camotra remains in place while the bank awaits approval for a successor.

The bank has already **submitted names for its next MD & CEO to the RBI**, reportedly around **the end of July 2026**, and people familiar with the process said the **RBI approval is expected in the next 2–3 weeks** from the article date. The article notes that appointment of a bank’s MD & CEO is **subject to prior RBI approval**, so the bank cannot finalize the new chief executive until the regulator completes its review.

For compliance and governance monitoring, the key point is that Unity Small Finance Bank is operating under a temporary extension for its incumbent CEO while the succession process is still pending. Camotra has been associated with Unity since inception; he was **an executive director at Centrum Financial Services**, the promoter entity of Unity, before being appointed **MD & CEO in August 2022**, and earlier served as **interim CEO** when the bank began operations. Unity Small Finance Bank itself began banking operations on **November 1, 2021**, after receiving final RBI approval.

rows.summary:
Mahindra Finance has expanded its Samur.AI multi-agent AI system so that it now covers about 70% of new-loan volumes, up from roughly 45% in Q1 FY27, indicating a rapid increase in automation across loan processing. The system is being used at the company’s central processing centre (CPC), not in the credit-decisioning layer, and its current role is to perform document and data verification rather than to approve or reject credit. It is designed to handle operational complexity, including regional-language documents and highly variable dealer documentation, and when a file is flagged for human review, the system provides a rationale for why the case was escalated.

From a compliance/process perspective, the key operational change is the shift from manual, decentralised handling toward a standardised, technology-driven workflow across the branch network, with centralised processing supporting loan origination. This implies greater reliance on automated verification controls and a structured exception/escalation process for cases that cannot be fully processed by AI. The article does not state any formal regulatory deadline or mandated compliance date, but it does show that the automation rollout is already in place and materially affecting underwriting operations. For compliance teams, the main items to monitor are the quality and auditability of the AI-driven verification process, the treatment of multilingual/regional documents, and the human-review controls for flagged cases, since the system is now processing the majority of new-loan flow.

rows.title: Extension of timeline for implementation of provisions of SEBI Circular dated June 15, 2026 on norms for base price, price bands, call auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)
rows.desc: Extension of timeline for implementation of provisions of SEBI Circular dated June 15, 2026 on norms for base price, price bands, call auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) Aug 28, 2026| Circular No.: HO/47/11/11(1)2026-MRD-POD3/I/19839/2026 Extension of timeline for implementation of provisions of SEBI Circular dated June 15, 2026 on norms for base price, price bands, call auction in pre-open session and Close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs)
rows.summary:
SEBI has issued a circular extending the implementation timeline for the provisions of its earlier circular dated June 15, 2026 on the norms for base price, price bands, call auction in the pre-open session, and the close-out procedure for Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs). The new circular is dated August 28, 2026 and is identified as Circular No. HO/47/11/11(1)2026-MRD-POD3/I/19839/2026. 

The material change is not a change to the substance of the ETF trading framework itself, but a postponement of when the June 15, 2026 requirements must be implemented. In other words, exchanges, trading members, and other market participants that would have had to operationalize the ETF-specific base price, price band, pre-open call auction, and close-out mechanics under the June 15 circular are being granted additional time before those rules become mandatory. Rajagopal Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited, Sundaram Towers, 1 st and 2 nd floor 46, Whites Road, Royapettah, Chennai, 600014 Dear Sir, Sub: Request for Informal Guidance by way of interpretive letter under the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 in connection with the provisions of Securities and Exchange Board of India (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012 (“AIF Regulations”) Ref: Your letter dated April 23, 2025 1. In the context of your letter under reference, you have, inter alia, stated that Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited (‘the Applicant’) is a SEBI registered Portfolio Manager bearing registration no. INP000006271 and also the Investment Manager for Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust, a Category III Alternative Investment Fund (“AIF”) having registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291 and Sundaram Category II AIF having registration no. IN/AIF2/17- 18/0340, and have sought an interpretive letter under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 (“Informal Guidance Scheme”) from SEBI in respect of the following query – i. Please clarify whether during the extended period, the close-ended Alternative Investment Fund is permitted only to liquidate its existing portfolio investments or allowed to make investments in portfolio companies. Page 2 of 4 2. Our Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the issues raised in your letter are as under: 2.1. In terms of Regulation 13(5) of AIF Regulations, extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Inve
rows.summary:
SEBI has issued an informal guidance letter dated **July 9, 2025** in response to Sundaram Alternate Assets Limited’s request regarding the **extension of tenure for close-ended Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)** under the **SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012**. The applicant, which is a SEBI-registered portfolio manager (**registration no. INP000006271**) and the investment manager for **Sundaram Alternative Investment Trust** (Category III AIF, **registration no. IN/AIF3/16-17/0291**) and **Sundaram Category II AIF** (**registration no. IN/AIF2/17-18/0340**), asked whether, during the extended period of a close-ended AIF, the fund may only liquidate existing investments or whether it may also make new investments in portfolio companies.

SEBI’s comment cites **Regulation 13(5)** of the AIF Regulations, which allows a close-ended AIF’s tenure to be **extended for up to two years** if approved by **two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment** in the AIF. SEBI’s guidance indicates that, during the extended tenure, the AIF is **not restricted only to liquidation** of its existing portfolio; rather, it is also **permitted to make investments in portfolio companies**. This means compliance teams should treat the extension period as a continued investment period, not a wind-down-only period, unless the fund’s own constitutive documents or other applicable rules impose stricter limits. The letter is issued as an **interpretive response under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003**, and addresses the specific operational question raised by the applicant for its close-ended AIFs.

rows.summary:
The document is a promotional/notice page for **MFCentral / MITRA**, described as a unified investor services gateway for mutual funds created by **KFintech and CAMS**. Its core message is that investors can use **one service request** to update or modify information across **all mutual fund folios**, instead of submitting separate requests to each fund house. It also states that the platform is intended to let investors view and manage their mutual fund portfolio on a single digital platform, with features for viewing holdings and performance by asset class, fund house, returns, and scheme level.

From a compliance perspective, the operational change emphasized is the move from paper-based servicing to a **digital, centralized servicing process** for mutual fund investors. The platform advertises support for common account and service actions such as **bank mandate changes, contact detail updates, changes in IDCW instructions**, and related folio-level service requests, with the stated benefit that a single request will apply across all folios. It also references quick links for **updating PAN details, PAN transmission requests, and transfer of units**, which suggests the portal is being positioned as a central workflow for investor servicing rather than a product-specific transaction site.

The only explicit regulatory requirement mentioned in the excerpt is the **Positive Pay System (PPS)** for cheques. The document says the **Reserve Bank of India announced PPS in September 2020** as an additional security layer for cheques **above Rs. 50,000**, and that banks indicated enforcement from **1 September 2021**. Investors are advised to take note of the PPS requirement, although the sentence is cut off in the provided content before the full instruction is shown. For compliance teams, this means cheque-based payments above that threshold may require adherence to the bank’s PPS validation process, and investor communications or operational SOPs should reflect the effective date and threshold.

The document also makes broad claims about the platform being **“highly secure”** and using **multiple layers of protection and data encryption** for mutual fund transactions. While these are marketing statements rather than detailed regulatory obligations, they indicate that the service is handling sensitive investor data and transaction requests, so firms using or referring investors to the platform should ensure privacy, authentication, and data-handling controls are aligned with those representations. Overall, the excerpt is more of a product announcement than a rulemaking notice, but the material compliance-relevant point is the PPS cheque requirement and the centralized digital servicing model for mutual fund folios.

rows.summary:
The document sets out the rights and obligations of a beneficial owner and a depository participant (DP) under the Depositories Act, 1996, SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 1996, and all related SEBI circulars, rules, regulations, depository bye-laws, business rules, operating instructions, and applicable government notifications in force from time to time. The DP must keep all beneficial-owner information from the account-opening form and supporting documents strictly confidential and may disclose it only where required by statutory, legal, or regulatory authority, while the beneficial owner must immediately notify the DP in writing of any change in the details previously provided in the account-opening form or later furnished to the DP.  

On fees and charges, the beneficial owner is required to pay only those charges for dematerialized holding, transfer, and depository services that have been mutually agreed between the DP and the beneficial owner and stated in the DP’s tariff sheet; the document specifically notes that no charges are payable for opening a demat account. It also states that for Basic Services Demat Accounts, the DP must follow the charge structure prescribed under the relevant applicable framework, though the excerpt provided cuts off before the detailed structure is shown. Overall, the operational compliance themes are account-opening controls, ongoing KYC/documentation discipline, confidentiality of client records, mandatory client notification of changes, and adherence to the applicable tariff/fee regime, including any special rules for Basic Services Demat Accounts.

rows.summary:
The document appears to summarize SEBI’s responses to comments on proposed changes for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs), and it indicates that SEBI is **not accepting several requests to relax the compliance framework**. On the proposal relating to **identification/validation of SWAGAT-FI status for existing FPIs**, commenters asked that existing FPIs not be required to provide additional proof because it would increase burden and paperwork; SEBI **disagreed**, saying the verification requirements will instead be aligned with the **existing exemption criteria under the Additional Disclosure Framework**, which the industry has already implemented. In practical terms, FPIs seeking the relevant status will still need to demonstrate the required conditions—such as diversification, independence of fund managers, regulator confirmation, blind pool status, and absence of segregated portfolios—but SEBI’s stated approach is to use a familiar verification model rather than introduce an entirely new process.

On **re-KYC and fee/payment periodicity**, commenters wanted the current periodicity to remain unchanged and opposed additional re-KYC requirements, arguing that material changes such as UBO updates would be caught through ordinary monitoring and that longer fee blocks would reduce SEBI’s flexibility. SEBI **disagreed with removing the re-KYC requirement**, stating that **material change reporting obligations remain in force** and that the additional re-KYC requirement is being retained for FPIs, consistent with treatment of other investors. The document also clarifies that there is **no yearly fee requirement currently**; instead, the proposal is to **increase the fee block period from 3 years to 10 years**, and this 10-year block is intended to **coincide with the re-KYC cycle**, rather than changing the underlying ability of SEBI to adjust fees.

A third item begins addressing comments that **FPIs should not be allowed to facilitate single demat accounts**, but the text provided is truncated, so the specific final regulatory outcome for that point is not visible in the excerpt. Based on the visible portions, the compliance takeaway is that SEBI is **preserving core identity, ownership, and status-verification controls for FPIs**, while trying to implement them through standardized existing frameworks rather than eliminating the obligations.

7.	Development of framework for information interchange with various government agencies. 
8.	Facilitating innovation in markets through SEBI’s Innovation Sandbox Framework.

rows.title: Settlement Application
rows.summary:
This document describes the online **SEBI Settlement Application** process and the required supporting filings for applicants seeking settlement under SEBI’s settlement framework. It states that once the **non-refundable settlement application fee** is paid online, the applicant must **physically submit the printed settlement application together with all required documents, including proof of payment, to the SEBI Settlement Division within 7 calendar days** from the date the payment is successfully made. It also directs applicants to **refer to SEBI Circular dated June 18, 2019** before filing.

The application form requires the applicant to choose the **type of application** from the available categories: **Summary Settlement (SS), Suo Motu (SM), Pre-SCN, Post-SCN, Post Appeal (SAT), Post SAT Order (SO), or Settlement with Confidentiality (SC)**. The form asks for the relevant proceeding identifiers depending on the case type, including **Show Cause Notice number/date, Summary Settlement Notice number/date, SAT appeal number, and Appeal number**. It also requires the applicant to provide the **matter to which the application relates**, and includes controls to **save or withdraw** the application details.

For each applicant, the form requires entry of **name, PAN number, applicant type, and proposed settlement amount**, along with documentary uploads. The settlement amount entered **cannot be less than ₹3 lakhs**, as expressly required under the Settlement Regulations. The applicant must upload **certified true copies of the ITRs for the last 3 financial years** in **PDF format only, up to 20 MB**, and a **certified true copy of the PAN card** in **PDF format only, up to 500 KB**. These requirements apply to the applicant whether the applicant is an **individual or a body corporate**.

The form also requires a detailed **correspondence address**, the applicant’s **GST number**, **state/territory selection**, **10-digit phone number**, and a **primary email address**, with the email noted as the address that will be used for all communications with the entity. Overall, the compliance obligation is not just to complete the online submission, but to ensure the offline physical filing is sent to SEBI within the 7-day window and that all required identification, tax, and payment documents are accurate, complete, and in the specified file formats and size limits.

rows.title: Settlement Calculator BETA

It is explicitly stated that the calculator is only a guide: the final settlement amount can be modified by the **Internal Committee**, **High Powered Advisory Committee**, and the **Panel of Whole Time Members**, and in some cases SEBI may also impose **non-monetary settlement terms** under **Regulation 9**.

For compliance purposes, the core monetary floor is that the **Indicative Amount (IA)** cannot be lower than **Rs. 3 lakh for a first-time applicant** or **Rs. 7 lakh for other applicants**. A “first time applicant” is defined as a person against whom **no order has been passed by the adjudicating officer or SEBI**, and who has **never obtained a settlement order from SEBI** as of the date of the current application. The calculator requires use of a **proceeding conversion factor (PCF)** depending on the **stage at which the relevant proceeding is pending** when the settlement application is filed. It further provides that, where a business or activity is **corporatized, converted into an LLP or partnership, or merged/taken over by new management**, the historical record of the erstwhile entity is treated as the record of the new entity. rows.title: Exim Bank’s GOI-supported Line of Credit (LOC) for ₹ 4,850 crores the Government of Maldives, for financing various developmental projects in Maldives
rows.desc: � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA www.rbi.org.in RBI/2026-2027/269 September 23, 2026 A.P. (DIR Series) Circular No. 22 All Category – I Authorised Dealer Banks Madam/Sir Exim Bank’s GOI-supported Line of Credit (LOC) for ₹ 4,850 crores the Government of Maldives, for financing various developmental projects in Maldives Export-Import Bank of India (Exim Bank) has entered into an agreement dated July 25, 2025, with the Government of the Republic of Maldives, for making available to the latter, Government of India supported Line of Credit (LoC) of ₹ 4,850 crores (Rupees Four Thousand Eight Hundred and Fifty crores only) for financing various developmental projects in Maldives. The export of eligible goods and services from India, as defined under the agreement, would be allowed, subject to their eligibility under the Foreign Trade Policy of the Government of India and whose purchase may be agreed to be financed by the Exim Bank under this agreement. Under this Agreement, goods, works and services of the value of at least 75% of the contract price (as may be applicable) shall be supplied by the Seller from India, and the remaining 25% of goods and services may be procured by the Seller for the purpose of the Eligible Contract from outside India. 2. The Agreement under the LoC is effective from August 27, 2026. Under the LoC, the last date for disbursement will be 48 months after scheduled completion date of the contract. Individual Credit Agreements will be signed under the ambit of Umbrella LOC (for a minimum value of ₹ 500 crores) subsequent to identification and approval of the projects to be financed under each individual credits under the LOC. 3. Shipments under the LoC shall be declared in Export Declaration Form/Shipping Bill as per instructions issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time. 4. No agency commission is payable for export under the above LoC. However, if required, the exporter may use his own resources or utilize balances in his Exchange Earners’ Foreign Cur
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has notified all Category-I Authorised Dealer banks that Exim Bank has entered into a Government of India-supported Line of Credit (LoC) of ₹4,850 crores with the Government of the Republic of Maldives to finance various developmental projects in Maldives, under an agreement dated July 25, 2025. The LoC may be used only for export of eligible Indian goods and services as defined in the agreement and only to the extent such exports are eligible under the Government of India’s Foreign Trade Policy; Exim Bank must also agree to finance the purchase under the agreement.

A key sourcing condition applies: at least 75% of the contract price must consist of goods, works, and services supplied by the seller from India, while the remaining up to 25% may be procured from outside India for the eligible contract. The agreement became effective on August 27, 2026, and the last date for disbursement is 48 months after the scheduled completion date of the contract. Individual Credit Agreements will be executed under the umbrella LoC only after the relevant projects are identified and approved, and each individual credit must be for a minimum value of ₹500 crores.

From a compliance and operational perspective, shipments under the LoC must be declared in the Export Declaration Form/Shipping Bill in accordance with RBI instructions as updated from time to time. The circular also states that no agency commission is payable for exports under this LoC. Exporters may, if needed, meet related costs from their own resources or by using balances in their Exchange Earners’ Foreign Currency account, but the circular does not indicate any other special procedural relief or exceptions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Amendment Directions, 2026

In order to ensure clarity and uniform practices in the valuation of units of Infrastructure Investment Trust (InvIT) and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REIT), there is a need to amend the extant instructions. 2. Accordingly, in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 45L of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (hereinafter called the Act) and all other laws enabling the Reserve Bank in this regard, the Reserve Bank, being satisfied that it is necessary and expedient in the public interest so to do, hereby, issues the Amendment Directions hereinafter specified. 3. (i) These Directions shall be called the Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Amendment Directions, 2026. (ii) These Amendment Directions shall come into effect from the date of issue. 4. The Reserve Bank of India (All India Financial Institutions - Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025, are amended as provided below. (i) Paragraph 58A shall be inserted as under: - “58A. Units of Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) (1) Quoted securities issued by InvITs and units of InvITs shall be valued mutatis mutandis as per instructions given in these Directions for quoted securities. (2) Unquoted instruments of InvITs shall be valued as under: i. Units: The valuation shall be done at the NAV as disclosed by the InvIT. Where an InvIT fails to comp
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has amended the 2025 Directions on classification, valuation, and operation of investment portfolios for All India Financial Institutions to create clearer and more uniform valuation rules for **Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs)** and **Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)**. The amendment is issued under **Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934**, and it **takes effect immediately from the date of issue, 22 September 2026**.

For **InvITs**, the amendment inserts a new paragraph 58A requiring that **quoted securities issued by InvITs and units of InvITs be valued mutatis mutandis in the same manner as other quoted securities** under the 2025 Directions. For **unquoted InvIT instruments**, the new rule says the **units must be valued at the NAV disclosed by the InvIT**. The document begins to specify a fallback where an InvIT **fails to comply** with the NAV disclosure requirement, but the provided text is cut off before the complete fallback procedure is shown.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that this amendment changes the investment valuation framework for AIFs holding InvIT-related instruments by making the valuation basis explicit and standardized, with immediate applicability. Institutions that hold or value **quoted or unquoted InvIT units/instruments** should update internal valuation policies, pricing controls, and periodic review processes to align with the RBI’s new instruction, and should also monitor whether the InvIT is properly disclosing NAV since that disclosure is now the stated basis for valuing unquoted units.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has finalized instructions governing the **novation of OTC derivative contracts** and has now embedded those rules directly into the existing directions for the relevant product classes rather than issuing a standalone operative framework. The circular explains that the final version was issued after considering feedback on the draft **Reserve Bank of India (Novation of OTC Derivative Contracts) Directions, 2025** that had been released by press notice on **July 9, 2025**, and that an annex to the circular summarizes the major feedback received. The consolidation affects the rules governing **OTC foreign exchange derivatives**, **OTC interest rate derivatives**, **government securities forward contracts**, and **credit derivatives**, through amendments made to the following instruments: the **Master Direction – Risk Management and Inter-Bank Dealings (July 5, 2016, as amended)**, the **Master Direction – RBI (Rupee Interest Rate Derivatives) Directions, 2025 (December 8, 2025, as amended)**, the **RBI (Forward Contracts in Government Securities) Directions, 2025 (February 21, 2025, as amended)**, and the **Master Direction – RBI (Credit Derivatives) Directions, 2026 (June 25, 2026, as amended)**.

The circular does not restate the detailed novation mechanics in the excerpt provided, but it makes clear that the instructions are now incorporated into the product-specific RBI directions and should be applied within the existing regulatory frameworks for those markets. The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk Directions, 2026** (issued **September 21, 2026**) set out the capital framework commercial banks must use for **market risk**, including how to draw the boundary between the **banking book** and **trading book**, how to treat **internal risk transfers**, and how to calculate **risk-weighted assets (RWAs)** and capital requirements for market risk. The document applies to **commercial banks** and is intended to standardize which positions are treated as trading versus banking book exposures, because that classification determines capital treatment. It also addresses a specific exception for **certain structural foreign exchange positions** that may be excluded from the **Net Open Position** measure, indicating that banks may need to evidence why such positions qualify for exclusion. The structure of the directions shows that they are not merely high-level policy but operational rules covering scope, classification, permitted reclassifications, and capital calculation methodology.

A major compliance point is the restrictions on moving instruments between regulatory books: the directions expressly regulate the **boundary between the banking book and the trading book** and restrict when instruments can be reclassified. The text also introduces detailed treatment for **internal risk transfers**, including (i) transfer of **credit risk** from the banking book to the trading book, (ii) transfer of **general interest rate risk (GIRR)** from the banking book to the trading book, and (iii) what counts as **eligible hedges for the CVA capital requirement**. For compliance teams, this means banks must have documented controls showing that internal transfers are recognized only in the circumstances permitted by the RBI framework, and that any capital relief or trading-book recognition tied to those transfers is supported by the required methodology and records. The inclusion of CVA hedge eligibility signals that banks need to review whether hedging instruments qualify for regulatory capital purposes, not just for internal risk management.

The directions also require banks to follow the RBI’s rules for **scope of application of market risk** and the corresponding **calculation of RWAs and capital requirements**, which implies an ongoing obligation to compute market-risk capital under the prescribed framework rather than relying on legacy or internal approaches that are inconsistent with the directions. The document’s chapter headings indicate that the RBI is formalizing the market-risk capital treatment in a way that affects both day-to-day classification of positions and periodic capital reporting. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed numeric formulas or a later implementation timetable, the issuance date of **September 21, 2026** is the key reference point for when the directions were promulgated. Compliance teams should therefore treat this as a governing regulatory framework for all commercial banks’ market-risk capital governance, classification controls, and reporting processes, with special attention to trading-book designation, internal risk-transfer documentation, structural FX position treatment, and RWA computation under the RBI’s prescribed rules.

The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026** on **September 18, 2026**, and they take **immediate effect**. These amendments modify the existing **RBI Rural Co-operative Banks KYC Directions, 2025** issued on **November 28, 2025**, which were originally framed under the **PMLA, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**.

After this amendment, **rural co-operative banks** may use the same alternative certified-copy process for **FPIs as well**, so institutions onboarding or maintaining accounts for FPIs must accept this document option where the applicable certification requirements are met.

The document does not introduce any new numerical threshold, rate, or deadline beyond immediate commencement; the substantive compliance change is the broader acceptance of certified copies for **FPI** KYC purposes under the existing RRB KYC framework.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026**, effective **immediately on September 18, 2026**. These amendments modify the **Local Area Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025**, which were originally issued in compliance with the **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002** and the **Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**. The RBI states that it reviewed the existing KYC facility allowing banks to obtain an **original certified copy** of documents—certified by one of the specified authorities/officials—for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** under paragraph 4(1)(v) of the 2025 Directions, and has decided to **extend the same facility to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)**.

For compliance purposes, the practical change is that **local area banks may now apply the same alternative documentary verification route for FPIs that was already available for NRIs and PIOs**. This means that where the 2025 Directions permit acceptance of an original certified copy in lieu of standard document submission, FPIs are now included in that scope, subject to the same certification requirements and the same categories of certifying authorities/authorized officials referenced in the underlying Directions. The amendment is issued under RBI’s powers under **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Banking Regulation Act (AACS), 1949 read with section 56**, **section 10(2) read with section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, **section 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and **Rule 9(14) of the PMLA Maintenance of Records Rules, 2005**.

The document does not introduce a delayed implementation date, grace period, threshold amount, or new numerical limit; instead, the operative requirement is an **immediate expansion of an existing KYC documentation flexibility**. Compliance teams at local area banks should therefore update onboarding/KYC procedures and staff instructions so that **FPI customers are handled consistently with the NRI/PIO certification-based alternative documentation process** from the date of issuance, ensuring the bank continues to meet AML/KYC and record-maintenance obligations under the 2025 Directions as amended.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Know Your Customer Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the earlier **2025 KYC Directions** for small finance banks. The substantive change is narrow but important: the existing KYC rule in **paragraph 5(1)(v)**, which already allowed banks to accept an **original certified copy** of identification/related documents for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** when certified by specified authorities or authorised officials under **FEMA 5(R)**, is now being **extended to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** as well.

For compliance purposes, this means small finance banks may now apply the same alternative document-acceptance facility to **FPIs** as they already do for NRIs and PIOs, rather than requiring only the original document path in every case. The amendment is issued under the RBI’s powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, the **Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and the **PML Rules, 2005**, indicating it is a binding regulatory instruction rather than guidance.

The amendment takes **immediate effect from September 18, 2026** (the date of issuance stated in the document). No monetary thresholds, reporting deadlines, or phased implementation periods are introduced in this text. Compliance teams at **small finance banks** should therefore update KYC procedures and staff instructions immediately so that FPI onboarding/document verification follows the same certified-copy option already available for NRIs and PIOs under the underlying 2025 Directions.

rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the existing **Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** and take **immediate effect** from **September 18, 2026**. The change is narrow but important: the RBI has expanded the existing KYC facility that already allowed banks, for **Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)** and **Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs)** under FEMA 5(R), to accept an **original certified copy** certified by specified authorities/officials instead of insisting on the usual form of document submission, and this same alternative documentation facility is now being extended to **Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs)** as well.

The amendment is made under the RBI’s powers, including **section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, **section 10(2) read with section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, **section 11(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999**, and **Rule 9(14) of the Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**. In practical compliance terms, commercial banks must update their KYC onboarding and document-acceptance procedures so that, where the directions permit certified copies, the same certified-copy route now applies not only to NRIs and PIOs but also to FPIs. The document states that paragraph **5(1)(v)** of the 2025 Directions is being substituted, but the text provided cuts off before the full revised wording, so the operative takeaway is the extension of the certified-copy exception to **FPIs** with no grace period or delayed implementation.

The above amendment sh
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Third Amendment Directions, 2026 revise the Priority Sector Lending Directions, 2025 by shortening the end date for a specific ANBC exclusion related to advances against fresh foreign currency and non-resident deposits. Under the earlier Second Amendment Directions issued on August 7, 2026, advances extended in India against fresh FCNR(B) deposits with a tenor of 3 to 5 years, and advances against NRE term deposits of at least 3 years, were excluded from Adjusted Net Bank Credit if the deposits were mobilized during the relevant windows ending September 30, 2026; this amendment changes that cutoff date from September 30, 2026 to August 31, 2026.

As amended, the exclusion applies only to advances against fresh FCNR(B) deposits mobilized between June 8, 2026 and August 31, 2026, and to advances against NRE term deposits mobilized between June 19, 2026 and August 31, 2026, including deposits renewed at maturity, subject to the same deposit tenor conditions stated in the prior directions. The amendment also updates the cross-reference in paragraph 6.1, item VI, to reflect the relevant Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio exemption directions, and clarifies that the amount excluded from ANBC for priority sector lending computation cannot exceed the amount of fresh outstanding FCNR(B)/NRE deposits that are actually eligible for CRR/SLR exemption under those directions.

For compliance teams, the operational impact is that banks must stop applying the ANBC exclusion for deposits mobilized after August 31, 2026, even if the original September 30, 2026 date had been used in prior guidance. The amendment is dated September 11, 2026, and it amends the Priority Sector Lending Directions, 2025 as updated on August 7, 2026.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Local Area Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio Second Amendment Directions, 2026** amend the existing **2025 directions** to reflect that a **Local Area Bank has been included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, which means it is now being treated under the framework applicable to **scheduled banks** for these reserve requirements. The amendment is issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Sections 18 and 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and it takes effect **immediately** on **September 11, 2026**.

The substantive change is the insertion of a new **“B. Incremental CRR”** provision after paragraph 7 of the 2025 Directions. The new paragraph **7A** states that, under **Section 42(1A) of the RBI Act, 1934**, the RBI may require **scheduled banks** to maintain, in addition to the balances required under **Section 42(1)**, an **additional average daily balance** at a rate specified by the RBI in a notification published in the **Gazette of India** (the text provided cuts off after “Ga…,” but the requirement clearly contemplates a Gazette notification). In practical compliance terms, this means affected institutions must monitor RBI notifications for any incremental CRR requirement and be prepared to maintain the additional average daily balance if the RBI imposes it.

Because the amendment is tied to the inclusion of a Local Area Bank in the Second Schedule, the key compliance point is that the affected bank(s) now fall within the regime applicable to **scheduled banks**, and the RBI has expressly preserved its power to impose an **incremental CRR** obligation over and above the normal CRR balance. No specific percentage, threshold, or implementation schedule for the incremental CRR is set out in this amendment itself; the operative rate will be whatever the RBI later specifies by separate notification.

rows.summary:
This RBI circular is part of the Reserve Bank of India’s continuing cleanup of the FEMA regulatory framework and specifically announces the withdrawal of seven older A.P. (DIR Series) circulars because they have become inoperative due to later amendments, duplication, overlap, or supersession. The circular is dated September 08, 2026 and is addressed to all Authorised Persons; they are instructed to bring its contents to the attention of their relevant constituents.  

The withdrawn circulars are: (1) AP (DIR) Series Circular No. 17 dated 29.09.2015 on ECB policy for issuance of rupee-denominated bonds overseas; (2) Circular No. 25 dated 03.09.2014 on ECB in Indian Rupees; (3) Circular No. 85 dated 06.01.2014 on liberalisation of the definition of “Infrastructure Sector” under ECB policy; (4) Circular No. 81 dated 24.12.2013 on borrowing and lending in rupees, specifically investments by persons resident outside India in tax-free, secured, redeemable, non-convertible bonds; (5) Circular No. 119 dated 26.06.2013 on ECB policy relating to import of services, technical know-how, and license fees; (6) Circular No. 49 dated 07.11.2012 on the Money Transfer Service Scheme list of sub-agents; and (7) Circular No. 48 dated 06.11.2012 on ECB policy for ECB by the Small Industries Development Bank of India.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is not a new substantive permission or restriction, but the removal from operative status of these seven specific circulars, meaning firms should not rely on them as current standalone guidance and should instead verify the applicable requirements against the latest FEMA/ECB/MTS scheme directions. The circular states it is issued under Section 10(4) and Section 11(1) of FEMA, 1999, and that it does not override any permissions or approvals that may still be required under other laws.

rows.desc: RBI/2026-27/253 DOR.AML.REC.219/14.06.001/2026-27 September 07, 2026 The Chairpersons/ CEOs of the Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, All India Financial Institutions Madam/Dear Sir, Implementation of Section 51A of UAPA, 1967: Updates to UNSC’s 1267/ 1989 ISIL (Da'esh) & Al-Qaida Sanctions List: Amendment of 2 Entries Please refer to Chapter IX on “Requirements/obligations under International Agreements - Communications from International Agencies” of the Reserve Bank of India - Know Your Customer, Directions, 2025 dated November 28, 2025 (amended as on December 29, 2025) (“Directions”), as applicable, as per which, regulated entity shall ensure that in terms of section 51A of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) (UAPA) Act, 1967 and amendments thereto, it does not have any account in the name of individuals / entities appearing in the lists of individuals and entities, suspected of having terrorist links, which are approved by and periodically circulated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). 2. In this connection, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Government of India has informed about the UNSC press release SC/16446, dated September 04, 2026 wherein the Security Council pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011) and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da’esh), Al‑Qaida and associated individuals, groups, undertakings and entities enacted the amendments specified with strikethrough and underline in the entries below on its ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban and arms embargo set out in paragraph 1 of Security Council resolution 2734 (2024), and adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations. 2 A. Individuals QDi.431 Name: 1: SANAULLAH 2: GHAFARI 3: na 4: na Name (original script): ثناء ﷲ غفار
rows.summary:
This RBI communication requires regulated entities to continue implementing Section 51A of the UAPA, 1967 in line with Chapter IX of the RBI KYC Directions, 2025 (dated November 28, 2025, as amended on December 29, 2025), meaning banks and other covered financial institutions must ensure they do not maintain accounts in the names of persons or entities appearing on the UNSC-approved terrorism-related lists circulated under UAPA. The letter is addressed to commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, regional rural banks, local area banks, non-banking financial companies, asset reconstruction companies, and all India financial institutions. It specifically updates the UN Security Council’s 1267/1989 ISIL (Da’esh) and Al-Qaida sanctions list based on UNSC press release SC/16446 dated September 4, 2026, which amended two entries on the sanctions list; the measures attached to listed persons/entities are the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo under UN Security Council Resolution 2734 (2024).

The document does not create a new sanctions framework, but it does require compliance teams to treat the updated UNSC list as operative and to screen/compare customer and counterparty names against the amended entries. The first amended individual listed in the excerpt is QDi.431, named Sanaullah Ghafari (original script: ثناء ﷲ غفار), indicating that the entry has been revised as shown in the UNSC notice. Because the RBI cites the UAPA Section 51A obligation and the KYC Directions, regulated entities must ensure they have no accounts in the names of any individuals/entities appearing on the circulated lists and must act on the updated designation information immediately upon receipt of this communication. The practical compliance action is to refresh sanctions screening/watchlists against the revised UNSC list and investigate any potential matches involving the amended entries without delay.

The document is dated September 07, 2026 and does not itself specify a separate internal deadline beyond the obligation to remain continuously compliant with the updated sanctions list.

rows.title: Master Directions on Relief/Savings Bonds
rows.summary:
This Master Direction consolidates and updates all operative RBI instructions on Relief/Savings Bonds as of June 30, 2018, and supersedes earlier scattered guidance by placing the current rules in one location; it was issued on July 2, 2018 and is stated to be updated whenever rules, regulations, or policy change. It applies to the designated Receiving Offices named in the circular: State Bank of India, all nationalized banks except Punjab and Sind Bank and Andhra Bank, Axis Bank Ltd., ICICI Bank Ltd., HDFC Bank Ltd., and Stock Holding Corporation of India Ltd. (SHCIL). The first operational change concerns broker enrollment/registration: Receiving Offices may use a simple registration process, under which a broker submits a request on business letterhead along with business data, and the Receiving Office must allot a code number that the broker must quote on all bond applications tendered for brokerage claims. The document also addresses appointment of sub-agents by Receiving Offices and notes a concern that some offices have engaged other banks as brokers/agents for receiving applications while those intermediaries use RBI’s name in publicity material and billboards, indicating that such arrangements and branding use are being scrutinized or should not misrepresent RBI involvement.

The directions also cover brokerage payment/rates for Savings Bonds and nomination facilities for Relief/Savings Bonds, with the detailed instructions contained in the later sections and appendix of the Master Direction. From a compliance perspective, the key obligation is to follow the updated RBI-prescribed procedures exactly, ensure only properly enrolled brokers are used for brokerage claims, and ensure the broker code system is implemented so applications can be tracked and brokerage paid only where properly claimed. Because the directions are a living compilation updated by RBI, compliance teams should treat this as a standing requirement to monitor subsequent amendments on the RBI website rather than a one-time circular.

rows.title: Master Direction – Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers (Updated as on November 22, 2018)
rows.summary:
This update to the RBI Master Direction on Operational Guidelines for Primary Dealers reiterates and clarifies several existing operational requirements for primary dealers (PDs) in government securities markets. First, PDs must follow the RBI’s rules for submitting non-competitive bids in G-Sec auctions, as set out in RBI/2008-09/479 dated May 22, 2009, as amended from time to time. It also confirms that PDs may sell securities allotted in primary issues on the same day they are received, but only in accordance with the specific circulars cited in the direction: IDMC.PDRS.No.PDS.1/03.64.00/2000-01 dated October 6, 2000; RBI/2005/461–IDMD.PDRS.4777/10.02.01/2004-05 dated May 11, 2005; and RBI/2012-13/133-IDMD.PDRD.188/03.64.00/2012-13 dated July 16, 2012. For such same-day sales, PDs are permitted to use brokers to execute the sale contracts.

A key settlement requirement is that primary auction settlement is independent of secondary market settlement and must therefore be funded separately. Successful PDs must ensure sufficient funds are available in their RBI current account on the auction settlement day before 3:00 p.m. to cover their auction subscriptions. If funds are short, the deficiency will be treated as an instance of “SGL bouncing,” which triggers the applicable penal provisions. Compliance teams should therefore treat auction-day liquidity management as a standalone obligation, not something that can be covered by secondary market settlement balances.

In the secondary market, PDs are required to act as market makers in Government securities by quoting two-way prices in G-Sec on the NDS-OM platform, in the OTC market, and on recognized stock exchanges in India, while also taking principal positions in the secondary market. The direction also imposes annual turnover targets: PDs must achieve a minimum turnover ratio of 5 times for Government dated securities and 10 times for Treasury Bills/Cash Management Bills, measured against average month-end stock holdings. For outright transactions specifically, the minimum turnover ratio is lower but still mandatory: at least 3 times for Government dated securities and 6 times for T-Bills/CMBs. The turnover ratio is defined as total secondary-market purchases and sales during the year divided by average month-end stocks.

The document also begins a separate requirement on short-selling in the secondary market, stating that PDs must comply with RBI-issued guidelines on that activity, but the excerpt provided cuts off before the full rule text. For compliance purposes, the material obligations visible in this excerpt are the funding deadline of 3:00 p.m. on auction settlement days, the prohibition on failing to fund primary auction obligations without incurring SGL bouncing treatment, the mandatory market-making function, the specified annual turnover ratios, and adherence to the cited RBI circulars governing same-day sale of auction allotments and non-competitive bidding.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India [Conduct of Government Business by Agency Banks (ABs) – Payment of Agency Commission and Oversight of ABs] Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2026 Directions on “Conduct of Government Business by Agency Banks (ABs) – Payment of Agency Commission and Oversight of ABs” set out the framework for appointing agency banks, paying commission for government business, and monitoring compliance. The directions are issued on April 30, 2026, and apply to agency banks conducting Government business under RBI appointment; the document’s operative details govern which government transactions are eligible for agency commission, how they must be reported, and what documentation is required to claim payment. It also specifically distinguishes transactions that do **not** qualify for commission, so banks need to check each transaction type against the eligibility rules rather than assuming all government collections or payments are compensable.

A major substantive part of the directions is the commission framework for government business: the RBI specifies the rates of agency commission, clarifies when a **single challan is to be treated as a single transaction**, and lays out the exact procedure ABs must follow to submit commission claims. The directions also require ABs to report government transactions to RBI in the prescribed manner, which is tied to the commission claim process, and to submit specified supporting documents when seeking payment. The document additionally includes clarifications on commission claims and introduces a penalty mechanism in the form of **penal interest for wrong claims of agency commission**, meaning banks may face financial consequences if they claim commission incorrectly or inconsistently with the directions.

For compliance purposes, the key operational issue is that the directions are not just fee-setting rules; they create an end-to-end control regime over government business conducted by agency banks. ABs must ensure their transaction tagging, challan treatment, reporting, and claim support are aligned with RBI’s prescribed rules, especially for transactions linked to Government schemes, which receive separate treatment in the directions. The final chapter on oversight indicates RBI will supervise government business conducted by ABs, so banks should expect ongoing monitoring of appointment compliance, transaction reporting, claim integrity, and adherence to the eligibility rules for agency commission.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India [Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs)] Directions, 2026 (Updated as on June 24, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Disbursement of Government Pension by Agency Banks (ABs) Directions, 2026”** (issued **April 30, 2026** and updated **June 24, 2026**) sets out the operating rules that **agency banks** must follow when paying government pension, including central, state, and related government pension disbursements routed through banks. The directions apply to **all agency banks authorized to disburse government pension**, and they replace/organize the compliance framework around pension payment timing, implementation of government orders (including **dearness relief (DR)** changes), error recovery, special handling for vulnerable pensioners, reimbursement, and life-certificate processing.

A core obligation is that agency banks must **promptly implement government orders** relating to pension changes, especially **DR and similar revisions**, and must keep themselves updated through the Government’s published orders available on the relevant government website. Banks are required to ensure pension is disbursed in line with the government’s instructions and at the prescribed time each month; the directions emphasize that pension should be credited **on the due date prescribed by the government/RBI framework**, not delayed by internal bank processing. Compliance teams should treat this as a strict operational requirement, because the directions place responsibility on the paying bank to avoid delayed credit and to ensure government-issued revisions are reflected without avoidable lag.

The document also addresses **recovery and refund of excess pension payments**. Where an excess payment occurs due to an error attributable to the **agency bank**, the bank is responsible for arranging recovery/refund in accordance with the directions and the applicable government instructions. Where the excess arises from a **government-attributed error**, the bank must still follow the prescribed process for correction, but the obligation and recovery mechanics differ from bank-attributed mistakes; this distinction matters for liability allocation, reporting, and reconciliation. Compliance staff should ensure the bank has controls to identify whether an overpayment originated from bank processing or from government input, because that affects how the excess is recovered and who bears the operational burden.

A separate chapter provides special instructions for **old, sick, disabled, and incapacitated pensioners**. These pensioners must be allowed to withdraw pension through the permitted modes set out in the directions, and banks are expected to use customer-friendly procedures to facilitate payment when the pensioner cannot personally visit the branch in the normal manner. The directions also require banks to **display the relevant withdrawal instructions prominently in branches**, so staff and customers can see how such pensioners may access their pensions. This is a branch-level compliance obligation, not just a back-office one, and should be reflected in staff training and inspection checklists.

The directions further cover **reimbursement of pension payments** made by agency banks and the associated documentation/processing expected for claiming reimbursement from the government system. In addition, the document contains a dedicated chapter on **life certificates**, indicating that banks must follow the prescribed life-certificate verification and submission process as a condition for continuing pension payments. For compliance purposes, the most important takeaway is that agency banks must maintain end-to-end controls over pension implementation: timely application of government orders, accurate monthly disbursement, proper handling of overpayments and recoveries, accessible procedures for vulnerable pensioners, visible branch instructions, and correct reimbursement and life-certificate processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026** were issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen internal grievance redress and require a meaningful review of customer complaints before final rejection by an apex-level authority inside the bank. The Directions take effect **immediately**, but compliance with **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)** is permitted until **June 30, 2026**. RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a particular regulated entity, and to extend any such suspension by further order.

The Directions apply to **Commercial Banks** that had **10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**, regardless of whether the bank is incorporated in India or abroad. For this purpose, “Commercial Banks” covers **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**, as well as **corresponding new banks** and **State Bank of India**. Accordingly, institutions below the 10-outlet threshold as of that date are outside the scope, while qualifying banks must implement the internal ombudsman framework required by the Directions.

The document specifically signals that banks must maintain an **Internal Ombudsman mechanism** as part of their customer complaint handling process, with review occurring **before rejection** so that complaints are not summarily dismissed without an internal apex-level reconsideration. Because the excerpt provided does not include the later operational clauses, a compliance team should expect additional detailed requirements in the full Directions on appointment, role, escalation workflow, and reporting, and should treat the immediate-effective provisions plus the June 30, 2026 implementation deadline as mandatory planning dates for any in-scope commercial bank.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks - Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026** are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** to strengthen internal grievance redressal by requiring an apex-level internal review before customer complaints are rejected. The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, except for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. RBI also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, generally or for a specified regulated entity, and to extend any such suspension period.

These Directions apply to **Small Finance Banks that had 10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**. They also apply to any Small Finance Bank that reaches that **10-outlet threshold after March 31, 2025**, but only **from six months after it first meets the eligibility criterion**. In other words, compliance teams at SFBs should first determine whether the bank meets or later crosses the 10-outlet trigger, because that determines whether and when the internal ombudsman framework becomes mandatory.

Substantively, the framework is intended to ensure that customer complaints are **reviewed by an internal ombudsman before rejection**, rather than being declined solely through ordinary complaint-handling channels. The document therefore requires banks in scope to maintain or enhance an internal grievance redress process with an **apex-level internal review function** that can independently assess complaints proposed for rejection.
