While the excerpt provided does not include the operative details of clauses 7 and 14, the document clearly signals that some specific implementation requirements tied to those provisions have a later compliance date of **June 30, 2026**, so affected banks should treat those as deferred mandatory steps and ensure their implementation plans and policies are aligned accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks - Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026** are intended to strengthen internal grievance redress by requiring an **apex-level internal review before customer complaints are rejected**. The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, except for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which may be implemented later but must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. The RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to extend any such suspension from time to time.

These Directions apply to **Payments Banks** that have **10 or more banking outlets in India as of March 31, 2025**. They also apply to any Payments Bank that reaches that threshold **after March 31, 2025**, but in that case the obligations begin **six months after the bank first meets the eligibility criteria**. In practice, compliance teams at affected Payments Banks need to assess their outlet count as of the March 31, 2025 cutoff and continuously monitor whether they cross the threshold later, because eligibility triggers a delayed but mandatory implementation timeline.

The document’s stated regulatory purpose is not merely procedural; it is to ensure complaints are not rejected without a meaningful internal review at the highest level within the bank. For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is to confirm that the bank’s internal grievance handling framework includes the mandated Internal Ombudsman review mechanism and that the delayed-effective clauses are fully in place by **June 30, 2026** at the latest. The excerpt provided does not include the substantive definitions or the later clauses themselves, so the material obligations visible here are the applicability test, commencement date, RBI suspension power, and the deadline for the specified deferred provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026** are intended to strengthen customer grievance redressal in NBFCs by requiring an **apex-level internal review before a complaint is finally rejected**. The Directions take **immediate effect**, but **clause 7(2), 14(2), and 14(4)** do not have to be implemented until **June 30, 2026** at the latest. The RBI also reserves the right to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to extend any suspension period.

These Directions apply to specified **NBFCs**, but explicitly **exclude** Housing Finance Companies, Core Investment Companies, Infrastructure Debt Fund-NBFCs, NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Companies, Non-Operative Financial Holding Companies, Primary Dealers, and Mortgage Guarantee Companies. Applicability is determined **as of March 31, 2025**, and the document begins listing categories such as **deposit-taking NBFCs**; the full regulation should be checked for all thresholds and subcategories covered, but the key compliance point is that the regime is targeted at NBFCs meeting the prescribed applicability criteria on that date. For in-scope entities, the core obligation is to maintain an Internal Ombudsman framework that allows customer complaints to be **reviewed before rejection**, rather than simply denied at the first-line grievance stage.

From a compliance perspective, the key operational dates are: **effective immediately upon issuance on January 14, 2026**, with a **hard compliance deadline of June 30, 2026** for the specified clauses. NBFCs that fall within scope should assess whether their current grievance-redress process already includes the required **independent internal review mechanism**, and if not, they will need to implement or revise procedures, governance, and escalation workflows to ensure complaints are routed for review before rejection. The document’s stated policy objective is not merely procedural formality; it is to ensure **speedy and meaningful resolution of customer complaints** through a higher-level internal authority within the NBFC.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Bank Prepaid Payment Instruments Issuers - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Non-Bank Prepaid Payment Instruments Issuers – Internal Ombudsman Directions, 2026”** require covered non-bank PPI issuers to strengthen their internal grievance redress framework by creating an **apex-level internal review mechanism** before customer complaints are finally rejected. The purpose is to ensure **speedy and meaningful resolution of complaints**, with an internal ombudsman-style review of grievances that would otherwise be denied.

These Directions apply to **non-bank prepaid payment instruments issuers** with **more than one crore (10 million) prepaid payment instruments outstanding as of March 31, 2025, or any time thereafter**. The text also indicates the Directions apply to **specified categories of PPI issuers under clause 4(1)(h)**, so compliance teams should assess applicability based on the formal definition in the instrument, not just business size. The Directions are issued under **Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.

The Directions take **immediate effect** upon issuance, but three specific provisions are subject to a later compliance deadline: **clause 7(2), 14(2), and 14(4)** must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. Compliance teams should therefore distinguish between obligations that are effective immediately and those that have the six-month implementation window. The Reserve Bank also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions for a specified period, either generally or for a particular regulated entity, and may **extend any suspension from time to time** by further order.

In practical terms, affected PPI issuers need to ensure they have an internal process that permits **review before rejection of customer complaints** by an internal authority at the highest level within the issuer. Because the document is a formal RBI direction rather than guidance, failure to meet the applicable deadlines or applicability threshold would create a direct compliance issue for in-scope issuers.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Credit Information Companies - Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Credit Information Companies (Internal Ombudsman) Directions, 2026** apply to all **Credit Information Companies (CICs)** and are intended to strengthen the CIC internal grievance redress system by requiring an **apex-level internal review before customer complaints are rejected**, so complaints are handled more speedily and meaningfully. The Directions take effect **immediately on January 14, 2026**, **except** for **clause 7(2), clause 14(2), and clause 14(4)**, which must be complied with **no later than June 30, 2026**. The RBI also reserves the power to **suspend any or all provisions** of the Directions, either generally or for a specific regulated entity, and to **extend any suspension** from time to time by order.

From the portion provided, the document begins defining key terms for implementation. It identifies the **“Competent Authority”** as the **Managing Director / Chief Executive Officer of the CIC**, indicating that senior management will have an explicit role in the complaint-handling framework. It also defines **“Complaint”** as a written representation or one made through the prescribed channel/mode (the text shown cuts off before the full definition), which signals that the obligations will turn on formal complaint intake and processing methods established by the Directions.

For compliance purposes, the material points are that CICs must ensure their internal grievance process is structured to allow an **independent or higher-level internal review before refusal/rejection of complaints**, and they should be prepared to implement the delayed provisions by **June 30, 2026**. Because the Directions are issued under **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**, they have statutory regulatory force for CIC operations. The excerpt provided does not yet include the full mechanics of appointment, tenure, reporting, escalation, or complaint timelines, so additional sections would be needed to identify the complete operational obligations.

rows.title: Master Direction - Reserve Bank of India (Internal Ombudsman for Regulated Entities) Directions, 2023
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Master Direction – RBI (Internal Ombudsman for Regulated Entities) Directions, 2023”** on **December 29, 2023**, to consolidate and update the internal-ombudsman framework previously set out separately for banks, NBFCs, non-bank system participants, and credit information companies. It applies to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding RRBs), all NBFCs, all Non-Bank System Participants, and all Credit Information Companies** addressed in the circular, and it is intended to strengthen the internal grievance-redress architecture by reaffirming the Internal Ombudsman as an **independent, apex-level authority for consumer grievance redress** within each regulated entity. The RBI states that the framework was reviewed in light of the integration of the three RBI Ombudsman schemes and to improve customer service standards, indicating that this direction is meant to harmonize and reinforce existing complaint-handling requirements rather than create an entirely new concept.

For compliance purposes, the key substance is that regulated entities covered by the direction must maintain an Internal Ombudsman mechanism that operates as a meaningful final internal review layer for consumer complaints, with the Ombudsman positioned independently from the business and complaint-handling functions. The document does not, in the excerpt provided, specify numerical thresholds, complaint types, appointment timelines, or reporting deadlines, but it clearly signals that the RBI expects the mechanism to function “as envisaged” and not merely as a formalistic process. The direction is issued under the RBI’s statutory powers, meaning it has mandatory regulatory force for covered entities and should be treated as a compliance obligation affecting governance, complaints escalation, and consumer grievance resolution processes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk) Directions, 2026
rows.desc: DOR/2026-27/472 DOR.MRG.REC.227/21-01-002/2026-27 September 21, 2026 Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk) Directions, 2026 Table of Contents Chapter-I: Preliminary ........................................................................................................... 3 A. Short title and Effective Date ......................................................................................... 3 B. Applicability ................................................................................................................... 3 C. Definitions ..................................................................................................................... 3 Chapter-II: Boundary between the banking book and the trading book ................................. 5 A. Scope of the trading book ............................................................................................. 5 B. Restrictions on reclassifying instruments between the regulatory books ....................... 5 C. Treatment of internal risk transfers ................................................................................ 6 C.1 Internal risk transfer of credit risk from banking book to trading book .................. 6 C.2 Internal risk transfer of general interest rate risk (GIRR) from banking book to trading book ................................................................................................................... 7 C.3 Eligible hedges for the CVA capital requirement .................................................. 8 Chapter-III: Scope of application of market risk ................................................................... 10 A. Exclusion of certain structural foreign exchange positions from Net Open Position .. 10 Chapter-IV: Calculating risk- weighted assets for market risk ............................................... 16 A. Risk-weighted assets and capital requirements .....................................
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Minimum Capital Requirements for Market Risk” Directions, 2026** set the supervisory framework for how commercial banks must classify positions, measure market risk, and calculate the resulting capital requirement. The document applies to the **commercial banks in scope under the RBI framework** and is organized around the boundary between the **banking book** and **trading book**, treatment of **internal risk transfers**, the **scope of market risk application**, and the **calculation of risk-weighted assets (RWA) and capital requirements** for market risk.

A key compliance theme is that banks must maintain and apply a disciplined distinction between instruments held in the banking book versus the trading book, and they are restricted in how they can move instruments between those books. The directions also govern **internal risk transfers** from the banking book to the trading book, including transfers of **credit risk** and **general interest rate risk (GIRR)**, and set rules for what counts as an **eligible hedge for the CVA capital requirement**. That means banks cannot rely on informal or opportunistic repositioning of exposures; any reclassification or internal transfer must fit the regulatory criteria in these directions and be supportable for capital purposes.

The document also addresses the **scope of market risk exposure** by identifying certain **structural foreign exchange positions** that may be excluded from the **Net Open Position** calculation, but only where the regulatory conditions for that exclusion are met. For compliance teams, this means FX positions that are part of the institution’s structural balance-sheet management must be reviewed carefully to determine whether they may be excluded, and if so, whether the exclusion is properly documented and consistently applied.

Finally, Chapter IV establishes how banks must compute **risk-weighted assets for market risk** and the related capital requirements, indicating that the directions are intended to be used operationally in capital measurement and regulatory reporting. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed formulas, thresholds, or specific effective-date text beyond the issuance date shown at the top (**September 21, 2026**), so a compliance team would need the full chapter text to identify the exact calculation mechanics, any implementation deadlines, and any transitional arrangements. Still, the document clearly requires banks to align their book classification, internal risk transfer treatment, FX structural position treatment, and market-risk RWA calculations with the RBI’s prescribed methodology.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach) Directions, 2026 (Effective from April 1, 2027)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach” Directions, 2026** (issued **April 27, 2026** and **effective from April 1, 2027**) establish the RBI’s updated framework for how **commercial banks** must calculate and apply **capital charges for credit risk** under the standardised approach. The directions apply across a broad range of exposure types and are organized into detailed rules covering **sovereigns, foreign sovereigns and central banks, public sector entities, MDBs/BIS/IMF, banks, corporates, subordinated debt/equity/other capital instruments, retail, MSMEs, real estate, NPAs, fund investments, specified categories, unhedged foreign currency exposure, other assets, off-balance sheet items, and securitisation exposures**. They also set out the framework for **external credit ratings**, including which rating agencies are eligible, how ratings are mapped and used, and how to handle long-term and short-term ratings, unsolicited ratings, multiple ratings, issuer-not-cooperating cases, and the use of issue ratings for issuer/other claims.  

From a compliance perspective, the directions require banks to follow explicit **general instructions and due diligence requirements** before assigning risk weights, including ensuring exposures are classified correctly and that any reliance on external ratings or credit risk mitigants meets the RBI’s standards. The document further lays down detailed rules for **credit risk mitigation**, including the legal certainty required for mitigation arrangements, how to treat **maturity mismatches and currency mismatches**, and the conditions for recognizing **collateral, on-balance-sheet netting, and guarantees** as valid forms of mitigation. The final chapter states that prior relevant directions are being **repealed**, meaning banks will need to transition their capital charge computation and related internal controls to this new framework by the **April 1, 2027** commencement date.  

For compliance teams, the key implication is that this is not a narrow amendment but a **full replacement framework** for determining risk weights and capital treatment for credit risk under the standardized approach. Banks will need to review their exposure classification logic, rating dependency controls, collateral and guarantee documentation, off-balance-sheet treatment, and securitisation capital calculations to ensure they align with the new directions before the effective date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Commercial Banks – Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions, 2026”** on **April 27, 2026** as **DOR/2026-27/398 / DOR.STR.REC.No.6/21.06.011/2026-27**. This document is the governing prudential framework for **commercial banks** on how to classify assets, recognize income, and make provisions, and it also introduces an **Expected Credit Loss (ECL)-based provisioning framework**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that it is not merely a guidance note: it is a set of binding directions that will affect banks’ credit impairment methodology, loan classification controls, provisioning calculations, and related reporting and governance processes.

The document is organized into a preliminary chapter, then rules for **classification as non-performing assets (NPAs)**, followed by a detailed chapter on **ECL-based provisioning**. The content shown indicates that the RBI is setting out the criteria for when an exposure must be classified as an NPA and the prudential norms that apply once a bank makes that determination. It then moves into a formal framework for calculating ECL, including **fair valuation on transition**, **initial recognition and subsequent measurement**, how to determine a **significant increase in credit risk (SICR)**, how ECL is measured for different financial instruments, the **period over which lifetime ECL is measured**, **probability-weighted outcomes**, and the use of the **effective interest rate**. A compliance team should treat this as a significant change to credit-loss governance because these topics imply new model, data, documentation, and controls requirements for expected-loss estimation.

Because the table of contents shows a dedicated section on **applicability**, compliance should confirm which entities within the bank group are covered and whether any branches, subsidiaries, or specific categories of commercial banking activity are excluded or subject to special treatment. The document also includes a definitions section, which will be important because the operational meaning of terms such as asset classification categories, default/NPA triggers, SICR, lifetime ECL, and effective interest rate will drive policy drafting and model calibration. In practice, the bank should expect to review and potentially revise its credit policy, accounting policy, provisioning methodology, internal escalation triggers, and management reporting so that they align with RBI’s required classification and impairment approach.

From a compliance standpoint, the most material obligations indicated by this draft are: determine when an exposure becomes an NPA under RBI-prescribed norms; apply the RBI’s prudential treatment once an asset is non-performing; build and maintain an ECL methodology that reflects **initial recognition, subsequent measurement, and SICR-based staging**; and ensure provisions are measured using the specified framework rather than legacy loss-incurred approaches. Since the document’s excerpt does not show the detailed thresholds or transition dates beyond the issuance date, the immediate action item is to review the operative chapters for any **effective date, implementation timeline, transitional arrangements, model governance expectations, or provisioning percentages** that will determine when the bank must change its systems and reporting.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend and Remittances of Profits) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividend and Remittances of Profits Directions, 2026** (issued as **RBI/2025-26/387, DOR.ACC.REC.No.427/21.02.067/2025-26 dated March 10, 2026**) establish the prudential framework commercial banks must follow before declaring dividends or remitting profits. The directions apply to **commercial banks** and specifically distinguish between **banks incorporated in India** and **foreign banks operating in India in branch mode**, with separate rules for dividend declaration and profit remittance. The document is organized around board oversight, eligibility criteria, dividend/profit limits, reporting, restrictions, penalties, and repeal/saving provisions.

For **boards and management**, the RBI requires explicit **board oversight** over any proposed dividend declaration or profit remittance, meaning the decision must be assessed against the prudential conditions in the directions rather than treated as a routine distribution matter. Banks must satisfy the prescribed **eligibility criteria** before any payment is made; if those conditions are not met, dividend or remittance is not permitted. For **banks incorporated in India**, the RBI sets the **quantum of dividend payable** through prudential limits, so compliance teams must verify that the proposed dividend amount falls within the applicable ceiling and is supportable by the bank’s financial position and regulatory status.

For **foreign banks operating in India in branch mode**, the directions instead govern **remittance of profits**, and the RBI also specifies categories of **profits that are ineligible for dividend payment or remittance**. That means not all profits can necessarily be taken out of India, and compliance must ensure the amounts proposed for remittance are drawn only from profits that qualify under the RBI’s rules. The directions also establish a **reporting system**, so banks will have to file the prescribed information to the RBI in the manner and form required before or in connection with distribution/remittance decisions.

The RBI further provides for **restrictions on payment of dividend and remittance of profits**, meaning even otherwise eligible banks can be barred from making distributions if regulatory conditions are not met. The document also includes **penal consequences for non-compliance**, indicating that violations may trigger supervisory or enforcement action in addition to the underlying prohibition on payment/remittance. Finally, Chapter III contains **repeal and saving provisions**, so compliance teams should check which prior RBI instructions have been superseded and whether any transitional or grandfathering treatment applies to actions already taken or pending when these directions took effect.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
This RBI circular, **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025**, reference **DOR/2025-26/174 / DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.93/13-04-001/2025-26**), consolidates and sets out binding directions for **commercial banks** on several operational and governance matters, with a significant focus on the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. The document is structured into chapters covering applicability and definitions, board governance requirements, DEAF credit/refund/registration/claim procedures, and returns/reporting, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal operating rulebook rather than a guidance note.

A key set of obligations applies at the **board level**: banks must have **board-approved policies**, the board is assigned specific oversight responsibilities, and the board must conduct periodic reviews of the relevant compliance areas. This means the bank’s senior governance framework is expected to explicitly approve, monitor, and periodically reassess the policies and procedures covered by the directions, rather than leaving them solely to operational teams.

The most substantive operational requirements concern the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund**. The directions define how amounts are to be **credited to the Fund**, how **refunds and interest** are to be handled, and the **registration guidelines** and **procedural requirements for transfer and claims**. Banks will need to ensure that dormant/unclaimed balances are transferred to the Fund in the manner prescribed by the RBI, that eligible refund claims are processed according to the specified procedure, and that any interest treatment tied to DEAF balances follows the new framework exactly. The inclusion of separate sections for credits, refunds, registration, and claims indicates that banks must maintain controls across the full DEAF lifecycle, from identification of eligible balances through transfer and eventual customer claim resolution.

The directions also impose **return/reporting obligations** (“Returns”), meaning banks will need to file whatever periodic or event-based reports the RBI specifies in the final text and ensure the underlying data is accurate, traceable, and reconciled to internal records. Because the document is titled as “Miscellaneous” directions and is expressly issued as a Reserve Bank of India direction for commercial banks, compliance should assume these are **mandatory requirements** effective from the date stated in the circular unless the operative chapters specify staggered implementation or separate deadlines. Where the final text includes precise thresholds, timelines, or filing formats for DEAF transfers, refunds, registration, or returns, those should be treated as direct compliance triggers for the relevant banking operations and IT/workflow teams.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions” Directions, 2025** is a comprehensive prudential capital framework for **commercial banks**, issued as RBI/DoR/2025-26/173 dated **November 28, 2025**. Its table of contents shows that it will govern three major areas: **counterparty credit risk capital for derivative transactions**, **capital requirements for exposures to central counterparties (CCPs)**, and **minimum capital requirements for operational risk**. From a compliance perspective, this is not a narrow clarification; it is a framework-setting direction that will affect how banks compute regulatory capital, determine exposure measures, and apply internal controls and reporting around derivatives, CCP clearing, and operational-risk capital calculations.

For **derivative transactions**, Chapter II introduces the **Standardised Approach for Counterparty Credit Risk (SA-CCR)** as the method for computing the **default risk capital charge**. This means affected banks will need to use the RBI-specified standardized counterparty credit risk methodology rather than ad hoc or legacy approaches for qualifying exposures. Compliance teams should expect operational requirements around correct trade classification, netting set identification, replacement cost and add-on calculations, and consistent application of the approach across all applicable derivative portfolios.

Chapter III sets out the **capital treatment for exposures to CCPs**, with separate rules for **qualifying CCPs (QCCPs)** and **non-qualifying CCPs**. Banks that clear through CCPs will need to distinguish whether the CCP meets the qualifying criteria, because the capital treatment differs materially depending on that status; exposures to **QCCPs** and **non-qualifying CCPs** are addressed in separate sections, and the chapter also includes specific requirements for recognizing **net replacement cost in close-out netting sets**. In practical terms, this implies the bank must have documented procedures to identify the CCP category, apply the correct exposure measure, and maintain evidence supporting any netting recognition used for capital purposes.

Chapter IV begins the framework for **minimum capital requirements for operational risk** and specifically includes an **interim arrangement**, indicating that the RBI is putting in place transitional treatment while the full operational-risk requirements are implemented. Even though the excerpt provided does not show the detailed formulae or phase-in dates, the presence of this chapter means commercial banks should prepare for updated operational-risk capital calculations, likely with transitional compliance steps and supervisory expectations during the interim period. Overall, the document is aimed at ensuring banks update capital computation processes, systems, and governance to align with RBI’s forthcoming standardized rules for derivatives, CCP exposures, and operational risk.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Climate Finance and Management of Climate Change Risks) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** (reference **DOR/2025-26/172** and **DOR.SFG.REC.No.91/30.01.021/2025-26**). The document is structured to impose two broad sets of requirements on **commercial banks**: first, governance and risk-management expectations for **climate finance and climate-related risks**, and second, a specific regulatory framework for **acceptance of green deposits**. The directions state a new/updated framework rather than a one-off disclosure requirement, so compliance teams should treat them as ongoing operational, treasury, product, disclosure, and board-governance obligations.

A central requirement is that the **board of directors** must oversee climate finance and climate risk management, meaning the bank cannot leave these matters solely to management-level committees. The directions require the board to approve and monitor the bank’s framework for dealing with climate change risks, which would typically include identifying exposures, setting internal controls, and ensuring appropriate reporting to senior management and the board. In practice, this means climate-related financial risks must be embedded into governance, strategy, and risk management rather than handled as a purely ESG or CSR matter.

The document creates a dedicated **Framework for Acceptance of Green Deposits**. Banks that choose to accept green deposits must have a formal **policy** approved by the board, and the framework governs how such deposits may be offered, priced, deployed, and reported. The directions specify rules for the **denomination, interest rates, and tenor** of these deposits, and require a **financing framework** that identifies the eligible use of proceeds, how funds will be tracked, and what internal controls apply. Green deposit proceeds must be used only for the stated green purposes under the framework; banks therefore need strong ring-fencing, tracking, and auditability so that deposited funds are not diverted to non-eligible activities.

The directions also require **third-party verification/assurance** and an **impact assessment** for the green-deposit framework. That means banks must obtain external confirmation that the proceeds are aligned with the stated green-use criteria, and they must assess and evidence the environmental impact of funded activities. In addition, the directions impose **reporting and disclosure** obligations, so banks must be prepared to disclose their green deposit framework, how proceeds were deployed, and the relevant impact/assurance information in a way that is transparent to regulators and depositors. This implies operational obligations around documentation, audit trails, internal certification, and periodic public/regulatory reporting.

Finally, the document includes **repeal and saving** provisions and states that other existing provisions may continue to apply as saved or supplemented by the new directions. For a compliance team, the key action is to map these directions against existing deposit-product approvals, treasury pricing, environmental/ESG claims processes, internal control frameworks, and board reporting, then determine whether the bank is offering—or intends to offer—green deposits and whether its climate-risk governance already meets the RBI’s expectations. Because the document content provided here is only the table of contents and headings, it does not expose the detailed numerical limits, specific tenor bands, interest-rate caps/floors, or exact reporting formats; however, those will be the critical implementation details to verify in the operative chapters before launch or ongoing compliance certification.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025**) replaces/sets a formal outsourcing-risk framework for **commercial banks** subject to RBI supervision, with the rules organized around board oversight, senior management accountability, and controls over outsourced financial services. The document establishes that each covered bank must have a **board-approved outsourcing policy** and a governance structure that clearly assigns responsibility for approving, monitoring, and reviewing outsourcing arrangements, including ongoing risk management and oversight of vendors/service providers. A key compliance theme is that outsourcing does **not** transfer responsibility away from the bank: the bank remains accountable for the outsourced activity, must maintain effective supervision, and must ensure the arrangement does not impair prudential control, customer protection, or regulatory compliance.

A central requirement is that **certain activities cannot be outsourced** at all; while the excerpt does not list the prohibited items, the directions expressly create a category of activities that banks are barred from delegating, so compliance teams must identify those exclusions in the operative text before entering any arrangement. For permitted outsourcing of financial services, the bank must implement an authorization process, maintain clear accountability lines, and ensure senior management performs active oversight, supported by a documented governance framework and a bank-wide outsourcing policy. The directions also require a risk-management approach tailored to outsourcing, meaning banks must evaluate the operational, legal, reputational, and business continuity risks associated with each outsourced function and ensure the service provider can meet the bank’s standards.

The document’s effective date is tied to its commencement provisions in Chapter I, so compliance teams should treat the **November 28, 2025** issuance as the key reference point and confirm the exact commencement/effective date in the full text. Because the table of contents shows dedicated sections on applicability, scope, definitions, board duties, prohibited outsourcing, authorization/accountability, governance framework, outsourcing policy, and senior management responsibilities, the directions are intended to be comprehensive rather than advisory: they require formal internal controls, documented approvals, and ongoing monitoring rather than ad hoc vendor management. Any bank using third parties for financial services should review existing outsourcing contracts, governance documents, and escalation procedures against these directions to identify whether changes are needed to policy wording, approval thresholds, risk reviews, or monitoring practices.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Commercial Banks – Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, updated as of **July 1, 2026**, and it applies to **commercial banks** covered by the RBI framework. The document replaces and consolidates a broad set of conduct, customer service, inclusion, payments, deposit, and lending requirements into a single binding directions framework, so compliance teams should treat it as the controlling operational standard for branch conduct, customer treatment, and lending behavior.

At a high level, the directions require banks to maintain a formal **institutional framework** for responsible business conduct, including governance, oversight, and internal accountability arrangements, and to implement prescribed customer-facing practices in branches. The customer-service chapters indicate that banks must meet detailed obligations on **branch-level service standards, customer guidance, complaint/protection measures, financial inclusion and accessibility, and payment/remittance service conduct**, with specific operational forms and notices provided in the annexes, including a **format for a comprehensive notice board** and **quick-reference rates**. This means banks must ensure the required disclosures, notices, and service procedures are in place at the branch and operational level rather than relying only on general policy statements.

The directions also impose specific requirements for **deposit and other liability accounts**, including standardized processes for account handling and claim settlement after death, reflected in the annexed forms for **settlement of claims** both **with a nominee or survivorship clause** and **without a nominee or survivorship clause**. Compliance teams should note that this signals mandatory process discipline around account documentation, nominee handling, and claim resolution, and the annexes suggest the RBI expects uniform forms and procedures rather than institution-specific variations. The document further addresses **responsible lending conduct**, meaning banks must align lending practices with RBI-prescribed conduct standards across origination and ongoing customer interaction, with chapter-level requirements likely affecting underwriting, disclosures, communication, and recovery behavior.

The table of contents shows the directions are organized to cover not just consumer-facing conduct but also **miscellaneous provisions** and a **repeal/transition section**, which indicates the 2025 directions likely supersede prior scattered instructions on these topics. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that affected banks must review their branch procedures, customer communications, complaint handling, inclusion/accessibility measures, deposit-claim workflows, payment/remittance practices, and lending conduct controls against the updated RBI framework and ensure the annexed formats and “rates at a quick glance” disclosures are implemented exactly as prescribed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer” Directions, 2025 are a consolidated KYC/AML compliance framework for commercial banks, issued under the RBI’s authority and updated as of December 29, 2025, with the base circular dated November 28, 2025. They apply to commercial banks and set binding requirements for customer identification, customer due diligence, risk-based controls, beneficial ownership identification, ongoing monitoring, and governance over KYC policies and procedures.  

For compliance teams, the key point is that banks must maintain a board-approved KYC framework with explicit policies and internal controls covering customer acceptance, identification, due diligence, risk categorization, periodic updating of records, and monitoring of transactions to detect suspicious activity. The directions also require ongoing due diligence rather than one-time onboarding review, meaning customer information must be periodically refreshed and transaction patterns monitored against expected activity throughout the relationship.  

The document’s structure shows separate obligations for individuals, sole proprietorships, and legal entities, with specific requirements for verifying identity, establishing the existence of the customer, and identifying beneficial owners where the customer is a legal entity or arrangement. It also includes enhanced and simplified due diligence procedures, indicating that the level of verification must be adjusted based on risk, with stricter checks for higher-risk relationships and streamlined measures permitted only where the rules explicitly allow lower-risk treatment.  

Because the table of contents also highlights chapters on applicability, definitions, risk management, and customer identification procedures, a compliance officer should expect the directions to prescribe who is in scope, what customer information must be obtained, how records are to be maintained, and how exceptions or special cases are handled. Any bank subject to these directions should review its KYC policy, onboarding workflows, periodic review schedules, beneficial ownership processes, and monitoring controls to ensure they align with the RBI’s current requirements in the updated 2025 text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI Directions document sets out the presentation, disclosure, and related accounting requirements that commercial banks in India must follow in their standalone and consolidated financial statements, replacing or updating earlier requirements under a single consolidated framework. It applies to commercial banks covered by the RBI’s regulatory perimeter, and the updated version is marked “as on July 01, 2026,” meaning the document incorporates revisions effective up to that date; however, the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative text or any transition provisions, so the compliance team should verify the full directions for exact applicability dates of each rule. The document is structured to require banks to prepare the balance sheet and profit and loss account in RBI-prescribed formats, follow specific notes and instructions for compilation, and apply RBI guidance where accounting-standard issues arise, especially where banking-specific presentation differs from generic corporate reporting.

A major portion of the directions is devoted to disclosure obligations in the notes to accounts, requiring banks to present detailed information in a specified manner rather than relying only on general financial statement formatting. The directions also require consolidated financial statements, so groups with subsidiaries or other entities that must be consolidated will need to ensure alignment between standalone and group reporting. In addition, the document contains separate operational instructions covering inter-branch account provisioning for net debit balances, reconciliation and treatment of outstanding Nostro account entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, and provisioning for fraud—each of which indicates that banks must maintain controls and accounting processes specific to these regulatory items. Because the table of contents references these as separate “Other Instructions,” they are not optional disclosures but compliance requirements that affect balance sheet and profit and loss recognition, reconciliation discipline, and internal governance over losses and reserves.

For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that the Directions are not just a presentation template; they are a binding reporting rulebook that controls how commercial banks classify, recognize, disclose, and explain financial information to the RBI and other users. The document’s focus on chapter-level instructions suggests detailed line-item and note-level requirements, including treatment of specific accounting standards issues and special banking exposures, so banks should review whether their chart of accounts, financial statement drafting process, and internal controls produce the exact RBI-prescribed outputs. No numerical thresholds, rates, or specific deadlines beyond the document date and “updated as on July 01, 2026” marker are visible in the excerpt, so any implementation date, exception, or threshold-based rule would need confirmation from the full text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** as **DOR/2025-26/166, DOR.FIN.REC.No.85/20-16-003/2025-26**. The stated purpose is to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent, and natural-justice-based process** for classifying a borrower as a **wilful defaulter** and to ensure that information on wilful defaulters is shared so lenders are cautioned and **further institutional finance is not extended** to them. The RBI issued the directions under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**.

From the content provided, the document is organized into chapters covering the board’s function, treatment of wilful defaulters, reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters, preventive measures and auditors’ role, and repeal/other provisions, with two annexures giving reporting formats. The excerpt does **not yet include the substantive operative clauses**, so the specific procedural requirements, thresholds, timelines, and definitions for “large defaulter” or the exact classification/reporting mechanics are not visible in the provided text. However, a compliance team should note that this is a **commercial-bank-focused regulatory framework** that will govern how banks identify, classify, report, and manage wilful defaulters, likely requiring internal controls, board oversight, documentation of due process, and information-sharing/reporting workflows once the detailed provisions are reviewed. If you share the remaining chapters, I can produce a full obligation-by-obligation compliance summary with all thresholds, deadlines, and filing requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets – Directions, 2025** (as updated **July 1, 2026**) consolidate and replace the RBI’s framework for how regulated commercial banks must identify stress early, report stressed exposures, attempt resolution, and make additional provisions when resolution is delayed. The directions apply to **commercial banks** covered by the RBI framework and set out a mandatory process for **board-approved stressed asset policies**, **early warning and reporting**, **time-bound resolution**, and **supervisory disclosure/review**. The document’s core compliance message is that banks must not wait for an account to become irrecoverable; instead, they must identify stress promptly, escalate it through internal governance, and act within specified timelines to either implement a viable resolution plan or face enhanced provisioning consequences.

Under the **general requirements**, each bank must maintain **board-approved policies** governing identification of stress, resolution strategy, inter-creditor coordination, and provisioning treatment. Banks are required to establish procedures for **early identification and reporting of stress** and to make the disclosures called for by the RBI framework, which are intended to support supervisory oversight and consistency across lenders. The document also makes clear that the RBI will exercise **supervisory review**, meaning banks’ treatment of stressed accounts, timelines, and provisioning decisions are subject to regulatory scrutiny rather than being purely internal credit-management decisions.

The **resolution process** begins with a formal **review period** once stress is identified, during which lenders must assess the borrower’s position and work toward a resolution plan. Where more than one lender is involved, the framework requires an **inter-creditor agreement**, so participating banks must coordinate decision-making rather than acting in isolation. A resolution plan must be prepared and implemented in accordance with the RBI’s prescribed process, and the framework ties the success or delay of that plan to the bank’s provisioning obligations.

A key compliance feature is the **additional provisioning requirement for delayed implementation of the resolution plan**. If a resolution plan is not implemented within the prescribed timeline, the bank must make **additional specific provisioning**, increasing the capital/earnings hit until the situation is resolved or regularized under the framework. Compliance teams should therefore treat these directions as both a governance requirement and a financial-control requirement: they affect how stressed loans are monitored, how quickly escalation occurs, how lender coordination is documented, and how provisioning is booked when deadlines are missed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the updated framework for **income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning (IRACP)** for **commercial banks** in India, and it is issued as **DOR/2025-26/164 dated November 28, 2025**, with the text marked **“updated as on July 01, 2026.”** It applies to the commercial banks covered by the RBI’s IRACP regime and replaces/updates the operating rules banks must use for identifying non-performing assets (NPAs), recognizing income only when permitted, and creating provisions in line with the prescribed standards. The document is organized to cover general governance, disclosure, automated processes, detailed classification rules, special cases, and provisioning requirements, so it is not just a technical accounting memo but a compliance framework for bank credit portfolios.

At a high level, the directions require banks to align board oversight, lending prudence, consumer education, and public disclosures with RBI expectations before moving into the detailed NPA rules. The “General Instructions” section indicates that the **board of directors has an explicit role** in governing IRACP compliance, and banks must maintain prudence in lending practices and consumer education processes, with disclosures prescribed separately. For compliance teams, this means the bank must have documented governance, controls, and reporting around how loan exposures are originated, monitored, classified, and disclosed, rather than leaving these decisions solely to operations or finance staff.

A significant operational requirement is the section on **automation of income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning processes**, which indicates that banks must use automated systems for these functions. That means classification and provisioning decisions should not depend on manual intervention where the rules can be system-driven, and the bank must ensure its core banking/credit systems correctly apply RBI’s asset classification logic. Compliance teams should expect an obligation to validate system configuration, exception handling, audit trails, and data integrity, because any automation error could directly affect whether an account is shown as standard, SMA, or NPA and how much provision is booked.

The document also contains detailed rules on **when an account becomes a non-performing asset**, how to treat **accounts regularized near the balance sheet date**, and how to handle **specific cases of asset classification** and **categories of NPAs**. That structure signals that timing matters: a borrower curing a delinquency close to year-end may not automatically eliminate the compliance impact if RBI’s prescribed timing or recognition rules require otherwise. The presence of a dedicated section on “specific cases” suggests there are special treatment rules for particular structures or account events, so compliance officers should verify how the bank classifies edge cases rather than relying only on generic overdue-based logic.

Finally, the directions include a separate chapter on **upgradation of NPAs** and another on **provisions**, which means banks must follow RBI’s rules not only for downgrading accounts into NPA status but also for when and how they can restore an account to performing status and release or adjust provisions. The document also includes treatment for **credit information/reporting**, **presentation/disclosure**, and other connected requirements later in the text structure, indicating that classification outcomes must be reflected consistently in financial statements, regulatory returns, and customer/consumer-facing disclosures. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this is a comprehensive IRACP rulebook: banks must ensure board oversight, system automation, timely and accurate NPA recognition, proper handling of special cases and year-end cures, and correct provisioning/upgradation practices across all relevant commercial-bank credit exposures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**) set out a comprehensive framework for how **commercial banks** must govern, measure, monitor, and report **asset-liability and liquidity risk**. The directions are structured to apply through board-approved policies and internal controls, and they replace/modernize RBI expectations for liquidity risk management by requiring banks to maintain formal governance over ALM, including documented strategies, risk measurement methods, limits, and review processes. The document’s content indicates that the central compliance focus is on ensuring banks can identify liquidity exposures, measure them under both **flow** and **stock** approaches, and monitor them on an ongoing basis under a Board-supervised framework.

A key requirement is that the **Board of Directors** must take explicit responsibility for ALM oversight: it must approve the bank’s policies, limits, and review mechanisms and ensure that management is operating within the approved risk appetite. This implies that banks need formalized, board-sanctioned ALM governance rather than ad hoc treasury management. The directions also establish that liquidity risk management must be embedded in policy and strategy, with clear procedures for identifying exposures, setting internal thresholds, and escalating exceptions, so compliance teams should expect detailed documentation requirements and evidence of periodic board review.

The document also indicates that banks must use recognized methods for **risk measurement**, specifically a **flow approach** and a **stock approach**, which suggests that liquidity assessment is not limited to one metric but requires analysis of expected cash inflows/outflows and balance-sheet stock positions. The chapter headings further show obligations for **risk monitoring**, implying continuous tracking of liquidity positions against limits and stress or scenario considerations. While the table of contents excerpt does not show the exact numerical thresholds, compliance teams should assume the directions contain RBI-specified or bank-specified limits and reporting requirements that must be incorporated into internal treasury, risk, and compliance workflows.

In practical terms, affected entities are **commercial banks in India** subject to RBI supervision, and the core compliance tasks will be to review whether existing ALM policies, committee charters, management information systems, and escalation processes meet the new directions. Banks will need to confirm that the ALM policy is current, approved by the Board, and aligned with the institution’s liquidity risk profile; that measurement and monitoring are performed consistently; and that management can evidence adherence through reports and reviews. Because the document is titled as a formal RBI direction, compliance officers should treat it as mandatory supervisory guidance requiring implementation and periodic proof of compliance rather than as a voluntary best-practice statement.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 22, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025** and updated **as of May 18, 2026**) set the current RBI framework for how commercial banks must classify, value, and manage their investment portfolios. The document is structured to govern the **board’s role**, the **investment policy framework**, and the **classification and valuation treatment** of investments, indicating that these directions apply at the level of a bank’s formal governance, accounting treatment, and ongoing portfolio operations. The title and table of contents show that the directions specifically cover **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Available for Sale (AFS)**, **Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVTPL)**, and the subcategory **Held for Trading (HFT)**, with additional provisions for **investments in subsidiaries, associates, and joint ventures**.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the document excerpt is that RBI has codified a **mandatory classification and valuation regime** for commercial banks’ investment portfolios, meaning banks cannot manage securities as a purely internal accounting matter but must follow RBI-prescribed categories and operational rules. The presence of a dedicated chapter on the **Role of the Board** indicates that the board is expected to approve and oversee the bank’s investment policy framework, rather than leaving portfolio classification and risk positioning solely to treasury or finance teams. The existence of separate treatment for HTM, AFS, and FVTPL/HFT also means banks must ensure investments are allocated to the correct bucket and valued according to the prescribed basis for that bucket, since classification directly drives whether and how fair-value changes flow through profit and loss or other accounting treatment.

The document excerpt does not include the substantive thresholds, exceptions, or detailed mechanics within each chapter, but it clearly signals that the updated directions are a comprehensive replacement/standard-setting instrument for commercial banks’ investment portfolio governance and accounting. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a core regulatory rulebook governing: how investment policy is drafted and approved, how portfolio categories are assigned, how valuation is performed, and how investments in controlled or affiliated entities are handled. Because the version is marked **“Updated as on May 18, 2026,”** firms should use that updated text as the operative version and verify whether any subsequent amendments, implementation timelines, or carve-outs appear in the full body of the directions before concluding their internal compliance mapping.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025**, effective **immediately upon issuance on November 28, 2025**. These Directions apply to **commercial banks** only—i.e., **banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks**—so compliance teams at in-scope banks need to review their lending-rate frameworks against these new instructions.

The document is a consolidated set of RBI directions issued under **Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. While the excerpt provided here does not include the substantive chapter text, the structure shows that the Directions govern the full set of lending-rate rules for commercial banks, including **general guidelines, benchmark requirements, other aspects of lending rates, foreign currency advances, exemptions, and repeal/transition provisions**. From a compliance perspective, this means the bank should expect binding requirements on how advances are priced, how benchmarks are selected and applied, and how any exceptions or special cases are handled.

Because the Directions are effective immediately, any existing lending policies, loan pricing systems, product programs, customer disclosures, and rate-reset mechanisms should be checked for alignment without delay. The document’s chapter headings indicate that compliance obligations likely extend beyond initial pricing to ongoing administration of advances, including treatment of **foreign currency loans** and any **RBI-prescribed exemptions**. A compliance officer should therefore treat this as a regulatorily binding rewrite of the commercial-bank lending-rate framework and verify whether prior instructions on interest rates on advances have been repealed or modified by the later chapters of the Directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Securitisation Transactions Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025**) set out a comprehensive prudential and operational framework for securitisation by commercial banks, replacing or consolidating the regulatory treatment for these transactions under RBI direction. The document applies to **commercial banks** and governs their role as originators, investors, servicers, and retainers in securitisation structures, including the requirements that must be met for assets to be securitised, the conditions under which securitisation exposures receive regulatory recognition, and the accounting treatment that applies. It also introduces a dedicated framework for **simple, transparent and comparable (STC) securitisations** for regulatory capital purposes, indicating that only transactions meeting specified criteria can receive the associated capital treatment.

A key requirement is that only **eligible assets** may be securitised, and originators must comply with prescribed **origination standards** before transferring exposures. The Directions impose a **Minimum Retention Requirement (MRR)**, meaning the originator must keep a specified economic interest in the securitised pool rather than fully offloading the risk; the document also limits the **total retained exposures by originators**, so banks cannot retain disproportionate residual risk or structure exposures in a way that undermines true risk transfer. The rules further require compliant **payment priorities and observability**, so cash flows and allocation waterfalls in the securitisation structure must be transparent and capable of supervision, and they establish conditions for the **special purpose entity (SPE)** to ensure the SPE is structured and operated in a manner consistent with securitisation requirements.

The Directions also regulate how securitisation transactions may be **issued and listed**, which is relevant where the securities are offered to investors or admitted to trading, and they specify **representations and warranties** that originators must provide, likely to address asset quality, enforceability, and transaction integrity. The accounting provisions require banks to account for securitisation transactions in a manner consistent with RBI standards, which affects recognition of transfer, derecognition, retained interests, and any profit/loss treatment on sale. For compliance purposes, banks will need to verify eligibility of underlying assets, document retention and risk-transfer compliance, maintain transaction-level transparency, ensure SPE and waterfall structures satisfy the prescribed conditions, and classify any transaction intended to obtain STC treatment against the detailed criteria in Chapter III. The document’s table of contents shows further detailed rules under Chapter III for **STC securitisations**, indicating that regulatory capital relief depends on meeting the specific STC framework rather than on securitisation alone.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** consolidate and replace the framework for **loan transfers, co-lending, consortium/multiple banking lending, inter-bank participations, and borrower-requested account transfers** for commercial banks. The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and appears to organize the regime into four parts: (A) transfer of loan exposures, (B) co-lending arrangements (CLAs), (C) other lending/risk-transfer arrangements, and (D) repeal/other provisions.

For **loan transfers**, the directions distinguish between **loans that are not in default** and **stressed loans**. Banks transferring or acquiring loan exposures must comply with the general conditions in the new framework, and the regulations set separate rules for loans that are performing versus those that are stressed, indicating different eligibility and procedural standards depending on the credit status of the exposure. A compliance team should treat this as a complete replacement-style framework for secondary transfer of credit risk on loan books and ensure internal policies, eligibility filters, approvals, documentation, and post-transfer treatment are aligned to the loan’s status at the time of transfer.

For **co-lending arrangements (CLAs)**, the RBI imposes prudential norms specifically for commercial banks participating in shared-lending structures. The document signals that banks involved in CLAs must follow defined scope and prudential requirements, meaning compliance obligations will extend beyond origination to the structuring, underwriting, monitoring, and ongoing administration of jointly originated loans. Any bank using co-lending should review whether its current operating model, risk allocation, servicing arrangements, and accounting/reporting procedures fit the RBI’s prescribed framework.

The directions also cover **consortium lending / multiple banking arrangements**, **inter-bank participations**, and **transfer of borrower accounts at the borrower’s request or instance**, which means the RBI is regulating not only outright sale/transfer transactions but also other mechanisms by which credit risk is distributed between banks. Compliance teams should expect requirements around governance, disclosures, borrower consent or request handling where applicable, and documentation to ensure the bank can evidence that the arrangement fits within the relevant permitted structure. The presence of annexes indicates additional operational or technical details are set out separately and may contain forms, procedures, or illustrative requirements that should be checked before implementation.

No specific numerical thresholds, rates, or effective dates for operational compliance are visible in the excerpt provided beyond the issuance date of **November 28, 2025** and the fact that the directions are issued under RBI reference **DOR/2025-26/159 / DOR.STR.REC.No.78/21.04.048/2025-26**. Because the text excerpt is only the table of contents and title page, a compliance officer would still need the body of the directions and annexes to identify exact transfer conditions, prohibited structures, reporting timelines, provisioning/accounting treatment, and any transition or repeal provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025** consolidate and update India’s prudential rules for managing concentration risk in **commercial banks**, replacing and organizing requirements across several exposure-related areas. The document states that RBI originally introduced exposure limits in **March 1989** because lending too much to one borrower or a connected group creates significant risk; these 2025 Directions continue that policy focus but now cover a broader, more structured framework across the board of directors’ responsibilities, large exposures, market-based credit supply for large borrowers, exposure norms, intra-group transactions, country risk, and inter-bank liabilities. The version provided is marked **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** so compliance teams should treat the text as the operative consolidated version as of that date.

At a high level, the Directions require banks to maintain formal governance and monitoring systems for concentration risk, with the **Board** responsible for oversight and for ensuring that internal policies, limits, and controls are set and followed. A major component is the **Large Exposures Framework**, which is the core prudential control on how much a bank may expose itself to a single counterparty or a group of connected counterparties; the document’s structure indicates that it also addresses how those exposures are measured, monitored, and reported, and how connected counterparties are identified. The Directions also include a separate chapter on **enhancing credit supply for large borrowers through market mechanisms**, signaling that large borrowers may need to be supported through market-based funding rather than through excessive bank concentration.

In addition, the Directions retain and organize the RBI’s broader **exposure norms**, including limits and prudential treatment for exposures that are not captured solely by the large-exposure framework. They also set **prudential limits on intra-group transactions and exposures**, meaning that banks must control transactions with their own group entities and cannot rely on affiliation to avoid concentration controls. Separate chapters cover **country risk exposure** and **inter-bank liabilities (IBL)**, so banks must also measure and manage sovereign/jurisdictional concentrations and liabilities to other banks under prescribed prudential limits.

The document is issued under RBI reference **DOR/2025-26/158** and **DOR.CRE.REC.77/07-03-001/2025-26**, dated **November 28, 2025**. For a compliance team, the key action is to determine which of the bank’s exposures fall into the large-exposure, intra-group, country-risk, and inter-bank categories and then confirm that internal policies, limit monitoring, reporting, and board-level oversight are aligned with the 2025 Directions as updated on **July 01, 2026**. The excerpt provided does not include the detailed numerical thresholds or exceptions, so those should be checked in the operative chapters before making any limit or reporting assessments.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India master direction, issued on November 28, 2025 and updated through July 1, 2026, consolidates and replaces the RBI’s requirements on commercial banks’ credit risk management. It applies to commercial banks and sets out mandatory board-approved policies, credit appraisal and monitoring expectations, statutory and regulatory lending restrictions, country-risk management, treatment of unhedged foreign currency exposure (UFCE), borrower Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) requirements, valuation standards for properties, security-interest filing requirements with CERSAI, account-operation controls for cash credit/current/overdraft accounts, and the loan-system framework for delivery of bank credit.

For credit risk governance, banks must maintain board-approved policies covering the entire credit lifecycle, including origination, appraisal, sanction, monitoring, renewal, restructuring, recovery, and portfolio concentration/risk appetite. The document also formalizes requirements for credit risk evaluation and borrower due diligence, including use of proper underwriting standards, financial analysis, and ongoing monitoring so that credit exposures are identified and managed consistently. Where the directions refer to limits, exposures, or prudential controls, banks must align internal processes with the RBI’s specified treatment rather than relying on ad hoc branch-level practices.

The directions also continue and organize the RBI’s lending restriction framework, including both statutory and regulatory restrictions that apply to commercial banks when extending credit. In addition, banks must manage country risk for cross-border exposures under a dedicated framework, with policies and internal controls to assess sovereign and transfer risk and to maintain the required monitoring/mitigation processes. The UFCE chapter requires banks to identify borrowers’ unhedged foreign currency exposures and incorporate that risk into credit appraisal and monitoring, so that FX risk is not ignored when assessing repayment capacity.

The LEI chapter requires applicable borrowers to obtain and maintain a Legal Entity Identifier where required by RBI rules, and banks must verify and record the LEI as part of onboarding and ongoing exposure management. The property-valuation chapter requires banks to use empanelled valuers in accordance with RBI standards when valuing immovable property collateral, while the CERSAI chapter requires filing of security interest for immovable assets other than equitable mortgage, as well as movable and intangible assets, in the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India. These filing and valuation requirements are compliance-critical because they affect the enforceability and perfection of bank security interests.

The direction also includes a specific operational framework for current accounts, cash credit accounts, and overdraft accounts, which affects how banks may maintain and operate such accounts for borrowers. Finally, the loan-system chapter requires banks to follow the RBI’s framework for delivery of bank credit, including the allocation and operation of loan and working-capital components, rather than using structures that obscure end-use or weaken monitoring. Chapter XI is deleted, and the final chapter contains repeal and savings provisions, meaning earlier instructions are superseded to the extent stated in the new master direction.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Credit Information Reporting Directions, 2025** (as updated through **July 1, 2026**) set out the mandatory framework for how commercial banks must report, correct, and use credit information through Credit Information Companies (CICs). The Directions apply to **commercial banks** that are members of CICs and govern both the content and timeliness of reporting, as well as downstream use of credit reports in lending decisions. The document replaces and consolidates earlier RBI instructions on credit information reporting for commercial banks, so compliance teams should treat it as the operative reporting rulebook for these activities.

The core requirement is that banks must submit credit information in the **prescribed RBI/CIC data formats** and must do so within the specified reporting cycle, with ongoing updates for changes and corrections. The Directions also impose obligations around **data quality**, including handling of **rejected records**, rectification of defective submissions, and periodic review of a borrower-level **Data Quality Index (DQI)** where applicable. Where credit information is found to be incorrect, banks must follow the prescribed **correction workflow** to ensure the borrower’s Credit Information Report is amended, rather than leaving disputes unresolved or relying on informal fixes.

The Directions also regulate how banks use credit information in **credit appraisal**: before sanctioning or reviewing credit, banks are expected to obtain and use credit information reports in accordance with the RBI’s instructions, rather than treating them as optional or purely advisory. The document further requires banks to ensure that credit information is **displayed or made available** in the manner prescribed by the RBI, which is intended to support transparency and borrower access to information. In addition, the Directions state how other existing RBI Department of Regulation instructions continue to apply alongside these rules, so compliance teams need to read this document together with any related RBI circulars on CIC membership, reporting, disclosure, and dispute resolution.

Because the document is an RBI directions instrument, the practical compliance burden is ongoing rather than a one-time filing.
