rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** apply to **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** and set out the RBI’s consolidated KYC/AML framework for customer acceptance, customer identification, ongoing due diligence, and record/monitoring controls. The document is a formal RBI direction issued **November 28, 2025** and updated **as of December 29, 2025**; it is organized as binding directions rather than guidance, so affected banks must align their internal policies, procedures, and system controls with these requirements. The excerpt provided shows the main scope of the directions: preliminary provisions, board and policy governance, customer acceptance policy, risk management, customer identification procedure, and customer due diligence for individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial ownership identification.

For compliance purposes, the key operational requirement is that UCBs must maintain a **board-approved KYC/AML governance framework** covering customer onboarding, risk rating, due diligence, and periodic review, rather than relying on branch-level discretion. The directions require banks to establish formal **Customer Acceptance Policy** criteria and a documented **Risk Management** framework so that customers are categorized and monitored according to their risk profile, with enhanced scrutiny for higher-risk customers and activities. The document also requires a defined **Customer Identification Procedure (CIP)** and **Customer Due Diligence (CDD)** process, with separate treatment for **individuals**, **sole proprietorship firms**, and **legal entities**, and a specific process for **identifying the beneficial owner** of entity customers.

Because the table of contents indicates dedicated sections for legal entities and beneficial ownership, compliance teams should expect the directions to require collection and verification of constitutional documents, ownership/control information, and person(s) acting on behalf of the customer before account opening and during the life of the relationship. The “general guidelines” and “board/policy-related” chapters indicate that banks must also maintain documented internal controls, staff accountability, and governance oversight for KYC implementation, rather than handling KYC as a one-time onboarding formality. No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or deadlines are visible in the excerpt provided beyond the document’s issue and update dates, so any detailed threshold-based onboarding exceptions, verification limits, or periodicity rules would need to be confirmed from the full text. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they took effect **immediately upon issuance**. The directions apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)** and are issued under **section 35A read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and other enabling provisions. For compliance purposes, the key point is that RBI has formally set prudential requirements governing **whether and when a UCB may declare dividends**, rather than leaving dividend declarations solely to internal board discretion.

The document indicates a dedicated framework in **Chapter II for declaration of dividend by a UCB**, meaning UCBs must review dividend decisions against RBI-prescribed prudential conditions before any declaration. Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds or tests in Chapter II, the title and structure make clear that these Directions create binding regulatory constraints on dividend distribution by UCBs and are intended to ensure dividends are declared only in a manner consistent with prudential soundness and regulatory compliance.

The document also includes **Chapter III on repeal and other provisions**, signaling that any prior RBI instructions on this subject may be superseded to the extent stated in the full text, while preserving actions taken or rights accrued under the earlier regime where applicable. It further states that the directions are **not intended to bar the application of other laws**, so UCBs must continue to comply with any parallel legal, accounting, corporate, or cooperative-law requirements that also govern dividend declaration. Finally, the document reserves RBI’s **interpretative authority**, meaning the central bank’s interpretation will control any ambiguity in these directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025”** (updated as of **April 1, 2026**) set out the mandatory format, presentation rules, note disclosures, and other accounting instructions for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**. The directions were issued by RBI on **November 28, 2025** and apply to the preparation of UCB financial statements from the specified effective date in the updated text; compliance teams should treat the April 1, 2026 update date as the operative reference point for the consolidated directions as presented here.

At a high level, the document requires UCBs to prepare their **balance sheet and profit and loss account in the RBI-prescribed format**, follow RBI’s detailed **notes and compilation instructions**, and apply specific guidance where accounting standards create presentation or disclosure issues. It also adds a separate chapter of **mandatory notes-to-accounts disclosures**, meaning the financial statements are not compliant unless the required qualitative and quantitative information is included in the prescribed presentation. Compliance officers should note that these are not merely “best practice” disclosures: the directions appear to convert several items into explicit regulatory reporting obligations for UCBs.

The document also contains additional operational/accounting requirements beyond the basic statement format. These include rules for **inter-branch account provisioning where there is a net debit balance**, **reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries**, and rules for **transfer to or appropriation from reserve funds**. It further addresses **provisioning for fraud**, indicating that banks must apply RBI-prescribed provisioning treatment when fraud events occur, rather than handling such exposures solely under internal accounting policy.

In practical compliance terms, the directions affect **all UCBs covered by RBI’s applicability clause**, and they require banks to align internal financial reporting, year-end close processes, note drafting, and reconciliation controls to RBI’s stated presentation/disclosure regime. Because the document is expressly focused on **financial statement presentation and disclosures**, compliance teams should review not only the chart of accounts and statement templates, but also procedures for gathering source data for disclosures, reconciling inter-branch and Nostro items, and ensuring reserve-fund and fraud-related accounting entries are posted and disclosed in the required manner.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. These Directions are intended to create a **non-discriminatory, transparent, and natural-justice-based process** for classifying borrowers of urban co-operative banks (UCBs) as wilful defaulters, and to ensure that credit information about such defaulters is shared so that lenders are cautioned against extending further institutional finance.

For compliance purposes, the document establishes a formal framework for **how UCBs must identify, classify, report, and monitor wilful defaulters and large defaulters**. It requires UCBs to follow prescribed procedures before making a wilful-defaulter determination, rather than using ad hoc or opaque internal practices, and it also sets up reporting obligations so that information on such cases can be disseminated to relevant credit-information channels and supervisory authorities. The Directions specifically cover both **wilful defaulters** and **large defaulters**, indicating that banks must maintain systems to detect, track, and report both categories, and not just internally flag them.

The document also makes clear that the **Board of the UCB has a defined role** in this process, which means compliance cannot be treated as only a branch-level or credit-officer function; governance oversight is required. In addition, the Directions include a chapter on **preventive measures and the role of auditors**, signaling that UCBs must have controls in place to prevent wilful default situations and that auditors have a responsibility in reviewing or validating the bank’s handling of such cases. The annexes provide the **required reporting formats** for submitting the **list of large defaulters** and the **data on wilful default cases**, so affected banks must ensure their internal data capture and reporting systems can populate those formats accurately and on time.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the beginning of Chapter I, it does **not yet show the detailed thresholds, deadlines, procedural steps, or classification criteria** that may appear later in the Directions. However, from the introductory material alone, the compliance impact is clear: any **urban co-operative bank** covered by these Directions must align its borrower-classification, credit-information sharing, governance, and audit processes with this RBI framework, and it should be prepared to use the prescribed annexed formats for reporting once the operative provisions apply.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (as updated on **July 1, 2026**) sets out the RBI’s framework for how urban co-operative banks must identify, report, disclose, restructure, classify, provision for, and recognize income on stressed borrower accounts. It applies specifically to **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** and is intended to replace or standardize the bank-level handling of stressed assets through **board-approved policies**, early warning processes, and prudential norms for restructuring. The directions were issued by RBI on **November 28, 2025**, and the updated text reflects the rules in force as of **July 1, 2026**.

A core requirement is that each UCB must maintain a **board-approved policy** for resolution of stressed assets, so compliance is not optional or ad hoc at branch level. The policy must cover how the bank identifies stress early, what triggers reporting/escalation, how restructuring proposals are evaluated, and how the bank ensures appropriate accounting and supervisory reporting. The directions also require **early identification and reporting of stress**, meaning banks are expected to monitor accounts proactively rather than wait until default or severe delinquency, and to ensure the stress is tracked and escalated internally in a timely manner. In addition, the document requires **disclosures** relating to stressed assets and restructuring, so compliance teams need to ensure the bank’s public/regulatory reporting reflects the prescribed information accurately and consistently.

The document then lays down detailed **prudential norms for restructuring of accounts**. It specifies general instructions for when and how accounts may be restructured, and it governs the **asset classification impact after restructuring**, so the classification treatment cannot be decided solely by the bank’s internal credit judgment. It also creates a **special regulatory treatment** regime for asset classification in specified cases, and addresses **additional finance** extended to a stressed borrower under a resolution plan, meaning any fresh lending provided as part of resolution has to be handled under the RBI’s stated prudential framework rather than as ordinary new credit.

The directions further prescribe when an account may receive an **asset classification upgrade after satisfactory performance**, which means a restructured account does not automatically return to a better category unless the borrower demonstrates performance meeting the RBI’s required standard over the relevant period. The document also sets out the **provisioning requirements after restructuring**, so banks must hold specific loss provisions against restructured/stressed exposures as required by the framework, and it includes rules for **income recognition** on such assets, meaning interest recognition cannot be assumed to follow standard accrual treatment if the account is stressed or under restructuring. For compliance purposes, the key operational implications are that UCBs must align credit, treasury/accounting, regulatory reporting, and board oversight processes to this RBI resolution framework, and they must apply the classification/provisioning/income rules exactly as prescribed for stressed accounts, including any additional finance and post-restructuring performance monitoring requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the income-recognition, asset-classification, and provisioning framework for urban co-operative banks (UCBs), with the document shown as **updated through July 1, 2026**. It applies to the regulated UCBs covered by the RBI’s prudential framework and replaces/updates the earlier rules on how loans and other credit exposures must be classified, when income may be recognized, and how much provision must be made. The key compliance point is that these are mandatory prudential requirements, so affected banks must align their board-approved policies, lending practices, system-based classification logic, disclosures, and provisioning calculations to the prescribed RBI standards.  

The directions require UCBs to follow RBI’s asset-classification norms in determining whether an exposure is standard, non-performing, or otherwise impaired, and to stop recognizing income on accounts once they become non-performing under the prescribed rules. The document includes detailed rules on general asset-classification principles, the conditions under which an account becomes an NPA, treatment of accounts regularized close to the balance-sheet date, special/edge-case classifications, NPA categories, valuation of security, and the conditions for upgrading loan accounts after they have been classified as NPAs. For compliance teams, the practical obligation is to ensure that overdue tracking, days-past-due logic, interest accrual, and NPA tagging are implemented consistently and reviewed regularly, because these classifications directly drive provisioning and financial reporting.  

The directions also emphasize the role of the board and senior management in prudence in lending and consumer education, and they impose disclosure requirements that UCBs must satisfy in relation to their asset quality and prudential reporting. In practice, this means the board must oversee credit-risk policy, monitoring, and compliance with RBI prudential norms rather than leaving classification/provisioning decisions entirely to operations or finance teams. UCBs must also ensure that any required public or regulatory disclosures accurately reflect asset quality, classification status, and related prudential information.  

Because the title says the document is “updated as on July 1, 2026,” the effective operating rule is that the version in force includes amendments through that date, so compliance should use the updated consolidated text rather than the original 2025 issue alone. The excerpt provided does not show the detailed numeric provisioning percentages or all threshold definitions, so a compliance review should verify the exact day-count triggers, provisioning rates, and any transitional or implementation dates in the full text before finalizing policies or controls.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Urban Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management Directions, 2025” sets out a formal, board-led framework for liquidity risk and asset-liability management (ALM) for urban co-operative banks, with the stated framework applying to UCBs and expressly noting that the liquidity risk management provisions also apply to Level I UCBs. The document appears to be a comprehensive replacement/updated supervisory standard issued by RBI on November 28, 2025 (reference DOR/2025-26/285 and DOR.LRG.No.204/13-10-006/2025-26), and its effective/commencement details are expected to be specified in Chapter I, though those details are not included in the excerpt provided. At a high level, the direction requires banks to maintain a structured ALM governance system, including a robust ALM information system, a defined ALM organization, and a formal ALM process, all under board oversight.

For compliance purposes, the most material requirement is that the board is made explicitly responsible for approving the bank’s ALM and liquidity-risk policies, setting and reviewing limits, and ensuring periodic review of the framework rather than leaving these decisions solely to management. The document establishes that liquidity risk must be actively managed, not merely monitored, and that banks must prepare a Structural Liquidity Statement (SLS) as part of their liquidity management process. It also indicates that behavioral pattern analysis is required, meaning banks cannot rely only on contractual maturities and must incorporate customer behavior and product behavior into their liquidity assessment and planning.

Because the document is organized around governance and process rather than a single numeric capital-style ratio in the excerpt, the key compliance obligation is ongoing internal control and reporting discipline: UCBs must maintain a documented ALM framework, ensure board-approved policies and limits, and operate a systematic process for measuring and managing liquidity mismatches and behavioral assumptions. The specific thresholds, time buckets, reporting frequencies, and any filing deadlines or implementation timelines are not visible in the excerpt provided, so a compliance team would need the remaining chapters to identify any exact ratios, limit bands, statement formats, escalation triggers, or submission timelines. Based on the visible portion alone, however, the direction clearly imposes a formalized, governance-heavy ALM regime on UCBs and extends liquidity-risk expectations to Level I UCBs as well.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on September 2, 2026)

The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** set out the governing framework for how **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** must classify, value, move, and otherwise manage their investment portfolios. At a high level, the directions require UCBs to maintain a formal **investment policy** approved and monitored at board level, and to manage investments through prescribed categories, including **Held to Maturity (HTM)**, **Held for Trading (HFT)**, and **Available for Sale (AFS)**. The framework also addresses **shifting securities among categories**, including movement **to and from HTM** and **between AFS and HFT**, which means banks must have internal procedures and documentation controls for reclassification decisions, valuation impacts, and any related accounting treatment. Because the document specifically distinguishes between classification and valuation requirements, compliance teams should expect obligations tied not only to where instruments are booked, but also to how they are marked, monitored, and reported over time.

The title and structure indicate that the directions regulate the **operation of the investment portfolio**, so they likely apply to all UCB investment activity covered by the RBI’s UCB framework, with particular attention to securities holdings and trading/investment book management. The board’s responsibilities and the “General Guidelines” section suggest the RBI expects governance over investment limits, approval processes, risk controls, and ongoing monitoring, rather than leaving these decisions solely to management. Any institution classified as a UCB should therefore confirm that its policies, accounting systems, trade capture, valuation practices, and internal approvals are aligned to the RBI’s category-specific rules and any permitted exceptions or transfer conditions.

Because the excerpt does not include the substantive chapter text, specific thresholds, percentages, valuation rates, time limits, or numerical limits cannot be confirmed from the provided content alone. From a compliance standpoint, the key action item is to review the full directions for any mandatory approval steps, permissible frequency and conditions for reclassification, valuation methodology for AFS/HFT securities, and any restrictions or caps on the HTM bucket. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply to **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under **Section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The directions are issued under RBI’s powers in **Sections 21 and 35A read with Section 56** of the Banking Regulation Act and take **effect immediately upon issuance**. The document defines “microfinance loan” by cross-reference to the **RBI (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025**, and defines “rests” as the **periodicity of charging interest to borrowers**; other undefined terms take their meanings from the Banking Regulation Act and related RBI framework.

For compliance purposes, the key operative change is that UCBs must follow RBI’s rules on how interest rates on advances are determined and applied, rather than relying on ad hoc pricing practices. The excerpt provided does not yet include the substantive rate-setting clauses, but it establishes that the directions are binding on all affected UCBs from the date of issue and that they are meant to govern the interest-rate framework for loans/advances, including the treatment of interest “rests.” The document also signals that these directions are part of a broader 2025 RBI overhaul for UCB credit regulation, so compliance teams should align this instrument with the linked **Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** when reviewing loan pricing, interest computation, and borrower disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued a new consolidated framework for urban co-operative banks on **transfer and distribution of credit risk**, titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025”** (issued **November 28, 2025**). The document is intended to replace and unify earlier RBI guidance covering **loan transfers, stressed-loan transfers, consortium lending, multiple banking arrangements, and other credit-risk transfer arrangements**, creating a self-contained regulatory regime for urban co-operative banks (UCBs). From a compliance perspective, the key change is not a single isolated rule but the creation of an overarching framework governing how UCBs may sell, transfer, participate in, or otherwise redistribute loan exposures and associated credit risk.

The directions are structured in three substantive parts: **Part A covers transfer of loan exposures**, including both general rules for all loan transfers and specific rules for **transfer of stressed loans**; **Part B covers other lending and risk-transfer arrangements**, specifically **lending under consortium and multiple banking arrangements**; and **Part C addresses repeal and related transitional provisions**. This means compliance teams should expect the directions to apply across the full lifecycle of loan exposure management, not just to sale transactions. The document signals that RBI is formalizing and tightening the regulatory treatment of credit-risk transfer activity by UCBs, so institutions engaged in loan sales, participation arrangements, syndications, or similar exposure-sharing structures will need to align internal policies, approval processes, documentation, reporting, and portfolio controls to the new framework.

The table of contents shows that the rules are organized into: **Chapter I – Preliminary**, followed by **Part A – Transfer of Loan Exposures** with separate chapters for **Scope and Definitions**, **General Conditions applicable for all loan transfers**, and **Transfer of stressed loans**; then **Part B – Other Types of Lending and Risk Transfer Arrangements**, consisting of **Lending under Consortium / Multiple Banking Arrangements**; and finally **Part C – Repeal and Other Provisions**. Even from the introductory material alone, the compliance implication is that UCBs must assess whether any of their lending or credit-risk sharing practices fall within the new definitions and conditions, because the framework is designed to govern “different avenues of credit risk transfer and distribution.” Where a bank uses loan transfer as a liquidity-management tool, to rebalance exposures, or to make strategic sales, those activities are now expressly within the RBI’s consolidated supervisory framework.

Because the excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative clauses, specific thresholds, procedural steps, or transitional deadlines from the chapters and annexes, the safest compliance takeaway is that this is a **new RBI directions circular dated November 28, 2025** that likely **supersedes prior fragmented guidance** and requires UCBs to review all existing loan-transfer, stressed-loan transfer, consortium, and multiple-banking arrangements for conformity with the new directions. A compliance officer should treat this as a prompt to update internal policies, transaction approvals, legal documentation, and monitoring controls for any credit-risk transfer activity, and to verify the repeal/transitional section for any grandfathering, effective-date, or reporting obligations once the full text is reviewed.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **“Urban Co-operative Banks (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025”** on **November 28, 2025** to consolidate and update prudential rules meant to reduce concentration risk in Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs). The document explains that RBI has long regulated UCB exposures because excessive lending to a single borrower or connected group can create asset-side concentration risk; these rules were originally introduced in **May 1994** using demand and time liabilities (DTL), then revised in **January 1996** to use **Capital Funds** as the reference base. The new Directions bring together the existing exposure limits on **individual borrowers**, **groups of interconnected borrowers**, **unsecured advances**, **inter-bank exposures**, and **small-value loans** into one consolidated framework.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the Directions apply specifically to **Urban Co-operative Banks** and are issued under RBI’s powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (including **Sections 21 and 35A read with Section 56**). The document signals that UCBs must continue to operate within prudential exposure limits designed to keep their loan book granular and prevent outsized exposure to very large borrowers. Although the excerpt provided does not yet state the detailed numerical caps, implementation mechanics, or reporting formats, it confirms that the new Directions are intended to govern how UCBs measure and manage concentration risk across all of the above exposure categories.

Because this is a consolidated directions circular, a compliance team should treat it as a potentially comprehensive replacement or restatement of prior RBI instructions on UCB exposure concentration, and should verify the full operative chapters for any revised definitions, limits, exceptions, and transitional provisions. The document’s structure indicates three parts: **Chapter I – Preliminary**, **Chapter II – Exposure Norms**, and **Chapter III – Repeal and other provisions**, which suggests that the final chapter likely identifies prior instruments being repealed or superseded and any savings/transitional treatment. Based on the excerpt, the immediate compliance takeaway is that UCBs remain subject to RBI prudential exposure controls, and any internal lending, risk, or treasury policies should be checked against the finalized norms in the complete text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India direction, issued on 28 November 2025 and updated as on 1 July 2026, sets out the credit risk management framework for Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs). It replaces and consolidates prior RBI instructions on credit exposure, credit administration, borrower identification, security-interest filing, account conduct, and related lending controls for UCBs. The document is structured into board-approved policies, credit risk evaluation, statutory and regulatory restrictions, loan administration, LEI requirements, property valuation, CERSAI filing, cash credit/current/overdraft account maintenance, and the loan system for bank credit.

The core compliance message is that UCBs must manage credit risk through formal board-approved policies and operational controls that govern how loans are originated, evaluated, documented, monitored, secured, and recovered. The directions impose specific obligations on the bank’s board and management to define credit policies, delegate powers, ensure proper appraisal of borrower creditworthiness, and maintain adequate documentation and security creation processes. Where the document refers to statutory or regulatory restrictions, UCBs must observe RBI-prescribed limits and prohibitions on lending concentration, connected lending, exposure norms, and other restrictions that apply to specific borrower categories or credit products.

The directions also require stronger borrower and security identification and tracking mechanisms. UCBs must require Legal Entity Identifiers (LEIs) for specified borrowers/exposures as prescribed, use approved valuation practices and empanelled valuers for property collateral, and file security interests in CERSAI for immovable assets (other than equitable mortgages), movable assets, and intangible assets where applicable. These filings are not optional administrative steps; they are part of the bank’s enforceable credit administration and security perfection obligations.

In addition, the document covers operating discipline for working-capital and overdraft lending, including maintenance of cash credit, current, and overdraft accounts by banks, and the “loan system” for delivery of bank credit. UCBs must comply with RBI’s requirements on how credit is disbursed and monitored, which may include segregation or structuring of working-capital limits, periodic review, and account conduct requirements designed to prevent misuse or diversion of funds. The updated directions therefore create a comprehensive compliance framework affecting virtually all lending activities of UCBs, and the operative date to follow for the consolidated directions is the updated version as of 1 July 2026, subject to any specific chapter-level timelines or exceptions contained in the full text.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting” Directions, 2025** (issued **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through July 01, 2026**) impose a formal framework for how **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** participate in the credit information ecosystem and report borrower data to credit information companies (CICs). The directions cover UCBs’ membership obligations with CICs, the data formats and reporting timelines they must follow, how reported data must be updated and corrected, and how credit information is to be used in credit appraisal and displayed in bank systems or customer-facing processes. They are intended to ensure that UCBs submit complete, timely, and accurate credit data and then promptly fix rejected or incorrect records when problems are identified.

For compliance purposes, the most important point is that the document creates **mandatory credit information reporting and maintenance obligations** for the affected institutions, rather than leaving reporting practices to internal discretion. UCBs are expected to adhere to RBI-prescribed reporting standards, including the specified data structures/formats, regular updation cycles, and any reporting rules on borrower records, account statuses, and other credit-related data fields that must be shared with CICs. The directions also establish a process for handling **rejected data**, requiring UCBs to rectify and resubmit such records, and they introduce oversight around the **Data Quality Index (DQI)** so that banks must review the quality of their reporting and address deficiencies where data quality is weak.

The directions also address the downstream use of credit bureau information in lending. UCBs must use credit information reports in **credit appraisal**, meaning lending decisions and underwriting processes are expected to incorporate CIC data rather than relying solely on internal records. In addition, there are instructions on the **display of information**, which means banks may need to ensure that relevant credit-information-related details are made available in the prescribed manner within their systems or to customers, consistent with RBI requirements. The document further states that other instructions issued by the Department of Regulation remain applicable where relevant, so this framework operates alongside existing RBI directions rather than replacing them wholesale.

Because the excerpt provided is only the heading, table of contents, and document metadata, it does **not** disclose the specific numeric deadlines, thresholds, form identifiers, submission frequencies, or exact technical file specifications; those details would need to be reviewed in the substantive chapters. For a compliance team, the immediate takeaway is that any UCB within scope must verify its CIC membership status, confirm its reporting processes against the RBI-prescribed formats and timelines, ensure a procedure for rejected-data remediation and DQI monitoring, and make sure credit bureau information is embedded in lending and disclosure workflows by the effective date of the operative provisions in the full directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025**, and they take **immediate effect**. They apply to **all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, whether referred to individually as a bank/UCB or collectively as banks/UCBs. The directions are issued under **Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, read with **Section 56** and other enabling provisions, and replace prior RBI instructions on these topics under the repeal and savings framework set out in Chapter VIII.

At a high level, the document consolidates and governs how UCBs may **issue, manage, and conduct credit card and debit card businesses**, including the conditions for issuance, customer conduct, and operational controls. It also addresses **debit card issuance**, **form factor requirements**, **co-branding arrangements**, and broader **general compliance rules** applicable to both credit and debit cards. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that these directions create a single binding framework for card lifecycle management by UCBs, rather than leaving such matters to ad hoc internal policy.

Because the excerpt provided stops at the beginning of the applicability section, it does not include the detailed operational rules, thresholds, prohibitions, customer disclosures, reporting obligations, or timelines that appear in later chapters. However, the document structure shows that the RBI intends the directions to cover: credit card business conduct, debit card issuance, acceptable card form factors, permissible co-branding, and general standards for both card types, followed by miscellaneous and repeal provisions. A compliance team should therefore treat this as a **new mandatory RBI framework effective immediately** and review the full text of all chapters to identify any required changes to product approvals, issuance controls, outsourcing/co-branding arrangements, customer onboarding disclosures, and internal governance procedures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and shown as **updated through July 15, 2026**) consolidates RBI requirements governing how UCBs may extend credit, with emphasis on board-approved lending policy, digital lending controls, and lending against **gold and silver collateral**. For a compliance team, the key takeaway is that these are **mandatory prudential and conduct requirements** for covered urban co-operative banks, and they impose ongoing governance, customer-protection, technology, reporting, and collateral-management obligations rather than optional guidance.

The document begins by defining its scope, commencement, and applicability, then requires the **Board** to approve and oversee lending-related policies. In practical terms, this means the bank’s board must formally set the institution’s approach to credit facilities and ensure that lending practices align with RBI requirements; compliance should expect board-level accountability rather than reliance on management discretion alone. The direction’s structure indicates that the rules are intended to govern both traditional lending and newer credit channels, especially where third parties or digital interfaces are involved.

A major component is **Chapter III on Digital Lending**, which imposes requirements on **bank–LSP arrangements** (where “LSP” refers to lending service providers), customer conduct protections, technology and data controls, reporting of credit information and digital lending apps, and default-related loss-sharing arrangements. The document specifically requires banks engaged in digital lending to maintain controls over how lending is originated and serviced through digital platforms, and to ensure that customer protection, data handling, and reporting processes are compliant. For compliance purposes, this means the bank must review all outsourced or partner-led digital lending models to confirm that responsibilities, disclosures, data access, reporting, and default-risk allocation are documented and operationalized in line with RBI standards.

The directions also include **technology and data requirements**, which signals that banks must have governance over data use, data security, and system controls in digital lending operations. In addition, there is a specific section on **reporting credit information and Digital Lending Apps (DLAs)**, so the bank must ensure the timely and accurate submission of required credit data and that any apps used in lending are handled according to RBI’s reporting and oversight expectations. The presence of a separate section on **loss sharing in case of default** means banks using third-party digital lending structures must have clear contractual allocation of default losses and related responsibilities, which should be reviewed carefully for regulatory alignment and consumer-risk implications.

Chapter IV addresses **lending against gold and silver collateral**, which is a significant area for UCBs. The title indicates that the directions contain both **general provisions** and **restrictions and ceilings**, meaning banks that offer gold- or silver-backed loans must comply with RBI’s limits on such lending and any operational controls governing valuation, lending amount, and collateral management. Because the table of contents specifically flags “Restrictions and Ceilings,” compliance should assume there are quantitative or procedural constraints that must be monitored closely, even where the excerpt does not reproduce the exact figures.

For a compliance officer, the practical action items are to verify that: the board-approved credit policy has been updated to reflect the 2025 directions; all digital lending partnerships, app-based lending processes, and credit reporting workflows comply with RBI’s conduct, technology, and loss-sharing requirements; and the bank’s gold/silver loan products are checked against the applicable restriction and ceiling provisions in Chapter IV. The document’s **effective regime is anchored in the 2025 issuance, with updates through July 15, 2026**, so the compliance program should be assessed against the latest consolidated version rather than the original text alone.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the interest-rate framework for **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** on **domestic rupee deposits** and related deposit-account practices, and it applies to the entities and activities covered under the document’s applicability section (i.e., UCB deposit-taking operations in India). The core compliance message is that UCBs must determine deposit interest rates in line with RBI’s prescribed framework rather than ad hoc or discriminatory pricing, and they must apply the specific rules for current accounts, savings deposits, term deposits, additional interest, overdue deposits, floating-rate term deposits, deceased depositor accounts, and premature withdrawals.

For **domestic savings deposits**, the direction requires a defined interest-rate method and periodic crediting of interest (the document’s chapter headings indicate that the periodicity requirement is separately addressed). For **domestic term deposits**, UCBs must follow RBI’s rules on the rate-setting framework, payment of interest, and treatment of premature withdrawal, including any penalty structure allowed by the directions. The document also specifically addresses **additional interest** on domestic deposits, meaning banks may need to identify depositors or circumstances that qualify for extra interest and ensure the correct calculation and crediting of such amounts.

The directions also require banks to handle **overdue term deposits** and **floating-rate domestic term deposits** under RBI-prescribed rules, which affects both operational systems and customer communications when deposits mature, are renewed, or reprice. In addition, banks must apply the RBI’s rules for interest payable on the **deposit account of a deceased depositor**, which typically governs how interest is calculated up to the date of settlement and the handling of balances pending transmission to legal heirs/nominees.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is shown as **updated through August 25, 2026**; however, the text provided does not include the operative paragraphs, so exact rate caps, thresholds, calculation formulas, or implementation deadlines cannot be extracted from the excerpt alone. A compliance team should therefore treat this as the controlling framework for UCB deposit interest administration and verify the full operative chapters for the precise numerical rates, exceptions, and effective-date mechanics before updating product terms, core banking systems, and customer-facing disclosures.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 16, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025** (updated through **June 16, 2026**) set out the capital adequacy framework that applies to urban co-operative banks, including how they must define regulatory capital, calculate risk-weighted assets, and meet minimum capital standards. The directions are issued under RBI’s prudential powers and are effective from the date specified in the instrument (**November 28, 2025**, subject to any chapter-wise implementation dates that may appear in the full text). For compliance purposes, the key point is that UCBs must determine their capital position under RBI’s prescribed definitions of **net worth, statutory capital requirements, minimum regulatory capital, and the composition of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital**, rather than relying on local accounting or legacy supervisory approaches.

The document is organized around three substantive compliance areas: **regulatory capital**, **computation of risk-weighted assets (RWA)**, and **other instructions**. Under the capital rules, banks must distinguish between **Tier 1 capital** and **Tier 2 capital** and apply RBI’s eligibility and deduction rules to each; this affects what instruments, reserves, and exposures can be counted for prudential purposes. The directions also specify the capital charge methodology for **credit risk** and **market risk**, meaning UCBs must assign prescribed risk weights to on- and off-balance-sheet exposures and hold capital against market-related positions using RBI’s framework. Compliance officers should therefore expect requirements not only on the amount of capital to be maintained, but also on the exact method used to compute the denominator of the capital ratio through RWA.

Because the table of contents shows dedicated sections on **net worth**, **statutory requirements**, **minimum regulatory capital**, and capital composition, the document is likely intended to align UCB prudential capital with a structured RBI formula rather than a discretionary or purely accounting-based measure. The updated version date (**June 16, 2026**) is important for monitoring whether any amendments, clarifications, or phased-in changes were incorporated after the original issuance. A corporate compliance team should treat this as a primary capital adequacy manual for UCBs: it governs which entities are in scope, how capital is classified, what exposures attract capital charges, and the ongoing obligation to monitor and report capital adequacy in RBI-prescribed form. If you want, I can also turn this into a **controls checklist** or a **“what changed / who must comply / action items”** briefing format for internal use.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)

The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025**, updated as of **August 25, 2026**, under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **RBI Act, 1934**.
