From the visible chapter headings, the directions require each affected NBFC to maintain a **board-approved outsourcing policy**, with the board retaining ultimate accountability for outsourced activities and senior management responsible for execution and oversight. The directions specifically distinguish **“outsourcing of financial services”**, indicate that some activities **must not be outsourced**, and require a governance framework covering **authorization, accountability, and oversight**. The table of contents also shows dedicated requirements for **risk management**, **business continuity and contingency planning**, **confidentiality and security of customer information**, **cross-border outsourcing controls**, **sub-contracting restrictions/oversight**, **handling of concentration and conflict risks**, **monitoring and control mechanisms**, **audit and inspection rights**, **customer grievance handling**, **reporting to the RBI**, and **compliance/effective-implementation obligations**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the RBI is moving outsourcing from a general third-party management issue into a **regulated compliance framework** with board-level oversight and documented internal controls. Any NBFC that outsources services should expect to review and likely update its policies, vendor due diligence, contract terms, monitoring procedures, incident escalation protocols, and contingency planning so they align with the new directions. However, **the excerpt does not include the operative effective date, transition period, numerical thresholds, or the exact list of prohibited activities**, so those details cannot be confirmed from the text provided and would need the full body of the directions to assess implementation timing and specific obligations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction set replaces and consolidates the conduct requirements for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) under the “Responsible Business Conduct” framework, with the document issued on **November 28, 2025** and updated through **July 1, 2026**. It applies to NBFCs covered by the RBI’s NBFC regulatory framework and is organized around board oversight, fair lending practices, customer disclosures, pricing/penalty rules, and loan servicing conduct. The compliance focus is on ensuring that NBFCs have board-approved policies and operational controls that make lending transparent, non-discriminatory, and customer-protective, especially for retail and personal lending.

A central requirement is that the **board** must approve and oversee the institution’s conduct framework, including policies that ensure fair treatment of borrowers, clear disclosures, grievance handling, and periodic review of compliance. NBFCs must maintain a **Fair Practices Code** and align loan origination and servicing with that code, meaning lending terms, communications, and recovery practices must be transparent and not misleading. The document also requires a **Key Facts Statement (KFS)** for loans and advances, so borrowers receive a standardized summary of key terms before or at disbursement, including pricing and charges; the document emphasizes that critical loan terms must be disclosed clearly and in a manner borrowers can understand.

The directions impose specific conduct rules on loan pricing and customer charges. **Penal charges** in loan accounts are regulated so that NBFCs cannot use punitive charges as a disguised interest-rate increase; such charges must be clearly disclosed and applied only for genuine non-compliance, not as a revenue substitute. The framework also addresses **reset of floating interest rates on EMI-based personal loans**, requiring NBFCs to disclose and manage resets in a way that prevents unexpected shocks to borrowers and ensures borrowers understand how their EMI, tenor, or other loan conditions may change when rates move. Similarly, the rules on **pre-payment charges** restrict or regulate charges for early repayment, with the compliance expectation that borrowers are told upfront whether prepayment is permitted and what costs, if any, apply.

The document also strengthens borrower protection at closure of a loan, especially for **personal loans**: upon **repayment or settlement**, NBFCs must promptly release the borrower’s **movable or immovable property documents** and follow a defined process for returning collateral/documents, reducing the risk of unnecessary retention after debt discharge. Separate conduct guidance applies to **lending against gold and silver collateral**, indicating that NBFCs must follow specific customer-protection and conduct standards in valuation, custody, and handling of pledged precious-metal assets. Overall, compliance teams should treat this as a borrower-conduct and disclosure regime: review board policies, loan documentation, pricing and penalty mechanics, EMI reset communications, prepayment terms, collateral release workflows, and gold/silver lending procedures to ensure they match the RBI’s prescribed conduct requirements as updated through **July 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025” consolidates and updates KYC/AML obligations for NBFCs and related regulated entities, with the stated purpose of preventing their use for money laundering and terrorist financing and preserving the integrity of the financial system. It is an RBI issued direction dated November 28, 2025 and marked “Updated as on December 29, 2025,” so compliance teams should treat the December 29 version as the operative text. The document is organized as a comprehensive KYC framework covering customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification, customer due diligence, recordkeeping, and FIU-India reporting, and it also addresses handling of communications from international agencies and other residual instructions.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that NBFCs are required to maintain a formal KYC/AML control framework rather than ad hoc onboarding practices. That framework includes policies for accepting customers, assigning and managing ML/TF risk, performing customer identification procedures, carrying out customer due diligence, retaining records, and reporting suspicious or prescribed transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India. The directions also indicate that requirements apply not only to the entity itself but to the activities and customer relationships that NBFCs establish and maintain, so onboarding, periodic review, transaction monitoring, and information sharing processes must all align with the RBI’s directions.

Because the provided excerpt does not include the operative clauses from the chapters, no specific numeric thresholds, deadlines, or rate-based requirements are visible in the supplied text. The table of contents shows that the document includes detailed rules on customer acceptance policy, risk management, CIP/C DD, record management, FIU reporting, obligations under international agreements, and a chapter on repeal and other provisions, suggesting there may be transition or supersession language elsewhere in the full text. A compliance team should therefore review the full updated directions to confirm any entity-specific exclusions, customer categories, transaction thresholds, retention periods, reporting timelines, or implementation dates that may be set out in the missing chapters and annexes.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction replaces and consolidates the prudential rules governing when non-banking financial companies may declare dividends. It is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends) Directions, 2025**, issued **November 28, 2025**, and shown as **updated through July 01, 2026**. The document is organized into provisions on commencement, applicability, dividend declaration standards, reporting, and repeal/savings, with separate reporting formats for a general **NBFC** and an **SPD** (systemically important deposit-taking/other specified category as defined in the document).

The core requirement is that an NBFC may declare dividend only if it satisfies the RBI’s prudential eligibility conditions and the board formally oversees the decision. The directions require management and the board to verify compliance with the specified financial soundness criteria before any dividend is recommended or paid, rather than treating dividend declaration as a purely discretionary corporate action. The document sets out a **quantum rule** for how much dividend can be paid, meaning the amount is not left solely to the board’s judgment but is capped by the prudential framework in the directions.

A compliance team should pay particular attention to the fact that the directions establish a **reporting obligation** when a dividend is declared. The NBFC must use the prescribed **Annex I reporting format**, and an **SPD** must use the separate **Annex II reporting format**, which implies that dividend decisions must be accompanied by the relevant regulatory submission in the form and manner the RBI specifies. The directions also include a repeal-and-savings clause, meaning earlier conflicting RBI instructions on the same topic are superseded to the extent covered, while any matters not inconsistent with the new directions continue to be governed by other applicable laws and directions. If you want, I can also turn this into a compliance checklist or a “who must do what by when” table.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures Directions, 2025** set the RBI’s required format and disclosure framework for NBFC financial statements, and the document is marked **updated as of July 1, 2026**. It applies to **non-banking financial companies** and is structured around how the **balance sheet, profit and loss account, notes to accounts, and consolidated financial statements** must be prepared and presented, together with detailed disclosure requirements and other instructions. The directions also state the **short title, commencement, and applicability** provisions, so a compliance team should treat this as the operative RBI framework governing NBFC statutory financial reporting from the effective date specified in the full text.  

At a substantive level, the document requires NBFCs to prepare financial statements in the prescribed RBI format, follow the **accounting standards specified by the RBI**, and comply with RBI guidance on the treatment of certain issues under those standards. It also contains a dedicated chapter on **specific disclosure requirements in the notes to accounts**, which means compliance is not limited to the face of the balance sheet and P&L but extends to the supporting explanatory disclosures that must accompany them. The directions further cover **consolidated financial statements**, indicating that entities with subsidiaries or other consolidation obligations must also align group reporting with the RBI’s presentation/disclosure requirements.  

The document includes a **repeal and saving** section, which means prior directions or instructions on the same subject are replaced to the extent stated, while preserving actions taken or rights/obligations already accrued under the earlier regime where the saving clause applies. It also clarifies that **other laws are not barred**, so these directions operate alongside any applicable Companies Act, accounting standards, SEBI requirements (if relevant), and other statutory obligations rather than displacing them unless expressly provided. Because the text shown is only the front matter and table of contents, the exact line-item disclosures, thresholds, and any institution-specific exceptions would need to be checked in the operative chapters before filing or auditing financial statements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025**, effective **November 28, 2025** and updated **as on July 1, 2026**, to require a **transparent, non-discriminatory wilful-default classification process** that follows **natural justice** and to ensure that information on wilful defaulters is shared so lenders can avoid extending further institutional finance to them. The Directions apply to **NBFCs** and are issued under RBI’s powers under **Section 45JA and Section 45L of the RBI Act, 1934** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005**.

For compliance purposes, the document establishes a formal regime for identifying, classifying, reporting, and preventing wilful default within NBFCs. It also introduces requirements for handling **“large defaulters”** and provides for standardized reporting to RBI using specified annexed formats: **Annex I** for submission of the **list of large defaulters** and **Annex II** for submission of **data on cases of wilful default**. The stated policy objective is not just internal classification, but dissemination of relevant credit information so that the market is warned and additional institutional credit is not extended to such borrowers.

The document’s structure shows that compliance obligations are organized around several operational areas: the **Board’s role**, the **treatment of wilful defaulters**, **reporting obligations for wilful and large defaulters**, and **preventive measures/auditor involvement**. This indicates that NBFCs must have board-level oversight, internal procedures for classification and escalation, reporting processes that match the RBI-prescribed formats, and controls designed to prevent misclassification or improper credit extensions to flagged borrowers.

Although the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds or procedural steps from the later chapters, the title and introduction make clear that the Directions are intended to govern both the **decision-making process for wilful-default classification** and the **subsequent reporting/dissemination obligations**. A compliance team should therefore treat these Directions as requiring a documented internal policy, fairness-oriented borrower treatment, board supervision, and timely regulatory reporting of both wilful default cases and large defaulters in the formats specified by RBI.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 1, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025** (dated **November 28, 2025** and noted as **updated as on July 1, 2026**) set a formal stress-resolution framework for certain NBFCs, with the main regime applying to **non-deposit-taking NBFCs with asset size of ₹500 crore or more** and to **all deposit-taking NBFCs**. The document establishes the legal structure for identifying stressed assets early, mandating board-approved resolution policies, and requiring disclosures and supervisory review by RBI. It is organized to cover definitions, governance and policy requirements, early detection and reporting of stress, and the mechanics of resolution through a review period, inter-creditor coordination, and an approved resolution plan.

For affected NBFCs, the directions require a **board-approved policy** for resolution of stressed assets and impose obligations for **early identification and reporting of stress** rather than waiting for default to become severe. The document also requires specified **disclosures** and subjects the institution’s actions to **supervisory review**, meaning compliance teams must expect RBI scrutiny of both process and outcomes. In practice, this means the NBFC must have documented internal triggers, escalation procedures, governance oversight, and reporting controls that allow stressed accounts to be identified and handled in a structured and auditable manner.

The resolution process itself is built around a defined **Review Period**, during which lenders/workout participants are expected to assess the account and finalize a workable plan. Where multiple creditors are involved, the directions require an **Inter Creditor Agreement (ICA)** so that the lenders can coordinate decision-making and implement the resolution plan consistently. The framework then contemplates a formal **Resolution Plan** that must be prepared and implemented within the regulatory process, rather than ad hoc restructuring outside the prescribed structure.

A key compliance implication is that this is not merely guidance on loan workout; it is a **prescriptive RBI directions framework** that can affect capital, provisioning, governance, and reporting obligations for covered NBFCs. Because the content provided here is a table-of-contents excerpt rather than the full operative text, no specific provisioning percentages, review-period lengths, or deadline dates can be extracted from the excerpt itself; however, the document clearly signals that those operational requirements are contained in the later chapters, including **additional provisioning** rules. Compliance teams should therefore treat the directions as immediately relevant to covered NBFCs and ensure they are reviewing the full text for the detailed triggers, timelines, provisioning norms, and any implementation deadlines tied to the July 1, 2026 updated version.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s updated **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025** set the prudential accounting and credit-risk rules that NBFCs must follow for loan income recognition, asset classification, provisioning, and related disclosures, with the document updated through **July 1, 2026**. It applies to **NBFCs** generally, and then imposes additional prudential norms on **NBFCs classified as NBFC–Base Layer (NBFC–BL)**. The Directions establish requirements on prudent lending and consumer education, define how assets must be classified, prescribe provisioning standards, and require disclosures, with an additional section specifically addressing **extra provisioning when a resolution plan is implemented under Chapter VI-A of the RBI’s 2025 Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that NBFCs must apply RBI-prescribed rules for recognizing income and for moving exposures through asset-quality buckets based on delinquency or impairment, and then create provisions accordingly rather than relying on internal accounting discretion. The document also contains a **Chapter II C2** that adds **specific provisioning** where an exposure is restructured/resolved under the referenced stressed-asset resolution framework, meaning firms need to coordinate these IRACP rules with the separate resolution regime. Chapter II also requires **disclosure obligations**, so firms must ensure their financial statement and regulatory reporting processes capture the asset-classification status, provisioning, and any other prescribed prudential information.

The table of contents shows a further **Chapter III** that imposes **additional prudential norms for NBFC–BLs**, including separate asset classification and provisioning requirements beyond the baseline NBFC rules. Although the excerpt provided does not show the detailed thresholds or percentages, the document’s structure makes clear that compliance teams should expect a layer-specific overlay for Base Layer NBFCs and should check the operative text for any stricter triggers, overdue-day cutoffs, provisioning percentages, or timing rules. In practice, this means NBFCs should review whether they fall within the scope of the base-layer provisions, update policies and systems accordingly, and ensure lending, collections, accounting, and regulatory reporting teams are aligned on the updated RBI framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI circular sets the **Asset-Liability Management (ALM) framework for non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)**, issued on **28 November 2025** and marked **“Updated as on 1 July 2026.”** It applies to **NBFCs within the scope stated in the Directions** and establishes mandatory requirements for board oversight, governance, information systems, liquidity risk management, maturity profiling, mismatch control, and currency-risk management. The document is structured as binding directions rather than guidance, so affected NBFCs must treat the provisions as compliance requirements and align internal policies, limits, monitoring, and reporting accordingly.

At a high level, the Directions require the **Board of Directors to approve ALM policies and limits and to review them periodically**, and they place responsibility on the NBFC to maintain an **ALM governance structure and information system** capable of measuring liquidity risk and producing maturity-based cash-flow data. NBFCs must maintain an **ALM organisation** and procedures to identify, measure, monitor, and control liquidity risk, including the preparation of **maturity profiles** and the management of liquidity mismatches. The framework also addresses **stock-based liquidity risk measurement** and **currency risk management**, indicating that NBFCs with relevant foreign-currency exposures must include those exposures in their ALM controls.

The document’s chapter structure shows that it contains specific compliance expectations on **liquidity mismatch management** and **measurement methodology**, which means entities must not only have policies but also operational processes for regular monitoring, escalation, and corrective action when mismatches emerge. Because this is an RBI prudential direction, compliance teams should treat the document as requiring documented governance, internal limits, periodic review, and data-driven reporting/monitoring rather than informal treasury management. Since the excerpt provided does not include the detailed thresholds or bucket-wise limits, a compliance officer would need to review the full text—especially the sections on maturity profiling and mismatch management—for exact numerical requirements, reporting frequencies, and any phase-in or transitional timelines beyond the stated effective/update date.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Classification, Valuation, and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025** (updated through **July 1, 2026**) set the accounting, valuation, trading, and reporting framework for NBFC investment portfolios, with distinct rules for **NBFCs in the Base Layer (NBFC-BL)** and other covered NBFCs as defined in the directions. The document is an operational compliance instrument: it governs how investment assets must be classified and valued, how government securities and corporate bond trades must be executed and reported, how income from investments is recognized, and how certain market products such as **Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), currency futures, and interest rate futures** may be used and accounted for. The directions are issued under the RBI’s supervisory authority and are intended to standardize investment portfolio treatment for NBFCs, so compliance teams should treat them as binding conduct, accounting, and reporting requirements rather than general guidance.

For **NBFC-BL**, the directions require a formal **investment policy** and establish specific **accounting and valuation rules** for the investment book, including the treatment of gains/losses, valuation methodology, and recognition of income from investments. They also prescribe how **Government Securities** transactions must be carried out and what operative procedures apply to such transactions, meaning NBFCs need controls around execution, settlement, and documentation of sovereign debt trades. The directions further require participation in a **reporting platform for corporate bond transactions**, so affected entities must ensure their transaction reporting processes, systems, and internal controls are aligned with the RBI-prescribed platform and timelines.

The document separately addresses **accounting for investments for non-Ind AS NBFCs**, indicating that entities not preparing financial statements under Ind AS must follow RBI-specified accounting treatment for investments and income recognition rather than relying on general policy. It also contains a dedicated section on **income from investments**, which is material for compliance because it determines when and how dividend, interest, and other investment income are recognized in the books. In addition, the directions regulate **investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**, imposing RBI requirements on whether and how NBFCs may invest in AIF units and how those exposures must be managed and reported.

The updated content also covers **currency futures** and **interest rate futures**, indicating that NBFCs using these instruments must follow the RBI’s specific operational and accounting rules for derivative use in the investment portfolio context. Because this is the **2025 direction set updated as of July 1, 2026**, the current version should be treated as incorporating all amendments through that date, and compliance programs should verify that policies, accounting manuals, portfolio controls, trade reporting, and investment approvals reflect the latest consolidated text. In practice, any NBFC with an investment portfolio—especially NBFC-BL and any entity using government securities, corporate bond reporting systems, AIF exposure, or futures instruments—should review these directions line-by-line against its existing procedures to confirm that classification, valuation, reporting, and income-recognition processes are fully aligned.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Securitisation Transactions) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Securitisation Transactions Directions, 2025** set the framework NBFCs must follow when originating, retaining, structuring, and accounting for securitisation transactions, and the document is marked **updated as of July 1, 2026**. It applies to **NBFC originators and related securitisation structures/SPVs** and is organized around what assets can be securitised, minimum retention by the originator, origination standards, payment waterfall/priority, limits on retained exposure, issuance/listing, SPV conditions, representations and warranties, accounting treatment, and a separate regime for **simple, transparent and comparable (STC)** securitisations for regulatory capital purposes. The compliance significance is that these directions replace a purely transactional approach with a rule-based regime governing both the **design of the securitisation and the ongoing treatment of the exposure**, so any NBFC considering securitisation must check eligibility, retention, structuring, and disclosure/listing requirements before execution.

A key requirement is that only **eligible assets** may be securitised, and the originator must satisfy a **Minimum Retention Requirement (MRR)**, meaning it must keep a prescribed portion of the securitised exposure rather than transferring the entire risk. The directions also require **origination standards** to be met, so the assets must be originated under defined underwriting and operational criteria before they can be packaged into a securitisation. The structure must include an enforceable **payment priority waterfall** and must be sufficiently **observable/transparent**, with the special purpose entity meeting specified conditions so the transfer is legally and operationally sound. The document also addresses **representations and warranties** and **accounting provisions**, meaning the originator cannot treat the transaction as a simple off-balance-sheet disposal without satisfying the RBI’s conditions on transfer, retained risk, and accounting recognition.

For compliance teams, the most important practical point is that the directions also cap the **total retained exposures** an originator can keep in connection with securitised assets, preventing excessive concentration of risk on the originating NBFC’s books. The directions further impose **issuance and listing** requirements, so if a securitised instrument is issued, it must follow the specified issuance process and, where applicable, be listed in accordance with the framework. In addition, the STC chapter creates a distinct pathway for securitisations that qualify as **simple, transparent and comparable**, which matters because such structures may receive **regulatory capital treatment** under the STC criteria only if they satisfy the RBI’s detailed qualitative and structural tests. Any NBFC engaging in securitisation after the effective regime should therefore review each transaction against the eligibility, retention, transfer, SPV, disclosure, and capital-treatment rules before closing, and ensure internal policies reflect the updated directions as of **July 1, 2026**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025** establish a **single, comprehensive framework** for how credit risk may be transferred or distributed by regulated lending institutions, replacing earlier piecemeal guidance on loan transfers, co-lending, consortium-style arrangements, and related credit-risk transfer structures. The directions are aimed at **NBFCs and other lending institutions covered by the framework** and are designed to govern transactions used for **liquidity management, exposure rebalancing, strategic portfolio sales, and co-lending**; the document states that it is intended to be self-contained and regulatory in nature, not merely advisory.

A major part of the framework concerns **transfer of loan exposures**, with separate treatment for **loans that are not in default** and **stressed loans**. For loans that are transferred, the directions set out **general conditions applicable to all transfers** and then impose additional rules depending on whether the loan is performing or stressed. For compliance purposes, this means institutions cannot treat transfers as a simple sale-and-exit transaction; they must determine the loan’s status, satisfy the relevant transfer conditions, and ensure the transaction is structured within the RBI’s permitted transfer mechanics before booking any derecognition, capital relief, or risk transfer treatment.

The directions also contain a distinct section on **co-lending arrangements**, reflecting RBI’s focus on shared lending models between regulated entities. These rules impose **prudential norms** on how such arrangements are to be structured and managed, meaning institutions participating in co-lending must ensure their arrangements meet the RBI’s required allocation, operational, and prudential standards rather than relying on bilateral commercial agreements alone. For compliance teams, this will typically require reviewing product structures, servicing arrangements, risk allocation, disclosures, and internal controls for any co-lending books or partnerships.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated as of July 01, 2026**, so compliance teams should treat the text as the operative consolidated version as of that update date. No specific numerical thresholds, rates, or deadlines are visible in the excerpt provided, but the title and structure indicate the framework is intended to be binding and comprehensive across all covered credit-risk transfer and distribution activities. The table of contents also shows a **Part C on repeal and other provisions**, indicating that some prior directions or guidance are being superseded or integrated into this new framework, so firms should check transition and repeal provisions carefully to confirm which older circulars, guidelines, or practices are no longer valid.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on August 25, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFC) – Concentration Risk Management Directions, 2025** formalize RBI’s framework for limiting concentration risk in NBFC credit and investment exposures. The document states that concentration of exposures to a single counterparty or connected group can create significant risk, so RBI requires applicable NBFCs to manage concentration through regulatory restrictions, internal exposure limits, and consideration of geographical concentration. It also notes that the RBI has already extended a **large exposure framework** to NBFCs in the **Upper Layer**, and this Directions set is issued under the RBI’s statutory powers to make those requirements binding.

The document is structured to apply differently by NBFC layer: **Base Layer, Middle Layer, and Upper Layer** each have their own chapter of requirements, which means compliance obligations are not uniform across the sector and must be mapped to the entity’s regulatory classification. The introduction makes clear that the directions are intended to regulate both **credit concentration** and **investment concentration**, and that firms must also ensure exposure norms are reckoned in line with RBI’s regulatory prescriptions rather than only internal policy definitions. The text emphasizes that NBFCs must actively avoid “undesirable concentration” in particular **geographical locations**, which indicates a need for location-based concentration monitoring in addition to counterparty-based limits.

The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is identified as **DOR/2025-26/351** and **DOR.CRE.REC.270/07-03-008/2025-26**, with an updated version noted as **updated on August 25, 2026**. Because the excerpt provided only includes the introduction and table of contents, it does not yet specify the exact numerical concentration limits, thresholds, carve-outs, reporting timelines, or implementation deadlines; those are expected to appear in the chapter-specific provisions and annexes. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway from the material shown is that NBFCs must determine their applicable layer, review concentration-risk controls for counterparties, connected counterparties, investments, and geography, and align internal limits and monitoring with RBI’s layer-based regulatory framework.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025** consolidate and update prudential requirements for NBFC credit-risk controls, including board governance, credit appraisal, concentration/other restrictions, CDS usage, borrower LEI identification, and CERSAI filing obligations. The document is an RBI direction dated **November 28, 2025**, and the version provided is **updated as on July 01, 2026**; compliance teams should treat the specific effective dates and transitional requirements in the operative chapters as controlling, especially where the text introduces phased implementation or updates existing rules. The stated regulatory intent is to address NBFC exposure to credit risk as one of the most significant risks in financial intermediation and to use a mix of internal controls and statutory restrictions/prohibitions because NBFC credit exposures span multiple sectors, borrower types, and products with interconnected systemic effects.

At a governance level, NBFCs are required to operate under **board-approved policies** governing credit risk, meaning the board must formally approve the institution’s credit-risk framework rather than leaving it solely to management. The directions also require **credit risk evaluation** processes, implying NBFCs must assess and monitor borrower creditworthiness and exposure risk using documented procedures rather than ad hoc judgment. In addition, the document contains a chapter on **regulatory restrictions**, indicating that certain credit-related activities are subject to RBI-imposed limits, prohibitions, or conditions; compliance teams should review this chapter for any activities the NBFC engages in that may be constrained by exposure thresholds, product restrictions, or counterparty limitations.

A separate chapter governs **Credit Default Swaps (CDS) for NBFCs acting as users**, meaning the rules are not for NBFCs as market makers but for NBFCs that use CDS for credit-risk management. The document also imposes a requirement on **borrowers to have a Legal Entity Identifier (LEI)** in specified circumstances, so any lending or exposure processes must be checked to determine when borrower LEI capture and validation are mandatory. Another chapter requires the **filing of security interests in CERSAI** for security interests relating to **immovable property other than equitable mortgage, movable assets, and intangible assets**, so NBFCs must ensure security creation documentation is followed by the prescribed registration/filing steps where those collateral types are involved.

The final chapter addresses **repeal and other provisions**, which means some prior RBI instructions are likely superseded, modified, or saved by these directions; compliance teams should identify legacy circulars or master directions replaced by this framework to avoid maintaining obsolete procedures. The document also includes **Annex I**, which likely contains operational or definitional material that supports implementation. Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter and introduction, it does not show the detailed numerical thresholds, deadlines, or procedural steps; those would need to be read from the operative chapters for exact compliance action items.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025** set out the mandatory framework for how NBFCs interact with credit information companies (CICs) and how they must report, correct, and use credit information. The document applies to **NBFCs** within RBI’s regulatory scope and governs their **membership in CICs, periodic credit data submission, data quality obligations, correction processes, and use of credit information reports in credit appraisal**. The directions are issued in RBI circular form **dated November 28, 2025** and are marked **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** so compliance teams should treat the incorporated text as the operative version as of that update date.

A key requirement is that affected NBFCs must maintain appropriate **membership and reporting arrangements with CICs** and submit borrower/account data in the **prescribed data formats** and within the **specified reporting timelines**; the framework also requires ongoing **updation** of reported information so that CIC records remain current. The directions further establish **reporting guidelines** that NBFCs must follow in compiling, validating, and transmitting credit information, and they create a formal process for handling **rejected data**, including the need to **rectify rejected submissions** and address them through a defined review of the **Data Quality Index (DQI)**. This means compliance is not limited to sending data on time—NBFCs must also maintain internal controls to monitor rejection rates, correct errors, and improve data quality continuously.

The directions also require NBFCs to have a process for **correcting Credit Information Reports** where errors or disputes arise, rather than relying on ad hoc adjustments. In addition, the RBI specifies how **credit information reports may be used in credit appraisal**, meaning NBFCs must use CIC outputs in a controlled and compliant manner when evaluating borrower creditworthiness. The directions also address **display of information**, indicating that certain credit information-related disclosures or presentation requirements apply, and they clarify how these instructions interact with other RBI directions issued by the **Department of Regulation**. Finally, the document references a **Technical Working Group**, indicating that implementation, reporting, or technical standards may be supported or guided through that mechanism; compliance teams should review the full operative chapters for exact file formats, submission cycles, correction workflows, and any institution-specific thresholds or reporting triggers that apply to their NBFC.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025

The directions are issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and are intended to govern the issuance and conduct of credit card business by the covered NBFCs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (updated as on July 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities Directions, 2025** are a consolidated set of binding rules for NBFC lending activities, with the version provided **updated as of July 15, 2026**. The document applies to **NBFCs** and, for the digital lending chapter, to NBFCs using **lending service provider (LSP)** arrangements and **digital lending applications (DLAs)**. It establishes board-level governance requirements, detailed conduct and customer-protection rules for digital lending, technology/data controls, reporting obligations, loss-sharing rules for defaulted loans, and specific restrictions and ceilings for lending against **gold and silver collateral**.

At a high level, the directions require the **board of an NBFC** to approve and oversee lending policies, including controls over outsourcing and digital lending arrangements, and to ensure the NBFC remains responsible for compliance even where third parties are involved. For **digital lending**, the NBFC must ensure that any LSP relationship is structured and monitored so that customer-facing practices, disclosures, consent, and grievance handling meet RBI requirements; the NBFC cannot shift regulatory responsibility to the platform or intermediary. The chapter also imposes **technology and data safeguards**, meaning data collected through digital lending must be limited, appropriately protected, and used only for permitted purposes, with controls over access, storage, sharing, and deletion as required by the directions.

The document further requires **credit information reporting** and oversight of any DLAs used in the lending process, so that loans originated or serviced digitally are properly reflected in credit bureau/reporting systems and the lender maintains traceability of the transaction chain. It also includes rules on **loss sharing in case of default**, which means NBFCs that enter arrangements with LSPs or similar service providers must allocate and document responsibility for default losses in a way that complies with RBI’s framework; this is intended to prevent hidden credit risk transfer and ensure the NBFC remains accountable for prudent underwriting and collection practices. In addition, the directions contain **general provisions** that govern implementation, compliance monitoring, and any residual obligations not covered by the chapter-specific rules.

For lending secured by **gold and silver collateral**, the directions establish dedicated rules that constrain how NBFCs can accept, value, and lend against precious-metal collateral. The document includes **restrictions and ceilings** for such lending, meaning compliance teams must check the specific collateral type, valuation practices, concentration limits, and any caps or prudential thresholds set by RBI before originating or renewing these loans. Because the excerpt does not include the detailed numerical ceilings, a compliance review would need to verify the full chapter text for exact loan-to-value limits, eligibility conditions, and any operational conditions attached to gold and silver-backed lending.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acceptance of Public Deposits) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
This RBI direction sets the framework for when and how NBFCs may accept public deposits and how deposit-taking NBFCs must manage repayment, liquidity, disclosures, reporting, and compliance after the rules take effect. It is issued under the RBI Act, 1934 and the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and is titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acceptance of Public Deposits) Directions, 2025**; the document shown is an **updated version as on April 15, 2026**. The introductory clause states that the Directions become effective **on the date they are placed on the official website** (the text provided cuts off after “official…”), so the operative start date is the publication/website-placement date rather than a fixed calendar date in the excerpt.

The core substance of the Directions is that they govern **non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)** that accept or propose to accept **public deposits** and impose the RBI’s framework on eligibility, restrictions, and ongoing conduct. The document is organized into chapters covering: preliminary definitions and application, **maintenance of liquid assets**, **restrictions on acceptance of public deposits by NBFCs**, **general provisions for repayment of public deposits**, **miscellaneous instructions**, **reporting requirements**, and **repeal/other provisions**, with two annexes. From the chapter headings alone, the compliance implication is that firms in scope will need to verify whether they are permitted to accept deposits at all, maintain the required liquid assets, follow prescribed repayment rules and timelines, and meet any recurring reporting obligations.

Because the excerpt provided ends in Chapter I before the substantive rules appear, the text available here does **not** include the specific numerical thresholds, deposit caps, liquidity percentages, maturity restrictions, reporting forms, or penalty/transition details that may be contained in later chapters and annexes. For compliance purposes, the key item visible in this excerpt is the **existence of a comprehensive RBI regime for NBFC public deposits** and the fact that it is a formal direction under statutory authority, meaning affected entities must treat it as binding once effective. If you share the remaining pages, I can produce a fuller operational summary with the exact limits, deadlines, filing requirements, and any amended or repealed provisions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025** (updated through **July 1, 2026**) set out the capital-adequacy framework for **non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)** and related entities covered by the applicability provisions. The document is organized around regulatory capital, risk-weighted assets, securitisation exposures, and leverage ratio, and it replaces/updates earlier prudential capital norms by prescribing how NBFCs must calculate eligible capital, deductions, and asset risk weights for regulatory reporting and compliance.

A core compliance obligation is that affected entities must determine **regulatory capital** by classifying capital into **CET1, Tier 1, and Tier 2**, and apply the RBI’s prescribed deductions and adjustments before using those amounts for capital-adequacy calculations. The directions also address the treatment of **owned funds**, **deferred tax assets (DTA)** and **deferred tax liabilities (DTL)**, and require specific regulatory adjustments to be made from capital rather than treating all balance-sheet items as freely available capital. The framework further introduces or maintains a **leverage ratio** requirement, meaning firms must monitor not only risk-weighted capital adequacy but also an exposure-based leverage measure.

The directions require NBFCs to compute **risk-weighted assets (RWAs)** under RBI-prescribed rules, which then drive the minimum capital requirement. The document specifically includes a separate section on **securitisation exposures**, indicating that NBFCs holding or originating securitised exposures must apply special capital treatment rather than relying solely on general asset risk weights. Compliance teams should therefore ensure that securitisation positions, off-balance-sheet exposures, and any other assets subject to special treatment are mapped to the correct regulatory buckets and risk weights.

Because the document is titled as **“Updated as on July 01, 2026,”** firms should treat that date as the version control point for the current requirements and verify whether any changes through that update affect their capital computation methods, deductions, or exposure classifications. The document’s structure indicates that the applicable rules begin with **short title and commencement** and **applicability** provisions in Chapter I, so compliance officers should confirm whether the firm falls within the defined NBFC categories and whether any exceptions or special applicability rules apply before implementing the capital and RWA calculations.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Governance) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on June 24, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Governance) Directions, 2025** set out the governance framework for NBFCs and, in several places, impose stricter requirements on **NBFCs in the Middle Layer (NBFC-ML) and Upper Layer (NBFC-UL)**. The directions are issued by the RBI under its supervisory powers and are intended to standardize board composition, committee oversight, fit-and-proper expectations, and senior management controls across regulated NBFCs. Because this document is titled as **updated as on June 24, 2026**, compliance teams should treat the updated version as the operative text and verify internal policies against that current version.

At a high level, the directions require each NBFC to have a **board-approved governance policy** and to **periodically review** it, rather than relying on informal practices. The board is expected to oversee governance, risk, compliance, and management succession/change control, and the directions specifically call for procedures addressing **changes in directors and/or management**. For all NBFCs, the document also addresses **board experience requirements**, meaning the board must have the appropriate level of expertise and collective capability to govern the institution; this is not a purely ceremonial requirement and should be reflected in board nomination, fit-and-proper assessment, and succession planning processes.

A separate set of obligations applies to **NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL**, which face enhanced governance expectations. These include requirements on the **constitution of the board and appointment of directors**, periodic **reviews** of governance arrangements, and mandatory **committees of the board** with specified oversight responsibilities. The document also introduces requirements around key control functions, including the appointment of a **Chief Risk Officer (CRO)** and a **Chief Compliance Officer (CCO)** for the relevant layers, signaling a formalized second-line control structure and clearer accountability for risk and compliance management. Compliance teams should ensure that the roles are not merely created on paper but are supported by documented reporting lines, authority, and independence consistent with the RBI’s governance expectations.

The directions are binding on the NBFCs within scope as defined in the document, and the practical compliance task is to map every applicable requirement to existing policies, board terms of reference, committee charters, and senior management appointments. Where the document specifies board reviews, appointment standards, or committee composition, those requirements should be checked against actual board minutes and governance documents, especially for NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL. In addition, any internal triggers for **director or management change approvals, notifications, and onboarding/offboarding controls** should be aligned to the RBI framework so that changes are handled through a documented governance process.

Because the provided excerpt is mainly the table of contents and title page, it does not show the detailed thresholds, exact committee composition rules, or any transitional deadlines in the visible text. However, from the portions shown, the compliance significance is clear: the RBI has issued a formal governance code for NBFCs, with heightened obligations for middle- and upper-layer entities, and firms in scope should confirm that their board structure, committees, senior appointments, and policy review cycles conform to the final updated directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Undertaking of Financial Services Directions, 2025** (updated **July 1, 2026**) consolidates the RBI’s rules on when and how NBFCs may expand into other financial services, with the document specifically covering governance by the board, investments in AIFs, overseas investments, expansion through the automatic route, and entry into insurance business. It applies to NBFCs within the scope of the Directions, and the table of contents indicates separate treatment for **NBFCs other than NBFC-CICs**, **NBFC-CICs**, and **HFCs** where relevant, so compliance teams should first map their entity type to the correct subchapter before assessing permissibility. The document is not just informational; it sets out the regulatory framework and procedural requirements that govern whether an NBFC may undertake new financial activities directly, through subsidiaries, joint ventures, or overseas investment structures, and it places responsibility on the board to oversee these expansions.

A key subject of the Directions is **investment in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs)**, which is addressed as a standalone compliance area in Chapter II. The inclusion of AIFs alongside board governance signals that NBFCs must review their investment practices against RBI’s specific constraints and any related approval/monitoring expectations before making such investments. The Directions also cover **overseas investment by NBFCs**—with separate provisions for **NBFCs other than NBFC-CICs** and for **NBFC-CICs**—indicating that foreign subsidiaries, JVs, or investment structures are regulated differently depending on the NBFC category. For compliance purposes, this means cross-border expansion is not presumed permissible and must be tested against the exact entity-specific conditions in the relevant section.

The document further addresses **expansion of activities through the automatic route**, meaning some service expansions may be allowed without case-by-case prior approval if the NBFC satisfies the prescribed conditions. It also includes a dedicated section on **entry into insurance business**, with separate rules for **NBFCs other than NBFC-CICs and HFCs**, implying that insurance forays are tightly controlled and depend on the institution’s regulated status. Because the table of contents shows multiple activity-specific chapters rather than a single omnibus permission, the compliance obligation is to verify the exact route, entity type, and activity before launching any new line of business, forming a subsidiary, entering a JV, or making an overseas investment.

The excerpt provided does not include the body text of the specific provisions, so no exact monetary thresholds, capital ratios, filing deadlines, or approval forms can be confirmed from the visible text alone. However, the document’s structure makes clear that it is intended to be the operative RBI framework for these expansion activities and that the relevant obligations are likely detailed in the later sections under each chapter. A compliance team should therefore treat this as the controlling document for business-expansion approvals and confirm the exact procedural requirements, restrictions, and any thresholds in the full text before proceeding with any AIF investment, overseas structure, or insurance-related activity.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 15, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation Directions, 2025** (as updated through **April 15, 2026**) set the framework for when and how NBFCs may open, close, or operate branches and overseas representative offices. The document applies to **NBFCs** subject to RBI supervision under these Directions and replaces earlier branch-authorisation guidance, with a **repeal-and-saving** structure preserving actions already taken under prior rules where applicable. Although the excerpt provided is only the table of contents, the operative structure shows that the Directions specifically regulate **opening branches in India, opening branches abroad, closing branches, and opening representative offices abroad**, with some prior provisions marked **deleted**, indicating a consolidation and revision of the earlier regime.

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that branch-related expansion or overseas presence by an NBFC is not treated as a purely internal business decision; it is governed by RBI authorization rules under these Directions. Any NBFC planning a new branch in India, a branch outside India, or a representative office abroad should assume a **pre-approval/authorisation-based process** rather than an automatic right to open such offices, and should confirm that the proposed activity falls within the specific permissions and procedural requirements in the relevant chapter. The document also contemplates **branch closures**, meaning compliance teams need controls not only for opening new locations but also for proper RBI-compliant winding down or closure of existing ones.

The title page indicates the Directions were issued on **November 28, 2025** and then **updated on April 15, 2026**, so compliance teams should treat the April 15, 2026 version as the current authoritative text. Because the excerpt does not include the body text of the rules, no specific numerical thresholds, filing deadlines, or approval criteria are visible here; however, the table of contents confirms that the Directions are organized around procedural requirements for branch authorization and overseas presence, so the full text should be reviewed before any expansion, relocation, or closure decision is implemented. In short, the document is a dedicated RBI rulebook for **where NBFCs may establish physical offices or representative presence and how those actions must be handled under RBI oversight**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Non-Banking Financial Companies (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** take effect **immediately** and apply to **all categories of NBFCs at all regulatory layers**, unless a specific provision says otherwise. The RBI issues these directions under its powers in **sections 45K, 45L, and 45M of the RBI Act, 1934**, and the purpose is to govern how voluntary amalgamations of NBFCs are to be handled under RBI oversight.

From the material provided, the document establishes the RBI’s framework for **granting a No Objection Certificate (NOC) and/or approval** for voluntary amalgamation transactions involving NBFCs. That means any NBFC seeking to merge voluntarily with another entity must follow the RBI’s prescribed process rather than proceeding purely as a corporate law matter; the RBI is asserting regulatory control over the transaction before it can be completed. Because the applicability is stated broadly, the compliance impact is not limited to a particular size or layer of NBFC unless later provisions carve out exceptions.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that these Directions create a **mandatory RBI approval/NOC route** for voluntary amalgamations of NBFCs, and they are not future-dated—they are operative immediately upon issuance on **November 28, 2025**. The document excerpt does not yet include the detailed procedural steps, eligibility conditions, forms, timelines, or substantive approval criteria, but it clearly signals that NBFCs contemplating amalgamation must treat RBI consent as a required precondition and align internal transaction planning, board approvals, and regulatory filings accordingly.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under Sections **45JA, 45K, 45L, 45M, and 45MA** of the RBI Act, 1934. The document is a replacement/updated framework governing **acquisition of shareholding or control in NBFCs** and is structured around when RBI prior approval is required, what information must be filed, what public notice must be given before a change in control/management, and how investments from **FATF non-compliant jurisdictions** are treated. It applies specifically to **non-banking financial companies (NBFCs)** and transactions that result in an acquisition of shareholding or a change in control or management of an NBFC.

For compliance purposes, the key substantive requirement is that **prior RBI approval is required before acquiring shareholding or control in an NBFC** where the transaction crosses the thresholds or otherwise falls within the scope set out in the Directions. The document also lays down a formal **application process for prior approval**, meaning the acquirer and the NBFC must prepare and submit the prescribed information to RBI before closing the transaction. In addition, where there is a proposed **change in control or management**, the Directions require a **prior public notice** to be issued, so the parties cannot treat the transaction as purely private; the notice obligation is intended to inform the market and stakeholders in advance of the change.

The Directions further impose restrictions or additional scrutiny for transactions involving **investment from jurisdictions identified by FATF as non-compliant**. That means any proposed acquisition funding or ownership chain involving such jurisdictions will trigger enhanced regulatory concern and may be disallowed or subjected to special conditions under RBI’s framework. The document also includes a **repeal and saving clause**, indicating that prior inconsistent directions are revoked while preserving actions already taken or rights/liabilities accrued under the earlier regime, and it clarifies that other applicable laws are **not barred** by these Directions.

Because the excerpt provided is only the front matter and table of contents, it does **not yet disclose the specific numerical ownership thresholds, exact filing forms, timelines, or the detailed content of the public notice**; those are likely contained in the body and annex. A compliance team should therefore treat this as confirmation that RBI has issued a formal new control-acquisition regime for NBFCs effective from the date of issuance, and should review the operative chapters immediately for any transaction involving acquisition of shares, voting rights, managerial control, or a change in ownership structure of an NBFC.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This document is the RBI’s consolidated 2025 framework for NBFC registration, exemptions, reporting, and scale-based regulation, issued under the RBI Act, 1934, the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011, and the National Housing Bank Act, 1987, and it applies to every Non-Banking Financial Company unless a specific exemption or carve-out is stated. It is dated November 28, 2025 and is presented as “updated as on July 01, 2026,” so compliance teams should treat it as the operative version incorporating amendments up to that date. The RBI states that the directions are issued in the public interest to regulate the financial system and to prevent NBFC affairs from being conducted in a way detrimental to depositors, investors, or the NBFC itself.

The document’s core substantive change is the creation and operation of a scale-based regulatory framework for NBFCs, meaning compliance obligations are not uniform across all entities but depend on the size, type, and risk profile of the NBFC. The framework is organized into chapters covering preliminary provisions, scale-based regulation, registration requirements, exemptions from the RBI Act, reporting obligations, and repeal/other transitional provisions. For a compliance team, this means the first task is to determine the entity’s classification under the RBI’s framework, because that classification will drive registration status, prudential requirements, reporting frequency/content, and which provisions of the RBI Act continue to apply versus which are exempted.

The document expressly addresses registration requirements, so any entity carrying on NBFC activities must assess whether registration with the RBI is required and whether any statutory exemption applies. It also creates a separate chapter on exemptions from the provisions of the RBI Act, 1934, indicating that certain NBFCs, activities, or classes of entities may be relieved from some statutory requirements only to the extent specified in these directions. Compliance teams should therefore review not just whether the business is an NBFC, but also whether it falls within an exempt category and whether the exemption is conditional or limited.

The reporting chapter indicates that NBFCs have ongoing reporting obligations to the RBI, and these obligations are part of the directions themselves rather than a separate standalone circular. Because the document is a consolidated framework, the compliance posture should be assumed to include continuing RBI reporting and internal controls to support classification under the scale-based regime, registration/renewal monitoring, and any exemption reliance. The final chapter on repeal and other provisions indicates that prior directions are being superseded or read together with transition rules, so teams should verify whether legacy policies, filings, or compliance calendars need to be updated to align with the 2025 framework as updated through July 1, 2026.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on December 29, 2025)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Asset Reconstruction Companies – Know Your Customer” Directions, 2025 (DOR/2025-26/377, DOR.AML.REC.No.296/14.01.010/2025-26, dated November 28, 2025; updated as on December 29, 2025) establish the KYC/AML framework specifically for Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) to prevent their use for money laundering or terrorist financing and to preserve financial-system integrity. The document is structured into eleven chapters covering preliminary provisions, general requirements, customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification, customer due diligence, recordkeeping, FIU-India reporting, handling communications from international agencies, other instructions, and repeal/transition provisions, with two annexes. From the excerpt provided, the core regulatory change is that ARCs are now expressly subject to RBI’s consolidated KYC expectations under these Directions, rather than only general AML principles, and the directions are intended to govern how ARCs identify customers, maintain records, and report suspicious or prescribed information.  

For compliance teams, the key implication is that ARCs must implement a formal customer acceptance policy, risk-based controls, customer identification procedures, and customer due diligence procedures tailored to the ARC business model, and must maintain records and reporting processes aligned to those obligations. The directions also require ARCs to report to the Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND) where applicable and to comply with obligations arising from international agreements and communications from international agencies. Chapter XI indicates there are repeal and other transitional provisions, meaning prior related instructions are superseded or modified and firms must confirm which legacy directions cease to apply once the new framework is in force.  

The excerpt you provided does not include the operative chapters’ detailed thresholds, dates, or procedural steps, so I cannot reliably state specific deadlines, numeric thresholds, or category-by-category customer requirements from the text shown. However, a compliance officer should treat the November 28, 2025 issue date and the “updated as on December 29, 2025” status as signals that the final, consolidated directions may contain amendments or clarifications relative to the original issue, and should review the full chapters and annexes for exact onboarding, identification, record retention, reporting timing, and escalation requirements before implementation.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 12 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002** and **Section 11 of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005** to create a formal system for **disseminating credit information on wilful defaulters** so lenders can be cautioned and **additional institutional finance is not extended** to such borrowers. The Directions are titled as above and **come into force immediately** on issuance. They apply to **all Asset Reconstruction Companies**; the document also states that the restrictions relating to **further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters** and the provisions on **large defaulters** apply to the relevant entities covered by the Directions, with detailed treatment to be administered through the reporting framework set out in the next chapter.

The substantive compliance focus of the document is the **reporting of wilful defaulters and large defaulters** by ARCs, with the objective of feeding reliable credit information into the financial system. The Directions introduce reporting requirements backed by prescribed formats: **Annex I** sets the **format for submission of the list of large defaulters**, and **Annex II** sets the **format for submission of data on cases of wilful default**. For a compliance team, the key operational implication is that ARCs must maintain internal processes to identify relevant default cases, compile the required borrower/case information in the RBI-prescribed templates, and ensure that the information used for cautioning the market is reported in a consistent and timely manner.

The document is also structured to include a **repeal and savings framework** in Chapter III, meaning prior directions or instructions on the same subject are being replaced or superseded to the extent covered by this 2025 instrument. No monetary thresholds, rates, or numerical limits are visible in the excerpt provided, so a compliance officer should review the full text and annexures for any definitions of “wilful defaulter,” “large defaulter,” reporting cutoffs, submission timelines, or specific data fields that create additional operational obligations. Based on the text shown, the immediate compliance takeaway is that **ARCs must be prepared to implement RBI’s mandatory reporting and caution-listing framework for wilful and large defaulters without delay**, using the annexed reporting formats.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) and credit information reporting set out the reporting, membership, data-quality, customer-service, and governance obligations that apply to ARCs in their role as credit information providers. The directions are issued by RBI under the cited circular reference and, according to the title, are updated as of July 1, 2026; the document itself is framed as the operative compliance instrument for ARCs with respect to credit information reporting and dissemination to credit information companies (CICs). At a high level, the directions require ARCs to participate in the CIC ecosystem, submit and maintain accurate credit information in the prescribed formats, and comply with RBI’s reporting timelines, rectification processes, and customer redress requirements.

A major substantive requirement is membership of CICs: ARCs must be members of credit information companies and operate in the manner specified by RBI for furnishing and receiving credit information. The reporting chapter then governs how ARCs must transmit loan/account-level data, including use of RBI-prescribed data formats and adherence to reporting timelines and periodic updation requirements. The directions also require ARCs to follow reporting guidelines designed to ensure data consistency and completeness, and they specifically contemplate rejection of non-compliant data submissions, with a mandated rectification process for rejected data and review of the ARC’s Data Quality Index (DQI), which implies that persistent data-quality failures may be tracked and assessed by regulators.

The document also addresses correction of Credit Information Reports, meaning ARCs must participate in correcting inaccurate bureau records when discrepancies are identified. It further requires ARCs to use credit information reports in credit appraisal, so credit decisions and recoveries must be supported by CIC data rather than handled informally. There is also a display/disclosure obligation for information, which indicates that certain prescribed credit-information-related details must be made available in the manner required by the directions.

Finally, the directions establish a Technical Working Group and a customer service and grievance redressal framework, which means ARCs will need internal processes and designated accountability for technical implementation, complaint handling, and escalation. For a compliance team, the key operational takeaway is that these directions are not merely advisory: they create ongoing obligations to become and remain CIC members, report accurately and on time, correct rejected or inaccurate data, monitor data-quality metrics, and maintain a functioning grievance process tied to credit information reporting.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on March 10, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) Directions, 2025** are a comprehensive regulatory framework for ARCs, issued under RBI authority on **November 28, 2025** and marked as **updated through March 10, 2026**. The document reorganizes and consolidates requirements across registration, governance, asset reconstruction and securitisation activities, prudential regulation, accounting/disclosure, and miscellaneous compliance obligations, so any entity operating as an ARC in India—or seeking to register as one—would need to treat this as its core rulebook. The title and structure indicate that the directions supersede prior fragmented instructions and create a single continuing framework for ARCs’ conduct, board oversight, reporting, and operational standards.

From a compliance perspective, the document specifically governs **the role of the board of directors, registration and related matters**, implying formal requirements around governance and eligibility before an entity can function as an ARC. It then sets out **guidelines on asset reconstruction and securitisation**, meaning the manner in which ARCs may acquire, manage, restructure, and resolve financial assets is subject to RBI-prescribed conditions rather than general commercial discretion. A separate chapter on **prudential regulations** indicates ongoing capital, exposure, asset-quality, provisioning, or similar risk-management requirements, while the **governance and conduct** chapter signals that ARCs must comply with conduct standards beyond pure prudential rules. The **accounting and disclosures** chapter means the directions also impose specific financial reporting and transparency obligations, and the **miscellaneous instructions** plus **repeal and other provisions** chapters indicate the document also addresses transition, applicability, and the treatment of prior directions.

For compliance teams, the most important operational takeaway is that these directions are meant to be **binding regulatory instructions for ARCs**, not merely guidance, and they likely require internal policies, board approvals, reporting controls, and monitoring procedures to be aligned with RBI expectations.
