rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Credit Information Companies – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Credit Information Companies – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025”** establishes a formal outsourcing-risk framework specifically for **credit information companies (CICs)**, with the stated aim of ensuring that outsourcing arrangements do not weaken governance, data protection, security, confidentiality, accountability, or regulatory compliance. The directions are issued by the RBI under its supervisory authority and apply to outsourcing of relevant activities by CICs; they are organized around board oversight, senior management responsibility, IT outsourcing governance, and risk management controls. The document indicates a structured compliance regime beginning with a board-approved outsourcing policy and ongoing oversight responsibilities, rather than leaving outsourcing decisions to operational teams or vendors.

At the governance level, the **Board must approve the outsourcing policy** and remains ultimately responsible for outsourced activities even when functions are performed by external providers. The board is expected to set the risk appetite, review material outsourcing arrangements, and ensure that the CIC has adequate systems to identify, manage, and monitor outsourcing risk. Senior management is tasked with implementing the policy, maintaining effective controls, and ensuring that business, IT, legal, and risk functions coordinate on outsourcing decisions; the IT function has a defined role in assessing technical risk, security, resilience, and vendor performance where technology services are outsourced.

For **IT outsourcing**, the directions require CICs to adopt a governance framework that provides **authorization, accountability, and oversight** over outsourced technology services. The compliance focus is on ensuring that outsourced IT arrangements are properly approved, risk-assessed, documented, and monitored, with attention to service continuity, cybersecurity, data access controls, and the ability of the CIC to supervise and audit the provider. The document also indicates that the outsourcing policy and controls must be designed to prevent over-dependence on third parties and to preserve the CIC’s capacity to meet its regulatory and operational obligations.

The directions further require a **risk management framework** for outsourcing, meaning CICs must identify and assess risks before entering into arrangements and continue monitoring them throughout the relationship. Although the excerpt provided does not show the later chapter details, the structure indicates the document will include requirements on risk assessment, contractual safeguards, due diligence, monitoring, and escalation/termination controls. The effective date is tied to the issuance date shown on the document—**November 28, 2025**—and compliance teams should treat the directions as operative from that date unless a later commencement date is specified in the omitted sections.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Credit Information Companies) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Credit Information Companies Directions, 2025** (as updated through **July 1, 2026**) set out the operating, governance, reporting, customer-service, and grievance-handling requirements for **credit information companies (CICs)** and the entities that participate in the credit-information ecosystem. The directions apply to CICs operating under RBI regulation and address their board oversight, statutory compliance, investment limitations, membership rules, data submission and dissemination processes, technical governance, and customer redress systems.

A key area is **governance and board responsibility**: the directions assign the board of a CIC explicit responsibility for ensuring compliance with the RBI framework and for overseeing the CIC’s policies, systems, and controls. They also restate the **statutory framework governing CICs** and the RBI’s authority over their functioning, meaning compliance teams must treat the directions as the operative regulatory baseline rather than just internal policy guidance.

The directions also cover **investment in CICs**, indicating that ownership and investment structures are regulated and that any shareholding or investment activity in a CIC must fit within the RBI’s prescribed framework. For compliance purposes, this means changes in control, investment arrangements, or ownership percentages need to be reviewed against the directions before implementation.

A substantial portion of the document governs **credit information reporting and dissemination**. It addresses **membership of CICs**, the obligations of **credit institutions (CIs)** when submitting data, and the CIC’s role in ensuring that information is collected, validated, maintained, and shared properly. The directions require CICs to have processes for receiving data from reporting institutions, handling errors and corrections, and disseminating credit information only in accordance with permitted purposes and access conditions. Compliance officers should note that this is not just a technical IT requirement: it imposes ongoing procedural obligations around data quality, timeliness, accuracy, and controlled access.

The document also establishes a **Technical Working Group (TWG)** and a **standing sub-group**, indicating an ongoing governance mechanism for technical standards, operational issues, and coordination within the credit-information framework. This signals that CICs may be expected to align systems and reporting practices with standards or decisions emerging from these bodies, so regulatory monitoring should include TWG-related developments.

Finally, the directions include a chapter on **customer service and grievance redressal**, which means CICs must maintain formal processes to handle consumer complaints, dispute resolution, and service-quality expectations. In practical terms, compliance teams should expect obligations around complaint tracking, turnaround times, escalation, and the correction of inaccurate credit information where required. Because the document is an updated 2026 version of the 2025 directions, compliance staff should use the updated text as the operative version and verify any implementation dates, thresholds, or procedural changes against the full chapters referenced in the table of contents before relying on prior versions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
This RBI circular titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026”** is a consolidated supervisory directions document for commercial banks, issued by the **Department of Supervision, RBI Central Office, Mumbai**, dated **July 31, 2026**. It brings together and standardizes compliance expectations across several operational areas, including **IT system access, monitoring end-use of funds, Prompt Corrective Action (PCA), fair practices in charging interest, inoperative accounts/unclaimed deposits, nomination facility, and fraud prevention**. The document is aimed at **commercial banks** and is intended to function as a supervisory framework that banks must follow, with chapter-wise requirements applying depending on the relevant business activity or control area.

For **IT systems access**, the directions require banks to establish controlled and monitored access arrangements to their information technology systems, implying governance over who can access systems and how access is tracked and restricted. The **monitoring of end use of funds** chapter indicates that banks must have procedures to verify that funds are used for their intended purposes, which would typically require post-disbursement checks, documentation, and escalation where misuse or diversion is detected. These requirements are compliance-relevant for lending, treasury, operations, and internal control teams because they affect the bank’s ability to demonstrate oversight of customer and borrower funds.

The document also contains a dedicated **Prompt Corrective Action Framework** chapter, meaning banks must comply with RBI’s intervention framework when financial or supervisory indicators weaken. Although the excerpt does not show the exact thresholds, the existence of a formal PCA chapter means banks should expect **trigger-based regulatory restrictions, monitoring, and remediation obligations** once RBI-prescribed capital, asset quality, profitability, or leverage benchmarks are breached. Compliance teams should treat this as a requirement to maintain continuous monitoring, board-level escalation, and readiness to implement RBI-imposed business restrictions if PCA thresholds are crossed.

Under **Fair Practices Code – Charging of Interest**, banks are required to follow prescribed fair-lending and disclosure standards when levying interest, which would ordinarily include transparent communication of rates and adherence to internal policy and contractual terms. The **Inoperative Accounts / Unclaimed Deposits** chapter requires banks to manage dormant or unclaimed balances according to RBI-prescribed procedures, which generally involves identifying such accounts, undertaking customer contact efforts, and maintaining safe custody and reporting controls. The **Nomination Facility** chapter requires banks to provide and administer nomination options in line with regulatory requirements, so account opening and maintenance processes must ensure customers are informed of nomination rights and that nominations are correctly captured and updated.

The final portion shown covers **fraud prevention measures**, including frauds arising from **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, **retail loan bulk proposal sanctions**, and **frauds involving fake title deeds of property**. This means banks must have stronger internal controls, segregation of duties, due diligence, and exception reporting around these specific fraud channels, with heightened scrutiny where staff collusion or document fraud is involved. Since the table of contents indicates more detailed subparts beyond the excerpt, compliance officers should assume the full directions contain operational obligations and reporting/escalation steps for fraud detection, sanction controls, and preventive monitoring, and should review the complete text for any explicit timelines, thresholds, or mandatory reporting formats not visible here.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Supervisory Returns Directions, 2026** are issued by the **Department of Supervision, RBI Central Office** and are dated **July 31, 2026**. They apply to **commercial banks** and establish the governance, data, and filing framework for RBI supervisory returns. The directions are organized around board/senior management accountability, reporting infrastructure, and detailed return-filing requirements.

A key requirement is that the **board and senior management remain responsible for the completeness, accuracy, and timeliness of supervisory reporting**, and banks must maintain appropriate oversight and internal controls over the return-filing process. The directions also require banks to have adequate **data architecture and IT infrastructure** to support supervisory reporting, with systems capable of producing reliable regulatory data and ensuring integrity of reporting across source systems, reconciliations, and submission workflows. Banks are expected to implement processes that ensure **accuracy and integrity in reporting**, which implies validation, review, and governance over data used in supervisory returns.

The document then sets out the **filing of supervisory returns**, including **operational guidelines, a list of applicable returns, timelines, exceptions, and penalties**. Although the excerpt does not list the individual returns or exact due dates, the directions clearly indicate that commercial banks must comply with the RBI’s specified reporting calendar and any prescribed formats/instructions for each return. Banks should therefore identify all returns covered by the directions and align internal reporting ownership, data collection, and sign-off processes accordingly.

For compliance purposes, the most important operational takeaway from the document excerpt is that the RBI is formalizing a structured supervisory-return regime with explicit expectations around governance, system readiness, accuracy controls, and punctual submission. Because the document includes a dedicated **penalties** section, failures in filing, data quality, or adherence to timelines may attract regulatory consequences. A compliance team should review the full schedule of returns and deadlines in the complete text and ensure the bank’s control environment is set up to meet the RBI’s reporting requirements from the applicable commencement date of the directions.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Commercial Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** on **31 July 2026** under the Department of Supervision, and these directions replace/update the RBI’s framework for the appointment, independence, tenure, and oversight of statutory auditors for commercial banks. The document applies to **commercial banks** and sets out mandatory requirements for the **board and senior management**, who must oversee the audit function and ensure compliance with the RBI’s appointment and governance standards. It also specifically governs the **number and coverage of Statutory Central Auditors and Statutory Auditors**, the **eligibility and independence criteria** for auditors, the **professional standards** they must follow, and the **rules on tenure and rotation**.

For banks, a major compliance obligation is that statutory audit appointments must be made only through the RBI-prescribed process, with the board and management responsible for ensuring that auditors meet the RBI’s **eligibility criteria** and do not compromise **independence**. The directions also address **audit fees and expenses**, meaning banks must structure compensation and reimbursements in line with the RBI framework rather than ad hoc arrangements. The document further indicates a formal **appointment procedure**, so banks will need to align internal governance, nomination/approval workflows, and documentation practices with the RBI requirements rather than relying solely on prior board-level practice.

Because the table of contents shows dedicated sections on governance, eligibility, independence, tenure, fees, and appointment procedure, compliance teams should expect these directions to impose both **substantive auditor-qualification requirements** and **process controls** around selection, rotation, and oversight. The key date visible in the document is the **issue date: 31 July 2026**; the excerpt provided does not include the detailed effective date or transition timetable, so those would need to be confirmed in the operative text before implementation planning.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Commercial Banks – Internal Audit Function” Directions, 2026** are a new supervisory framework issued by the RBI’s Department of Supervision on **31 July 2026** (circular reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/413**, **DoS.CO.PPG.7/11.01.005/2026-27**). The document is directed at **commercial banks** and sets out mandatory requirements for how the internal audit function must be governed, structured, and operated. Its stated focus is to strengthen the **risk-based internal audit framework**, with explicit expectations for board oversight, senior management accountability, functional independence, audit planning, and communication/reporting processes.

From the table of contents, the Directions apply across several core compliance areas: **preliminary applicability and commencement**, **governance and oversight**, and **risk-based internal audit framework**. Under governance, the document assigns specific responsibilities to the **Board** and to **senior management**, indicating that internal audit can no longer be treated as a purely operational function; it must be actively overseen at the highest levels. The internal audit framework chapter shows that banks must have a formal **policy on internal audit**, ensure **functional independence** of the function, conduct structured **risk assessment**, define the **scope** of audits, establish **communication** channels for findings, and implement **performance evaluation** of the function itself.

The excerpt provided does not include the detailed operative text of each requirement, so the precise thresholds, deadlines, reporting formats, or transition periods are not visible here. However, the document clearly signals that compliance officers should expect a formal RBI-mandated internal audit regime for commercial banks that likely requires board-approved policy governance, documented risk-based audit planning, and demonstrable independence from the business and control functions being audited. The effective date is tied to the issuance date in the title block (**31 July 2026**), but because the substantive commencement clause is not visible in the excerpt, any implementation date or transitional grace period would need to be confirmed from the full text before finalizing compliance actions.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Commercial Banks – Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2026** (issued **31 July 2026**) establish a consolidated fraud-risk governance and detection framework for **commercial banks** subject to RBI supervision. The document requires banks to put in place a formal **governance structure for fraud risk management**, including board and senior-management oversight, so that fraud prevention, detection, reporting, and remediation are handled through defined institutional responsibilities rather than ad hoc responses. It also introduces a structured **Early Warning Signal (EWS)** and **Red Flagging Account (RFA)** framework for identifying stress or suspicious activity in advance of a confirmed fraud.

For **credit facilities and loan accounts**, banks must implement an EWS/RFA process that can identify red flags early, escalate them through internal governance, and support timely classification and follow-up before loss crystallizes. The document also separately requires an **EWS framework for non-credit banking transactions** and other banking activity, meaning fraud monitoring is not limited to loans but extends to broader transaction types and service channels. Where an account is **classified as a red-flagged account**, the bank must follow the prescribed process for **reporting fraud** and related internal/external actions, rather than treating the issue as a normal credit-monitoring matter.

The directions further require banks to obtain **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**, when such external parties are involved in the transaction, account, or underlying documentation, reflecting a stronger control over reliance on outsourced or professional certifications. The title and chapter structure indicate that the directions cover both the **governance layer** and the **operational controls** for detection and reporting, so compliance teams should expect obligations around policy updates, escalation protocols, account tagging, reporting triggers, and evidence preservation. The document excerpt provided does not include specific monetary thresholds, date-based transition periods, or detailed procedural timelines beyond the issuance date, so those would need to be confirmed from the full text if implementation planning is required.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Commercial Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls” Directions, 2026 establish mandatory cybersecurity, fraud-prevention, authentication, reconciliation, and customer-protection controls for commercial banks that offer digital payment services. The document is issued by RBI’s Department of Supervision and is intended to strengthen the security of payment channels such as internet/mobile banking and other digital payment applications operated by covered banks. It is a supervisory direction, so compliance is not optional: banks must align their internal governance, technology controls, and customer-facing processes with the requirements in the directions.

A key compliance obligation is that the bank’s Board must approve a policy framework for digital payment security and oversee implementation through governance arrangements that assign accountability for security risk management. The directions require banks to maintain structured security controls across the full application life cycle, including secure development, testing, change management, deployment, and ongoing vulnerability management. They also require stronger authentication controls for customer access and transaction approval, meaning banks must ensure authentication frameworks are risk-sensitive and resilient against unauthorized access, rather than relying only on weak or legacy login methods.

The document also places explicit obligations on fraud risk management and reconciliation. Banks must have systems to detect suspicious or fraudulent digital payment activity, respond to it promptly, and reconcile digital payment transactions with internal records and settlement outcomes to identify breaks or failures. In addition, banks must maintain customer protection measures, including customer awareness initiatives and a grievance-redressal mechanism so customers can report issues and receive timely resolution for failed, disputed, or unauthorized digital payment transactions.

The document’s title page shows it was issued on July 31, 2026, and the directions are identified as RBI/DoS/2026-27/411 and DoS.CO.CSITEG.5/31.01.015/2026-27. The excerpt provided does not include the substantive chapter text beyond the table of contents, so the specific technical thresholds, implementation timelines, exemptions, and any channel-specific requirements in later chapters cannot be confirmed from the supplied text alone. For compliance purposes, however, a bank should treat the directions as requiring a formal, board-approved digital payment security framework, documented operational controls, customer complaint handling, and end-to-end oversight of digital payment risk across all covered payment services.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **“Commercial Banks – Cybersecurity, Technology: Risk, Resilience and Assurance Framework) Directions, 2026”** on **31 July 2026** under reference **RBI/DoS/2026-27/410** and **DoS.CO.CSITEG.4/31.01.015/2026-27**. The directions establish a comprehensive supervisory framework for **commercial banks** covering governance, cybersecurity, technology risk, operational resilience, and assurance requirements. In practical terms, the document replaces or strengthens prior expectations by requiring banks to have formal board oversight, documented policies, management accountability, and more structured controls around IT, information security, cyber risk, resilience testing, assurance, and incident handling.

A major theme is **board accountability**: each covered bank must have **board-approved policies** and board-level oversight for IT/cyber risk. The board is required to oversee the institution’s technology risk posture through appropriate committees and to ensure that management implements controls, monitors incidents, and remediates weaknesses. The directions also require an **IT governance framework**, an **information security policy**, a **cybersecurity policy**, and clearly defined responsibilities for senior management, the IT steering committee, the head of IT, and information security functions. This means compliance teams should expect formal documentation, assigned ownership, regular reporting to the board/committees, and evidence that policy decisions are being approved and monitored at the top level.

The document further addresses **technology risk and resilience** as a bank-wide compliance obligation, not just an IT function issue. Banks are expected to maintain controls that support **availability, confidentiality, integrity, and resilience** of information systems, and to operate processes for monitoring vulnerabilities, managing technology change, and responding to incidents. The framework also implies a need for periodic testing and assurance so the bank can demonstrate that safeguards are effective, not merely documented. Compliance officers should anticipate requirements for internal controls, independent review, testing/assurance exercises, and management reporting that prove the bank can continue critical services during cyber or technology disruptions.

Although the excerpt provided does not show the full chapter-by-chapter operative text, the structure of the directions indicates coverage of multiple compliance domains: **preliminary provisions, board governance, IT governance and oversight, business continuity/resilience, cybersecurity operations, assurance, and ongoing supervisory compliance**. The applicable entities are **commercial banks**, and the operative obligations would typically attach to their whole organization, including outsourced technology arrangements and digital channels where relevant. Because the document is framed as RBI “Directions,” the requirements should be treated as **mandatory supervisory instructions**, with compliance expected by the date stated in the operative clauses and any transitional provisions in the full text. The Reserve Bank of India’s **Small Finance Banks – Statutory Audit Directions, 2026** (issued **July 31, 2026**) set out the mandatory framework for appointing, rotating, supervising, compensating, and replacing statutory auditors of **small finance banks (SFBs)**. The directions apply to all SFBs and are intended to govern the statutory audit process under RBI supervision, with emphasis on board responsibility, auditor independence, and regular rotation of audit firms and partners.

For governance, the document requires the **Board and senior management** of each SFB to take active responsibility for the audit process rather than treating it as a routine administrative exercise. They must ensure proper appointment procedures, monitor auditor performance and independence, and maintain oversight over any issues that arise during the audit cycle. The directions also establish detailed rules for how many statutory central auditors/statutory auditors may be appointed and how branch coverage is to be allocated, meaning the scope of audit work must be structured in accordance with RBI-prescribed limits rather than left entirely to bank discretion.

The directions specify **eligibility criteria** for auditors, including requirements intended to ensure competence, independence, and professional standing, and they impose explicit restrictions to prevent conflicts of interest. Auditors must comply with professional standards, and the bank must verify that the chosen audit firms and partners are not disqualified under RBI rules or otherwise impaired in their independence. The document also addresses **tenure and rotation**, requiring periodic rotation of audit firms and, where applicable, audit partners, so the same auditor cannot continue indefinitely in a way that would compromise objectivity.

The directions further regulate **audit fees and expenses**, implying that compensation must be structured and approved in a manner consistent with RBI expectations and not in a way that could undermine auditor independence. They also provide a formal **appointment procedure**, meaning the bank must follow a prescribed process rather than making ad hoc appointments. Overall, the compliance impact is that SFBs must review their auditor appointment governance, independence screening, rotation tracking, and board oversight processes to ensure they align with the RBI’s 2026 statutory audit requirements from the date the directions take effect.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks - Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Small Finance Banks (Internal Audit Function) Directions, 2026** on **31 July 2026** under **RBI/DoS/2026-27/422**. The directions are aimed specifically at **Small Finance Banks (SFBs)** and replace/standardize how their internal audit function must be governed, staffed, scoped, and reported, with a strong emphasis on **risk-based internal audit** and **independence from management**. The document applies to all SFBs covered by RBI supervision, and it requires the board and senior management to take direct responsibility for establishing an effective internal audit framework rather than treating audit as a purely operational function.

A key requirement is that the **board** must approve and oversee the internal audit policy and ensure the audit function has adequate authority, resources, independence, and access to records and personnel. **Senior management** must implement the framework, ensure timely remediation of audit observations, and support the internal audit team without interfering with its objectivity. The directions also require a formal **risk assessment process** to determine audit priorities and frequency, meaning audit coverage must be driven by the bank’s risk profile rather than a fixed or purely calendar-based plan.

The internal audit function must be **functionally independent**, properly documented, and structured to cover the bank’s material activities, processes, systems, and control environment. The directions set expectations for the **scope of audit**, including review of governance, operations, compliance, risk management, and internal controls, and require that audit findings be formally communicated and tracked through corrective action and closure. The framework also contemplates clear reporting lines, escalation of significant issues, and periodic reporting to the board or its audit committee so that unresolved weaknesses and high-risk issues receive prompt attention.

Where the document becomes operationally important for compliance teams is that it creates an enforceable requirement for each SFB to maintain a **policy on internal audit**, ensure **adequate staffing and competence**, and conduct audits using a documented, risk-based methodology. Compliance officers should expect to review whether the bank’s existing audit charter, reporting structure, issue-tracking process, and board oversight arrangements align with these directions once they take effect. The excerpt provided does not show any separate transitional deadline, so the main effective date appears to be the date of the directions themselves unless the full text specifies otherwise.

The directions require an **early detection framework** built around **early warning signals and red-flagging of accounts**, with separate treatment for **credit facilities/loan accounts** and for **other banking/non-credit-related transactions**. The document also introduces general instructions for cases where a **credit facility or loan account is classified as a “red-flagged account”** and for the **reporting of fraud**. The directions further reference **independent confirmation from third parties** in the general instructions section, indicating that banks may need external verification in certain cases rather than relying only on internal records or borrower representations.

In practical compliance terms, this directive is aimed at ensuring that SFBs have documented controls to detect fraudulent conduct in both lending and transactional activities, formally escalate suspicious activity, and apply consistent classification/reporting standards. Compliance officers should treat this as requiring a bank-wide fraud risk management framework with board/senior-management oversight, formal EWS and red-flagging processes, and clear procedures for classifying, investigating, and reporting fraud-related accounts.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Small Finance Banks – Digital Payment Security Controls) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:

It is a supervisory direction from the Reserve Bank of India’s Department of Supervision and applies to the covered entities from the commencement date stated in the full text, so compliance teams should treat it as a binding operating requirement rather than guidance. The document is structured to require board-approved policies, operational controls, and customer-facing processes, with specific expectations around security risk governance, application security, authentication, fraud monitoring, and grievance handling.

At the governance level, the direction requires the **Board of Directors** to approve policies and oversight arrangements for digital payment security, with management responsible for implementing security controls and monitoring risks across digital channels. It also expects SFBs to maintain “general controls” over security risk management, including formal processes for identifying, assessing, mitigating, and reporting digital payment and cyber/security risks, as well as controls over access, system configuration, and secure operations. The document also calls for an **application security life cycle** approach, meaning security must be built into development, testing, deployment, and change management for all relevant digital payment applications rather than added only after launch.

A major compliance area is the **authentication framework**, which requires banks to use stronger customer authentication protections for digital payment transactions and internet banking. The direction also addresses **fraud risk management**, requiring banks to put in place mechanisms to detect suspicious activity, investigate fraud trends, and respond to emerging fraud patterns, together with **reconciliation mechanisms** so customer transactions, internal ledgers, and external payment systems are matched and discrepancies are promptly resolved. In addition, the direction mandates **customer protection, awareness, and grievance redressal mechanisms**, meaning banks must inform customers of security risks and remedies and maintain a process for complaints and dispute handling tied to digital payment failures or unauthorized transactions.

The title and contents indicate that the document is not limited to one product but covers the full digital payments control environment of SFBs, including internet banking. Compliance officers should therefore assess whether their institution has documented policies, board approvals, technical safeguards, fraud monitoring, reconciliation controls, and customer complaint workflows that align with RBI’s prescribed framework, and confirm the exact effective date and any transition periods in the operative chapters of the direction. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Payments Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Payments Banks – Miscellaneous Supervisory Directions, 2026** were issued on **July 31, 2026** under RBI supervision powers and are intended to apply specifically to **payments banks**. The document sets out a consolidated set of supervisory requirements covering IT-system access, inoperative and unclaimed deposits, nomination processes, fraud-prevention controls, legal compliance reporting, and related governance obligations. It is not a general banking circular; it is directed at payments banks and the activities and controls they must maintain for account handling, fraud management, and regulatory compliance.

A major requirement concerns **access to IT systems**: payments banks must ensure that access to core and supporting IT systems is controlled, traceable, and limited to authorized personnel, with proper segregation of duties and records that support accountability. The document also requires payments banks to maintain proper handling of **inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits**, meaning they must identify accounts that have become inactive, move them through the required internal classification process, and follow the applicable RBI-prescribed steps for customer contact, reactivation, and transfer/maintenance of unclaimed balances. Compliance teams should note that this area typically requires periodic review of dormant accounts, documentation of outreach efforts, and evidence that the bank’s processes can demonstrate compliance during supervisory review.

The directions also reinforce the **nomination facility**: payments banks must provide and administer nomination in the manner required by RBI, ensuring customers are informed and the bank’s forms, records, and internal processes support valid nominations, changes, and claims settlement. In the fraud control section, the RBI requires tighter controls for **frauds involving collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, and the **safe custody of critical documents**. The document further addresses **accounts opened by employees**, indicating additional scrutiny and internal controls where staff open or maintain accounts, and it requires a **Legal Compliance Certificate** and a **Legal Compliance Audit** so that the bank can formally evidence adherence to legal and regulatory requirements. Where the directions contemplate **forensic scrutiny/investigation** of fraud-related events, the bank must be prepared to preserve records and cooperate with such reviews.

From a compliance-program perspective, the operative requirement is that payments banks must have documented procedures, control ownership, and audit trails for each of these subject areas, and they must be able to show implementation to RBI supervisors. Because the title and issuance date indicate these are **2026 supervisory directions**, banks should treat them as applicable from the effective date stated in the final text and align internal policies, operating procedures, and audit calendars accordingly. rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Local Area Banks – Miscellaneous) Supervisory Directions, 2026

These directions are a supervisory framework for **local area banks** and consolidate multiple operational, conduct, deposit, fraud-prevention, and governance expectations into one set of binding directions. The document is organized into chapters covering: preliminary matters, fair practices in charging interest, inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits, fraud prevention measures, and a protected disclosure scheme.

A key substantive requirement concerns **fair practices in charging interest**. Local area banks must ensure their interest-charging practices comply with RBI’s fair-practice expectations, meaning interest must be levied transparently and in a manner that is not arbitrary or misleading to customers. The direction is meant to govern how banks calculate, disclose, and apply interest so that borrowers and depositors are treated consistently and the bank’s internal systems align with RBI’s supervisory standards.

The directions also impose requirements for handling **inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits**. Local area banks must maintain processes for identifying accounts that have become inactive/inoperative and for dealing with balances that remain unclaimed, with the aim of protecting customer funds, preventing misuse, and ensuring proper recordkeeping and follow-up. Compliance officers should expect obligations around periodic review, customer outreach, and internal controls so that dormant balances are not neglected and can be properly reported or transferred in accordance with RBI’s rules.

A substantial portion of the document is devoted to **fraud prevention measures**. The RBI specifically addresses frauds arising from **collusion of bank officials**, **large-value frauds**, and **frauds involving fake title deeds of property deposits**. It also requires safeguards for the **safe custody of critical documents** and sets expectations for **accounts opened by employees**, indicating that banks must have internal controls to detect conflicts of interest, unusual transactions, document tampering, and staff misuse of account-opening processes. The document further includes “other instructions,” indicating that fraud controls are not limited to the enumerated scenarios and that banks must maintain broader anti-fraud governance, escalation, and monitoring arrangements.

The final major area is a **Protected Disclosure Scheme**, which establishes a channel for confidential reporting of wrongdoing. The table of contents shows that the scheme covers **scope and coverage**, indicating that the directions will specify who can make protected disclosures, what types of misconduct can be reported, and how such reports are to be handled. For compliance teams, the practical implication is that the bank must have procedures to receive, protect, investigate, and escalate whistleblower-style complaints without retaliation, while maintaining confidentiality and documentation.

Overall, the document is a supervisory instruction package for local area banks that tightens expectations on customer fairness, dormant-account management, anti-fraud controls, document security, employee-account controls, and protected reporting. Because the excerpt provided shows the structure but not the detailed chapter text, the compliance significance is that the bank should treat these chapter headings as mandatory control areas requiring operational procedures, monitoring, and staff accountability effective from the direction’s issuance date unless a chapter specifies a different implementation timeline in its detailed provisions.

The document is organized into chapters on preliminary matters, governance and oversight, and the risk-based internal audit framework, indicating that obligations likely cover not only audit execution but also reporting lines, escalation, and management responses to findings. The document excerpt provided does not include the later chapters or any specific numerical thresholds, deadlines for phased implementation, or exemptions, so those details would need to be checked in the full text before determining whether any bank-specific transition period or size-based carve-out applies.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Fraud Risk Management) Directions, 2026
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Urban Co-operative Banks – Fraud Risk Management” Directions, 2026** were issued on **July 31, 2026** and are directed at **urban co-operative banks (UCBs)**. The document is a comprehensive fraud-risk governance framework, so the key compliance takeaway is that UCBs must maintain a formal, board-supervised fraud risk management structure, with clear accountability for detecting, escalating, investigating, and reporting fraud or suspected fraud across credit and non-credit banking activities. The directions appear to replace or update earlier RBI expectations by codifying a more structured regime around governance, early warning signals, third-party confirmations, and fraud incident handling.

A central requirement is the establishment of a **governance structure for fraud risk management**. UCBs must have a defined internal framework overseen at senior levels, with responsibility for fraud prevention and detection not left to ad hoc operational handling. The bank must ensure that fraud risks are monitored at the institutional level, with escalation channels and oversight mechanisms sufficient to identify suspicious activity early and prevent concealment or delay in reporting. Compliance teams should treat this as requiring board/management ownership, documented internal roles, and ongoing supervisory review of fraud-control effectiveness.

The directions also introduce a formal **Early Warning Signal (EWS) framework** for detecting fraud in **credit facilities/loan accounts** and in **other banking or non-credit transactions**. This means banks must implement systems and processes to identify indicators of suspicious behavior before a fraud fully crystallizes, rather than relying only on post-event detection. The document specifically distinguishes between loan-account risk indicators and other transaction types, so institutions need separate controls appropriate to credit exposures and to operational/payment/service activities. The compliance burden here is to ensure these warning signals are built into internal monitoring, reviewed consistently, and acted upon promptly through defined escalation and investigative procedures.

Another material requirement is the need for **independent confirmation from third-party service providers, including professionals**. Where a bank relies on external entities or professionals in connection with transactions, underwriting, verification, valuation, audit, legal certification, or related services, it must not treat those representations as automatically reliable; instead, the framework requires independent confirmation in the circumstances contemplated by the directions. This is aimed at reducing fraud risk arising from forged, manipulated, or collusive third-party inputs. For compliance purposes, banks should review vendor, professional, and outsourced-service controls to ensure they can verify external confirmations and detect inconsistencies before relying on them.

The document’s structure also indicates **general instructions** for handling cases where credit facilities, loan accounts, or other banking transactions show indications of fraudulent activity. That implies banks must have a formal response process once red flags arise, including internal review, documentation, escalation, and compliance with any RBI reporting requirements. While the excerpt does not show the detailed reporting timelines or thresholds, the title and chapter headings make clear that the directions are intended to impose institution-wide obligations on UCBs to detect, investigate, and control fraud risk systematically. A compliance team should therefore map the full text into policies, controls, investigation protocols, and staff training, with particular attention to how early warning signals are generated, who reviews them, and how suspicious cases are escalated.

The circular serves as the authoritative compilation for internal policy, loan monitoring, NPA recognition, provisioning, and reporting controls, so banks should ensure their credit policies, classification engines, board-approved processes, and reporting templates are aligned to the consolidated instructions contained in the circular and its annexures.

This RBI Master Circular, issued on 1 April 2025 as RBI/2025-26/09 (DOR.CAP.REC.03/09.18.201/2025-26), applies to all Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs) and supersedes/consolidates the earlier master circular dated 1 April 2024. It states that it updates all instructions and guidelines on prudential norms for capital adequacy issued up to 31 March 2025, with the detailed rules collected in the annexures referenced in the circular.

Substantively, the circular reiterates that capital is a buffer against losses and a licensing/continuation requirement for a bank, and then restates the statutory minimum capital position for co-operative banks under the Banking Regulation Act (AACS): a bank may not commence or carry on banking business unless its aggregate paid-up capital and reserves are at least ₹1 lakh. It also indicates that the circular covers the computation of net worth, capital adequacy norms/CRAR, risk weights, market risk capital, share-linking to borrowings, refund of share capital, and investor-protection measures for regulatory capital instruments, with specific operational guidance contained in Annexes 1 through 5.

For compliance purposes, the key practical point is that UCBs must use this Master Circular as the current consolidated source for capital adequacy compliance as of 31 March 2025, and must follow the detailed requirements in the annexures on: how to compute net worth; the applicable risk weights for capital adequacy calculations; the rules for issuing preference shares and debt capital instruments; the format for returns; and any procedural safeguards for investors in such instruments. The document also includes a section on returns, implying ongoing reporting obligations under the prescribed pro forma.

No new numerical capital adequacy ratio, deadline, or rate is stated in the excerpt beyond the ₹1 lakh statutory minimum paid-up capital and reserves threshold; the circular’s primary compliance change is the consolidation and update of the earlier instructions into one current master circular effective from 1 April 2025.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular updates and consolidates all RBI instructions on the **Board of Directors of Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, superseding the prior circular dated **April 1, 2024**. It is addressed to the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of all UCBs and reiterates that boards must consist of persons of **high integrity and knowledge**, with the bank required to maintain **at least two professional directors at all times**—meaning directors with suitable banking experience (at middle/senior management level) or relevant professional qualifications. The circular applies to the governance of UCBs under the RBI’s supervisory powers under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **RBI Act, 1934**.

The document covers the **constitution of the Board**, the **role and responsibilities of directors**, the **committees of the Board**, the **calendar of reviews and matters to be placed before the Board**, and controls relating to **donations to trusts/institutions where directors or their relatives have an interest or position**. It also includes rules on **payment of fees and allowances to directors**, and it consolidates earlier RBI circulars and the related guidance annexed in the master circular, including the **Madhava Das Committee recommendations** and the prescribed **reviews to be submitted to the Board**. For compliance purposes, the key requirement is that UCBs must ensure their governance structure, board composition, committee oversight, and periodic review mechanisms continue to satisfy RBI expectations as set out in the updated consolidated instructions.

The circular is effective from **April 1, 2025** and is intended to be read as the current master reference on board governance for UCBs. Compliance teams should treat the circular as the governing compilation of all existing instructions on this subject, and should verify that board composition, director suitability, board committee structure, agenda/calendar items, donation approvals, and director compensation arrangements are aligned with the consolidated RBI framework.

The table of contents also shows specific treatment for items such as **counterparty credit risk on off-balance-sheet exposures**, indicating that the circular is not merely high-level policy but a detailed operational rulebook that affects how banks calculate risk weights and capital charges across major asset classes.

For compliance purposes, the key action is that affected banks must ensure their **capital adequacy calculations, exposure classifications, deductions, and transitional treatment** are aligned with the updated consolidated instructions as of **April 1, 2025**. Because the circular consolidates prior instructions rather than creating a single isolated rule change in the excerpt provided, a compliance team would need to check the annexed consolidated circular list and the body of the Master Circular for any **new or revised risk weights, deduction thresholds, reporting expectations, or capital composition requirements** applicable to their portfolios and regulatory filings.

This RBI Master Circular, dated **June 16, 2025** and addressed to **all Scheduled Commercial Banks, including Small Finance Banks**, consolidates all Reserve Bank instructions issued up to that date on **credit facilities to Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs)**. It does not introduce a single new standalone rule in the excerpt provided; rather, it restates and consolidates the RBI’s existing requirements and expectations for banks to **step up advances to SC/ST borrowers**.

A key compliance point is the **planning and coordination framework** banks must use. The **District Level Consultative Committees (DLCCs)** under the Lead Bank Scheme remain the principal coordination mechanism between banks and development agencies, and the **district credit plans** prepared by Lead Banks must clearly show how credit is linked with **employment generation and development schemes**. Banks are also expected to maintain **closer liaison with District Industries Centres (DICs)** in the districts for promotion of **self-employment** opportunities. At the **block level**, planning must give **weightage to SC/ST communities**, meaning credit planning is not to be neutral in a purely population-agnostic way but should deliberately reflect SC/ST participation and needs.

For a compliance team, the practical obligation is to ensure the bank’s **district credit planning, branch/block-level business planning, and developmental coordination processes** explicitly incorporate SC/ST lending objectives and can demonstrate that linkage in records and planning documents. Because the circular is a **master consolidation**, the operative compliance requirement is not just monitoring one policy note, but ensuring internal credit policy, rural and priority sector planning, and reporting systems align with the consolidated RBI instructions listed in the appendix. The document excerpt does not specify numerical lending targets, caps, dates for phased implementation, or special pricing terms; the material requirement shown is the **institutional obligation to plan, coordinate, and weight credit delivery in favor of SC/ST borrowers through formal district and block-level mechanisms**.

This Master Circular consolidates RBI’s Lead Bank Scheme instructions issued up to March 31, 2025 and is addressed to SLBC/UTLBC convenor banks and lead banks, superseding/compiling prior guidance rather than introducing a single isolated rule. For compliance teams, the key point is that the circular is a consolidated operational framework covering the governance structure for Lead Bank Scheme forums, credit-planning and monitoring responsibilities, data-flow requirements, and banking-penetration obligations, with the detailed operative instructions contained in the circular’s sections and the appendix of source instructions. It applies to institutions participating in the Lead Bank Scheme framework, especially lead banks, convenor banks, and the bodies they service at district, state, block, and local levels.

The document establishes the fora under the Lead Bank Scheme, including Block Level Bankers’ Committees, District Consultative Committees (DCCs), District Level Review Committees (DLRCs), and State Level Bankers’ Committees (SLBCs), and lays out requirements for their constitution, meeting conduct, agendas, annual meeting calendars, and related reporting/review processes. It specifically identifies the role of Lead District Managers (LDMs), requires quarterly public meetings and grievance-redressal mechanisms at the district level, and standardizes the SLBC website information/data architecture and liaison with state governments. It also calls for capacity-building, training, and sensitization programmes, indicating that compliance is not just documentary but includes active operational coordination and stakeholder engagement.

On implementation, the circular covers preparation of credit plans and Potential Linked Credit Plans (PLPs), monitoring performance against those plans, and a revised mechanism for data flow for Lead Bank Scheme forum meetings. That means banks and convenor institutions must ensure timely, accurate submission and consolidation of data used for LBS meetings and reviews, and must maintain planning and monitoring processes that can evidence progress against district/state credit objectives. The circular also includes rules on assignment of Lead Bank responsibility, which is relevant for any institution taking on or continuing that role.

A material compliance area is banking penetration and branch/service expansion. The circular continues the roadmap for providing banking services in unbanked villages and the roadmap for opening brick-and-mortar branches in villages with population above 5,000 where there is no branch of a scheduled commercial bank, while also aligning the roadmap for such unbanked villages with revised branch authorization guidelines. Even though the text provided here does not state the detailed thresholds or timelines beyond the “population more than 5,000” criterion, the compliance implication is that affected banks must track coverage gaps, service delivery obligations, and branch-opening priorities for eligible villages under the revised framework. The circular itself is dated April 1, 2025, and consolidates guidance effective through March 31, 2025.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by the RBI on 1 April 2025 (RBI/2025-26/01, FIDD.CO.FID.BC.No.4/12.01.033/2025-26), is addressed to the Chairman/Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of all scheduled commercial banks and consolidates all RBI instructions on the Self Help Group (SHG)-Bank Linkage Programme up to 31 March 2025. It does not itself announce a new standalone policy change in the excerpt provided; rather, it restates and compiles the existing regulatory framework governing SHG lending and related bank obligations.

The document explains the policy rationale for SHG-bank linkage: SHGs are intended to connect the formal banking system with the rural poor, with NABARD studies cited as showing higher SHG loan volumes, a shift from consumption/non-income-generating borrowing toward productive activities, near-100% recovery in some cases, lower transaction costs for banks and borrowers, and rising member incomes. It also notes that around 85% of bank-linked SHGs were formed exclusively by women, highlighting the program’s gender dimension. On this basis, banks have been advised to meet the entire credit requirements of SHG members, following the Union Budget 2008-09 direction on “Total Financial Inclusion.”

The excerpted text says scheduled commercial banks should meet the full credit needs of SHG members for: income-generation activities, social needs, and other approved purposes referenced in the underlying Budget language. For a compliance team, the key point is that this Master Circular is the authoritative consolidation of RBI guidance on SHG-bank linkage as of 31 March 2025, so internal policies, credit processes, product structures, and monitoring arrangements for SHG lending should be checked against the consolidated RBI instructions contained in the full circular and its appendix.

rows.summary:
On August 12, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued for public comment the draft **“Reserve Bank of India (Interest Rates on Loans and Advances) Directions, 2026”**, following the announcement in the RBI’s **Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies dated August 05, 2026**. The draft is intended to replace the current patchwork of interest-rate instructions with a **harmonized, principles-based framework for all regulated entities (REs)** covering both **fixed-rate and floating-rate loans and advances**, with the framework to be calibrated to the **nature, complexity, and scale** of each RE’s operations.

The RBI says the existing regime is uneven: for **Commercial Banks** (including **Small Finance Banks** and **Local Area Banks**), there are detailed rules already in place for **internal and external benchmark-based lending**, including the setting of **spreads over benchmarks**; by contrast, the rules for **NBFCs, All India Financial Institutions, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Cooperative Banks, and Rural Cooperative Banks** are mostly limited to conduct-related requirements. The RBI also notes that among commercial banks it has observed **divergent practices in determining the MCLR (internal benchmark) and its components**, and that current guidance on **fixed-rate loans** is very limited. The proposed directions are meant to address these gaps and align interest-rate setting practices more consistently across REs.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is still a **draft consultation document**, so the immediate obligation is to **review and submit comments/feedback** rather than to implement final rule changes yet. However, the substance of the proposal signals that, once finalized, it may impose a more uniform supervisory standard on all REs for how loan and advance interest rates are determined, including both benchmark-linked floating-rate structures and fixed-rate lending. The document excerpt provided does not yet give a final effective date, transition period, or operative thresholds/rates; those would need to be checked in the final directions once issued.

rows.title: RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’
rows.desc: August 7, 2026 RBI invites public comments on the draft Directions on ‘Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework’ Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) reflects the adjustment to the default risk-free prices of derivatives to account for potential counterparty default. CVA risk refers to losses resulting from changes in CVA values, driven by shifts in counterparty credit spreads and market risk factors. The CVA capital charge ensures banks hold sufficient capital to cover these risks. 2. The extant CVA framework was issued by the Reserve Bank in 2011, which was based on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) standards issued in 2010. The BCBS has, since, issued revised CVA guidelines under the final Basel III framework. Accordingly, it has been decided to issue revised instructions on CVA framework permitting banks in India to adopt the basic approach (BA-CVA). Banks may choose to implement either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. Alternatively, in line with BCBS guidelines, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may calculate their CVA capital charge as 100 per cent of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge. 3. The revised instructions: (a) allow eligible banks to choose a simpler approach; (b) clarify the eligibility and recognition of CVA hedges; (c) increase the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties by sector and credit quality; and (d) separate systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation, addressing imperfect alignment of indirect CVA hedges. These revisions enhance risk sensitivity and improve consistency in the CVA framework. 4. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has released today the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026. 5. rows.summary:
On August 7, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued draft revised Directions on the Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA) Framework and invited public comments by August 28, 2026. The draft replaces the RBI’s existing CVA framework issued in 2011, which had been based on the 2010 Basel Committee standards, and is intended to align Indian rules with the Basel III revisions to CVA treatment.

Substantively, the RBI is proposing to allow Indian banks to use the Basel “basic approach” for CVA capital calculation (BA-CVA), with banks permitted to adopt either the full or reduced version of BA-CVA. In addition, banks with an insignificant volume of non-centrally cleared derivatives may, consistent with BCBS guidance, calculate their CVA capital charge at 100% of their counterparty credit risk (CCR) capital charge instead of using the BA-CVA methodology. The draft also clarifies when CVA hedges are eligible for recognition, increases the sensitivity of supervisory risk weights for counterparties based on sector and credit quality, and separates systematic and idiosyncratic CVA risk components in the full BA-CVA calculation to better reflect indirect CVA hedges.

The RBI states that these changes are meant to make the framework more risk-sensitive and more consistent with current international standards. The new draft Directions, titled the **Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Credit Valuation Adjustment Framework) Directions, 2026**, apply to commercial banks in India that are subject to RBI regulation and to their CVA capital computation for derivative exposures. The consultation is open to regulated entities, market participants, and other interested parties, who may submit comments up to the August 28, 2026 deadline.

rows.summary:
On August 6, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released draft directions for public comment to update the concentration risk framework applicable to rural co-operative banks (RCBs). The package consists of two instruments: a new **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2026**, which would replace the existing **2025** concentration risk directions, and a **Draft RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Amendment Directions, 2026**, which would amend certain provisions of the **2025 Credit Facilities Directions**.

The draft changes are intended to set out prudential exposure limits for **single and group counterparties**, raise **housing loan limits**, and specify prudential limits for **unsecured advances**. RBI also proposes to give **larger RCBs with deposits above ₹1,000 crore** more flexibility to determine the **tenor and moratorium** for housing loans, while for **other RCBs** it proposes to **increase the ceilings** for those housing-loan parameters. In addition, RBI proposes to **withdraw the general prudential sectoral exposure limits**, with the stated exception that the **real estate sector** exposure limit would remain in place.

For compliance purposes, the key operational point is that these are **draft directions** open for consultation, not yet final rules. RBI has set **August 28, 2026** as the deadline for comments/feedback from regulated entities and other stakeholders, which may be submitted either through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** portal on the RBI website or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on (full name of the draft Directions)”**. Compliance teams at RCBs should review the draft closely for any changes to counterparty exposure, unsecured lending, and housing finance policies, especially where deposits exceed the **₹1,000 crore** threshold.

rows.title: Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments
rows.desc: July 21, 2026 Rationalisation of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 – Draft Rules for Comments Foreign investment into India is presently governed by the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 ('NDI Rules'). The Union Budget 2026- 27 announced a comprehensive review of the NDI Rules to create a more contemporary, user-friendly framework for foreign investments, consistent with India's evolving economic priorities. Pursuant thereto, a committee was constituted by the Central Government to undertake a comprehensive review of the extant regulatory framework. Based on the recommendations of the Committee, and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, the Reserve Bank of India has prepared a draft of the rationalized Rules. The salient features of the proposed draft Rules, inter alia, are as under: a) Simplified and principle-based framework: Rationalization of provisions, harmonization of definitions and a simplified regulatory architecture to enhance clarity and reduce regulatory complexity. b) Alignment with the FDI Policy: Clear demarcation of procedural FEMA provisions from policy and sector-specific requirements, improving regulatory coherence and facilitating timely policy changes. c) Enhanced ease of doing business: Streamlined procedures, reduced compliance burden and greater operational flexibility through a transparent and investor-friendly regulatory framework. d) Future-ready regulatory framework: Adoption of principle-based, investee-neutral and investor-neutral provisions aligned with evolving business practices, while preserving necessary regulatory safeguards. � � PRESS RELEASE � � RESERVE BANK OF INDIA : www.rbi.org.in/hindi , �� , � , , - 400 001 Website : www.rbi.org.in Department of Communication, Central Office, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, - /email : helpdoc@rbi.org.in Mumbai - 400 001 /Phone: 022 - 2266 0502 The Rules will be finalized after wider public consultations
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued **draft rationalised Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (NDI Rules)** for public comments on **July 21, 2026**, following the Union Budget 2026–27 announcement of a comprehensive review of the foreign investment framework. The draft is intended to update and simplify the existing foreign investment rules in India by creating a more contemporary, user-friendly structure that better aligns with India’s current economic priorities and the evolving foreign investment environment.

For compliance teams, the key substantive change is that the RBI, based on a committee review and in consultation with the Central Government and other stakeholders, is proposing a **simplified, principle-based framework** with **harmonized definitions** and a more coherent regulatory architecture. The draft also aims to **separate FEMA procedural requirements from FDI policy and sector-specific requirements**, which should make it clearer which obligations arise under FEMA rules versus sectoral policy conditions and may allow policy changes to be implemented more efficiently. The document also emphasizes **reduced compliance burden, streamlined procedures, and greater operational flexibility**, with the stated goal of improving ease of doing business and making the regime more investor-friendly while retaining necessary safeguards.

No specific numeric thresholds, ownership caps, rates, deadlines, or sector-specific eligibility changes are stated in the press release itself. The only procedural deadline mentioned is that the draft will be **finalized after wider public consultations**, meaning the current publication is a consultation stage rather than an immediately effective rule change. Compliance officers should therefore treat this as a signal that the NDI Rules are likely to be materially reworked, but should wait for the final notified text to identify any actual legal obligations, transition requirements, or date-specific implementation steps.

rows.summary:
On July 15, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) released a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance”** for public comment. The draft is aimed at a broad set of RBI-regulated entities: **commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, regional rural banks, urban co-operative banks, rural co-operative banks, all India financial institutions, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), asset reconstruction companies, and credit information companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as potentially applicable to their data governance frameworks and control environment.

The RBI’s stated objective is to respond to the increasing digitalisation of financial services and the growing dependence on technology-driven business models, where data has become a critical asset. The draft explains that as data volume, variety, and velocity increase, regulated entities need stronger governance so that data remains **accurate, consistent, secure, and fit for purpose** across business functions and systems. The RBI also highlights that weak data governance can create **financial, operational, compliance, and reputational risks**, indicating that the guidance is intended to support broader risk management and supervisory expectations, not just IT controls.

The RBI is seeking comments from regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders **by August 17, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted via the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email using the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Expectations for Data Governance.”** No final compliance obligations are imposed yet in this press release, but the issuance of the draft signals that regulated entities should review their data governance practices and be prepared for future final guidance once the consultation closes.

rows.summary:
On June 24, 2026, the Reserve Bank of India released for public comment a draft **“Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management”**. The draft is intended to broaden and update RBI’s earlier August 5, 2024 draft **“Regulatory Principles for Management of Model Risks in Credit,”** reflecting the fact that model use has expanded significantly across regulated entities and that entities are increasingly using models, including those based on **Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning**. The stated policy objective is to strengthen governance and risk-management practices for the use of models, and the draft appears to shift the focus from only credit-related model risk to a wider model-risk framework.

The draft Guidance would apply to a wide set of RBI-regulated entities: **Commercial Banks, Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Local Area Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Urban Co-operative Banks, Rural Co-operative Banks, All India Financial Institutions, Non-Banking Financial Companies, Asset Reconstruction Companies, and Credit Information Companies**. Compliance teams at any of these entities should treat the draft as relevant to their model governance, validation, oversight, and risk-control frameworks, particularly where models are used in credit, decisioning, or AI/ML-enabled processes. The press release does not state final requirements yet, but it clearly signals that RBI is moving toward formal principles for identifying, governing, and managing model risk across these institutions.

RBI is seeking comments from **regulated entities, members of the public, and other stakeholders** by **July 24, 2026**. Feedback may be submitted through the **“Connect 2 Regulate”** section on the RBI website, or sent to the **Chief General Manager, Operational Risk Group, Department of Regulation, Central Office, Reserve Bank of India, Shahid Bhagat Singh Marg, Fort, Mumbai – 400 001**, or by email with the subject line **“Feedback on Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management.”** There are no monetary thresholds, rates, or implementation dates stated in the press release itself beyond the comment deadline; the immediate compliance action is to review the draft, assess whether the institution falls within the listed regulated entities, and determine whether to submit feedback before the deadline.
