For filings under the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018, the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011, and the SEBI (Buyback of Securities) Regulations, 2018, fees are currently paid through the Payment Gateway available on the SEBI Intermediary Portal. If a particular application is not supported on that portal, listed companies must follow the payment method set out in SEBI’s attached communication rather than using any alternate method.

The key compliance point is that, effective from October 13, 2021, filings where fees have been paid using modes other than the specified ones may be delayed in processing. The circular does not introduce a new fee amount or rate, but it does create an operational requirement for listed companies to review their filing/payment process and ensure that any SEBI-related filing is accompanied by payment through the correct channel. Compliance teams should verify internal procedures for SEBI filings, confirm which applications are portal-supported, and avoid non-prescribed payment modes so that regulatory filings are not held up.

rows.title: Master Circular on Scheme of Arrangement
rows.summary:
This NSE circular does not itself create new substantive requirements; it is a forwarding notice from the National Stock Exchange of India to all listed companies alerting them to SEBI’s circular no. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL2/CIR/P/2021/0000000665 dated November 23, 2021, titled “Master Circular on Scheme of Arrangement.” The NSE states that a copy of the SEBI circular is enclosed “for your reference and for necessary action at your end,” which means listed issuers should review the SEBI master circular and apply any scheme-of-arrangement requirements to any current or future merger, demerger, restructuring, or similar arrangement they are proposing or processing through the listed-entity approval and disclosure framework. The circular is addressed to the Company Secretary of all listed companies and was issued by NSE on November 24, 2021 under download ref. no. NSE/CML/2021/48.

Because the text provided is only the NSE covering communication, it does not specify the operative procedural changes, thresholds, timelines, filing requirements, or conditions contained in the underlying SEBI master circular itself. From a compliance perspective, the key action item in this document is to obtain and review the enclosed SEBI circular immediately and ensure that any scheme of arrangement being contemplated or already underway is checked against the updated SEBI framework, with necessary action taken at the company level to comply with whatever requirements the SEBI circular prescribes.

rows.title: Disclosure obligations of listed entities in relation to Related Party Transaction
rows.summary:
This NSE circular (Ref. No. NSE/CML/2021/47, dated November 23, 2021) is a forwarding notice to the Company Secretary of **all entities that have listed their specified securities**. It informs them that SEBI has issued a new notification/circular titled **“Disclosure obligations of listed entities in relation to Related Party Transactions”** under SEBI Notification No. **SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD1/CIR/P/2021/662 dated November 22, 2021**.

The document itself does **not** set out the substantive disclosure requirements; instead, it directs listed entities to the enclosed SEBI circular for the actual obligations and states that the SEBI circular is available for reference and necessary action. From a compliance perspective, the immediate requirement is to **review the SEBI notification/circular and implement whatever related-party-transaction disclosure changes it contains** for listed entities with specified securities. No explicit effective date, deadline, threshold, or procedural detail is stated in the NSE covering circular itself beyond the issuance date and reference to the underlying SEBI action.

rows.title: Addendum to SEBI Circular dated November 16, 2021 relating to Schemes of Arrangement by Listed Entities
rows.summary: This communication is an addendum/covering notice from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited to the Company Secretary of all listed companies, drawing attention to SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL2/CIR/P/2021/0000000659 dated November 18, 2021, titled “Schemes of Arrangement by Listed Entities.” The notice itself does not introduce new substantive requirements, thresholds, timelines, or procedures; instead, it serves to forward the SEBI circular and state that it is enclosed “for your reference and for necessary action” by recipients. The affected parties are all listed companies, particularly their company secretarial/compliance functions, to the extent they are considering or implementing schemes of arrangement. Because the actual compliance obligations are contained in the referenced SEBI circular and not in this addendum, a compliance officer should treat this document as a notification requiring review of the enclosed SEBI circular and any related action needed for ongoing or proposed scheme-of-arrangement filings.

rows.title: Schemes of Arrangement by Listed Entities
rows.summary: The National Stock Exchange of India issued this circular on November 17, 2021 to all listed companies, forwarding SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL2/CIR/P/2021/0000000657 dated November 16, 2021, titled “Schemes of Arrangement by Listed Entities.” The NSE notice itself does not set out the detailed substantive requirements; it serves as a communication that SEBI’s circular on schemes of arrangement for listed entities is enclosed and should be reviewed for necessary action. For compliance purposes, the affected entities are all listed companies, and the subject matter is any scheme of arrangement involving a listed entity. No separate effective date, deadline, threshold, or procedural requirement is stated in the NSE cover circular beyond the instruction that the SEBI circular is for the recipient’s information and necessary action.

rows.title: Common and Simplified Norms for processing investor’s service request by RTAs and norms for furnishing PAN, KYC details and Nomination
rows.summary:
This NSE communication is a forwarding circular, not a standalone substantive rule, but it matters because it notifies all listed companies that SEBI has issued new requirements on **common and simplified norms for processing investor service requests by RTAs** and on **furnishing PAN, KYC details, and nomination**. The NSE circular is **Ref. No. NSE/CML/2021/44 dated November 03, 2021**, and it is addressed to the **Company Secretary of all listed companies through recognized stock exchanges**. NSE states that it is enclosing **SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD_RTAMB/P/CIR/2021/655 dated November 03, 2021** for reference and “necessary action,” meaning listed issuers should review and implement the SEBI circular’s requirements as applicable to their investor servicing and registrar/transfer agent processes.

The document itself does **not restate the operative SEBI requirements, thresholds, procedures, or deadlines**; it only points recipients to the SEBI notification for the actual compliance obligations. From a compliance standpoint, the key action item is to **obtain and operationalize the underlying SEBI circular** because this NSE letter signals that the new framework affects the handling of investor requests by RTAs and likely touches issuer-side processes around **PAN/KYC/Nomination collection and validation**. No specific effective date other than the **November 03, 2021** issuance date is provided in this NSE letter, and no numerical thresholds, forms, or timelines are set out here.

rows.title: Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)on application filed under Regulation 37 of SEBI (Listing Obligation and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 w.r.t. Scheme of Arrangements
rows.summary:
This SOP applies to all listed companies/listed entities that file a draft Scheme of Arrangement with the stock exchange(s) seeking the exchange’s no-objection/observation under Regulation 37 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, read with the SEBI circulars dated March 10, 2017 and subsequent amendments. The key filing deadline is that the scheme application, together with all documents required by the exchange checklist, must be submitted within 15 working days of the board meeting that approves the draft scheme; if the company misses that 15-working-day window, it must obtain fresh board approval based on fresh financial statements, a fresh valuation report, and similar updated materials before reapplying.

For schemes involving unlisted company(ies), the listed entity must submit audited financial statements for the last 3 years, and those financials must not be older than 6 months at the time of submission. The circular states that these audited financials are to be used by the valuer for the valuation report under the Income Approach. In addition, when the stock exchange issues its observation letter, it will require an undertaking from the listed entity confirming that the unlisted company’s financials will still be no more than 6 months old at the time the scheme is submitted to the National Company Law Tribunal (the text cuts off after “submi…”, but the obligation clearly described is the freshness requirement for NCLT submission).

For compliance purposes, the operational change is that companies must tightly coordinate board approval, financial reporting cut-off dates, valuation work, and exchange filing timing so the application is not delayed beyond 15 working days and the unlisted-company financials remain within the 6-month age limit. Missing these timing conditions triggers a re-approval and re-documentation process rather than simply curing the filing, so companies should treat the dates of the board meeting, financial statements, valuation report, and intended filing/submission as a single controlled compliance timeline.

rows.title: Transmission of Securities to joint Holder(s)
rows.summary:
This NSE circular dated **October 19, 2021** is a forwarding notice to **all listed companies** (through the stock exchanges) regarding a new **SEBI notification dated October 18, 2021** titled **“Transmission of Securities to joint Holder(s).”** The circular itself does **not restate the full operative requirements** of the SEBI notification; it advises listed companies that the SEBI circular is enclosed, available on the NSE website, and should be reviewed for **necessary action**.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that this communication is a **directive to take note of and implement the SEBI transmission framework for securities held in joint names**, if applicable to the company’s registrars, transfer agents, and investor servicing processes. The document does **not provide any specific effective date, deadlines, thresholds, or procedural details** beyond the fact that the SEBI notification was issued on **October 18, 2021** and the NSE circular followed on **October 19, 2021**. Because the actual rules are contained in the referenced SEBI notification rather than reproduced here, a compliance team would need to review that underlying circular to determine the precise obligations, impacted transactions, and any changes to transmission processing for joint holders.

rows.title: XBRL based filing of Related Party Transactions for Listed Companies at NSE
rows.summary:
NSE Circular NSE/CML/2021/42 dated October 19, 2021 clarifies the earlier requirement under Circular NSE/CML/2021/34 dated September 6, 2021 that all listed companies file Related Party Transactions disclosures under Regulation 23(9) in XBRL format only. The new circular creates an exception for **listed banking companies**: the XBRL submission requirement **does not apply for the half year ended September 30, 2021** for these entities.

For that reporting period, listed banking companies must **continue filing Related Party Transactions in PDF format** instead of XBRL. The circular does not change the underlying obligation to file Related Party Transactions; it only postpones the XBRL-only filing requirement for banking companies for the September 30, 2021 half-year filing cycle. All other listed companies remain subject to the original XBRL-based filing requirement under Regulation 23(9) as stated in the September 6, 2021 circular.

rows.title: Contact details of NSE’s Listing department officials
rows.summary: NSE has informed all listed companies that the contact details of its Listing department officials, together with the profiles/domains they handle, are now available on the NEAPS portal under **Help > Contact Us**. The stated purpose is to improve operational convenience and the overall experience for companies, and the notice directs companies to use this resource when seeking assistance on listing-related matters. Companies may call the relevant NSE officers for query resolution **between 9:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. on all working days**. The notice also expressly states that **NSE Circular No. NSE/CML/2018/34 dated November 27, 2018 is repealed**, so any prior reliance on that circular should be discontinued and replaced with this updated contact-information arrangement.

rows.title: Amendments to manner and mechanism of providing exit option to dissenting unit holders pursuant to Regulation 22(6A) and Regulation 22(8) of SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014 (“SEBI (REIT) Regulations”)
rows.summary:
This NSE circular dated October 5, 2021 is addressed to all Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and serves as a transmission notice for a SEBI notification issued the same day, SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/640. The circular does not itself set out the substantive legal changes; instead, it states that SEBI has amended the manner and mechanism for providing an exit option to dissenting unit holders under Regulation 22(6A) and Regulation 22(8) of the SEBI (REIT) Regulations, 2014, and directs REITs to review the enclosed SEBI circular and take necessary action.  

For compliance purposes, the operative impact is that REITs must align any exit-option process for dissenting unit holders with the amended SEBI framework referenced in the notification. The document does not specify the mechanics, thresholds, pricing, timelines, or procedural steps within the NSE notice itself, nor does it mention any separate compliance deadline beyond the effective date implied by the SEBI notification dated October 5, 2021. The notice also indicates that the SEBI circular is available on the NSE website and is enclosed for reference, so REIT compliance teams should obtain and implement the full SEBI text to determine the exact obligations created by the amendments.

rows.title: Amendments to manner and mechanism of providing exit option to dissenting unit holders pursuant to Regulation 22(5C) and Regulation 22(7) of SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014 (“SEBI (InvIT) Regulations”)
rows.summary:
This circular from the National Stock Exchange of India is a forwarding notice dated October 5, 2021, addressed to all Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) and their company secretaries, pointing them to a SEBI notification of the same date: SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/639. The subject of the underlying SEBI action is amendments to the manner and mechanism for providing an exit option to dissenting unit holders under Regulation 22(5C) and Regulation 22(7) of the SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014. 

For compliance purposes, the operative regulatory change is not described in detail in this NSE cover letter itself; rather, the letter states that SEBI has issued the amendment circular and that InvITs should review the enclosed SEBI notification and take “necessary action” as applicable. The notice therefore signals that any InvIT involved in a transaction or governance action covered by Regulation 22(5C) or 22(7) must ensure its exit-option process for dissenting unit holders is aligned with the amended SEBI mechanism. 

The document does not specify the substantive procedural changes, fees, thresholds, timelines, or other numerical requirements in the NSE letter itself, nor does it provide an implementation deadline beyond the circular date of October 5, 2021. Compliance teams should treat this as an alert that a binding SEBI amendment has been issued and should obtain and review the enclosed SEBI circular directly to determine the precise obligations, affected transactions, and any updated steps for offering and administering the exit option.

rows.title: Relaxations relating to procedural matters - Issues and Listing
rows.summary:
This notice is a forwarding communication from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited to the Company Secretary of all listed companies, alerting them to SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL2/CIR/P/2021/633 dated October 1, 2021, titled “Relaxations relating to procedural matters – Issues and Listing.” The NSE letter itself does not introduce new substantive requirements or change any rules; it simply encloses the SEBI circular and asks recipients to take “necessary action” as applicable.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the operative guidance, if any, is contained in the referenced SEBI circular rather than in this cover letter. The document does not state any deadlines, thresholds, rates, or specific procedural steps in the letter text provided, and it does not identify a narrower class of issuers beyond “all listed companies.” Accordingly, the only immediate compliance takeaway from this document alone is that listed companies should review the attached SEBI circular for any procedural relaxations or obligations affecting issues and listing activities, and act on those requirements if they are relevant to the company.

rows.title: Guidance note on Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulation 23(9) regarding disclosure of related party transactions
rows.summary:
The National Stock Exchange of India issued this guidance note on September 29, 2021, to clarify how listed entities must make the related party transactions disclosure required under Regulation 23(9) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. It references an earlier NSE guidance circular dated April 1, 2021, and a subsequent circular dated September 6, 2021 on XBRL-based filing of related party transactions for listed companies at NSE, and specifically clarifies the answer to question 3 of the prior guidance note.

The substantive requirement clarified is the basis on which related party transactions must be filed. If a listed entity submits only standalone financial results under Regulation 33 of the SEBI LODR Regulations, it must submit its related party transactions disclosure on a standalone basis under Regulation 23(9). If, however, a listed entity submits both standalone and consolidated financial results under Regulation 33, then it must submit related party transactions disclosure only on a consolidated basis under Regulation 23(9). In other words, the filing format follows the scope of the financial results being submitted: standalone-only filers disclose standalone related party transactions, while filers of both standalone and consolidated results disclose only consolidated related party transactions.

This clarification applies to all listed entities covered by Regulation 33 and Regulation 23(9), and it affects the compliance process for periodic disclosure of related party transactions to the exchange, including the XBRL-based filing process referenced in the earlier circulars. The circular does not introduce a new deadline, rate, threshold, or numerical requirement; it is a procedural clarification on the required reporting basis for the disclosure.

rows.title: Bank accounts for payment of fees to SEBI under the SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014, SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003, SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-convertible Securities) Regulations, 2021 and SEBI (Issue and Listing of Securitized Debt Instruments and Security Receipts) Regulations, 2008
rows.summary:
This NSE circular (dated **September 28, 2021**) communicates SEBI’s updated procedure for paying various fees under the **SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014**, **SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014**, **SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003**, **SEBI (Issue and Listing of Non-convertible Securities) Regulations, 2021**, and **SEBI (Issue and Listing of Securitized Debt Instruments and Security Receipts) Regulations, 2008**. It applies to **all InvITs, all REITs, and all issuers making public issues of non-convertible securities, securitised debt instruments, and security receipts**.

The key change is that **fees must be remitted only to the specified ICICI Bank virtual accounts**; SEBI has designated **ICICI Bank Ltd.** as the bank, with **IFSC code ICIC0000106** and beneficiary name **Securities and Exchange Board of India**. The circular lists the required **virtual account codes** for each fee type: **Filing Fee – InvITs (SEBIRCINVITFILFEE)**, **Filing Fee – REITs (SEBIRCREITFILFEE)**, **Regulatory Fee – Public Issue of Debt Securities (SEBIRCDEBTPUBLICPLC)**, **Regulatory Fee – Public Issue of Non-convertible Redeemable Preference Shares (SEBIRCNCRPSPUBLICPLC)**, **Filing Fee – Public Issue of Securitised Debt Instruments (SEBIRCSDIPUBLICPLC)**, **Registration Fees – Trustee/Special Purpose Distinct Entity, including application/registration/annual fees (SEBIRCSPDE)**, **Exemption Fees under LODR/NCS (SEBIRCEXEMPTFEE)**, and **Informal Guidance (SEBIRCIG)**. This means the payment method is now tightly controlled and fee payments must map to the correct virtual account depending on the transaction or regulatory filing.

For **REIT and InvIT registration matters**, SEBI requires that the **application fee and registration fee be paid only through the SEBI Intermediary Portal**; they are not to be paid through the general virtual account mechanism described for other fees. The circular explicitly warns filers **not to transfer or pay fees by any other means or mode**, because doing so will create reconciliation problems and **delay processing**. As an additional compliance step, remitters must send the **particulars of remittance by email to od-ddhs@sebi**. There are no other effective dates, thresholds, or fee amounts specified in the circular—its operative requirement is the exclusive use of the designated payment channels and the email notification of payment details.

rows.title: XBRL based filing of Related Party Transactions for Listed Companies at NSE
rows.summary:
NSE has introduced **mandatory XBRL-only filing** for **Related Party Transactions disclosures under Regulation 23(9) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015** for **all listed companies**. This replaces prior filing methods for this disclosure on the NSE platform: companies must now submit the related party transactions report **only in XBRL mode** through NSE’s NEAPS system.

The filing requirement remains tied to **Regulation 23(9)**, which requires listed entities to submit **within 30 days from the date of publication of their standalone and consolidated financial results for the half year** the disclosures of related party transactions on a consolidated basis. NSE states that the XBRL filing facility is being introduced **with immediate effect** to improve accuracy and efficiency, so compliance teams should treat XBRL submission as already operative from **September 6, 2021** (the circular date).

For submission, companies must use the **Excel utility attached as Annexure 1** to generate the XBRL/XML file, or use the utility provided by another stock exchange to generate the XML file, and then upload it on the **NEAPS portal** via **Compliance > Common XBRL upload > Related Party Transactions** by selecting the relevant **financial year** and **period type**. After a successful upload, the system displays **“File Uploaded successfully”** and an **acknowledgement email** is sent to the registered email address.

The circular does not change the underlying disclosure content required by Regulation 23(9), but it does impose a **new procedural/compliance obligation**: listed companies must ensure their related party transactions disclosure is prepared in the prescribed XBRL format and filed electronically through the NSE’s XBRL workflow, rather than in a non-XBRL format. For any issues or clarifications, NSE directs filers to contact **nsexbrl@nse**.

rows.title: Guidelines on issuance of non-convertible debt instruments along with warrants (''NCDs with Warrants’) in terms of Chapter VI – Qualified Institutions Placement of SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
rows.summary:
This notice is an informational forwarding letter from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited to all listed companies, drawing attention to SEBI Circular No. SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL/CIR/P/2021/614 dated August 13, 2021 on “Guidelines on issuance of non-convertible debt instruments along with warrants (NCDs with Warrants)” under Chapter VI on Qualified Institutions Placement of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018. The NSE letter itself does not introduce new obligations, thresholds, or deadlines; it simply encloses the SEBI circular and states that it is being circulated for information and necessary action by recipients.

For compliance purposes, the relevant operative requirements are in the referenced SEBI circular, not in this cover note. Based on this document alone, the only clearly affected entities are listed companies, which are being notified that SEBI has issued guidance governing issuances of NCDs together with warrants under the QIP framework. No implementation date, filing deadline, quantitative limit, pricing rule, or procedural amendment is stated in the text provided here, so a compliance team would need to review the enclosed SEBI circular directly to determine the exact issuance conditions and any action items.

rows.title: Disclosure of shareholding pattern of promoter(s) and promoter group entities

rows.title: Automation of Continual Disclosures under Regulation 7(2) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 - System driven disclosures - Ease of doing business
rows.summary:
This NSE circular is an intimation to **all listed companies** that SEBI has issued a new framework for **automation of continual disclosures under Regulation 7(2) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**, described as **“system driven disclosures”** and issued as an **ease-of-doing-business** measure. The NSE circular itself does not set out the technical mechanics; instead, it directs companies to SEBI Notification **SEBI/HO/ISD/ISD/CIR/P/2021/617 dated August 13, 2021**, which is attached for reference and necessary action, and notes that the same circular is available on the NSE website.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the disclosure process under **Regulation 7(2)** is being moved toward an **automated, system-generated regime**, so listed entities should expect that continual disclosure reporting connected with insider trading obligations will be driven by system data rather than solely manual filing. The circular does not specify a separate deadline, threshold, or numerical trigger in the NSE note itself, but the operative date referenced for the SEBI action is **August 13, 2021**, with the NSE circular issued on **August 16, 2021**. Companies should review the enclosed SEBI circular immediately to understand any implementation steps, internal process changes, or reporting adjustments required for their compliance and disclosures under the insider trading framework.

rows.title: Holding of Annual General Meeting (AGM) by top 100 listed entities by market capitalization
rows.summary:
This NSE communication dated 23 July 2021 is a forwarding notice to all listed entities that fall within the top 100 listed companies by market capitalization, drawing attention to SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD1/P/CIR/2021/602 issued the same day on “Holding of Annual General Meeting (AGM) by top 100 listed entities by market capitalization.” The letter itself does not set out new substantive rules; it advises recipients that the SEBI circular is enclosed and that they should take “necessary action” in accordance with that SEBI requirement.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that the affected population is specifically the top 100 listed entities by market capitalization, not all listed entities. The document contains no implementation mechanics, deadlines, numerical thresholds beyond the “top 100” criterion, or procedural details for how AGMs must be held; those obligations are contained in the referenced SEBI circular, not in this NSE cover letter. The only explicit administrative instruction in this notice is to review the enclosed SEBI circular (also available on the NSE website) and act accordingly.

rows.title: Continuous disclosures in compliances by InvITs -Amendments
rows.summary:
This NSE communication simply forwards SEBI’s July 22, 2021 notification, titled **“Continuous disclosures in compliances by InvITs - Amendments,”** to the Company Secretaries of **all Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs)**. The letter itself does **not** spell out the amended disclosure requirements; it says the SEBI notification is enclosed and should be reviewed for “necessary action,” with the circular also available on the NSE website. For compliance purposes, the key point is that **SEBI has issued amendments affecting continuous disclosure/compliance obligations for InvITs**, and any InvIT should treat this as a regulatory update requiring review against its current disclosure processes and reporting calendar.

The notice is dated **23 July 2021** and references the underlying SEBI notification dated **22 July 2021**. No thresholds, rates, filing dates, or specific procedural changes are described in the body of this NSE letter, so the operative requirements are contained only in the attached SEBI circular/notification, which is not reproduced here. Therefore, from this document alone, a compliance team should note the **applicability to all InvITs**, the **effective regulatory update date of July 22, 2021**, and the need to obtain and implement the enclosed SEBI amendment text.

rows.title: Continuous disclosures in compliances by REITs - Amendments
rows.summary:
This communication from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited dated 23 July 2021 is a forwarding notice to all Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) about SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/599 dated 22 July 2021, titled “Continuous disclosures in compliances by REITs - Amendments.” The NSE letter itself does not spell out the revised compliance requirements; it states that the SEBI notification/circular is enclosed and is to be reviewed and acted on by the recipients, and that the circular is also available on the NSE website for reference.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that SEBI has amended the continuous disclosure framework applicable to REITs, so REIT issuers and their compliance teams must review the underlying SEBI circular to identify what periodic or event-based disclosures have changed, what reporting formats or timelines now apply, and whether any additional filings, certifications, or internal controls are required. The notice is addressed to the Company Secretary of all REITs, indicating the change is relevant to all REIT entities subject to SEBI’s continuous disclosure regime. No specific effective date, deadline, thresholds, or quantitative requirements are provided in the NSE forwarding letter itself; those details are expected to be contained in the enclosed SEBI notification dated 22 July 2021.

rows.title: Guidance note for companies undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
rows.summary:
This NSE guidance note, issued on 9 July 2021 and addressed to all listed companies, does not create a new standalone rule; it points companies to a January 3, 2018 circular of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) and reminds them that companies undergoing a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) must continue to comply with listing regulations and all other applicable laws as amended from time to time. The note is explicitly described as guidance for assistance only, so the underlying obligations remain those in the applicable regulations and the IBBI circular.

The cited IBBI circular places responsibility on the Interim Resolution Professional, Resolution Professional, or Liquidator (as applicable) to exercise reasonable care and diligence and take all necessary steps to ensure that the corporate debtor complies with applicable laws during CIRP or liquidation. It also clarifies that if the company incurs any loss, including any penalty, because of non-compliance with applicable laws during the process, that loss is not to be treated as insolvency resolution process cost or liquidation process cost under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. However, if non-compliance occurs because of the insolvency professional’s conduct, the insolvency professional can be held responsible for that non-compliance.

For listed entities, the practical compliance message is that CIRP does not suspend legal and disclosure obligations under SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) and related regulations; the company and the appointed insolvency professional must still ensure timely compliance with all applicable filing, disclosure, and governance requirements throughout the process. No new thresholds, monetary limits, or specific deadlines are introduced in this note beyond the issuance date, but companies are instructed to review and comply with the current version of all applicable listing and regulatory requirements during CIRP.

rows.title: Standard Operating Procedure for listed subsidiary company desirous of getting delisted through a Scheme of Arrangement wherein the listed parent holding company and the listed subsidiary are in the same line of business
rows.summary: This NSE communication is a forwarding notice to all listed entities that have issued listed equity shares or listed convertible securities, pointing them to a SEBI notification dated 6 July 2021 on a new “Standard Operating Procedure” for delisting a listed subsidiary company through a Scheme of Arrangement when both the listed parent holding company and the listed subsidiary operate in the same line of business. The document itself does not set out the procedure in detail; instead, it announces that SEBI has issued the controlling circular and that the circular is attached and also available on the NSE website for reference and necessary action. The operative change for compliance teams is that any listed group structure contemplating this specific delisting route should review and follow the SEBI-issued SOP referenced by circular number SEBI/HO/CFD/DIL1/CIR/P/2021/0585, dated 6 July 2021. No separate deadline, threshold, rate, or filing date is stated in this NSE covering letter beyond the circular’s issue date, and the only affected parties identified here are listed entities with equity and convertibles, particularly listed parent-subsidiary groups in the same business line considering delisting of the subsidiary through a scheme of arrangement.

rows.title: Issue of No Objection Certificate for release of 1% of Issue amount

A compliance team should therefore treat this as a notice to retrieve and assess the underlying SEBI circular for operative obligations, implementation steps, and any filing/approval conditions that may apply to issuers or other market participants involved in public issues.

rows.title: Guidance Note on Analyst/Institutional Investors meet
rows.summary:
This guidance note, issued by NSE on June 29, 2021, explains the effect of SEBI’s May 5, 2021 amendments to the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, specifically the enhanced disclosure requirement under point 15 of para A of Part A of Schedule III. For listed companies, disclosure of **group meetings** with analysts/institutional investors is now **mandatory**, including both the **schedule** of such meetings and the **post-meeting disclosures**; however, disclosure of **one-on-one meetings** is **not mandatory** under this clarification. The note also requires that **all audio/video recordings and transcripts of post-earnings or quarterly investor calls**, whether held physically or digitally and whether organized by the listed entity or any other entity, must be **disclosed to the recognized stock exchange**.

In addition, the Exchange says it has been advised to issue further guidance under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 to strengthen disclosures where **Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)** is shared during analyst/research/investor meetings. This second requirement is explicitly limited to situations where UPSI is in fact shared during the meet, and it applies even if the meeting was **not organized by the listed company**, because the possibility of sharing price-sensitive information in such meetings cannot be ruled out. The practical compliance implication is that listed entities must treat analyst/institutional investor interactions as potentially disclosure-relevant when UPSI may be discussed, and ensure the required disclosures and filings are made in line with these clarified expectations.

rows.title: FAQ’s - LODR amendments dated May 05, 2021
rows.summary:
SEBI’s May 5, 2021 amendments to the LODR Regulations, 2015, as explained in this NSE FAQ circular dated June 28, 2021, clarify how listed entities should determine applicability and the compliance timeline for certain risk-management-related changes. For Regulation 3(2), the market-capitalization cutoff date to determine whether a listed entity is subject to the relevant provisions is **March 31, 2021**. Listed companies are also reminded that they must comply with the amended LODR requirements and any other applicable regulations as updated from time to time; the FAQ is only interpretive assistance and does not replace the regulations.

The substantive amendment addressed in the FAQ is to **Regulation 21(2)**, which now requires the **Risk Management Committee (RMC)** to have **at least three members**, with a **majority from the board of directors**, including **at least one independent director**; and for entities with **outstanding SR equity shares**, **at least two-thirds of the RMC must be independent directors**. Regulation **21(3A)** changes the frequency requirement from **“once” to “twice”**, and Regulation **21(5)** changes the threshold from **500 to 1000** (as amended in the regulation text). The amendment to **Schedule III, Part D** requires formulation of a **detailed risk management policy**.

On timing, the FAQ says compliance periods are available for the amended provisions, but the visible text in the provided document cuts off before the full timing table is shown. It does clearly indicate that the time available differs by provision, and specifically references **Regulation 21(2), 21(5), and Schedule III, Part D** as items for which a compliance period is being provided. The circular is addressed to **all listed companies** and issued by the **National Stock Exchange of India Limited** as a response to common implementation questions about the SEBI amendment.

rows.title: Action(s) to be initiated against listed companies for non-payment of outstanding Annual Listing Fees (“ALF”)
rows.summary:
This circular informs all listed entities that have not paid their outstanding Annual Listing Fees (ALF) that the NSE will initiate enforcement action in line with SEBI’s SOP on non-payment of ALF. The process is staged: first, the Exchange will issue reminder letters during the six-month period after the ALF invoice is issued; second, once those six months expire, the Exchange will send a formal notice requiring payment within 15 days, and if the entity still does not pay within that 15-day period, the Exchange will withhold approval for any further listing of securities by that defaulting listed entity.

If the listed entity still fails to clear the ALF after that notice period, the Exchange will escalate the matter to the promoter(s) of the defaulting entity. A notice will be sent to the promoter(s) using the information available with the Exchange, requiring them to ensure compliance and arrange payment of the outstanding ALF within 30 days from the date of that promoter notice. The circular also states that the concerned promoter(s) may submit a representation to the Exchange by email at listingsop@nse.in (the text provided cuts off immediately after this, so any additional filing details or subsequent steps are not visible in the excerpt).

For compliance purposes, the key obligation is to ensure ALF is paid promptly after invoice issuance, because the enforcement timeline begins with the invoice date and quickly escalates from reminders to formal notice, then to restriction on further listing approvals, and finally to promoter-level action. The document applies specifically to listed entities with unpaid ALF and, at the final stage, to their promoter(s); no other fee amounts or numeric thresholds are specified beyond the six-month reminder window, the 15-day cure period, and the 30-day promoter payment period.

rows.title: Automation of Continual Disclosures under Regulation 7(2) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 -System driven disclosures for inclusion of listed Debt Securities

rows.title: Relaxation from the requirement of minimum vesting period in case of death of employee(s) under SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014
rows.summary:
This NSE communication informs all listed entities that SEBI has issued Circular No. **SEBI/HO/CFD/DCR2/CIR/P/2021/576 dated June 15, 2021** on **“Relaxation from the requirement of minimum vesting period in case of death of employee(s) under SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014.”** The notice itself does not set out the full operative rule change, but it clearly indicates that SEBI has granted a relaxation to the usual **minimum vesting period** requirement when an employee covered by a share-based employee benefit arrangement dies.

The practical compliance implication is that listed companies administering employee share plans under the **SEBI (Share Based Employee Benefit) Regulations, 2014** should review their plan rules and internal procedures so that vesting treatment on an employee’s death follows the SEBI circular rather than any default minimum vesting timeline. The circular is addressed to **all listed entities**, so any company with SEBI-governed share-based employee benefit schemes may be affected.

The document is dated **June 16, 2021** and states that the SEBI circular is enclosed for information and necessary action, with a copy also available on the **NSE website**. No numeric thresholds, percentage limits, or other deadlines are mentioned in this NSE covering letter beyond the dates of the SEBI circular and the NSE communication.

rows.title: Guidance note on communications by Listed Entities
rows.summary:
This guidance note, issued by NSE on 11 June 2021 under confidential reference NSE/CML/2021/18, applies to all listed companies and is aimed at how they communicate publicly through the Exchange website/platform and other disclosures. It reminds listed entities that they often publish performance updates, awards and recognition, leadership claims, and interview-based statements by key managerial personnel or other representatives about prospects or future plans, but that stakeholder protection remains paramount and such communications must not compromise market integrity.

The core requirement is that no price-sensitive information may be disclosed to the public unless it has first been disclosed to the stock exchanges. In addition, any public statement made by the listed entity must be truthful, fair, evidence-based, and not manipulative, deceptive, distorted, untrue, or misleading; the entity must not make unsubstantiated promises or forecasts. Communications must also be written in clear, concise, understandable, simple, and easy-to-understand language, avoiding excessive technical, legal, or otherwise complex wording.

If the company presents financial data, it must include corresponding data for the past three years, and that disclosure must cover sales, gross profit, net profit, share capital, reserves, earnings per share, dividends, debts, and book values. The note also says companies should provide a link to the company’s website where the underlying details are available and can be verified. Finally, the level of detail must be adequate and appropriate so that investors are not misled or distracted by incomplete or promotional presentation.

rows.title: Format of compliance report on Corporate Governance by Listed Entities
rows.summary:
This notice from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited is a forwarding/intimation letter to all listed entities, issued on 31 May 2021, referencing SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD-2/P/CIR/2021/567 dated 31 May 2021. Its subject is the “Format of compliance report on Corporate Governance by Listed Entities,” and the practical action for compliance teams is to review and follow the SEBI circular it encloses, because it announces the required format for corporate governance compliance reporting by listed companies. The letter itself does not set out the substantive reporting fields or thresholds, nor does it specify any new implementation date beyond the SEBI notification date; it simply confirms that the SEBI circular is enclosed and available on the NSE website for necessary action.

For a corporate compliance team, the key takeaway is that this communication applies to all listed entities and is aimed at ensuring they use the updated SEBI-prescribed compliance report format for corporate governance disclosures. Because the letter does not reproduce the actual form or filing instructions, any operational changes, reporting frequency, certification requirements, or revised disclosure obligations would need to be taken directly from the attached SEBI circular dated 31 May 2021. The notice is informational in tone, but it clearly signals that listed entities should treat the SEBI circular as requiring compliance action.

rows.title: Relaxation from compliance to REITs and InvITs due to the CoVID -19 virus pandemic
rows.summary:
This NSE communication, dated 17-May-2021, is a notice to the Company Secretaries of all Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) and all Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) that SEBI has issued a COVID-19-related relaxation circular, SEBI Notification No. SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS_Div3/P/CIR/2021/563 dated 14-May-2021, titled “Relaxation from compliance to REITs and InvITs due to the CoVID-19 virus pandemic.” The NSE letter itself does not set out the underlying relaxations in detail; it simply forwards SEBI’s notification and states that the circular is enclosed, available on the NSE website, and is being circulated “for necessary action” and “for your information.”

For compliance purposes, the material point is that REITs and InvITs should review the SEBI circular dated 14-May-2021 to determine what compliance requirements have been temporarily relaxed because of the pandemic and what actions, if any, are still required. This NSE communication does not specify any deadlines, thresholds, reporting dates, or affected obligations on its own, and it does not impose a separate substantive requirement beyond alerting the affected entities to the SEBI relaxation and directing them to take appropriate action based on the enclosed circular.

rows.title: Business responsibility and sustainability reporting by listed entities
rows.summary:
This notice from the National Stock Exchange of India Limited informs all listed entities that SEBI has issued a new circular, SEBI/HO/CFD/CMD-2/P/CIR/2021/562, dated 10 May 2021, titled “Business responsibility and sustainability reporting by listed entities.” The NSE letter itself does not set out the substantive reporting rules; it only forwards the SEBI circular and states that listed companies should take “necessary action” in line with it. From a compliance perspective, the material point is that this is a new SEBI-mandated business responsibility and sustainability reporting requirement applicable to listed entities, and the underlying circular must be reviewed for the actual reporting framework, disclosures, timelines, and any phased applicability.

The document also notes that a copy of the SEBI circular is enclosed and is available on the NSE website for reference. No deadlines, thresholds, reporting formats, or entity carve-outs are specified in the NSE covering letter itself, so the compliance obligation here is essentially to treat the SEBI circular as operative guidance and assess whether the listed entity must update its sustainability/business responsibility reporting processes accordingly.

rows.title: Comprehensive FAQs and Compilation of informal guidance- SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (Period October 2015 - March 2021)
rows.summary:
This NSE circular, dated **04-May-2021** and addressed to **all listed companies via stock exchanges**, does not itself impose a new substantive insider-trading rule; instead, it **informs companies that SEBI has issued updated interpretive guidance** on the **SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015**. Specifically, it points compliance teams to two SEBI publications: **“Comprehensive FAQs on SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015” dated 29-Apr-2021** and **“Compilation of Informal Guidance Relating to SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015 for the period Oct 2015–Mar 2021” dated 03-May-2021**.

The practical compliance takeaway is that listed entities should **review these SEBI clarifications and align internal insider-trading controls, policies, and interpretations accordingly**, because the documents consolidate SEBI’s responses to common questions and informal guidance issued over the stated period. The circular does not specify a filing deadline, reporting threshold, or penalty change; its operative effect is to **direct listed companies and their company secretaries/compliance officers to use the referenced SEBI FAQs and guidance as current reference material** for PIT compliance.

The notice also provides the **official SEBI URLs** for the two documents and states that copies are enclosed and available on the **NSE website**. In short, the document is an informational dissemination from NSE for **all listed companies**, alerting them that SEBI has published updated PIT-related FAQs and informal guidance that should be consulted for compliance interpretation from that point forward.

rows.title: Addendum to SEBI Circular on “Relaxation in adherence to prescribed timelines issued by SEBI due to Covid 19” dated April 13, 2020
rows.summary:
This NSE communication is a forwarding notice to all listed companies, issued by the National Stock Exchange of India Limited on 29-Apr-2021, informing them of a SEBI notification dated the same day: SEBI/HO/MIRSD/RTAMB/P/CIR/2021/558. The subject of the SEBI action is an addendum to SEBI’s earlier COVID-19 relaxation circular dated 13-Apr-2020 concerning adherence to prescribed timelines. The NSE letter itself does not create a new standalone compliance obligation or set out any numerical thresholds, deadlines, or procedure changes; instead, it directs listed companies to review the enclosed SEBI circular and take any “necessary action” at their end.

For a compliance team, the key point is that this notice applies to all listed companies communicated through the stock exchanges, and it indicates that SEBI has modified or supplemented its prior COVID-related timeline-relaxation framework as of 29-Apr-2021. Because the NSE communication does not reproduce the substantive contents of the addendum, the actual operational requirements, any revised filing/processing timelines, and any affected transactions or market participants must be taken from the attached SEBI circular itself. The notice also states that the circular is available on the NSE website for reference.

rows.summary:
This Gazette notification of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), dated **10 September 2026** and published in **The Gazette of India on 14 September 2026**, is a formal **delegation of powers** issued under **section 23(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999 (41 of 1999)**. It states that IRDAI has delegated authority relating to **imposition of penalties and issuance of directions** under the **Insurance Act, 1938**, as well as under applicable **regulations and guidelines**, with the delegation taking effect through the notification itself; no separate implementation date is stated beyond the notification/publication date.

The delegation covers specific enforcement powers under the Insurance Act and certain 2015 regulations. Under **section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, the power to issue **directions to any insurer or insurance intermediary** in an enforcement proceeding for identified violations is delegated to the **Chairperson**. Under **section 102 of the Insurance Act, 1938**, the power to impose penalties on any person who fails to: **(a)** furnish any document, statement, account, return, or report to the Authority, **(b)** comply with directions, **(c)** maintain the solvency margin, or **(d)** comply with directions on insurance treaties, is delegated to a **Whole Time Member**, a **panel of the Chairperson and one Whole Time Member**, or a **panel of two Whole Time Members**, with the specific forum to be chosen by the Chairperson.

The notification also delegates the power under **section 104** to impose penalty for failure to comply with the relevant statutory requirements, and under **section 105(2)** it delegates the power to impose the specified penalty for non-compliance with that provision. In addition, for the **IRDAI (Issuance of Captive Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, the notification delegates the power under **regulation 22(6)** to the competent authority specified in the same framework, and for the **IRDAI (Registration of Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, it delegates powers under **regulations 48 to 53** and **section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938** in relation to the relevant compliance/enforcement actions.

For a compliance team, the practical significance is that **enforcement actions, directions, and penalty proceedings no longer necessarily need to go to the full Authority**; they may be exercised by the Chairperson, a Whole Time Member, or specified panels, depending on the provision. This means compliance failures involving **document/reporting obligations, solvency margin maintenance, insurance treaty directions, or violations identified in enforcement proceedings** can now result in action from these delegated decision-makers, so escalation, response, and legal review processes should be aligned to receive and handle orders issued by those officials as valid IRDAI action.

Substantively, the required percentage cession of the sum insured on each general insurance policy to Indian reinsurer(s) is fixed at 4% for insurance attaching during the financial year from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2027. It applies to **Indian re-insurers and other applicable insurers** covered by Section 101A, and it requires that, for **general insurance policies attaching between 1 April 2023 and 31 March 2024**, a **4% cession of the sum insured on each policy** must be reinsured with the Indian reinsurer(s). For compliance purposes, the key point is that this is a mandatory annual cession requirement for the specified policy period, and insurers subject to Section 101A must ensure their reinsurance arrangements, premium treatment, and placement workflow reflect the **4% compulsory cession** and the stated **NIL treatment** for terrorism and nuclear pool premiums.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI (Other Forms of Capital) Regulations, 2022 were notified on 5 December 2022 and are intended to replace and standardize the framework under which insurers can raise capital through instruments other than ordinary share capital. The regulations apply to insurers regulated under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDA Act, 1999, and they sit within the broader IRDAI regulatory framework governing capital raising and solvency. They define key terms such as “equity share capital,” “other forms of capital,” “preferential issue,” “private placement,” “promoter,” “controlled,” and related expressions, so companies using or issuing non-equity capital must align their instrument structures and disclosures with these regulatory meanings.

A major substantive requirement is the creation of a regulatory framework for issuance, treatment, and monitoring of “other forms of capital,” including instruments that are not pure equity but are intended to count toward an insurer’s capital base subject to conditions. The regulations provide for classification and treatment of instruments based on their features, including terms around priority, redemption, maturity, and loss absorption, and they require insurers to ensure that these instruments are structured so they do not undermine policyholder protection or solvency. Where instruments are held by promoters or related parties, or are issued through private placement or preferential issue, the regulations impose additional scrutiny and compliance conditions. The document also sets out the regulatory expectations for disclosures, approval processes, and ongoing compliance in relation to these instruments.

The regulations appear to include an explicit quantitative treatment for a particular category of capital instruments, showing a phased recognition or crediting of capital value over time. The text references a table in which the recognized value declines in steps from 100% to 80%, 60%, 40%, 20%, and then 0% as maturity approaches, with the example indicating a value of 1.50 plus 20% = 1.80 at one stage, which suggests the instrument’s regulatory value is amortized or progressively reduced before maturity. Compliance teams should treat this as a key capital-adequacy feature: instruments may not retain full regulatory capital recognition throughout their life, and the insurer must monitor residual tenor and the corresponding amount eligible for capital credit.

The regulations also specify conditions around the number and type of investors and the mechanics of issuance. The text references a threshold of 50 and mentions private placement/procedural requirements, suggesting limits or gating conditions for certain offers or placements, and it also refers to a 15-day timeline in at least one procedural context. In addition, the instrument documentation must contain prescribed features and cannot conflict with the regulatory definition of capital; the regulations appear to require careful drafting of offering documents and issuer resolutions before issuance. Where instruments are to be issued or transferred, the insurer must ensure the transaction is approved and documented in the manner prescribed by IRDAI.

Finally, the regulations include amendments or references to prior IRDAI regulations dated 2022 and 2015, indicating that this notification integrates with or modifies existing capital and insurer governance rules rather than operating in isolation. The practical compliance impact is that insurers planning to raise capital through hybrid, subordinated, or otherwise non-equity instruments must review the new definitions, valuation/recognition rules, issuance procedures, and ongoing reporting requirements before launching any transaction. In short, the document does not merely permit alternative capital forms; it imposes a structured legal and prudential framework that controls what can be issued, how it is recognized in capital calculations, and what approvals/disclosures are required.

It also includes representatives from key industry and technical institutions: the Director of the National Insurance Academy; the President of the Institute of Actuaries of India; the Secretary General of the Insurance Institute of India; the President of the Insurance Brokers’ Association of India; and the President of the Indian Institute of Insurance Surveyors & Loss Assessors. The document continues with additional committee membership beyond the excerpt shown, including the Insurance Ombudsman, but the core compliance point is that the committee’s constitution has been formally reset and becomes operative on the stated effective date.

For a compliance team, the practical obligation is to ensure internal governance materials, committee references, and any stakeholder engagement or regulatory communication involving the Insurance Advisory Committee are aligned to this 10 August 2021 reconstitution, rather than any prior composition. No monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or substantive operational rules are introduced in this notification beyond the change in committee membership and effective date.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued the **IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021** on **7 July 2021**, and the amending text appears to take effect from the date of publication unless a specific provision in the underlying regulations says otherwise. The amendments revise several provisions of the **IRDAI (Indian Insurance Companies) Regulations, 2015**, and also make related changes to the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Regulations, 2015** and the **Indian Insurance Companies (Indian Owned and Controlled) Regulations, 2015**.  

A key change is the insertion of a new **regulation 31** in the 2015 Indian Insurance Companies Regulations, stating that an insurer must comply with **regulation 5** of the 2021 amendment framework, which appears to introduce updated requirements tied to the insurer’s structure and governance. The document also amends **regulation 5(2)(vi)** of the 2015 regulations to update the cross-reference language, replacing earlier references so that the provision now points to the relevant clause(s) under the amended framework; similarly, **regulation 7** is amended to change the wording around **promoter/promoter group ownership and control** and the related cross-references to the 2000 and 2015 rules.  

The amendment makes conforming edits to **regulations 16 and 17** of the 2015 regulations by replacing the prior cross-references with references to **regulation 5(2)** of the amended 2021 framework, indicating that compliance obligations under those provisions now track the updated ownership/control standard. It also deletes or updates references in **regulations 29, 30 and 31** to align them with the new 2021 rule set, and amends the textual reference in the older rules so that the compliance regime is read together with the **2015** and **2021** amendments.  

In the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Regulations, 2015**, the amendment substitutes the cross-reference in **regulation 5(2)(vi)** and updates **regulation 7** and **regulation 13** to reflect the revised 2021 wording and the applicable ownership/control concepts. The same type of conforming changes are made in the **Indian Insurance Companies (Indian Owned and Controlled) Regulations, 2015**, again updating **regulation 5(2)(vi)**, **regulation 7**, and **regulation 13** so that those provisions refer to the amended regime rather than the superseded language.  

For compliance purposes, the practical effect is that insurers, and especially those affected by **foreign investment**, **Indian ownership and control**, and the linked **promoter/promoter group** provisions, must apply the updated cross-references and the new/modified compliance standard introduced by the 2021 amendment. The document does not set out a monetary threshold or percentage in the extracted text provided here, but it clearly requires regulated entities to realign their internal compliance, ownership-control assessments, and regulatory filings/interpretations to the amended regulatory structure immediately upon the amendment’s commencement.

The Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) issued the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2021** on **19 May 2021** (G.S.R. 337(E)), after publishing draft rules on **15 April 2021** and inviting public comments for **15 days** from publication. The amendments were made under **section 114(2)(aaa)** read with **section 2(7A)(b)** of the **Insurance Act, 1938**, and they amend the **Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2015**.

The most significant substantive change is a revised definition of **“foreign investment”** in the 2015 rules. The amendment also revises related definitions and references in the rules (including terms used in rule 2 and rule 5, and an updated statutory citation in rule 8), so compliance teams should treat this as a definitional and cross-reference update rather than a stand-alone licensing regime. The document specifically changes rule 4 to state that **foreign investment up to 74%** of the paid-up equity share capital is permitted in an Indian insurance company, subject to the conditions in the rule and the broader insurance-law framework. In practical terms, the rule change reflects the increase in the foreign investment ceiling for Indian insurance companies from the earlier level to **74%**, and compliance teams should ensure ownership tracking, board/governance checks, and foreign investor reporting are aligned with that cap.

The amendment applies to **Indian insurance companies** and the foreign investment they receive, so any insurer with existing or proposed foreign shareholding must review whether its capital structure, approvals, and internal compliance procedures now fit within the revised **74%** limit and the conditions attached to rule 4. Because the document is an amendment notification rather than a full restatement of the rulebook, affected firms should read it together with the **2015 Foreign Investment Rules** and the **Insurance Act, 1938** to identify every updated definition and cross-reference that may affect filings, ownership monitoring, and regulatory correspondence. The notification does not set a separate operational deadline beyond its issuance date, but it became effective upon publication on **19 May 2021**.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued Circular No. IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/122/9/2026 dated 22 September 2026 to all insurance intermediaries, repealing the earlier “Guidelines on repatriation of dividends by insurance intermediaries having majority by foreign investors” (Ref. No. IRDAI/INT/GDL/MISC/004/01/2020 dated 03.01.2020). The stated reason is that IRDAI notified the IRDAI (Insurance Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 on 30.07.2026 to align the intermediary framework with the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 and the Indian Insurance Companies (Foreign Investment) Amendment Rules, 2025.

For compliance purposes, the substantive change is that the earlier requirement for prior IRDAI approval before repatriating dividends has been removed, and the related condition governing related-party payments has also been eliminated. As a result, the 2020 guidelines that imposed these restrictions no longer apply, and they are expressly repealed effective 30.07.2026.

This means insurance intermediaries with majority foreign investment should no longer follow the superseded 2020 dividend-repatriation approval process for actions occurring on or after 30.07.2026, and they should update internal compliance manuals, approval matrices, and any foreign-investor distribution procedures to reflect that IRDAI pre-approval is no longer required under the repealed guideline. The circular itself does not introduce any new thresholds, filing deadlines, or replacement approval procedure; it simply withdraws the prior guidance in line with the amended regulations.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **27 August 2026** to **all insurers** permitting investment in **New Development Bank (NDB) “Maharajah INR Bonds” / onshore rupee bonds** as part of insurers’ **approved investments**. NDB has requested this permission to support issuance of bonds with a proposed total size of **INR 25,000 crore over a five-year period**, and the stated use of proceeds is for **general corporate purposes** and **financing/onward lending for sustainable development, sustainable infrastructure, and green/social projects in India**.

The circular clarifies that these NDB onshore rupee bonds are treated as **“securities” under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956**. IRDAI’s permission is not unconditional: insurers may invest only if the bonds are governed by **any applicable Government of India norms**, the **public issue is duly approved by SEBI**, and insurers comply with **Section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938** when making the investment. The bonds must also satisfy the **rating criteria for “Approved Investments” under Schedule III of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024**, as amended from time to time; the circular further notes that where **SEBI exempts the rating requirement** because the bonds have been rated by an **international rating agency**, that SEBI position is relevant to the compliance assessment.

For compliance teams, the practical impact is that NDB onshore rupee bonds are now eligible for insurer investment, but only within the existing statutory and regulatory framework for approved investments. Insurers should verify, before investing, that each issuance has the necessary **SEBI approval**, that any **Government of India conditions** are satisfied, that the investment remains consistent with **Section 27E limits/requirements**, and that the issue meets the applicable **Schedule III approved-investment rating standards** or a valid SEBI exemption applies. The circular is a **permission to invest**, not a relaxation of existing insurer investment controls, and there is no separate date-specific operational deadline beyond the effective applicability of the circular from its issuance on **27 August 2026**.

The IRDAI has issued a circular dated 07-08-2026 requiring all life insurers, and all general and health insurers other than reinsurers, to begin monthly submission of specified financial information for the purpose of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s Index of Service Production (ISP). The reporting starts from **July 2026 onward** and requires insurers to provide, on a monthly basis, the relevant income and claims data used for ISP compilation.

For **general and health insurers (excluding reinsurers)**, the required monthly data are **Gross Direct Premium, Claims Paid (Direct), and Investment Income of Policyholders and Shareholders**. For **life insurers**, the required monthly data are **Gross Premium, Benefits Paid (Gross), and Investment Income for Policyholders and Shareholders**. The information must be submitted through the **National Informatics Centre (NIC) online data templates** created for this purpose; IRDAI says the **online link will be shared separately**, and the template formats are identified as **Annexure A for life insurers** and **Annexure B for general and health insurers**.

The filing deadline is strict: the NIC form must be submitted **on or before the 15th day of the month following the reporting month**. IRDAI also expressly instructs insurers to ensure the information is **complete and accurate at the time of submission**. The circular is issued under **Section 14(2)(h) of the IRDA Act, 1999** and is stated to be for the limited purpose of meeting ISP data needs only; it **does not change** the disclosure requirements or financial statement preparation requirements under the **Insurance Act, 1938** or the **IRDA framework**.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **31 July 2026** and addressed to **all CEOs/CMDs of all insurance companies, including life insurers and stand-alone health insurers**, responds to the **flood-related natural disaster in Assam** that began on **19 July 2026** and affected the districts of **Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, and Golaghat** (declared a natural disaster). IRDAI states that insurers must take **immediate steps** to reduce hardship to affected policyholders and accelerate **claim registration and settlement**.

The circular requires insurers to **mobilize all resources immediately**, including **surveyors and investigators**, and to appoint **senior Nodal Officers** to oversee claims in the affected areas. The appointment of the Nodal Officer must be **communicated immediately to the Chief Secretary**, and claims in each district may be handled by a designated **District Claims Service Head**. Insurers must also activate and publicize **24x7 customer support/helplines** to assist claimants, and they must run an **extensive awareness campaign** describing the measures being taken; the **contact details of the district heads** must be published on the insurer’s website and additionally publicized through **press and digital media**.

On claims handling, insurers are directed to use **special, empowered district desks** so claims can be processed quickly in the affected districts. The document’s focus is operational readiness and speed of service delivery rather than changing policy coverage terms: the compliance obligation is to ensure rapid claim intake, escalation, and settlement support for customers impacted by the Assam floods, with visible local points of contact and continuous assistance availability.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued a circular dated **23 July 2026** to **all insurers except reinsurers** requiring them to improve the timeliness and completeness of submissions made to the **Office of the Insurance Ombudsmen (IO)**. The regulator says that, based on a recent orientation programme for Insurance Ombudsmen, insurers have been causing **inordinate delays** by submitting **Self-Contained Notes (SCNs)**, supporting documents, and follow-up information **piecemeal** and **late**, which in turn delays resolution of policyholder/beneficiary complaints.

The circular emphasizes that SCNs and any further documents requested by the Ombudsman are essential for deciding complaints, and that insurers must provide the materials sought under **Rule 15(2) of the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017** promptly. This is tied to **Rule 17(4)**, which requires that a complaint be decided **within 90 days of receipt of all required information from the complainant**; delayed insurer responses undermine this statutory timeline. To improve disposal efficiency, IRDAI advises insurers to submit the required SCNs **duly supported by relevant documents**, rather than sending information in fragments after repeated follow-ups.

Although the excerpt cuts off before listing every procedural instruction, the document clearly establishes a compliance expectation that insurers must treat Ombudsman requests as time-sensitive and provide complete, organized, and prompt responses to avoid delaying complaint adjudication. The practical compliance impact is on all insurer complaint-handling and Ombudsman-response processes: insurers should ensure that SCNs and requested documents are compiled and submitted without unnecessary delay, and that subsequent information requests are tracked and answered comprehensively, since the regulator views delayed or partial submissions as a matter of concern.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 14 July 2026 and addressed to all insurers, issues additional clarifications on implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS), building on Circular No. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/45/4/2026 dated 1 April 2026. The stated purpose is to ensure consistent implementation of the regulatory framework and it specifically clarifies three areas: the role of the Appointed Actuary, the requirement for independent validation, and the use of Ind AS-compliant financial statements for consolidation.

On the Appointed Actuary’s role, the circular says that under Clauses 6 and 7 of Part II of Schedule I of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, the Appointed Actuary must provide actuarial expertise and support for preparation of financial statements under applicable Ind AS, but this role is limited to actuarial inputs and valuation-related support; the Appointed Actuary is not the person responsible for actually drafting or signing the financial statements. The circular then clarifies that the insurer’s management remains responsible for the preparation and approval of Ind AS financial statements, while the Appointed Actuary contributes required actuarial inputs, assumptions, and valuations.

A major change concerns independent validation and timing. For the financial year 2026–27, and for every year thereafter, an independent validation of the insurer’s Ind AS financial statements is required before finalization. The circular specifies that this independent validation must be completed by 31 August 2026 for the 2026–27 financial year, and similar timelines will apply in subsequent years in line with the year-end reporting process. The validation is intended to cover the proper application of Ind AS, including actuarial assumptions, policy liability measurements, and consistency of disclosures, and it must be carried out by an independent professional or firm with the relevant expertise and no conflict of interest.

The circular also clarifies how Ind AS-compliant financial statements are to be used for consolidation. For any insurer that is part of a group, the Ind AS financial statements prepared by the insurer are to be used for group consolidation purposes, provided they are prepared in accordance with the applicable Ind AS and have undergone the required independent validation. The document implies that insurers must ensure their subsidiary/parent consolidation packs are based on validated Ind AS numbers rather than on separate local-compliance figures.

Finally, the circular indicates that insurers must align their internal processes, governance, and reporting timelines with these requirements immediately for the 2026–27 cycle. Compliance officers should ensure the Appointed Actuary’s responsibilities are properly documented and limited to actuarial support, that an independent validation mechanism is in place well before the 31 August 2026 deadline, and that finance, actuarial, and consolidation teams are coordinating so that the validated Ind AS financial statements can be used for reporting and consolidation without delay.
