rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated **8 July 2026** and addressed to **all insurers and reinsurers**, updates the **formats for publishing financial results under SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015** for listed insurance entities. It explains that SEBI’s master circular on financial-results publication already required listed insurers to use IRDAI-prescribed formats, but those formats now needed revision because of the **adoption of Ind AS by insurers**. As a result, the circular says the **unaudited/audited quarterly financial-results formats submitted to stock exchanges have been updated** for **all listed Life Insurers, General Insurers, Health Insurers, and Reinsurers**.

The updated requirements apply specifically to listed insurers/reinsurers **that are required to prepare financial statements under Ind AS**. For these entities, **quarterly financial results must be presented in the format set out in Annexure I**, and the **segment-wise Revenue, Results, and Capital Employed** must also be reported along with the quarterly results, in the format prescribed in **Annexure II**. The circular also refers to a further format in **Annexure III** and indicates another annexure tied to **SEBI LODR Regulation 47(1)(b)**, implying additional publication-format obligations where applicable to listed entities.

The circular also notes an important exception: insurers that have been granted **forbearance for Ind AS implementation for FY 2026–27** are treated differently, because the format changes are driven by Ind AS adoption and therefore apply to the entities that are actually operating under Ind AS. It further references earlier IRDAI directions/circulars from **25 January 2016** and **30 January 2017**, indicating that the current update is a replacement or revision of prior publishing formats rather than a wholly new reporting regime. For compliance purposes, listed insurers should ensure their stock-exchange financial-result disclosures are revised immediately to match the new annexed formats, including the quarterly statement and the required segment reporting, so that their disclosures remain aligned with IRDAI’s standards under the SEBI LODR framework.

rows.summary:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the transitional arrangements governing **payment of annual fee and issuance of Certificate of Registration** for insurance intermediaries, and for surveyors/loss assessors where applicable. These arrangements had originally been issued by Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/41/3/2026 dated 16 March 2026**, with applicability extended to surveyors and loss assessors by Circular **IRDAI/INT/CIR/MISC/54/4/2026 dated 7 April 2026**. The earlier transitional framework was due to expire on **30 June 2026**, but IRDAI has now decided that it will continue **beyond 30 June 2026 until the date the relevant amended Regulations are notified**.

More specifically, the circular amends the timing in the earlier circulars so that the period referenced in **paragraph 4.3 of Circular 41/3/2026** is extended from **30 June 2026 to 31 August 2026, or to the date of notification of the relevant amended Regulations, whichever is earlier**. It also states that **paragraph 4.1 of Circular 54/4/2026** is to be read in line with this extension. The practical effect is that entities covered by those circulars should continue following the interim process for annual fee payment and certificate issuance until the new regulations are formally notified, rather than assuming the transitional mechanism ends on 30 June 2026.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that firms in the affected categories must keep using the existing transitional arrangement and should monitor closely for the notification of the amended Regulations, because that notification will end the transitional regime even if it occurs before **31 August 2026**. No new fee rate or threshold is introduced in this circular; the only substantive change is the **extension of the interim compliance period and related operational process** pending the final regulatory amendments under the **Insurance Act, 1938**, as amended by the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025**.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular, dated 25.05.2026 and issued under Ref. IRDAI/F&I/CIR/MISC/72/5/2026, amends the remuneration framework for Key Managerial Persons (KMPs) under the IRDAI (Corporate Governance for Insurers) Regulations, 2024. It specifically modifies Regulation 8.1(b) and 8.3, and also updates the related definitions/wording in Regulation 9.2, so insurers must review their KMP pay structures under the 2024 corporate governance regime rather than treating this as a standalone guidance note.

The core change is a new cap methodology for KMP remuneration for FY 2026–27, with a formula driven by the insurer’s size/financial metrics and thresholds. The document lays out a graded structure with three bands and corresponding maximum remuneration percentages: for one band the cap is linked to 90% of a benchmark amount, for another it references a 30/40/50 threshold structure tied to the “(G + …)” measure, and for another it uses 15, 30, and 60 as review/approval trigger points; in addition, the circular mentions a “10%” and “50%” limit in connection with certain components and an overall ceiling for specific KMP remuneration categories. It also explicitly distinguishes fixed and variable compensation and sets out how variable pay should be computed, including a formula based on a ratio of one amount to another, and it describes that certain remuneration components may be excluded or restricted depending on the applicable band and conditions.

For compliance purposes, insurers must examine remuneration proposals not only for whole-time KMPs but also for other managerial/technical roles covered by the revised wording, and they must apply the new calculation rules when determining whether pay is within the permitted ceiling. The circular indicates that some remuneration arrangements require prior approval/escalation when they cross specified thresholds, and it introduces a staged approach using annual compensation levels and band-based percentage caps rather than a flat, universal limit. It also appears to require that remuneration be split and evaluated by component, with special treatment for variable pay and other allowances, so boards and nomination/remuneration committees will need to document the basis for each KMP package under the new framework.

The practical compliance action is to reassess FY 2026–27 KMP compensation plans, map each KMP into the relevant category under the amended regulations, and ensure that any proposed fixed pay, variable pay, or other perks comply with the new formula and ceiling structure before approval or payment. Because the circular amends the underlying regulations themselves, insurers should update internal remuneration policies, committee approval templates, and governance papers to reflect the revised provisions, and they should be prepared to justify any compensation above the lower benchmark percentages only where the circular’s conditions and approval route are satisfied.

rows.summary:
This circular from IRDAI clarifies how the post-amendment annual-fee and certificate-of-registration transition applies to **Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs)** under the **Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025**. It states that the circular applies to **all SLAs** and is issued in continuation of IRDAI’s earlier circular dated **16 March 2026** on transitional arrangements for annual fee payment and CoR issuance for intermediaries. The background noted is that the SBSR Act amended **Section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938** so that intermediary registration continues in force subject to payment of the annual fee prescribed by regulation, unless suspended or cancelled by the Authority.

The key operational change is the treatment of the **annual fee for SLAs for the period 5 March 2026 to 30 September 2026**. The circular provides the applicable fee structure and the **18% GST** component: for the first fee slab, the base fee is **₹400**, GST is **₹72**, and the total payable is **₹472**; for the second fee slab, the base fee is **₹2,000**, GST is **₹360**, and the total payable is **₹2,360**. The document also indicates that the annual-fee mechanism must be read in light of the transitional framework, with SLAs continuing to be subject to registration and fee requirements during the transition rather than falling outside the regime.

The circular also clarifies timing around the transition. It states that **from 5 March 2026 to 5 March 2027**, the relevant arrangements continue, and it specifically notes the applicability of the clarified fee and registration treatment during that period. It further references that the earlier circular had already set transitional arrangements for intermediaries generally, and this document narrows that guidance to SLAs because of their distinct operational and fee structure. The practical compliance takeaway is that SLAs should ensure their annual fee payments are made in accordance with this updated structure and timeline so that their **registration remains in force** and their **Certificate of Registration** is properly issued/maintained under the revised framework.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI has issued this circular on 1 April 2026 to all insurers, under Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938, Section 14 of the IRDA Act, 1999, and Regulations 7 and 8 of the IRDAI (Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers) Regulations, 2024, to provide implementation clarifications on Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS). The circular follows amendments notified to the 2024 Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions Regulations, and the clarifications are intended to govern how insurers should apply the amended Ind AS framework from 1 April 2026 onward.

The document is structured around multiple specific issues, with the clarifications stated in the body and Annexure-II. It covers, among other things, the treatment of items in relation to the insurer’s balance sheet and financial reporting under Ind AS, including references to products, liabilities, and other insurer-specific accounting items. The circular also clarifies the handling of certain matters under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDAI regulatory framework, including the application of provisions linked to Sections 11, 13, 49, and 64 of the Insurance Act, 1938, as well as references to regulatory reporting/filing obligations and treatment of assets or investments under the revised regime.

A key operational deadline in the circular is 30 April 2026, which is mentioned as a required date for a specified submission/action under the clarifications. The circular also refers to the 2026–27 period in connection with implementation, indicating that insurers must align their accounting and related compliance processes for that financial year. The document points insurers to Annexure-I and Annexure-II for the detailed question-and-answer clarifications that drive the actual implementation requirements.

The circular makes clear that insurers should follow the clarified interpretations for their Ind AS implementation and related regulatory compliance, rather than relying on prior practice that may be inconsistent with the new amendments. It also references the need to comply with linked provisions of the Insurance Act, 1938, including Sections 11, 13, 49, and 64, implying that the accounting treatment cannot be viewed in isolation from statutory insurance reporting and investment requirements. If insurers need clarification, they are instructed to contact IRDAI at the email address provided: indas-team@irdai.gov.in.

IRDAI has issued a transitional circular for insurance intermediaries under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025 (“SBSR Act”), which became effective on 5 February 2026. Exercising powers under section 42D(4A), IRDAI is changing the mechanism for two compliance areas: the payment of annual fee and the issuance of the Certificate of Registration for insurance intermediaries.

The circular applies broadly to all registered insurance intermediary categories, specifically Insurance Brokers, Corporate Agents, Insurance Marketing Firms (IMFs), Web Aggregators, Common Service Centres (CSCs), Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors, Insurance Repositories, Third Party Administrators (TPAs), and any other entities registered as insurance intermediaries under the applicable regulations. It states that the SBSR Act has amended section 42D of the Insurance Act, 1938, and the new transitional framework is meant to govern the move to the amended regime.

The key operative dates are 5 February 2026, when the SBSR Act came into force, and the transitional payment/registration window from 5 March 2026 to 30 June 2026. During this period, intermediaries are required to follow the transitional arrangements prescribed by IRDAI for annual fee payment and certificate issuance; the circular refers to specific forms/annexures and procedural provisions to be used in this period, indicating that existing or legacy procedures are not simply continuing unchanged.

For compliance teams, the practical point is that annual fee and registration certificate administration is no longer just a routine pre-existing renewal process; it is now governed by a statutory transition under the amended law, with a defined compliance window and IRDAI-specified procedures. Intermediaries in any of the listed categories should ensure their registration status, annual fee payments, and certificate issuance/renewal activities are aligned with the new transitional requirements applicable from 5 March 2026 through 30 June 2026.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a clarification circular on insurers’ investments in Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), dated 12/02/2026, to supplement para 1.5 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17/05/2024. The circular confirms that the existing framework already permits insurer investment only in Fund of Funds (FoFs) that comply with section 27E of the Insurance Act, 1938; insurers must have the FoF’s offer documents include a clause preventing that FoF from investing into AIFs that invest in overseas companies or funds; insurers must ensure AIFs do not invest in securities of companies incorporated outside India; and an insurer cannot invest in an AIF that has exposure to a FoF in which that insurer already has exposure.

The new circular is being issued because insurers sought clarification on how these rules apply where AIFs use “excuse rights” and how investee limits should be treated for direct and indirect exposure through FoFs. IRDAI states that compliance with the newly clarified conditions will satisfy sub-paras 4(b), 4(c), and 5 of para 1.5 of the Master Circular, and it introduces a specific exception-based framework for AIFs using excuse rights. Under the clarified approach, insurers may invest only in AIFs that do not, either directly or indirectly, breach the section 27E restriction on overseas exposure, and the insurer must ensure the relevant AIF/FoF structure is consistent with the clarified investment restrictions before committing funds.

The circular therefore broadens the permissible avenues for insurer investment in AIFs, but only within the clarified compliance guardrails. For compliance teams, the key action is to review AIF and FoF structures, fund offer documents, and any excuse-rights mechanics to confirm that the underlying investment chain does not create prohibited overseas exposure or impermissible cross-exposure through FoFs. The document does not state a separate implementation deadline beyond the circular date itself, so the clarifications should be treated as effective from issuance unless a later operative date is specified in the full text.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular dated **6 January 2026** to **all insurers and insurance intermediaries** directing them to implement TRAI’s mandatory **1600-series** calling framework for consumer-facing communications. The circular responds to TRAI’s **16 December 2025 Direction**, issued under **section 13 read with section 11(1)(b)(i) and (v) of the TRAI Act, 1997**, intended to curb **Unsolicited Commercial Communication (UCC)**, reduce impersonation-based fraud, and improve consumer trust.

The key compliance requirement is that **all service and transactional voice calls** to consumers must be moved to the **1600 series**, and this adoption must be **completed by 15 February 2026**. After that date, insurers and intermediaries **must not initiate service or transactional voice calls from any number other than one allocated under the 1600 series**, and this restriction applies **regardless of whether customer consent is explicit or implied**. In other words, consent does not create an exception for using non-1600 numbers for these call types.

The circular also warns that **any UCC complaint** against an entity that does not comply will be dealt with under the **regulatory provisions applicable to unregistered telemarketers under TRAI**, and this is **in addition to any further action** that the Authority (IRDAI) may deem appropriate. For compliance teams, this means firms should urgently confirm allocation of 1600-series numbers, complete technical and operational migration before the deadline, and ensure all outbound service/transactional calling workflows, vendor arrangements, and telephony systems are blocked from using non-1600 numbers after **15 February 2026**.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued a circular permitting **insurers and reinsurers** to invest not only in bank AT1 and Tier 2 instruments, but also in the **same types of capital instruments issued by RBI-regulated All India Financial Institutions (AIFIs)**. Specifically, insurers may now invest in **AT1 bonds** and in **Debt Capital Instruments and Preference Share Capital Instruments (excluding Perpetual Cumulative Preference Shares)** that form **Tier 2 capital** of such AIFIs. The circular states that this expansion is intended to broaden insurers’ investment options and support portfolio diversification.

This permission is tied to the fact that **RBI enabled AIFIs to issue Additional Tier 1 Bonds and Tier 2 capital effective 1 April 2024** under its Basel III prudential framework. IRDAI’s instruction is not a new standalone investment regime; instead, insurers must apply the **existing IRDAI investment provisions already applicable to investments in banks**, specifically the rules in **paragraphs 1.6(b) and 1.6(d) of Chapter 3 of the Master Circular on Actuarial, Finance and Investment Functions of Insurers dated 17 May 2024**. In other words, compliance teams should treat these AIFI instruments as fitting within the same framework used for bank AT1/Tier 2 investments, rather than creating a separate internal policy basis.

The circular also imposes an administrative/compliance requirement: insurers must use the **existing category codes specified for investments in PSU banks** when recording these investments. The document does not introduce a separate later implementation date beyond the circular date itself; it is dated **19 December 2025**, and the permission is presented as effective immediately from that issuance. For compliance purposes, the key action is to ensure that investment policy, limits, approvals, classification/reporting, and system coding are updated so that investments in these AIFI AT1 and Tier 2 instruments are processed consistently with the bank-investment framework and mapped using the existing PSU-bank category codes.

rows.summary:
This IRDAI circular dated **10 October 2025** announces a **full cessation of the earlier practice of allowing individual Surveyors and Loss Assessors (SLAs) to add an additional line of business/department to their surveyor licence on the basis of the categorization letter issued in 2001–02**. It applies to **all licensed Surveyors and Loss Assessors**, and specifically addresses the category of individual SLAs who had been categorized into multiple lines of business before the **IRDA Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors (Licensing, Professional Requirements and Code of Conduct) Regulations, 2000** took effect. The circular explains that, under the earlier system, an individual SLA was categorized in several lines of business/departments, and later was permitted to retain only **3 LOBs** from among those categorized on the licence.

The regulator had already relaxed this framework through **Circular Ref. IRDA/SUR/CIR/MISC/042/02/2020 dated 4 February 2020**, which allowed an individual SLA to **add LOBs based on the 2001–02 categorization letter** if the person had the relevant educational qualification and had maintained **continuous renewal of the licence without break** up to the date of filing the modification application. That 2020 circular also removed the earlier **cap of 3 LOBs** on an individual surveyor licence. However, IRDAI states that it has now received multiple applications under this 2020 route from SLAs who are seeking to add new LOBs but have **not carried out the required survey work in the relevant line(s) of business in recent times / as required under the applicable norms**, indicating that the earlier concession was being used beyond its intended scope.

As a result, IRDAI is ending this practice: **the option to seek addition of LOB/department to an SLA licence solely on the basis of the old 2001–02 categorization letter is no longer available**. Compliance teams should treat this as a change affecting the **licensing and scope of work of individual surveyors/loss assessors**, particularly those who may have been relying on the 2020 circular to expand their licence coverage. Going forward, any SLA licence modification requests should be reviewed under the current regulatory framework rather than the old categorization-based relaxation, and firms should ensure that internal records, authorizations, and engagement assignments reflect that the prior facilitation for adding LOBs from the 2001–02 categorization has been discontinued.

rows.summary:
IRDAI has issued Circular No. IRDAI/RBC/CIR/MISC/94/8/2025 dated 14 August 2025 on **Quantitative Impact Study-2 (QIS 2)** under the Risk Based Capital (RBC) framework for the Indian insurance industry. The circular explains that RBC implementation is a key IRDAI initiative to align Indian insurance regulation with global best practices, and that QIS 2 follows the first quantitative impact study (QIS 1) conducted in 2023. Based on the results of QIS 1 and feedback from insurers, IRDAI is requiring a second impact study to refine the framework further.

The requirement applies to **all Life Insurers, General Insurers, Standalone Health Insurers, Reinsurers, Branches of Foreign Reinsurers, and Lloyd’s India**. Insurers must complete QIS 2 **using the Technical Guidance document** and must base the exercise on the **data used for actuarial valuation as at 31 March 2025**. IRDAI says the technical guidance, the data submission template, the requirements for the associated template used to submit results, the submission mode, and the supplementary information will be communicated separately to insurers.

The circular states that **QIS 2 is a pivotal step toward the RBC framework**, so compliance teams should treat it as a formal regulatory exercise rather than a voluntary consultation. The only deadline explicitly visible in the text provided is the use of the **31 March 2025 valuation data**; the circular also references that the separate technical guidance and submission instructions will follow, so insurers should monitor for those documents and prepare to meet any resulting submission requirements promptly.

This IRDAI guideline, dated **11 February 2026** and issued under reference **IRDAI/F&I/GDL/MISC/27/02/2026**, replaces/updates the earlier framework referenced in the document (including the prior **17 October 2022** guidance) and sets out the rules for **insurance companies registered outside India** that want to **establish or close a liaison office in India**. It is aimed at foreign insurers, and it ties the liaison-office process to Indian regulatory oversight rather than treating it as a purely corporate-filings matter.

On **establishment**, the document requires the foreign insurance company to make an application to IRDAI in the prescribed format and with the supporting information listed in the annexures. The application package is structured to cover the applicant’s identity and regulatory status, details of the parent/foreign insurer, proposed India liaison-office activity, and the required declarations/undertakings. The guideline indicates that the liaison office is limited to permitted liaison-type functions and is not a full operating insurance business presence; the office is subject to conditions and oversight, and the document’s annexures specify the reporting, declarations, and compliance documentation that must accompany the request.

The guidance also imposes **ongoing compliance and reporting obligations** on the liaison office after approval, including maintaining the office only for the purposes allowed under the framework and complying with the regulator’s information requests and procedural requirements. The document points to defined annexures for the detailed contents of the application, the declarations to be furnished, and the requirements for closure, which means compliance teams need to treat the annexures as operative parts of the rule, not just explanatory notes. If the office ceases to be needed or the insurer wants to terminate it, closure is not automatic: the foreign insurer must follow the prescribed closure process, submit the required closure request/documents, and ensure that the office’s activities are wound down in accordance with IRDAI’s instructions.

The guideline is therefore relevant to any **non-Indian registered insurer** considering a liaison presence in India or already operating one. The practical compliance takeaway is that both **entry** and **exit** are regulated events requiring prior/structured regulatory filings, prescribed declarations, and adherence to the conditions attached by IRDAI; firms should review the annexures closely to confirm the exact form, supporting documents, and any office-specific obligations before making changes.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework Guidelines, 2025** under **Section 34 of the Insurance Act, 1938** and **Section 14(1) of the IRDAI Act, 1999** to create a regulatory framework for how insurers and distribution channels must identify, monitor, and manage insurance fraud risk. The guidelines apply broadly to **all insurers and distribution channels**, unless a specific exemption is stated elsewhere in the document, and they are intended to cover fraud risk arising across the insurance business and its external intermediaries. The document is titled and effective as the **IRDAI (Insurance Fraud Monitoring Framework) Guidelines, 2025**, with the reference date shown as **09.10.2025** and an applicability/commencement date indicated in the text as **1 January 2026**.

A key requirement is that insurers must implement a formal fraud monitoring framework, with governance and controls designed to detect, prevent, report, and respond to fraud. The document defines terms relevant to the framework, including “fraud,” “distribution channels,” and other operational concepts, and then sets out obligations for insurers and distribution channels to maintain appropriate systems, records, controls, and escalation processes. The framework is meant to cover both **internal fraud** and **external fraud** affecting the insurer’s operations, policy servicing, claims, procurement, and distribution-related activities.

The guidelines require insurers to establish specific internal arrangements for fraud risk management, including procedures to identify suspicious patterns, investigate incidents, and ensure escalation to the appropriate authority/committee/management level. The document also contemplates formal roles and responsibilities, including accountability at senior-management and governance levels, so that fraud risks are not handled ad hoc but through a defined process. Insurers are expected to maintain documentation and oversight mechanisms, including records of suspected and confirmed fraud, outcomes of investigations, and remediation steps.

The guidelines also impose obligations on **distribution channels**, meaning intermediaries and other entities involved in selling or servicing insurance products, to cooperate with the fraud monitoring framework and follow the insurer’s fraud-related controls and reporting requirements. Where fraud risk arises in distribution activity, the insurer must ensure that the channel is subject to monitoring and that suspicious conduct is escalated and acted upon. The document indicates that the framework is intended to apply across the insurance value chain, not only within the insurer’s own employees and systems.

The later sections of the document refer to implementation, reporting, and compliance expectations, and the annexure/appendix structure suggests that additional procedural details, formats, or timelines are prescribed there. Because the text provided is partially truncated and OCR-extracted, the exact annexure contents and some clause-specific sub-requirements are not fully visible in the excerpt, but the compliance significance is clear: insurers and their distribution partners must be ready by the commencement date to operate under a formal fraud-monitoring regime, with governance, detection, reporting, and remediation controls in place. For compliance planning, the practical takeaway is that affected entities should treat this as a mandatory enterprise fraud-control framework effective from **1 January 2026**, and should ensure their policies, oversight structure, investigation procedures, recordkeeping, and intermediary oversight are aligned before that date.

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has amended Clause 15(a) of the “Revised Guidelines on Insurance Repositories and Electronic Issuance of Insurance Policies” (originally issued 29 May 2015). The substantive change is to the annual review requirement for an insurance repository’s controls, systems, procedures, and safeguards: instead of requiring the review to be conducted by an “external system audit firm approved by the Authority” on a yearly basis, the clause now requires that the review of the controls, systems, procedures and safeguards established under Clause 14 be conducted **at least once a year**, **at the repository’s own cost**, by an **external auditor** who is **either** a **Certified Information System Auditor (CISA)**, a **Chartered Accountant with DISA (ICAI) qualification**, or a **CERT-In certified expert**.

For compliance purposes, this means insurance repositories must ensure their annual audit/review program is performed by a suitably qualified individual auditor meeting one of those three credentials, rather than by a generic external system audit firm, and must budget for the review themselves. The amendment applies specifically to entities operating as insurance repositories under the referenced IRDAI guidelines and to the review of the controls/systems/procedures/safeguards described in Clause 14. The circular is stated to come into force **with immediate effect**; no transition period, later effective date, or numerical threshold beyond the “at least once a year” frequency is provided.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued the **“Guidelines on Hedging Through Equity Derivatives”** on **28 February 2025** to **all life, general, and health insurers**. These guidelines replace/operate in the context of earlier IRDAI investment directions, including the **2004** and **2012** investment-related circulars and the broader **IRDAI (Investment) Regulations, 2016**, and they are intended to govern how insurers may use equity derivatives for hedging. The document makes clear that the new framework is about **permitted hedging**, not speculative trading, and that insurers must use equity derivatives only within the specific limits and controls prescribed.

The guidelines allow insurers to hedge equity exposure using derivative instruments only in relation to their own underlying equity investments, and they distinguish between use by **life insurers** and **general/health insurers** through the applicable investment and risk-management limits. A key requirement is that hedging activity must be tied to an identifiable underlying equity exposure and must not exceed the exposure being hedged; insurers are expected to maintain a documented link between the derivative position and the underlying asset/investment. The document also requires insurers to put in place internal policies, approvals, and governance controls for derivative use, including board-level oversight and documented procedures for authorizing, monitoring, and closing hedge positions.

The document sets specific quantitative constraints on hedging and derivative usage. It states that the **maximum hedge ratio is 1:1** in relation to the underlying exposure, and it provides that the aggregate use of certain derivative positions is subject to limits linked to the insurer’s equity holdings and the scope of permissible investments. It also specifies an exposure cap in one area of hedging activity at **20%** and imposes a value band of **80–125** for another monitored metric under the hedging framework, indicating that insurers must track positions against prescribed tolerance ranges rather than treat derivatives as open-ended risk-transfer tools. Where relevant, the rules require ongoing valuation, risk measurement, and compliance monitoring so that positions remain within the approved hedge parameters throughout their life.

The guidelines further require insurers to implement a formal **risk management framework** for derivative hedging, including segregation of duties, limits-setting, independent monitoring, valuation controls, and periodic reporting. The document calls for derivatives to be used only by authorized personnel and under a clearly approved policy, with records retained to evidence the hedge rationale, underlying exposure, transaction terms, valuation, and compliance with prescribed limits. It also indicates that insurers must ensure the instruments, counterparties, and execution mechanisms are appropriate and that all hedging activity is capable of being reviewed by the insurer’s internal control function and by IRDAI supervision.

In practical compliance terms, insurers need to review their investment policies, board approvals, operational procedures, and reporting controls to ensure their equity derivative activity fits the new framework from **28 February 2025** onward. Any insurer with equity exposures should assess whether existing positions qualify as hedges under the new rules, confirm that derivative usage is not speculative, and verify that hedge ratios, exposure caps, and valuation controls are being met continuously. If you want, I can also turn this into a **compliance action checklist** or a **gap-assessment template** for insurers.

For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that the insurance ecosystem now has a **single revised cybersecurity baseline** that applies across insurers and intermediaries, with obligations focused on strengthening information security controls and governance. Companies should verify whether they fall within the listed covered entities, determine whether they already completed the FY 2022-23 security audit, and if so, prepare to align with the new requirements starting the next financial year. rows.summary:
IRDAI’s 28 September 2022 guidelines address conflict-of-interest risks arising when multiple entities in the same group apply for, or hold, Certificates of Registration (CoR) as intermediaries or insurance intermediaries, and when directors are shared across such entities. The document applies to entities that are “intermediaries” or “insurance intermediaries” under section 2(f) of the IRDAI Act, 1999, and specifically references groups as defined in section 2(g) of the IRDAI (Investment) Regulations, 2018.

The key substantive requirement is that, where IRDAI has granted or is granting CoR to more than one entity within the same group, or where common directors already exist or are being appointed within the same group or across different groups, the number of directorships must comply with section 165 of the Companies Act, 2013. In other words, the guideline does not create a separate IRDAI numerical cap; it ties allowable common directorships to the Companies Act limit. When common directors are in place, each affected intermediary/insurance intermediary must maintain a Board-approved policy for dealing with related-party transactions, with “related party” determined under section 2(76) of the Companies Act, 2013.

The guidelines also require that every related-party transaction undertaken by the intermediary or insurance intermediary comply with section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and applicable Accounting Standard AS 18. In addition, the statutory auditor of the intermediary/insurance intermediary must certify to IRDAI that the entity is compliant with section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013. rows.desc: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India Survey No.115/1, Financial District, Nanakramguda, HYDERABAD 500 032. IRDAI/NL/GDL/MISC/244/09/2021 8 th September, 2021 To The Chairman-Cum- Managing Directors/Chief Executive officers of General Insurance Companies (except ECGC Ltd and AIC Ltd) Madam/Sir, IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines, 2021 The revised guidelines on Trade Credit insurance are hereby issued considering the evolving insurance risk needs of various sectors and response to changing market conditions. The guidelines shall come into force with effect from 1 st November, 2021. The guidelines have been placed on the IRDAI website (https://www.irdai.gov.in). Yours faithfully, Sd/- (Yegnapriya Bharath) Chief General Manager (NL) IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines,2021 Page 1 of 9 IRDAI (Trade Credit Insurance) Guidelines, 2021 1. Introduction 1.1 Trade credit insurance protects businesses against the risk of non-payment for goods and services by buyers. It usually covers a portfolio of buyers and indemnifies an agreed percentage of an invoice or invoices that remain unpaid as a result of protracted default, insolvency / bankruptcy. It contributes to the economic growth of a country by facilitating trade and helps in improving economic stability by addressing the trade losses due to payment risks. 1.2 These guidelines set out the regulatory framework; (a) to promote sustainable and healthy development of trade credit insurance business. (b) to facilitate general insurance companies to offer trade credit insurance covers to suppliers as well as licensed banks and other financial institutions to help businesses manage country risk, open up access to new markets and to manage non-payment risk associated with trade financing portfolio. (c) to enable general insurance companies to offer trade credit insurance with customised covers to improve businesses for the SMEs and MSMEs, considering the evolving insurance risk needs of these sectors.
rows.summary:
IRDAI issued revised **Trade Credit Insurance Guidelines, 2021** by circular dated **8 September 2021** to all **general insurance companies in India, except ECGC Ltd. and AIC Ltd.** The guidelines are stated to take effect on **1 November 2021**, and IRDAI says they were updated in response to evolving insurance risk needs and changing market conditions. The document’s core purpose is to regulate trade credit insurance in a way that supports sustainable market development, enables insurers to offer cover to **suppliers, licensed banks, and other financial institutions**, and allows more customized protection for **SMEs and MSMEs**.

The document explains that trade credit insurance protects businesses against **non-payment for goods and services** by buyers, typically by covering a **portfolio of buyers** and indemnifying an agreed percentage of unpaid invoices when default is prolonged or when the buyer becomes insolvent/bankrupt. This product is presented as a tool to support trade, improve economic stability, open access to new markets, and manage payment and country-risk exposure in trade financing.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the guidelines establish the regulatory framework under which affected insurers may offer trade credit insurance products, including customized covers for smaller businesses and coverage arrangements involving financial institutions. Affected entities should review their trade credit insurance underwriting, product design, and distribution arrangements to ensure they conform to the new IRDAI framework once it becomes effective on **1 November 2021**.

rows.summary:
IRDAI issued these guidelines on **5 May 2021** to all **general and health insurers** to standardize a **Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product (SDTIP)** for travel **within India**. The stated purpose is to make domestic travel insurance easier for consumers to compare and to ensure all insurers offer a product with the same core protections; insurers are required to use the **mandatory covers specified in the guidelines**, and they may offer **only the optional covers expressly permitted** in the document. Premium pricing is not fixed by the regulator, but insurers must set premiums in compliance with the **IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016** and the guideline framework.

From a compliance perspective, the document establishes a product-structuring obligation rather than a claims-only rule: insurers that market domestic travel insurance must ensure the policy form, coverage terms, and customer information sheet conform to the standard template in the annexures. The guidelines also anticipate a formal filing requirement, with the document including an **Annexure-3 form for filing the Standard Domestic Travel Insurance Product**, meaning insurers must submit the product in the prescribed format before offering it. The product is intended to cover common domestic travel risks with uniform features across the market, so companies should review existing domestic travel offerings to confirm they do not deviate from the required base cover or add unapproved optional features.

The excerpt provided does not include the full list of mandatory benefits, exclusions, limits, waiting periods, or filing timelines, so those details would need to be checked in the annexures and full guideline text before implementation. However, the key compliance takeaway is that **domestic travel insurance is being standardized**: the insurer’s discretion is narrowed to pricing and any optional covers specifically allowed by the IRDAI guidelines, and product documentation must match the prescribed policy terms and customer disclosure format.

rows.summary:
The IRDAI issued these guidelines on 31 March 2021, under Ref. IRDA/SUR/GDL/MISC/068/03/2021, to all licensed surveyors and loss assessors, building on the earlier circular dated 1 December 2020 on practical training required for fresh and renewal licences. The circular is issued under Section 14 of the IRDAI Act, 1999 and Regulation 3(2)(b) and (c) of the IRDAI (Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors) Regulations, 2015, so the training requirements are not optional and are part of the licensing framework. The document’s core requirement is that surveyors/loss assessors seeking fresh or renewal licences must complete practical training, including a two-month institutional practical training at either the National Insurance Academy (NIA) or the Insurance Institute of India (III).  

The institutional training is intended to cover practical insurance and surveying fundamentals, starting with introduction to different types of policies, endorsements, insurance terminology, and the nature of survey/loss assessment work. The document indicates that this training is structured and specific to surveyor/loss assessor functions, rather than generic insurance education, and is designed to support competency for licensing. The circular also references that additional aspects of practical training are to follow under the guidelines, implying that the institutional component is only one part of the overall training framework.  

For compliance purposes, the key point is that licensed surveyors and loss assessors must ensure they meet the prescribed practical training requirements before obtaining or renewing their licence, and they must do so through the specified institutions and format laid down by IRDAI. The effective date of this circular is 31 March 2021, and it supersedes/implements the earlier 1 December 2020 guidance on the same subject.

A report by the Board shall be attached to the financial statements, which shall include, inter alia, an important statement called Directors’ Responsibility Statement. According to sub-section 5 of Section 134, this statement shall disclose the Board’s assertions regarding certain critical aspects, such as adherence to applicable accounting standards; selection and application of accounting policies and making of judgements/estimates on reasonable and prudent basis; maintenance of adequate records for safeguarding the assets of the company and preventing and detecting fraud and other irregularities; preparation of accounts on a going concern basis; implementation of adequate
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 07.01.2026, is addressed to all listed companies, companies and bodies corporate covered under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the statutory auditors of those entities. It does not create a new standalone legal regime, but signals NFRA’s expectation that communication between statutory auditors and those charged with governance (TCWG), including audit committees, be materially strengthened and brought into closer alignment with the Companies Act, 2013, the Standards on Auditing under that Act, and related rules and regulations.

The circular explains that the Companies Act, 2013 already imposes key responsibilities on the board of directors, independent directors, audit committees, and auditors in relation to financial statements and audit. It specifically highlights Section 134, under which the board must approve the financial statements, including consolidated financial statements where applicable, and attach a board’s report that includes the Directors’ Responsibility Statement. That statement must cover the board’s assertions that applicable accounting standards have been followed; accounting policies have been selected and applied with reasonable and prudent judgment/estimates; adequate records are maintained to safeguard assets and prevent and detect fraud and other irregularities; the accounts have been prepared on a going-concern basis; and adequate internal financial controls are in place and operating effectively.

The compliance message is that auditors and governance bodies must treat these statutory obligations as requiring more effective and timely two-way communication during the audit and financial reporting process, particularly with the audit committee. While the excerpt provided does not yet set out any new numeric thresholds, filing deadlines, or penalties, it clearly indicates NFRA has observed deficiencies in current practice and is issuing the circular to reinforce existing statutory and audit-standard-based communication requirements. Compliance teams should therefore expect a heightened supervisory expectation that management, the board, audit committees, and auditors actively exchange information on matters affecting financial statements, internal controls, and audit findings, rather than treating audit committee interaction as merely formal or periodic.

Complex group structures including special purpose vehicles, auto pilot structures, cross holdings of interests across group entities and shared servi
rows.summary:
The NFRA’s circular dated 3 October 2024 addresses the responsibilities of the principal auditor and other auditors in group audits for entities covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018. It reiterates that statutory audits of both standalone financial statements and consolidated financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013 must comply with the Standards on Auditing, the Standard on Quality Control, and the Code of Ethics, including independence requirements. The circular explains that audits of group financial statements—such as audits of companies with branches, subsidiaries, associates, and other components—require special attention because the principal auditor remains ultimately responsible for the group audit opinion, even where component work is performed by other auditors, and that SA 600 governs the use of another auditor’s work.

The document’s central point is that group audits often involve material or significant-risk areas because of modern group structures and business arrangements. It specifically notes complex structures such as special purpose vehicles, “auto pilot” structures, cross-holdings, and shared-services arrangements as examples of the kinds of group features that can make audit risk higher and component reliance more difficult. The circular is therefore aimed at ensuring that auditors treat group audits as a heightened compliance and audit-quality area, with the principal auditor actively managing and overseeing the work of other auditors rather than merely relying on their reports.

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that audit teams involved in group audits must ensure full adherence to the applicable auditing framework, with documented compliance to the quality-control standards, the 35 standards on auditing, and ethical/independence requirements. The circular is directed to auditors of entities under NFRA’s jurisdiction and is intended to reinforce the existing legal and professional duties in group audit engagements, especially where the work of component auditors is used in forming the final group opinion. No monetary thresholds, filing deadlines, or new reporting forms are set out in the excerpt provided, but the effective date of the circular itself is 3 October 2024.

rows.title: NFRA circular on Statutory Auditors’ responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company
rows.desc: / Government of India / National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi NF-25013/2/2023 Dated 26.06.2023 Circular To 1. Auditors of the Entities Regulated by the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) Subject: Statutory Auditors’ Responsibilities in relation to Fraud in a Company In course of discharge of its statutory functions, NFRA has noticed that auditors are not fulfilling their statutory responsibilities relating to reporting of fraud as mandated under the Companies Act, 2013 (CA 2013) read with the relevant Rules and the applicable Standards on Auditing (SAs). 2 The CA 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO) and the Standards on Auditing (SAs) place mandatory reporting obligations on auditors to report fraud and/or suspected fraud to the Central Government and the Board/Audit Committee. 2.1 Section 143 (12) of CA 2013 and related Rules places certain reporting obligations on the auditor, in relation to frauds: “Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, if an auditor of a company in the course of the performance of his duties as auditor, has reason to believe that an offence of fraud involving such amount or amounts as may be prescribed, is being or has been committed in the company by its officers or employees, the auditor shall report the matter to the Central Government within such time and in such manner as may be prescribed: ....” Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules 2014, prescribes detailed steps that need to be followed by the auditor if he has reason to believe that an offence of fraud, which involves or is expected to involve individually an amount of rupees one crore or above, is being or has been committed against the company by its officers or employees. The auditor is required to report the matter to the Board or Audit Committee and to the Central Government in the form of a statement as specified in Form ADT-4. 2.2 Clause (xi) of Companies
rows.summary:
The NFRA has issued this circular because it has observed that statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated entities are not consistently carrying out their legal duties to report fraud, or suspected fraud, as required under the Companies Act, 2013, the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order (CARO), and the applicable Standards on Auditing. The circular is addressed to auditors of entities regulated by NFRA and reiterates that these reporting duties are mandatory, not discretionary.  

For fraud involving a company’s officers or employees, section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires an auditor who, in the course of audit work, has reason to believe that a fraud offence has been or is being committed to report the matter to the Central Government within the prescribed time and in the prescribed manner. Rule 13 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 specifies the process where the suspected or actual fraud involves, or is expected to involve, an amount of **₹1 crore or more**: the auditor must report first to the **Board or Audit Committee** and also report to the **Central Government** in **Form ADT-4**.  

The circular also points auditors to the separate reporting obligation under **Clause (xi)** of the Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, which requires disclosure of fraud and suspected fraud matters in the auditor’s reporting. In substance, NFRA is reminding auditors that fraud-related reporting must be completed through the correct statutory channels, using the prescribed form and process, whenever the threshold and legal test under the rules are met.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational takeaway is that auditors of NFRA-regulated entities must ensure they have procedures to identify, document, escalate, and report any fraud or suspected fraud meeting the statutory threshold, and they must not limit themselves to internal reporting alone. The circular signals NFRA scrutiny of auditor non-compliance in this area and reinforces that failure to report as required under section 143(12), Rule 13, CARO, and the SAs may constitute a breach of statutory audit responsibilities.

Para 46 of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, requires that the entity shall recognise as revenue the amount of the transaction price, excluding the estimates of variable conside
rows.summary:
This NFRA circular, dated 29 March 2023, is addressed to all listed companies, unlisted companies covered by Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, and the auditors of those companies. It states that, in exercising NFRA’s statutory mandate under section 132(2)(b) and 132(2)(d) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 4(2)(c) and 4(2)(g) of the NFRA Rules, NFRA has identified apparent non-compliance in recent financial statement reviews in two linked areas: revenue recognition/measurement and the initial measurement of the related trade receivables.

The circular specifically flags compliance issues under Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, beginning with paragraph 46, which requires revenue to be recognized at the transaction price, excluding estimated variable consideration until the amount can be reliably determined in accordance with the standard. NFRA says these are critical areas because they affect both how revenue is measured and how the corresponding receivables are initially recorded, and it highlights the concern to the company’s management, audit committee, and statutory auditors for urgent attention. The document makes clear that the issue is not a general accounting reminder but a warning based on NFRA’s review findings that some companies are not following the prescribed Ind AS requirements.

For compliance purposes, the affected population is broad: every listed company and every unlisted company that falls within NFRA Rule 3 is expected to ensure its revenue policies, estimates, and trade receivables accounting are fully consistent with Ind AS 115. The circular does not introduce a new quantitative threshold, fee, or deadline, but it does require immediate review of existing accounting policies and practices, especially around transaction price determination, treatment of variable consideration, and the measurement of receivables arising from customer contracts. Management, audit committees, and statutory auditors should treat the circular as a prompt to verify that the company’s Ind AS 115 policy documentation, estimates, and financial statement presentation are compliant and supportable under the standard.

NFRA found that he did not exercise due diligence and acted with gross negligence in meeting his obligation to identify and report fraud under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 and SA 240, despite there being several indicators of fraud. For a compliance team, the practical significance is that the order reinforces that a disclaimer of opinion does not relieve an engagement partner of the duty to perform fraud-risk procedures, respond appropriately to fraud indicators, or gather sufficient appropriate evidence before concluding an audit. It also shows that NFRA is actively using its powers to scrutinize auditors’ conduct in prior-period audits of public interest entities, and that failures tied to fraud reporting and audit evidence can be treated as serious professional misconduct. rows.summary:
NFRA has issued a draft revision of SA 600, “Special Considerations—Audits of Group Financial Statements (Including the Work of Component Auditors),” for public comment, with comments due by 30.10.2024. The draft applies to audits of group financial statements for PIEs under Rule 3 of the NFRA Rules, 2018, but specifically excludes PSUs, PSBs, PSIs, and their branches. The standard explains that group financial statements cover more than one entity or business unit brought together through a consolidation process, and that this includes not only consolidated financial statements under the relevant reporting framework but also combined financial statements and aggregation of information from branches, divisions, or similar units.

The revised SA 600 is intended to address the special risks and responsibilities that arise in group audits, especially where component auditors are involved. It cross-references and builds on other auditing standards, particularly SA 220 (Revised), SA 230, SA 300, SA 315 (Revised), and SA 330, meaning group audit teams must apply those standards with the additional requirements in SA 600. The document also notes that the guidance may be useful outside a formal group audit when the engagement team includes individuals from another firm—for example, for attending physical inventory counts, inspecting property, plant and equipment, or performing procedures at a remote shared service center.

For compliance teams, the immediate action item is the consultation deadline: public comments must be submitted by 30 October 2024. Substantively, the draft signals heightened focus on how group structures are organized and how auditors evaluate and coordinate work across components, so affected PIEs should expect tighter scrutiny over consolidation structures, the involvement of component auditors, and audit planning and supervision in group engagements.

rows.title: Annual Transparency Report by Statutory Auditors of PIEs-Invitation for public comment
rows.desc: / Government of India � � � � � � � /National Financial Reporting Authority ***** 7 th Floor, Hindustan Times House, Kasturba Gandhi Marg, New Delhi Dated: 16.01.2023 Invitation for Comment To Statutory Auditors of the NFRA Regulated Public Interest Entities (PIEs) Subject: Publication of Annual Transparency Reports (ATR) by Auditors/Audit Firms Auditors have a critical role in the financial reporting supply chain of PIEs. Audit of financial reports of PIEs by Independent Auditor enhances the credibility and integrity of the general purpose financial reports of PIEs. Therefore, the need for high-quality comprehensive financial information covering both financial and non-financial aspects of PIEs cannot be overemphasised. 2. Regulators have been prescribing obligations for PIEs to provide high-quality comprehensive financial and non-financial information commensurate with the nature, size and complexity of their operations to the various stakeholders. The role and responsibilities of the independent auditors of such entities have also evolved significantly with focus on the need to build commensurate professional and operating capabilities within the auditing profession. Audit professionals have been augmenting their capabilities and resources including building a network or alliances of firms, domestically and globally, developing in-house multi-disciplinary professionals or professional units, delivering variety of non-audit services, increasing use of digital audit tools and techniques, separating management and governance structures and so on. 3. In this backdrop, Regulators and Oversight Authorities in some overseas jurisdictions 1 require audit firms carrying out audit of PIEs to prepare and publish information in the form of Transparency Reports on annual basis. Accordingly, the audit firms in those jurisdictions have been publishing the Transparency Reports 2 4. Indian companies have become significant constituents of the global economy and India has evolved
rows.summary:
The National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) issued an invitation for public comment dated 16 January 2023 to statutory auditors of NFRA-regulated Public Interest Entities (PIEs) on the proposal to require publication of Annual Transparency Reports (ATR) by auditors/audit firms. The notice explains that because auditors of PIEs play a critical role in the financial reporting supply chain, and because audit quality increasingly depends on robust professional and operational capabilities, regulators in some overseas jurisdictions already require audit firms auditing PIEs to prepare and publish annual transparency reports. NFRA notes that Indian companies are now important participants in the global economy and implies that Indian audit firms and PIEs should align with higher transparency expectations seen internationally.  

The document is a consultation notice rather than a final rule, so it does not itself create an enforceable compliance obligation or set a specific effective date, deadline, filing format, or threshold in the text provided. However, the subject matter makes clear that the contemplated requirement would affect statutory auditors and audit firms serving NFRA-regulated PIEs, and would likely require them to disclose information annually about their firm’s capabilities, resources, governance, quality-related arrangements, and possibly other transparency information comparable to overseas ATR regimes. Compliance teams at affected audit firms should treat this as an early policy signal that public annual disclosure obligations for PIE auditors may be introduced, and should monitor NFRA’s next consultation or final issuance for the precise content, timing, and scope of any mandatory ATR requirement.

This document is a **Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA)** from the **National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA)** dated **28.09.2021** to the **Secretary, Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)** regarding **ICAI’s recommendations for revising the existing Accounting Standards under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013**. It records that ICAI had submitted an Approach Paper and draft revised texts for **18 revised Accounting Standards**, as part of a broader project expected to result in **32 revised Accounting Standards** in total, intended for companies **not required to follow Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)**. NFRA notes the historical context: the revision project was developed after Ind AS implementation for certain classes of companies, and ICAI’s 2020 revision of its 2014–15 approach paper reflects the view that accounting recognition and measurement should, as far as possible, be broadly the same across companies.

The core compliance point is that the **revised ASs will apply to companies for which Ind AS is not mandatory**, meaning the regime will cover a **large number of Micro, Small and Medium-size Companies (MSMCs)** and will **replace the existing Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules**. NFRA emphasizes that this is not a minor technical update: because these standards are intended for a very large non-Ind AS population, the revision could have a **significant economic and administrative impact** on affected entities. The letter indicates NFRA is evaluating ICAI’s recommendations in light of that broad impact, especially because the changes would govern financial reporting for companies outside the Ind AS framework.

For a compliance team, the practical implication is that organizations **not currently on Ind AS** should monitor the final outcome of this standards-revision exercise, because their accounting and reporting policies may need to change once the revised ASs are notified. The document itself does **not** set a new effective date, transition date, or threshold numbers for application in this excerpt, but it clearly signals that the revised standards are intended to become the **mandatory baseline** for non-Ind AS companies. The key obligation area is therefore readiness for updated accounting recognition/measurement requirements once NFRA/MCA complete the revision process and the revised standards are formally prescribed.

This consultation paper/report from the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA), Government of India, was issued as a March 2021 Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) report under the title “Enhancing Engagement with Stakeholders,” and it is framed as a consultation document released in June 2021. Its purpose is not to impose a specific new rule immediately, but to recommend how NFRA should interact more effectively with the financial reporting ecosystem—especially auditors, preparers, users of financial statements, regulators, academics, and others—and to strengthen transparency, guidance, enforcement, and communication.

The report explains that financial reporting is viewed as a “supply chain” involving auditors, preparers, users, regulators, academics, and other stakeholders, and it assesses NFRA’s role in each part of that chain. It records stakeholder views gathered through consultation, including expectations that NFRA should be more visible, clarify its scope relative to other regulators, provide timely guidance, use data more effectively, and improve engagement before and after enforcement actions. The report also discusses the Indian accounting and auditing landscape, the need for a clear road map, and the importance of building NFRA’s regulatory capacity and accountability.

The main recommendations are organized around stakeholder engagement, inspection/investigation/enforcement, settlement of disciplinary matters and remediation, communication and advocacy, data dissemination, a road map, regulatory capacity building, decision-making, timely guidance, and audit quality indicators/audit firm evaluation. In practical compliance terms, the document signals an expected shift toward more structured engagement by NFRA, stronger transparency around its decision-making and enforcement approach, and greater emphasis on audit quality measurement and firm-level evaluation. It also specifically points to settlement and remediation mechanisms for disciplinary matters, suggesting that entities subject to NFRA oversight may face not only enforcement but also processes aimed at corrective action and resolution.

No binding deadlines, numeric thresholds, fee rates, or immediate filing obligations are set out in the text provided. Instead, the document should be read as a policy and reform roadmap for NFRA’s future functioning, with implications for any audit firms, companies, auditors, or other market participants that fall within NFRA’s jurisdiction or are affected by its guidance, inspections, investigations, or disciplinary processes. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this report anticipates a more proactive, data-driven, and communication-heavy regulator, so affected entities should be prepared for closer scrutiny, more formalized interaction, and potential future changes in oversight practices.

rows.title: The PCAOB announced that Addison Scott and Zian Xi have been named as the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellows.
rows.desc: PCAOB Announces New Audit Practitioner Fellows WASHINGTON, Sep. 15, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Addison (Addi) Scott and Zian Xi have been named as the two Audit Practitioner Fellows, as part of the recently launched Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program within the PCAOB’s Office of the Chief Auditor. Effective immediately, Ms. Scott and Ms. Xi will serve two-year terms supporting the Board’s standard-setting and research agendas, bringing recent audit experience to strengthen the PCAOB’s oversight activities and advance the public interest. “Standards are the foundation of the PCAOB’s work, establishing the rules of the road for auditors of public companies and SEC-registered brokers and dealers, providing the framework against which we conduct inspections and, where appropriate, pursue enforcement. However, to develop principles-based standards that are scalable, practical, and effective, we need a clear understanding of today’s audit environment.” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “Addi and Zian will provide real-world insights to help us develop standards that improve audit quality while appropriately balancing costs and benefits.”Before joining the PCAOB in September 2026, Ms. Scott spent more than 11 years with Ernst & Young (EY), including three years in the firm's Professional Practice Group focused on audit methodology and the implementation of PCAOB, AICPA, and international auditing and quality management standards. rows.summary:
The PCAOB announced the appointment of Addison (Addi) Scott and Zian Xi as the two inaugural Audit Practitioner Fellows under its recently launched Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program in the Office of the Chief Auditor. Their appointments are effective immediately, and each will serve a two-year term supporting the PCAOB’s standard-setting and research work. The stated purpose of the program is to bring recent, practical audit experience into the PCAOB’s work so it can develop standards that are more scalable, practical, and effective for oversight of auditors of public companies and SEC-registered brokers and dealers.

For compliance purposes, the announcement does not create a new substantive rule, deadline, or filing obligation for registrants, but it signals the PCAOB’s continued focus on principles-based standards and on balancing audit quality with costs and benefits when setting requirements that will affect firms subject to PCAOB oversight. Chairman Demetrios Logothetis specifically tied the fellowship to the Board’s inspections and enforcement framework, indicating the fellows will contribute to the standards that govern audited public companies and SEC-registered broker-dealers.

The release provides background on the fellows’ qualifications: Ms. Scott joins after more than 11 years at Ernst & Young, including three years in EY’s Professional Practice Group focused on audit methodology and implementation of PCAOB, AICPA, and international auditing and quality management standards, followed by service as a Senior Manager in assurance; she is a CPA licensed in Arkansas. Ms. Xi joined after serving as a Senior Manager in Deloitte & Touche LLP’s national office, with specialization in audit transformation, data and technology, artificial intelligence, and technical consultations. The practical compliance takeaway is that the PCAOB is adding recently practiced audit professionals into its standards-development process, which may influence the direction and real-world applicability of future PCAOB requirements.

rows.title: A new PCAOB staff resource, QC 1000 Questions and Answers, provides answers to questions about certain matters related to the implementation of QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control.

This resource does not address provisions that are the subject of the proposed or conforming amendments that the Board issued for public comment on June 9, 2026. QC 1000 Questions and Answers is the latest in a range of materials – including videos, online knowledge checks, and more – that the PCAOB has released to assist firms and auditors with the implementation of QC 1000 and other new standards and rules in order to improve audit quality and protect investors. For further questions regarding the application of the requirements of QC 1000, contact the PCAOB’s Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA) at 202-591-4395. Registered public accounting firms may also request a consultation with OCA through the Firm Consultation Process on the interpretation and application of PCAOB standards, including QC 1000.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. rows.summary:

rows.title: Advancing its strategic planning process, the PCAOB has requested public input on draft goals and objectives for its 2026-2030 strategic plan.

Comments should reference “Request for Public Comment Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives.” The document provided does not state a specific comment deadline in the excerpt shown.

The PCAOB announced on July 9, 2026 the membership of its new Inspections Modernization Council (IMC), a resource group made up of outside stakeholders with an interest in PCAOB inspection activities. The IMC is not described as a rulemaking body, but as an advisory/resource group intended to provide outside perspectives to help the PCAOB modernize its inspection program and, in turn, improve audit quality. The modernization topics the PCAOB says the IMC will help evaluate include producing more useful inspection-report outputs for users, using technology such as automation and artificial intelligence, and shifting inspections toward firms’ systems of quality control.

For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that this announcement signals the PCAOB’s direction of travel rather than an immediate new compliance deadline or filing requirement. The PCAOB is considering inspection-process changes that could affect how audit firms are evaluated and how inspection findings are presented, which may in time change internal quality-control expectations, documentation practices, and technology-related audit oversight. The Board said it received more than 100 applications from across the financial reporting ecosystem and selected the following IMC members: David J. Cohen (Forvis Mazars, LLP), Kyle D. Crockett (Ford Motor Company), Ashley “Ash” Dalnoot (Grant Thornton Advisors LLC), Alicia R. Ramirez (RJI International), Jen Sisson (International Corporate Governance Network), Dan G. Sunderland (Northeastern University), Huong Tran (Instacart), Brendan Whalen (S.R. Snodgrass, P.C.), and Lucia M. Wind (Committee of Sponsoring Organizations).

The practical compliance relevance is prospective: firms subject to PCAOB inspections should monitor future PCAOB actions stemming from the IMC, especially any changes tied to inspection reporting, quality-control emphasis, or the use of automation and AI in the inspection process.

rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George Kostolampros as General Counsel.
rows.desc: George Kostolampros Named PCAOB General Counsel WASHINGTON, Jul. 1, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George Kostolampros has been appointed the PCAOB’s General Counsel. As General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros will provide legal advice and counsel on all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC). “OGC’s work underpins the PCAOB’s ability to execute its mission to protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We are grateful that George is joining us to fill this critical leadership role.” Mr. Kostolampros brings more than 25 years of experience advising organizations and senior leaders on complex legal, regulatory, governance, compliance, and risk-management matters. Prior to his appointment as General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. Before returning to private practice, he served as Senior Counsel in the Division of Enforcement at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Kostolampros received his J.D., magna cum laude, from Widener University School of Law and his B.A. from Syracuse University. “I am honored to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the talented OGC staff to advance the PCAOB’s priorities and mission,” said Mr. Kostolampros. Matt Goldin, who was named Acting General Counsel in January 2026, will resume his role as Deputy General Counsel, advising the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assisting with OGC’s management. “Matt is a valued member of the OGC team, and we thank him for his distinguished service as Acting General Counsel,” said Chairman Logothetis.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corp
rows.summary:
The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) announced on July 1, 2026 that George Kostolampros has been appointed General Counsel, replacing the acting arrangement that had been in place since January 2026. In this role, he will provide legal advice and counsel across all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC), which the PCAOB described as central to carrying out its investor-protection mission. The PCAOB highlighted Kostolampros’s background as a Venable LLP partner advising public companies, boards, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, as well as his prior service as Senior Counsel in the SEC’s Division of Enforcement. The only date-specific operational point in the release is the transition itself: January 2026 for Goldin’s acting appointment and July 1, 2026 for Kostolampros’s permanent appointment.

There are no statutory, regulatory, or procedural changes described in this document, and no action is required by issuers, audit firms, or other outside parties based solely on this announcement.

rows.summary:
