OERA’s role is to provide independent, evidence-based economic and risk analysis that supports PCAOB oversight work, including inspections, investigations, rulemaking, standard setting, and post-implementation reviews; the announcement is an internal leadership change and does not itself impose a new compliance rule, filing requirement, or deadline on registrants or audit firms. rows.title: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB after more than 17 years of service.
rows.desc: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich to Depart the PCAOB WASHINGTON, Jun. 26, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB on July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. “I have greatly valued Barb’s expert advice – her accomplishments at the PCAOB have been extraordinary,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We thank her for her leadership and dedication, and we wish her well as she embarks on a new professional opportunity.” Ms. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009. After serving in several roles at the PCAOB – including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor – she was named Chief Auditor in October 2022. During her tenure as Chief Auditor, the PCAOB adopted several new standards that represented important milestones in the PCAOB’s work to improve audit quality and protect investors. Most notably, the PCAOB in May 2024 adopted QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control. The standard, which will become effective December 15, 2026, features a risk-based approach designed to drive continuous improvement in audit quality. Additionally, Ms. Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, the creation of resources to help audit firms with implementation of new standards, the launch of the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process through which registered public accounting firms can submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. “It has been an honor to advance the PCAOB’s investor-protection mission, together with my talented colleagues in the Office of the Chief Auditor and so many others across the PCAOB,” said Ms. Vanich. The PCAOB is beginning a search to fill the Chief Auditor

The consultation process is available only to **registered public accounting firms**, and it covers the interpretation and application of **PCAOB auditing, attestation, and quality control standards**, along with the **related rules and forms**, and the PCAOB’s **ethics and independence standards and rules**. If a firm wants to use the process, it must submit a request by completing the **Consultation Intake Form**. The PCAOB stated that it **does not plan to make consultation requests public**, although it may later issue **public guidance** if questions are commonly asked or broadly useful.  

For compliance teams, the practical effect is that firms now have a more structured mechanism to seek PCAOB staff input before finalizing interpretations or implementation approaches, which may help reduce inconsistency across engagements and support compliance with evolving PCAOB requirements. The announcement does not specify a filing deadline, approval timeline, or mandatory use requirement, and it does not impose a new compliance obligation beyond the submission process if a firm chooses to consult.

rows.title: The PCAOB has launched an open comment period for stakeholders to provide input on its standard-setting and research agendas.
rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued **Release No. 2026-005 on June 23, 2026** to open a **public comment period** seeking stakeholder input on its **standard-setting and research agendas**. The document does **not** itself adopt a new auditing rule or impose an immediate compliance requirement on registrants or auditors; rather, it asks firms, investors, audit committees, preparers, and other interested parties to comment on **which topics the PCAOB should prioritize** in future standard-setting and research work.

For a compliance team, the key point is that the PCAOB is signaling where future requirements may emerge and is inviting feedback on the most pressing audit-related issues. The agenda discussion specifically highlights **data and technology**, with focused attention on **artificial intelligence** and **digital assets**, indicating these are likely areas of regulatory development or updated guidance. The release also discusses the PCAOB’s **approach to standard setting**, including its **conceptual framework**, its **standard-setting process**, and its consideration of **other standard setters** and **possible alignment with international auditing standards**.

Because this is a request for comment rather than a final standard, the practical obligation is external-facing: organizations that want to influence future PCAOB rulemaking should review the agenda and submit comments during the open comment period. The document’s material significance is that it may foreshadow future auditing standards affecting how audits are performed in technology-heavy areas, especially where AI tools or digital assets are involved, but it does not specify new thresholds, rates, deadlines for compliance, or effective dates for substantive obligations in the excerpt provided.

rows.summary:

This report is issued under PCAOB Rule 4020T, which governs interim inspection reporting for broker-dealer audits.

While the excerpt provided does not include the specific deficiencies or statistics, the report signals that broker-dealer audit oversight remains an active compliance focus and that firms auditing broker-dealers should expect PCAOB scrutiny of audit execution, documentation, and conformity with PCAOB standards. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that broker-dealers must continue using qualified PCAOB-registered auditors for their annual audited filings, and those auditors should ensure their broker-dealer audit work is aligned with PCAOB requirements because inspection findings may affect regulatory posture, audit quality assessments, and supervisory expectations.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued an order on January 13, 2026, imposing sanctions on Zwick CPA, PLLC and its owner Jack Zwick, CPA, based on violations of PCAOB rules and standards in connection with the audit of one issuer client’s financial statements. The Board censured both the firm and Zwick and revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, which means the firm cannot continue practicing before the PCAOB as a registered public accounting firm unless it later reapplies and is approved. The order also bars Zwick from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, although he may file a petition for Board consent to re-associate only after three years from the date of the order; similarly, the firm may reapply for registration only after three years from the date of the order.

Financially, the PCAOB imposed a civil money penalty of $50,000, assessed jointly and severally against the firm and Zwick. In addition to the monetary penalty, the firm must complete specified remedial quality-control measures before submitting any future registration application, and it must provide evidence of those measures with any such application. Zwick must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education focused on PCAOB auditing standards, on top of any CPE required for his professional license, before he can file any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The sanctions indicate the PCAOB viewed the conduct as serious enough to require not just punishment but pre-clearance remediation and training before either respondent can seek to return to PCAOB-regulated practice.

The PCAOB’s December 18, 2025 Order sanctions CPA Jennifer A. Crofoot for violations tied to her work on audits of four issuer clients, and it also addresses quality control failures at her former registered audit firm. The Board censured Crofoot, barred her from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education on PCAOB auditing standards before she may seek Board consent to associate with a registered firm again. The document also signals that the disciplinary action is intended to protect investors and the public interest in accurate, independent audit reports, so any registered firm or associated person should view this as an enforcement reminder that audit evidence and quality control failures can trigger both individual sanctions and firm-related scrutiny.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB instituted disciplinary proceedings against TPS Thayer LLC and issued an order on December 4, 2025 censuring the firm, imposing a $100,000 civil money penalty, and requiring contingent remedial actions under Section IV of the order. The sanctions stem from TPS Thayer’s use, in five issuer audits, of audit work performed in a substantial-role capacity by a public accounting firm that was not registered with the PCAOB; the PCAOB found that TPS Thayer did not appropriately plan those audits and did not reasonably supervise the unregistered firm. The order notes that TPS Thayer had filed a Form 1-WD on April 7, 2025 seeking withdrawal from PCAOB registration, and that request would be handled under PCAOB Rule 2107; that withdrawal request is separate from the sanctions in this order.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB issued an Order on September 23, 2025 censuring Marcum Asia CPAs LLP (also referred to as MarcumBP or the Firm), imposing a $100,000 civil money penalty, and requiring the firm to conduct training on communications between predecessor and successor auditors. The sanctions were based on findings that the firm violated PCAOB rules and standards governing those auditor-to-auditor communications, which are the procedures used when a new auditor is considering engagement and contacts the prior auditor about the client.

(“Firm” or “Centurion”) and CHAN Kam Fuk (Dominic) (“Chan”) (collectively, “Respondents”); b. revoking the Firm’s PCAOB registration; c. barring Chan from being an associated person of a public accounting firm registered with the PCAOB; and d. imposing a civil money penalty in the amount of $75,000, jointly and severally, on the Firm and Chan. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that: (a) Respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with performing audits of the 2021 financial statements of two issuer clients and audit procedures for subsidiaries of a third issuer; (b) the Firm violated PCAOB rules and standards concerning audit reporting in connection with the two issuer audits; (c) the Firm filed inaccurate and/or untimely Form APs required by PCAOB rules; (d) the Firm violated PCAOB quality control standards; and (e) Chan directly and substantially contributed to the Firm’s audit reporting violations. I. The Board deems it necessary and appropriate, for the protection of investors and to further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, that disciplinary proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted against Respondents Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Centurion ZD CPA & Co. and CHAN Kam Fuk, Respondents. In anticipation of the institution of these proceedings, and pursuant to PCAOB Rule 520
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s July 22, 2025 Order permanently revoked the PCAOB registration of Hong Kong audit firm Centurion ZD CPA & Co. and permanently barred its owner, CHAN Kam Fuk (Dominic), from being an associated person of any PCAOB-registered public accounting firm. The Board also censured both respondents and imposed a $75,000 civil money penalty, jointly and severally, against the firm and Chan. These sanctions were based on findings that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with audits of the 2021 financial statements of two issuer clients and audit procedures performed for subsidiaries of a third issuer.

For compliance purposes, the order indicates that the firm’s audit failures were not limited to substantive audit work; the PCAOB also found audit reporting violations in the two issuer audits, meaning the firm failed to comply with PCAOB requirements governing the form and content of audit reports. In addition, Centurion filed inaccurate and/or untimely Form APs, which are the PCAOB’s required audit reporting forms identifying the engagement partner, other accounting firms, and certain roles in the audit. The PCAOB further found that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards, and that Chan directly and substantially contributed to the audit reporting violations.

The action was brought under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), with the Board stating the sanctions were necessary to protect investors and promote informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. For any firm or personnel involved in PCAOB-regulated audits, the key compliance takeaway is that deficiencies in issuer audit execution, audit reporting, Form AP filing accuracy/timeliness, and quality control can lead to registration revocation, individual industry bars, and monetary penalties.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s July 8, 2025 Order against PWR CPA LLP censures the firm, imposes a $60,000 civil money penalty, and requires remedial actions before the firm can submit any future registration application; PWR must also provide evidence of those remedial actions with any future registration filing. The Board based the sanctions on findings that PWR violated PCAOB rules and standards in an audit of one issuer and repeatedly failed to comply with PCAOB reporting requirements, including failures tied to required fraud-risk inquiries. 

A key compliance point is that PWR filed a Form 1-WD on January 17, 2025 to withdraw from PCAOB registration, but the Board states that withdrawal will not be allowed to proceed until PWR first establishes, revises, or supplements its policies and procedures as required by Paragraph IV.C.1 of the Order and submits the written certification required by Paragraph IV.C.2. In other words, any future registration-related action by PWR is conditioned on completing the ordered remediation and proving it to the PCAOB. 

For compliance teams, this order underscores that PCAOB enforcement can target both audit-performance failures and recurring regulatory-reporting failures, and it shows that a withdrawal from registration does not eliminate the obligation to remediate prior deficiencies before the PCAOB will process the withdrawal or any future registration request. The Order was issued under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1).

The PCAOB issued an order on July 8, 2025, censuring Goldman & Company, CPA’s, P.C. and imposing a $25,000 civil money penalty after finding that the firm failed to comply with PCAOB audit documentation standards in connection with an audit of a broker-dealer. The order also requires the firm to undertake remedial actions described in Section V of the order, so the sanctions are not limited to the monetary penalty and censure; the firm must implement whatever corrective measures the PCAOB specifically directed there.

The document does not provide the full Section V text in the excerpt, so the specific remedial obligations and any deadlines for those actions are not visible here. This matters to any registered audit firm performing broker-dealer work, because the action underscores that incomplete or noncompliant audit documentation can trigger public discipline, financial penalties, and mandatory remediation.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s July 8, 2025 Order censures Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C. and imposes a $50,000 civil money penalty because the firm repeatedly failed to comply with PCAOB engagement quality review requirements on 17 broker and/or dealer audits. The Board found that across those engagements the firm did not obtain an engagement quality review from a qualified engagement quality reviewer, which is a required safeguard for audit quality and independence under PCAOB rules and standards. The disciplinary action was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the firm resolved the matter through an Offer of Settlement under PCAOB Rule 5205, consenting to the Order without admitting or denying the findings except as to jurisdiction.

In addition to the public censure and monetary penalty, the firm must complete remedial actions described in Section IV of the Order. The document does not provide the specifics of those remedial steps in the excerpt, but compliance teams should treat this as a signal that the PCAOB views failure to secure a qualified engagement quality review as a serious, repeated violation, especially in broker-dealer audit work. No separate prospective deadline is stated in the excerpt beyond the Order date itself, July 8, 2025, but the sanctions and remedial obligations are effective as part of the PCAOB Order.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 order against Deloitte Accountants B.V. (“Deloitte Netherlands”) imposes a formal censure, a $3 million civil money penalty, and required remedial measures because the firm violated PCAOB rules and quality control standards over several years in connection with its internal training program. The order requires Deloitte Netherlands to implement additional remedial actions described in Section IV of the order, meaning the firm must take corrective steps beyond paying the penalty and accepting the censure. rows.title: The PCAOB has permanently barred Michael T. Studer, CPA, and permanently revoked the PCAOB registration of his firm, Michael T. Studer CPA P.C.
rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-022 June 24, 2025 By this Order Making Findings and Imposing Sanctions (“Order”), the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“Board” or “PCAOB”) is: (1) censuring Michael T. Studer CPA P.C. (“Firm”) and Michael T. Studer, CPA (“Studer”) (collectively, “Respondents”); (2) revoking the Firm’s registration; (3) barring Studer from being an associated person of a registered public accounting firm; and (4) imposing a civil money penalty in the amount of $20,000, jointly and severally, on the Firm and Studer. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that: (a) Respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in connection with performing the audit of the financial statements of an issuer client; (b) Studer failed to properly supervise the work of the engagement team on that audit; (c) the Firm violated PCAOB standards by failing to obtain an engagement quality review (“EQR”) in connection with that audit; (d) the Firm violated PCAOB quality control standards; and (e) Studer directly and substantially contributed to the Firm’s EQR and quality control violations. I. On June 20, 2024, the Board instituted disciplinary proceedings against Respondents pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, as amended (the “Act”), and Order Making Findings and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Michael T. Studer CPA P.C. and Michael T. Studer, CPA, Respondents. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-022 June 24, 2025 2 PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1). The Board determined, under Section 105(c)(2) of the Act and PCAOB Rule 5203, that good cause was shown to make the hearing in this proceeding public, and the Division of Enforcement and Investigations consented to making the hearing public. As permitted by Section 105(c)(2) of the Act and PCAOB Rule 5203, Respondents did not consent to make the hearing in this proceeding public. II. In response
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 24, 2025 Order permanently sanctions both Michael T. Studer, CPA P.C. and Michael T. Studer, CPA for audit-quality and supervision failures in connection with an issuer audit. The Board censured both respondents, permanently revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, permanently barred Studer from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $20,000 civil money penalty against the firm and Studer jointly and severally. The stated basis for the sanctions is that they violated PCAOB rules and standards during the audit of an issuer’s financial statements, Studer failed to properly supervise the engagement team, the firm failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR), the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards, and Studer directly and substantially contributed to the EQR and quality control violations.

For compliance teams, the key point is that the order is a final PCAOB disciplinary action affecting a registered public accounting firm and its CPA principal. The revocation means the firm can no longer operate as a PCAOB-registered firm, and the bar means Studer cannot serve in an associated-person role at any registered public accounting firm. The proceeding itself was instituted on June 20, 2024 under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1); the PCAOB also noted that it found good cause to make the hearing public under Section 105(c)(2) and Rule 5203, while the respondents did not consent to a public hearing. No broader industry-wide rule change is announced in this excerpt; the document is an enforcement order imposing firm- and individual-specific sanctions for failures in audit supervision, EQR, and quality control.

rows.title: The PCAOB has sanctioned a firm and one of its partners for, among other violations, failing to properly document five audits.

Heaton may file a petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm after two years from the date of this Order. Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Heaton & Company, PLLC, and Kristofer Heaton, CPA, Respondents. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-021 June 12, 2025 2 The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that: (a) the Firm failed to timely assemble for retention a complete and final set of audit documentation in connection with the audits of five issuers, (b) Heaton failed to adequately perform an engagement quality review (“EQR”) for five issuer audits, (c) the Firm violated PCAOB quality control standa
rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s June 12, 2025 Order against Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) and partner Kristofer Heaton is a disciplinary action based on findings that the firm failed to timely assemble and retain complete and final audit documentation for five issuer audits, that Heaton did not adequately perform engagement quality reviews on those same five audits, and that the firm violated PCAOB quality control standards. As sanctions, the PCAOB censured both respondents, revoked the firm’s PCAOB registration, barred Heaton from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, and imposed civil money penalties of $35,000 on the firm and $25,000 on Heaton. The order also imposes forward-looking remedial conditions: if the firm later seeks to reapply for PCAOB registration, it must first complete certain remedial measures described in Section IV of the Order, and Heaton must complete 40 hours of continuing professional education beyond any CPE required by his professional license before he may file a petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm.

The order specifies a two-year waiting period from the date of the Order before either the firm may reapply for registration or Heaton may petition for consent to associate again. The affected activities are audits of issuers, so the action is relevant to registered public accounting firms, partners performing EQRs, and any firm with PCAOB inspection/registration obligations. For compliance teams, the key takeaways are that the PCAOB treated failures in audit file completion, EQR performance, and quality control as sanctionable violations, and it paired the sanctions with reinstatement hurdles—remedial steps for any future firm registration application and a mandatory 40-hour CPE condition for Heaton before any future association request.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered an April 22, 2025 disciplinary order against registered public accounting firm Adeptus Partners LLC and partner Howard S. Krant, CPA, based on violations tied to supervision, audit review, and quality control in connection with the audits of two issuers. The Board censured both Adeptus and Krant; suspended Krant from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm for one year starting on the date of the Order; imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty on Krant; imposed a $75,000 civil money penalty on Adeptus; and required Adeptus to retain an independent consultant to review its quality-control system and make recommendations as specified in Section IV of the Order. The proceeding was instituted under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), and the matter was resolved through offers of settlement accepted by the Board under PCAOB Rule 5205. The order is relevant to any registered public accounting firm, particularly those auditing issuers, because it underscores PCAOB enforcement exposure for failures in supervision, audit review, and quality control systems.

rows.title: The PCAOB has sanctioned James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner for audit failures.

rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s March 25, 2025 order against James Pai CPA PLLC and its sole partner, Yu-Ching James Pai, imposes significant disciplinary sanctions for audit-related violations involving two audits of one issuer client. The Board found that the respondents violated PCAOB rules and standards in performing those audits, and that the firm specifically failed to obtain the required engagement quality review (EQR). The order also states that the firm filed inaccurate PCAOB Form APs in connection with those engagements, which is a separate reporting/compliance failure.

As sanctions, the PCAOB censured both the firm and Pai, revoked the firm’s registration, barred Pai from being an associated person of any registered public accounting firm, and imposed a $40,000 civil money penalty jointly and severally on the firm and Pai. In addition, the firm is required to undertake remedial actions to its system of quality control before it can submit any future registration application, and it must provide evidence of those remedial measures with any future application. Pai is required to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education, on top of any CPE required for licensing, before he may file a petition for PCAOB consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm.

The order provides that the firm may reapply for PCAOB registration only after three years from the date of the order, and Pai may file a petition for Board consent to associate only after three years from the same date. The Board based these sanctions on findings that Sellers violated PCAOB rules and auditing standards in connection with two issuer audits and also violated auditor independence requirements in one of those audits. The Order was issued under Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1), following Sellers’ settlement offer under Rule 5205, which the Board accepted.

rows.title: The PCAOB has sanctioned a former engagement partner for violating multiple PCAOB rules and standards, including failure to cooperate with a PCAOB inspection.
rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-006 February 25, 2025 By this Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions (“Order”), the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (“Board” or “PCAOB”) is: (1) censuring Natalie Murphy, CPA (“Murphy” or “Respondent”); (2) barring Murphy from being associated with a registered public accounting firm; 1 (3) imposing a $50,000 civil money penalty on Murphy; and (4) requiring Murphy to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education (“CPE”), in addition to any CPE required in connection with any professional license she holds, before filing any petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that Murphy: (1) failed to cooperate with the PCAOB’s 2022 inspection of Heaton & Company, PLLC (d/b/a Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah) (“Heaton & Co.” or the “Firm”) by providing misleading information to PCAOB inspectors in connection with two issuer audits; (2) failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two issuer audits; and (3) failed to timely assemble for retention a complete and final set of audit documentation in a total of five issuer audits. 1 Murphy may file a petition for Board consent to associate with a registered public accounting firm after five years from the date of this Order. Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions In the Matter of Natalie Murphy, CPA, Respondent. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-006 February 25, 2025 2 I. rows.summary:
The PCAOB entered a disciplinary order against former engagement partner Natalie Murphy, CPA, based on misconduct tied to issuer audit work and her cooperation with a PCAOB inspection of Heaton & Company, PLLC (doing business as Pinnacle Accountancy Group of Utah). The Board censured Murphy, barred her from being associated with any registered public accounting firm, imposed a $50,000 civil money penalty, and required her to complete 40 hours of continuing professional education before she can even petition for PCAOB consent to associate with a registered firm; any such petition cannot be filed until five years after the date of the Order, February 25, 2025.

The conduct leading to the sanctions was that Murphy failed to cooperate with the PCAOB’s 2022 inspection by providing misleading information to inspectors regarding two issuer audits, failed to adequately document work paper additions and modifications made after the documentation completion date for those two audits, and failed to timely assemble a complete and final set of audit documentation for retention in a total of five issuer audits. For compliance purposes, the order underscores that engagement partners and other personnel at registered public accounting firms must provide truthful, complete, and timely responses during PCAOB inspections, and must properly document post-completion changes to audit workpapers and finalize audit files within the required retention timeline.

The practical effect is that Murphy is prohibited from working in any capacity that would constitute being “associated with” a registered public accounting firm unless and until the PCAOB grants consent after the five-year period and she satisfies the additional 40-hour CPE شرط. The order is aimed at protecting investors and reinforcing the PCAOB’s expectations for audit documentation integrity, timely file completion, and full cooperation with inspection staff.
